decks.title: Story bank (S1–S13)
decks.blurb: Your thirteen stories in STAR form, tagged by the leadership principles they answer.

cards.f: S1 — Ford Feature Management: redesign under a migration deadline
cards.b:
Situation. At Ford I led architecture for Feature Management, the service that decides which features each vehicle supports from about fifteen parameters. Thirty million requests a month, growing to eleven million vehicles with the F-150 Lightning. P99 latency was over 300 milliseconds, every request recomputed capability and called four downstream systems synchronously, and leadership had just mandated an Azure-to-GCP migration on a date that left no room for a redesign.
Task. I was accountable for the architecture and for hitting the migration date. The default plan was lift-and-shift, which would have moved every problem to a new cloud.
Action. I benchmarked the per-request computation and projected it at eleven million vehicles to show the cost and latency curve. I designed the alternative: subscribe to manufacturing and configuration events, compute capability when the vehicle changes, persist it in a document store with a Redis cache, and reconcile fully every fifteen days — so the read path had zero synchronous dependencies. Then I phased it: I split the roadmap so the core event-driven path shipped with the migration and non-critical enhancements followed, and I presented benchmarks, cost projections, and a risk analysis to the platform team, the migration program, and leadership to get all three aligned.
Result. We hit the migration date. P99 went from over 300 milliseconds to under 100. The read path no longer went down when downstream systems did. Compute cost dropped [X%] because it scaled with configuration changes instead of reads, and vehicle capability was visible before the sale for the first time.
Learning. I'd start the benchmarking a month earlier. The numbers are what moved people, and I spent two weeks arguing before I had them.

cards.f: S2 — Stellantis: the provisioning defect that was bricking vehicles
cards.b:
Answers: "Tell me about a time you took on something outside your job." "Tell me about a difficult decision under pressure." "Tell me about the most challenging problem you solved." "Tell me about aligning many teams with conflicting priorities." "Tell me about a time you found a problem by digging into data."

Situation. At Stellantis I was managing delivery of over-the-air updates in the Uconnect organization. Customers started calling in. Remote start, lock and unlock, and other phone features had stopped working on their vehicles. The volume was growing every day.
Task. OTA was mine. The failing features depended on it. I had to find out why and stop it spreading.
Action. I went to the data. The affected vehicles were not connecting to the OTA server and were not sending any telemetry over MQTT. So it wasn't my feature — it was connectivity. I kept digging. The root cause was in provisioning: when a vehicle was activated, the factory-installed IMEI was supposed to be replaced with the carrier's AT&T IMEI. That swap was failing. Without it, the vehicle had no cellular connection at all. Provisioning was not my responsibility. But it was breaking my features and, worse, bricking vehicles. Every bricked vehicle meant a dealership visit to manually re-flash it — effectively a recall, at huge cost. So I took it on. Provisioning was a workflow across three companies' systems: the Stellantis cloud, SiriusXM, and the AT&T cloud. Nobody owned the whole thing. I set up an onsite workshop with more than fifty people from every team involved. We mapped the workflow end to end, found exactly where the IMEI swap was failing, and agreed on a fix and who owned each piece. Each team delivered their part. I tracked it to closure.
Result. The provisioning fix stopped new vehicles from bricking. [How many vehicles were affected before the fix; how many were at risk; rough recall cost avoided per vehicle × volume]. OTA and the remote features came back. We avoided a recall.
Learning. The failure lived in the gap between three organizations, which is exactly where failures hide. Afterward I pushed for a single owner for the end-to-end provisioning workflow and monitoring on the step that had failed — a vehicle that never sends its first telemetry within an hour of activation should page someone. Measure the boundary, not just the pieces.
Say "I" for the investigation and the workshop; say "the teams" for the fix. If asked "why you?": "Because the customer calls were landing on my feature and nobody else could see the whole workflow."

cards.f: S3 — Cindia → a graph-based digital thread
cards.b:
Answers: "Tell me about a time you challenged the status quo." "A build-vs-buy decision." "Getting leadership to fund something." "A customer asked for one thing but needed another." "A decision without enough data."

Situation. I joined ARV to implement the digital thread for the XM30 program. The company had already bought an integration product, Cindia. Within a few months it was clear it could not do the job: it could not connect all of our PLM, simulation and engineering tools, it needed manual mapping for everything, and it assumed a linear requirements → design → BOM flow when our program reverse-engineered BOMs and block diagrams. It was an ETL tool, not a digital thread. The ask I was given was "make Cindia work."
Task. I owned the digital-thread architecture. I had to decide whether to keep forcing the purchased tool or replace it — against sunk cost and a vendor relationship.
Action. I validated with the engineers and with the vendor that no off-the-shelf option modeled our reality. I designed a graph-database digital thread: assets, BOMs, requirements and PLM items as nodes with flexible relationships, so engineers could ask questions nobody had anticipated. Then I built the case the way leadership needed to hear it — not technology but risk and ROI: a $50K-a-year renewal that would never do the job, versus a larger upfront build with a mitigation plan and a payback. I got it approved.
Result. A scalable digital thread that now spans Teamcenter, Plex, Cameo, Creo, Zuken, GitLab and Jira, with a Power BI manufacturing dashboard on top; manual mapping eliminated; engineers in control of their own data. [ROI number or hours saved per month; number of systems connected on day one vs now]
Learning. Sunk cost is not a reason to keep a tool that doesn't model the business. And the customer's ask ("make the tool work") and the customer's need (a thread across six systems) were different things — I had to sit with the engineers to see it.
Not a failure story — the vendor's tool failed, you decided. Use it for build-vs-buy, challenging the status quo, and Think Big. Use S5 for "a time you failed".

cards.f: S4 — ARV: from no process and a failing security score to enterprise governance
cards.b:
Answers: "Tell me about transforming an organization." "Improving operational health from nothing." "Your largest project." "Security or compliance under pressure." "Sequencing a lot of change."

Situation. ARV had just won a multi-billion-dollar Army program and was growing fast — 130-plus engineers, a PLM ecosystem, an ERP rollout, defense cybersecurity requirements — with no delivery process, no change management, fragmented ticketing, no monitoring, no DR, manual onboarding, and a security score of 7.3 against an 8.1 standard.
Task. I owned IT and digital-engineering architecture. I had to get a 250-person company to enterprise-grade governance and defense compliance without stopping the program.
Action. I sequenced it deliberately: visibility first, then control, then automation — you cannot automate what you cannot see. Visibility: enterprise Jira and Confluence, Kanban for IT and Scrum for software, Nagios observability with proactive alerting and capacity planning. Control: DLP, AD-based identity across applications, endpoint hardening, patch automation, a DR strategy for the mission-critical platforms. Automation: vendor, license, asset and onboarding automation, automated laptop provisioning. I set the order, wrote the plan, and ran the weekly review that kept it moving.
Result. Security score 7.3 → 8.1+; [uptime / outage numbers; onboarding time from X to Y; license cost saved]; a foundation that scaled with the program instead of breaking under it.
Learning. The sequence is the strategy. Teams that start with automation automate chaos. Visibility → control → automation.
t: Success and Scale Bring Broad Responsibility

cards.f: S5 — Cameo/MBSE turnaround — inherited, failing, leaderless (and the failure version)
cards.b:
Situation. At Rheinmetall our monthly SysML model deliveries to the Army were failing on import every month — performance, broken dependencies, validation errors. It was a reputational problem with the customer and the CTO asked me to own it, though the systems engineering team didn't report to me and SysML wasn't my background.
Task. Make the deliveries reliable, and do it without losing the team, which had been operating without technical leadership under heavy pressure.
Action. My first month was wrong. The visible symptom was an undersized single-cluster server and an old Cameo version with known defects, so I started there — procurement, upgrade planning, infrastructure. It helped at the margin. What actually fixed it came from going deeper: I met every engineer, read every defect ticket and every vendor escalation, and learned enough SysML and Cameo to read the models myself. The models had cyclical dependencies created by engineers taking shortcuts under monthly pressure, with no shared framework. So I changed approach: I negotiated a one-month delivery extension with the program office myself so the team wasn't absorbing the pressure, restored ownership of model packages, brought in an MBSE consultancy and adopted a UAF-based framework, and only then finished the infrastructure — Teamwork Cloud, multi-cluster, Cameo 2024, coordinated across our environment and the government's.
Result. The recurring failures stopped. Dependency graphs were clean, imports reliable, delivery predictable, and [retention through the turnaround].
Learning. I told the team I'd spent the first month on the wrong thing, and that's the moment they started telling me what was actually going on. Now I start with the people and the process, and I treat the infrastructure fix as the easy part.

cards.f: S6 — Grid monitoring — pushing back on an unrealistic plan
cards.b:
Situation. On a remote-monitoring and predictive-analytics platform for commercial electrical grids across the US and Canada, the RFP and the plan assumed one device type, one message format, and two VMs. In the first weeks I found five module types with multiple variants, real-time streaming ingestion, and fault-tolerance and scale requirements the plan couldn't meet. My manager wanted the original plan delivered as sold.
Task. I was the architect accountable for the technical plan. The choice was deliver and fail, or escalate against my own manager.
Action. I quantified it — effort, infrastructure, risk, and cost — and built a short deck: why the assumptions were invalid, what architecture was needed, what it would cost, and what failure would look like for the client. Before going up, I reviewed it with a senior enterprise architect and got his agreement so I wasn't a lone voice. Then I presented it jointly to the VP with three options, not a complaint.
Result. Leadership took the facts to the client transparently and renegotiated scope, budget, and timeline. We delivered a scalable platform that materially improved fault detection and the client relationship became a long-term one. The alternative was a failed project and a financial loss.
Learning. Options with numbers, and an ally before the room. And if the VP had said "proceed as planned," I would have delivered that and tracked the metrics that would have shown whether I was right — which is the commit half of the principle.

cards.f: S7 — Production AI in a CUI environment: RheinMan and RheinCoder (the hands-on detail behind S13)
cards.b:
Answers: "How hands-on are you?" "Tell me about responsible AI." "Build vs buy under constraints." "A measurable productivity improvement." "How do you keep learning?"

Situation. Engineers were losing hours a week searching Teamcenter, Confluence and work instructions. No cloud AI was allowed — the data is CUI.
Task. Put useful AI into production on-prem, with guardrails, in a defense environment — and keep my own hands on it so the senior engineers would trust the architecture.
Action. I built RheinMan: an n8n-orchestrated RAG with Qdrant and on-prem models, work-relevance input filtering, and tool-calling passthrough where permitted. I built RheinCoder: a VS Code multi-agent extension, migrated from a classifier pipeline to a LangGraph tool-calling loop, with per-hunk diff approval, a flight recorder, a semantic index and a substantial automated test suite, targeting Spring Boot and embedded C. I scoped a Presidio-based CUI log anonymizer. I evaluated Hermes, Nemotron, Eigent and OpenClaw and rejected Eigent for the secured slot on security grounds. I still write code for it.
Result. [Productivity up N% — say how measured; adopted by N engineers]; compliance maintained throughout.
Learning. Constraints clarify architecture. Guardrails and evaluation are the product, not an afterthought — and a manager who still ships code earns a different kind of trust from senior engineers.
t: Success and Scale Bring Broad Responsibility

cards.f: S8 — Growing people: the mentorship pyramid and one person who became a lead
cards.b:
Answers: "Tell me about someone you developed." "How do you build high-performing teams?" "How do you manage your strongest performers?" "How have you helped a strong engineer advance?"

Approach. Four pillars I run every team on: a mentorship pyramid (I mentor the seniors, they mentor the next level, so growth scales without me); a culture that questions designs and understands the business context; DevSecOps and automation so quality is the default rather than heroics (at Rheinmetall: CI/CD with SonarQube, Astrée, Tessy; IaC; observability); and business cases for modern tooling so teams are equipped — the AI assistants in S13 came from that.
The one person. [Name/role when you got them → what you gave them: a scope with its own customers, a stretch project, visibility in front of leadership, feedback they did not enjoy → where they are now]
Learning. People grow on scope and honest feedback, not on praise. The manager's job is to hand over decision rights in writing and then stay out of the way.
This is the one story still missing its person. Fill the bracket before the call — it is referenced by four answers in Parts 10 and 10C.
t: Strive to be Earth's Best Employer

cards.f: S9 — How I lead (the two-minute answer to "describe your leadership style")
cards.b:
Answers: "Describe your leadership style." "How would your team describe you?" "How do you make decisions?"

Three principles. Lead by example — hands-on, keep learning, earn credibility with senior engineers by still being able to do the work. Trust, respect, empowerment — psychological safety, real ownership with decision rights written down, and I am available for guidance without taking the work back. Data-driven, transparent decisions — debate the trade-offs openly, decide openly, course-correct openly when wrong.
Effect. Teams that feel respected, trusted, heard and challenged exceed expectations; retention of top talent through hard periods (S5); morale under pressure.
The honest weakness to pair with it. [One real thing your last upward feedback said — e.g., taking too long on staffing decisions — and the fix you put in place]
t: Strive to be Earth's Best Employer

cards.f: S10 — Letting go a senior systems engineer
cards.b:
Answers: "Tell me about managing an underperformer." "Tell me about a time you had to let someone go." "Tell me about a hard people decision." "Tell me about a hiring mistake" (the résumé was exceptional; the signal I missed was delivery).

Situation. At Rheinmetall I hired a senior systems engineer and architect. Over thirty years of experience. NASA, Air Force programs. Her job was to model the whole digital engineering ecosystem — every tool, and the data flow between them — so we could see where the digital thread needed to connect.
Task. I was her manager. I owned her delivery and her growth.
Action. I set a regular cadence on progress from the start. After a few weeks, all I saw was a template and fragments of the model. In our meetings she would brainstorm instead of going out and gathering information from department leads. She said departments weren't cooperating. So I removed the blocker myself: I set up the stakeholder meetings and sat in them. The information still didn't make it into the model. I gave direct, specific feedback — here is what I expected, here is what I got. Then I went closer and managed the work at a task level to see if structure helped. It didn't. She became hard to reach — hours without a response. I asked her directly whether something outside work was going on and how I could help. She didn't open up. After six months with no deliverable, I made the decision to let her go.
Result. The role was refilled and the ecosystem model was delivered by [who, and how long after]. The digital thread now spans six systems.
Learning. Two things. I should have set a 30-day deliverable with a concrete artifact in the first month instead of trusting the résumé. And I waited too long — at month three the pattern was clear. Now I use a written improvement plan with a date as soon as I see a pattern, not a bad week.
If they ask "what would you do differently": say the 30-day deliverable and acting at month three. Do not blame her. Keep it factual and kind.

Answers: "Walk me through your most severe outage." "Tell me about a crisis you ran." "Tell me about a time you had to act fast with incomplete information." "Tell me about a security issue you handled."

Situation. Early in the Ukraine war, cyber activity against defense suppliers went up. Almost all our applications are on-prem and not on the internet. The few that are use two-factor and IP whitelisting. One application — the Vendor Portal, used to onboard suppliers and keep their annual defense-compliance certifications — was public. It had a known vulnerability (a CVE) in the .NET file-upload code. Attackers used it to inject malicious code into our network. Our managed security provider, Arctic Wolf, detected the injection and alerted us.
Task. I owned the application and the response. Contain it, find out how far it went, fix it, and make sure it couldn't happen again.
Action. First hour: I took the site down, and then every internet-facing site, at the firewall — contain first, diagnose second. I opened a live bridge that ran the whole day: Arctic Wolf's analysts, our developers, and our network admins. We worked to pinpoint and isolate the attack path. Then we scanned the entire network for every known vulnerability, not just the one that was exploited. We fixed the code, patched everything we found, and redeployed. Then the long-term decisions: I moved the server into a DMZ, and we implemented FIPS-compliant encryption end to end.
Result. Contained the same day. [Hours of downtime; confirmed no data exfiltration; number of other vulnerabilities found and fixed]. No recurrence. This incident is part of why our security score went from 7.3 to above 8.1.
Learning. The vulnerability was known before it was exploited. The real fix was a mechanism: automated dependency and vulnerability scanning in the pipeline, and a rule that nothing internet-facing deploys without passing it. Fix the class, not the instance.
Amazon vocabulary to use: "I treated it as a Sev-1," "I was the incident commander on the bridge," "the correction of error produced three actions," "blast radius."
t: Success and Scale Bring Broad Responsibility

cards.f: S12 — Ford: lift-and-shift vs re-architecture, and committing to the hybrid
cards.b:
Answers: "Tell me about a time you disagreed with a decision and committed anyway." "Tell me about a time you pushed back on leadership." "Tell me about a decision that went against your recommendation."

Situation. At Ford, management mandated a move from Azure to GCP on a tight date. The plan was lift and shift — including rewriting our C# monolith into Java to use GCP serverless. I disagreed. The same serverless pattern was available in Azure, and the monolith could be broken into microservices in place. I was already mid-way through a redesign: a Redis cache and a dynamic, rules-driven engine replacing static logic.
Task. I owned the architecture. I had to make my case, and then deliver whatever was decided.
Action. I presented the risks in writing: rewrite risk, timeline risk, the cost of moving before fixing the architecture, and the option to migrate without the language rewrite. I did it once, clearly, with data. Leadership decided on a hybrid: lift and shift the code, but include the Redis cache and the event-driven capability computation I had designed. That wasn't my full recommendation. I committed to it completely — I phased the roadmap so the redesign pieces that mattered for scale landed with the migration, and I stopped relitigating the rewrite.
Result. We hit the migration date. Latency went from over 300 ms to under 100. The platform scaled to 11 million vehicles. [What happened with the language rewrite — was it done later, dropped, or did it cause the problems you predicted?].
Learning. Making the argument once, with numbers, and then committing fully got me more influence than winning would have. Leadership took the cache and the event design because I didn't fight on everything. Pick the hill.

cards.f: S13 — Think Big: one AI layer for the whole enterprise, not one chatbot
cards.b:
Answers: "Tell me about a time you thought big." "When was the last time you did something innovative?" "Tell me about a bold idea you drove." "Tell me about a time you simplified something complex." "How do you keep learning?" "Tell me about building something nobody had built before."

Situation. At Rheinmetall every team wanted "AI" and every team meant something different: engineers wanted answers from documents spread across PLM, requirements tools and SharePoint; systems engineers spent weeks hand-building SysML models in Cameo; developers wanted a coding assistant but nothing could leave the building — the data is CUI, so public tools were off the table. The obvious move was five point solutions. The obvious move was wrong.
Task. I owned architecture. I had to decide whether we built five tools or one platform, with a small team and no cloud.
Action. I framed it as one governed AI layer with products on top: on-prem models, a vector store (Qdrant), an orchestration layer (n8n and MCP so any internal app could be a tool), guardrails and audit — built once, and then every product is a thin layer that reuses it. Then I picked the products by customer pain, not by novelty:
  • RheinMan — enterprise-grade RAG in production on n8n, connected to multiple internal business apps and engineering tools, so an engineer asks one question and gets an answer grounded in the systems of record, with citations.
  • Campilot — a Cameo plugin that turns natural language into SysML v1 elements. The innovation is the hybrid of AI and deterministic code: the model proposes, deterministic rules generate the actual model elements, and defense frameworks and an ontology constrain what is allowed — so the output is valid SysML, not plausible-looking text. No vendor had shipped this for MBSE.
  • RheinCoder — an in-house VS Code coding agent, moved from a fixed pipeline to tool-calling agents so it could choose its own steps.
  • SOP Sentinel — factory video turned into electronic work instructions: watch the operator, extract the steps, produce the instruction set that quality can review, instead of someone writing it by hand weeks later.
  • Log Distillery — scrapes logs across systems and distills them into a root-cause narrative for system administrators, so a two-hour grep session becomes a two-minute read.
I sequenced them so the first one (RheinMan) paid for the platform and the rest rode on it.
Result. [Adoption: number of users / queries per week on RheinMan; time to build a SysML model before vs after Campilot; developer time saved with RheinCoder; hours per work instruction before vs after SOP Sentinel; mean time to diagnose with Log Distillery]. Five products on one platform, from a team of [N], entirely on-prem and compliant.
Learning. Think Big is not "a bigger feature" — it is choosing the layer instead of the feature, so the fifth product costs a tenth of the first. And the most innovative part was not the model; it was constraining the model with deterministic code and an ontology so engineers could trust the output. Innovation that engineers trust is innovation that is checkable.
If asked "what was the risk?": "That I was building a platform nobody asked for. I de-risked it by shipping RheinMan first — a product people did ask for — on the platform, so the platform was never on the roadmap by itself." Say "I" for the architecture decision and the sequencing; "the team" for each product.

decks.title: How answers are scored, follow-ups & pitfalls
decks.blurb: STAR-L, the bar, the follow-ups interviewers always ask, and day-of pitfalls.

cards.f: STAR, and where the points are
cards.b:
PartHow longSay thisDon't do this
Situation20 secondsTwo sentences. Where, what scale, what was at stake.Five minutes of backstory
Task10 seconds"I was responsible for…""The team needed to…"
ActionHalf your timeWhat you did, step by step. Your decisions. Your tradeoffs.Describing the system instead of your actions
Result20 secondsNumbers. Before and after."It went well." "Significantly improved."
LearningOne sentenceWhat you'd do differently.Skipping it, or "nothing"

• Say "I", not "we". They can't score "we". If it was a team effort: "the team built it; my part was the design and the decision to phase it."
  • Every result has a number. 300 milliseconds to under 100. Security score 7.3 to 8.1. Thirty million requests a month. If you don't have the exact number, give an honest estimate and say it's an estimate.
  • Expect follow-ups. The chain is always: what did you do → why that option → what else did you consider → how did you know it worked → what went wrong → what would you change. Prepare each story three levels deep.
  • Two to three minutes, then stop. Let them ask. Long answers mean fewer data points.
  • Failure stories must be yours. "The vendor failed" scores zero. "I spent a month on the wrong fix" scores well.
  • Recent and big. Last five years, largest scope.
  • Don't reuse a story. They notice. You now have twelve.
Words that make interviewers nod: working backwards from the customer · mechanism, not good intentions · blast radius · correction of error (COE) · two-way door vs one-way door decision · dive deep · disagree and commit · raise the bar · operational metrics · root cause vs contributing factors · ownership end to end · invent and simplify

• Twelve stories on one page: headline, three numbers, the learning line. Keep it in front of you — it's a phone screen.
  • The four unwritten stories written: Stellantis OTA, disagree-and-commit where you lost, a hiring mistake, an underperformer.
  • Every amber bracket filled with a number.
  • Job description re-read; the team's customer named in your "why Amazon."
  • Quiet room, headset, Chime tested, water. Phone screens are often recorded in notes; speak in complete sentences at a measured pace.

• Answer the question asked, then stop. Two to three minutes. Let the follow-up come.
  • "I", not "we". If you catch yourself, correct it: "the team did X; what I personally did was Y."
  • Give the number even when they don't ask. Give the learning even when they don't ask.
  • If you don't have an example for a principle, say so and offer the closest one — don't invent.
  • If asked "what would you do differently?" have a real answer. "Nothing" is scored as a lack of self-awareness.
  • Don't disparage a former employer or a current one. Don't say you're leaving defense because it's slow.

• Generic answers about philosophy with no incident, no date, no number.
  • Stories where someone else was the actor (the vendor failed, the team did it).
  • Repeating the same story for three principles.
  • Long situation, short action.
  • Treating "tell me about a failure" as an invitation to describe a success in disguise.
  • Not asking questions at the end — it's read as low curiosity.

cards.f: The five follow-ups that come after every story
cards.b:
Amazon interviewers are trained to probe; expect two of these after each answer. Having the answers ready is worth more than polishing the story.

They askYou have ready
"What was your role, specifically?"One sentence starting with "I decided / I wrote / I told" — not "we".
"What was the number?"The before and after figure, and how it was measured. Fill every amber bracket in Parts 3B and 5 before the call.
"What would you do differently?"One real thing. "Nothing" is scored as low self-awareness.
"How did you know it worked?"The metric and when you looked at it. A result without a measurement is an opinion.
"What did you learn, and where have you used it since?"The principle in one line, plus one later situation where it changed what you did.

decks.title: Leadership principles → what they test
decks.blurb: Sixteen leadership principles (the Amazon set, a superset of most companies’ competencies): definition, what they check, typical questions, your story.

cards.b:
Leaders start with the customer and work backwards. They work vigorously to earn and keep customer trust.

What they probe
Did you make a decision that favored the customer over what was easier for your team or leadership? Do you know who your customer is and what they experience?
Questions
"Tell me about a time you went above and beyond for a customer." "Tell me about a time you had to balance customer needs against business constraints." "Who was your customer and how did you learn what they needed?"
Your story
S2 Stellantis provisioning — it started with customer calls and ended with a recall avoided; the strongest Customer Obsession story you have. Also S1 Ford Feature Management. The customer was the vehicle owner opening FordPass and the dealer at the point of sale; capability visible before sale and sub-100 ms responses were customer outcomes, not technical ones. Secondary: S7 RAG assistant — engineers as internal customers, hours lost searching Teamcenter measured first.
Headline
"I redesigned a platform that decided what every Ford vehicle could do, because the customer-facing latency and the gaps before sale were costing trust — and I measured it from the customer side first."

Leaders are owners. They think long term and don't sacrifice long-term value for short-term results. They never say "that's not my job."

What they probe
Did you take on something outside your remit because it mattered? Did you choose the long-term fix over the quick one?
Questions
"Tell me about a time you took on something outside your job description." "Tell me about a time you chose a long-term solution at short-term cost." "Tell me about a problem you saw that nobody owned."
Your story
S2 Stellantis provisioning — "not my job" is literally the principle's text, and you owned it anyway. Also S5 Cameo/MBSE turnaround — the CTO asked, but the team wasn't yours and the domain (SysML) wasn't your specialty; you learned it, took ownership of the delivery to the Army, and fixed the framework rather than the servers. Backup: S4 ARV IT transformation — security, process, and DR nobody owned.
Headline
"When our monthly SysML deliveries to the Army kept failing, I took ownership of a team and a domain that weren't mine, learned the tooling, and fixed the root cause rather than the symptom."

Leaders expect and require innovation and invention from their teams and always find ways to simplify. They are not limited by "not invented here."

What they probe
Did you create something new or remove complexity, and did it scale?
Questions
"Tell me about a time you invented something." "Tell me about a time you simplified a process or system." "Tell me about an innovative idea that was initially misunderstood."
Your story
S1 Ford — replacing per-request computation with event-driven computation is the simplification; one code path, zero synchronous dependencies. S3 Cindia → graph digital thread is the invention: a graph model instead of a linear ETL tool. S7 RheinCoder — migrating a classifier pipeline to a tool-calling loop removed brittle heuristics.
Headline
"The simplification was to stop recomputing on every read: compute once when the vehicle changes, serve from a cache, reconcile every fifteen days. It removed four synchronous dependencies and took p99 from over 300 ms to under 100."

Leaders have strong judgment and good instincts. They seek diverse perspectives and work to disconfirm their beliefs.

What they probe
A decision with incomplete information that turned out right — and how you tested your own belief. Also: a time you were wrong.
Questions
"Tell me about a decision you made with limited information." "Tell me about a time you were wrong." "How do you make sure you're not fooling yourself?"
Your story
S3 Cindia — validated with engineers and the vendor before deciding; a time-boxed, reversible first step. For "wrong": S5 — the first month on infrastructure when the cause was modeling discipline.
Headline
"I'd bought nothing yet and had to decide whether a purchased tool could ever model our reality. I set a time box, tried to make it work with the vendor, asked three engineers to break my alternative, and chose a reversible first step."

Leaders are never done learning and always seek to improve themselves.

What they probe
Something you learned recently that you didn't need to; how you learn.
Questions
"Tell me about something you learned recently." "Tell me about a time you had to learn a new domain quickly." "What are you reading or building?"
Your story
S5 — learned SysML and Cameo to lead a team credibly. S7 — building RheinCoder and RheinMan, evaluating Hermes/Nemotron/Eigent/OpenClaw; the AWS labs and the two curricula you've authored.
Headline
"I still write code. In the last year I built a multi-agent coding platform on LangGraph, evaluated four open models for a secured RAG slot and rejected one, and wrote a manufacturing-systems curriculum — because I don't trust my judgment on things I haven't built."

Leaders raise the performance bar with every hire and promotion. Leaders develop leaders.

What they probe
Your hiring bar, a specific person you grew, a hiring mistake, and how you manage out.
Questions
"Tell me about the best hire you made." "Tell me about someone you developed into a leader." "Tell me about a hiring mistake." "How do you raise the bar?"
Your story
S8 mentorship pyramid — but Amazon wants a named trajectory. [One person: what you gave them, timeline, where they are now]. Hiring process: rubric, work-sample round, independent scoring before debrief.
Headline
"I grew the architecture function from [N to M] with a written competency framework and a work-sample round; the hire I'm proudest of is [role], who [outcome]."

Leaders have relentlessly high standards. They ensure defects do not get sent down the line and that problems are fixed so they stay fixed.

What they probe
Did you refuse to ship something that wasn't good enough, at a cost? Did you fix the class of problem?
Questions
"Tell me about a time you refused to compromise on quality." "Tell me about a time you raised the bar for your team." "Tell me about a time you found a defect others missed."
Your story
S5 — negotiated a delivery extension rather than ship another broken model; then a framework and CI gates so it stayed fixed. Also the GitLab partner pipeline: SonarQube, Astrée, Tessy on every partner commit, no lower bar for contractors.
Headline
"I'd rather be late once than wrong every month. I negotiated a one-month extension with the program office, fixed the root cause, and put gates in place so the failure class couldn't recur."

Leaders create and communicate a bold direction that inspires results.

What they probe
Did you propose something bigger than what was asked, and did it change the organization's trajectory?
Questions
"Tell me about a time you proposed a bold idea." "Tell me about the most ambitious project you've led." "Tell me about a time you changed the direction of a program."
Your story
S3 — the enterprise digital thread spanning Teamcenter, Plex, Cameo, Creo, Zuken, GitLab, when the ask was "make the integration tool work." S4 — enterprise governance for a company that had just won a multi-billion-dollar program.
Headline
"The request was to make one integration tool work. What I proposed was the digital thread for the whole program — a graph of every engineering artifact — and it's now the backbone connecting six systems."

Speed matters in business. Many decisions are reversible and do not need extensive study. We value calculated risk taking.

What they probe
Did you act without full information because waiting was worse? Did you distinguish reversible from irreversible?
Questions
"Tell me about a time you had to act quickly." "Tell me about a calculated risk." "Tell me about a time you decided without consensus."
Your story
S1 — phasing the redesign into the migration deadline instead of waiting to finish it. S6 — escalating in the first weeks of the grid project rather than waiting for the plan to fail.
Headline
"Three weeks in, I had enough evidence that the plan couldn't work. I didn't wait for it to fail — I quantified it, got an ally, and put options in front of the VP that week."

Accomplish more with less. Constraints breed resourcefulness, self-sufficiency, and invention.

What they probe
Did you deliver with fewer resources than asked, or cut cost without cutting outcome?
Questions
"Tell me about a time you accomplished something with limited resources." "Tell me about a time you reduced cost." "Tell me about a time you said no to more headcount."
Your story
S1 — compute cost [X% lower] because cost scaled with configuration changes instead of reads. S4 — license-management system that [recovered $X]; on-prem inference priced against cloud. S7 — built AI platforms with open models and n8n rather than buying.
Headline
"The cheapest compute is the computation you don't do. Moving Feature Management to compute-on-change cut cost by [X%] and made cost scale with the right variable."

Leaders listen attentively, speak candidly, and treat others respectfully. They are vocally self-critical.

What they probe
A time you admitted a mistake publicly; a time you rebuilt trust with a team or stakeholder; how you deliver bad news.
Questions
"Tell me about a time you had to earn the trust of a team." "Tell me about a time you were vocally self-critical." "Tell me about delivering bad news to leadership."
Your story
S5 — a leaderless, burned team; listening tour; negotiating the extension so they weren't absorbing pressure; admitting the first month was spent on the wrong thing. S6 — telling a VP the plan was wrong, with numbers.
Headline
"I told the team the first thing I'd done was wrong — a month on infrastructure when the problem was modeling discipline. Saying that out loud is what made them tell me the rest."

Leaders operate at all levels, stay connected to the details, audit frequently, and are skeptical when metrics and anecdote differ.

What they probe
A time you went into the details yourself and found what the summary hid.
Questions
"Tell me about a time you found a problem by digging into the data." "Tell me about a time metrics and reality disagreed." "How deep do you go as a manager?"
Your story
S5 — read every defect ticket and vendor escalation, learned the tool, found cyclical dependencies. S6 — read the RFP against the device specs and found five module types where the plan assumed one. S4 — Plex-to-Teamcenter mapping across 245 fields and 452 attributes, personally.
Headline
"The status reports said 'import failures.' I read every ticket and every Dassault escalation and learned enough SysML to see the models had cyclical dependencies created under pressure — a people problem wearing a technical costume."

Leaders respectfully challenge decisions when they disagree, even when uncomfortable. Once a decision is determined, they commit wholly.

What they probe
Both halves: a time you pushed back on a superior, and a time you lost and committed anyway.
Questions
"Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager." "Tell me about a time you committed to a decision you disagreed with." "Tell me about a time you were the only dissenting voice."
Your story
Backbone: S6 grid project — against your own manager, to the VP. Commit: [A real case where you lost the argument and delivered it well — write this].
Headline
"My manager wanted the original plan delivered. I thought it would fail the client. I built the case in numbers, found an ally, and took it to the VP — and if the VP had said proceed, I'd have delivered it and tracked the metrics that would show whether I was right."

Leaders focus on the key inputs for their business and deliver them with the right quality and in a timely fashion. Despite setbacks, they rise to the occasion.

What they probe
A hard commitment delivered despite obstacles — with numbers.
Questions
"Tell me about the most difficult delivery of your career." "Tell me about a time you had to deliver under a tight deadline." "Tell me about a goal you didn't meet."
Your story
S1 — redesign plus migration, on the mandated date, with the numbers. S2 Stellantis OTA — fleet fix, recall avoided [vehicles, dollars]. For "didn't meet": the first failed Cameo delivery after you took over, and what you changed.
Headline
"Leadership mandated a cloud migration date. I delivered the migration and a redesign on that date: sub-100 ms, horizontal scale to eleven million vehicles, lower compute cost."

cards.f: Strive to be Earth's Best Employer
cards.b:
Leaders work to create a safer, more productive, higher performing, more diverse, and more just work environment. They lead with empathy.

What they probe
Did you make a team's working life better in a measurable way? Did you protect people?
Questions
"Tell me about a time you improved your team's work environment." "Tell me about a time you supported someone through a hard period." "How do you know your team is healthy?"
Your story
S5 — negotiated the extension so engineers stopped absorbing the Army's pressure; restored psychological safety. S7 — the assistant that gave engineers hours back. Retention through the turnaround: [number].
Headline
"The team had been failing publicly every month with no leader. The first thing I did was take the pressure off them — I owned the extension conversation with the program office — and then I gave them a framework to succeed with."

cards.f: Success and Scale Bring Broad Responsibility
cards.b:
We must be humble and thoughtful about even the secondary effects of our actions. Leaders create more than they consume.

What they probe
Did you consider second-order effects — security, privacy, safety, the broader organization — beyond your immediate goal?
Questions
"Tell me about a time you considered the broader impact of a decision." "Tell me about a time you chose the responsible path over the expedient one."
Your story
S7 — responsible AI guardrails in a CUI environment: on-prem only, work-relevance filtering, retrieval-level access control, log anonymization — when cloud AI would have been faster. S4 — security posture 7.3 to 8.1 for a defense supplier.
Headline
"The fast path was a cloud model. The responsible path for controlled data was on-prem with guardrails I had to build. I chose the second and still shipped it to production."

decks.title: Reported manager questions — 60-second answers
decks.blurb: Questions reported from real engineering-manager screens and loops, each with the story to use, a spoken answer and the follow-up.

cards.b:
Answer from: Part 8 opener
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"I lead architecture and engineering at American Rheinmetall — about [N] engineers through [N] leads, across the digital-engineering platform, PLM/MBSE tooling and an on-prem AI platform for CUI data. Before that I was an architect at Ford on the Feature Management platform and at Stellantis on connected-vehicle OTA. The through-line is platforms many teams depend on, correctness under scale, and turning around teams that were struggling. I'm talking to you because BDT is that same problem at Amazon's scale." Ninety seconds, then stop.

Then they will ask: "How many report to you directly?" — have the exact numbers ready; this is leveling.

cards.f: Walk me through your current org. How many engineers report to you, and what do they own?
cards.b:
Answer from: Say the numbers
Say it (about 60 seconds)

Draw it in words: "[N] direct reports, of which [N] are leads with teams of [N]; total span [N]. Pod A owns [X], pod B owns [Y], pod C owns [Z]. I also own the roadmap and the budget for [area]." Then one sentence on what you personally still do (architecture reviews, hiring bar, executive updates). Direct reports, span, what each pod owns, what you personally own.

Then they will ask: "Do your leads manage people or are they tech leads?" — answer precisely; manager-of-managers is the L7 signal, so do not inflate.

cards.f: How do you decide what your team works on next quarter?
cards.b:
Answer from: Part 6; S1 phasing
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"I start from the customer's top three pains, not from our backlog — for a platform that means the teams who depend on us, so I run a quarterly listening pass with the biggest consumers. Then operational debt gets a fixed share — about 20% — because platforms die from neglect, not from missing features. The rest is ranked by value divided by effort with risk as a tie-breaker, written down as a one-page plan with what we are explicitly not doing, and reviewed with my leads before it goes up." Give one real example from S1: the migration date vs the redesign.

Then they will ask: "How do you say no to a senior stakeholder?" — "With data and an alternative: here's the cost, here's what it displaces, here's a smaller version we can do."

cards.f: Walk me through a system your team owned. Which parts would you redesign?
cards.b:
Answer from: S1 Feature Management; or the OTA platform
Say it (about 60 seconds)

Pick one system and draw it in the generic shape: producers → ingestion → the core → consumers. Give three numbers (volume, latency, team size). Then the redesign with a reason: "the reconciliation ran as a nightly batch and I'd make it event-driven with idempotent handlers, because the batch window became the bottleneck and the on-call pain." What broke, why, what you'd change is the whole answer.

Then they will ask: "What breaks first at ten times the traffic?" — name the single component and its symptom.

cards.f: How do you manage projects? What's your process for managing resources?
cards.b:
Answer from: Part 6
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"Three mechanisms. A written plan with milestones, owners and the risks ranked — I keep a risk register and review it weekly. A dependency map so partner commitments are visible before they slip. And a weekly metrics review — delivery predictability, operational health, hiring pipeline — so I manage from numbers, not from the loudest voice. Resourcing is a quarterly conversation: I show what the team can do at current size, what it cannot, and what I would add with one more engineer."

Then they will ask: "Give me an example of a project that was behind — what did you do?" — have S5 or S6 ready with the specific change.

cards.f: Tell me about the most challenging project you worked on.
cards.b:
Answer from: S1 or S5
Say it (about 60 seconds)

STAR with numbers. Situation in two sentences; your personal actions in four; result with a figure; one sentence of learning. For S5: "I inherited a failing, leaderless program with a customer-visible deadline. In my first month I got the diagnosis wrong — I treated it as a staffing problem when it was a requirements problem. I corrected by [specific action], we delivered [what] by [date], and the learning was diagnose before you staff."

Then they will ask: "What would you do differently?" — never "nothing"; have the one real thing.

cards.f: What was the largest project you've executed?
cards.b:
Answer from: S4 ARV transformation or S1
Say it (about 60 seconds)

Size it in numbers first — teams, budget, duration, users affected — then the hardest part, then the outcome. "Largest by blast radius was the ARV digital-engineering transformation: [N] teams, [N] systems, [duration]. The hard part was sequencing — nothing could be cut over at once. The outcome was [metric]."

Then they will ask: "What did you personally do versus your team?" — be precise; "I" for decisions, "the team" for the building.

cards.f: Tell me about a time you coached an engineer through underperformance. What changed?
cards.b:
Answer from: S10 (3B)
Say it (about 60 seconds)

Name the gap specifically, the plan, the timeline, the check-ins, and the outcome — including the case where it ended in a departure. "A senior systems engineer was not delivering designs the team could build from. I named the gap in writing, set a six-week plan with two concrete deliverables, met weekly, and brought in a peer to pair. By week six [what happened]. The learning: early, specific, documented, humane — and that letting someone go kindly is also a form of respect for the rest of the team."

Then they will ask: "How long did you give it, and how did you know it was time?" — the timeline and the evidence.

cards.f: What approach do you take with low performers?
cards.b:
Answer from: Part 6
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"Early — the first miss gets a conversation, not the third. Specific — behaviors and outputs, not adjectives. Documented — so the person and I agree on what was said. Humane — the plan is designed to succeed, and if it doesn't, the exit is handled with dignity. And I ask myself first whether the role, the manager or the setup is the problem before I decide the person is."

Then they will ask: "Have you ever been wrong about a low performer?" — a short honest example earns trust.

cards.f: How do you measure engineering manager performance?
cards.b:
Answer from: Part 6
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"Three lenses. Team outcomes: delivery predictability, operational health of what they own. People outcomes: retention of strong people, promotions they sponsored, quality of their hires. And what their team says in skip-levels — whether people understand the why, feel safe disagreeing, and know where they stand."

Then they will ask: "Which of those is the leading indicator?" — the skip-level signal; the others lag by two quarters.

cards.f: How would you write a job description for an engineering manager?
cards.b:
Answer from: Part 6
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"Outcomes owned, not activities. The scope in numbers. The three or four competencies that matter for this team — for a platform team: operational rigor, customer empathy for internal teams, hiring bar. And one line on what raising the bar looks like at this level, so candidates self-select."

Then they will ask: "What's the one competency you won't compromise on?" — pick one and say why.

cards.f: Give an example of how you helped another employee grow.
cards.b:
Answer from: S8
Say it (about 60 seconds)

One named trajectory: where they were, what you gave them (scope, a stretch project, visibility, feedback), what you removed (a blocker, yourself), and where they are now. Role, what you gave, where they are now.

Then they will ask: "What did you personally do that a good peer wouldn't have?" — the specific sponsorship moment.

cards.f: Tell me about the best hire you made and the worst.
cards.b:
Answer from: S10 (3B)
Say it (about 60 seconds)

Best: the signal you saw that others missed and how it played out. Worst: the signal you missed, what it cost, and the change to your interview loop afterwards — "I added a working session on a real problem because the résumé and references did not show how the person thinks under ambiguity."

Then they will ask: "How has your hiring process changed?" — the concrete mechanism you added.

cards.f: How do you keep a distributed team aligned?
cards.b:
Answer from: Partner-team experience
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"Written-first: decisions in a doc, not a call. Handoff notes at the end of each day across time zones. A decision log so nobody re-litigates. And one synchronous hour a week that is sacred. I learned this across Wipro, Cognizant and partner teams in [regions]."

Then they will ask: "How do you handle a time-zone conflict on an urgent issue?" — the escalation path agreed in advance.

cards.f: Walk me through your most severe outage. How did you handle detection and mitigation?
cards.b:
Answer from: S11 (3B)
Say it (about 60 seconds)

Timeline with times. Detection (how you found out, and whether a customer found out first), containment before diagnosis, communication cadence, the fix, the COE, and the mechanism that came out of it. "The vendor portal breach: detected at [time] by [what]; I isolated [what] within [minutes]; customers were told at [time]; root cause was [what]; the lasting change was [mechanism]."

Then they will ask: "What would have caught it earlier?" — name the missing alarm or control.

cards.f: How would you improve the operational health of a system your team owns?
cards.b:
Answer from: ARV observability-from-zero
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"In order: define SLOs on what the customer feels; replace cause-based alerts with symptom-based ones; a runbook for every alert; a COE for every customer-visible incident with tracked actions; a monthly pattern review that fixes the class, not the instance. At ARV I built this from zero — we went from [before] to [after] in [time]."

Then they will ask: "How do you keep the action items from dying?" — they are reviewed in the same weekly meeting as delivery.

cards.f: How do you structure on-call so it stays sustainable?
cards.b:
Answer from: Part 11C SRE
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"Rotation of at least six so nobody is on more than one week in six. Pages per shift is a metric I review; above a threshold, fixing the pager is the next sprint's top priority. On-call is compensated or time-banked. And the manager is in the rotation for the first quarter of any new service."

Then they will ask: "What's your threshold?" — have a number: e.g., more than two pages a night for two shifts triggers the fix.

cards.f: How do you handle a recurring issue that keeps paging the team?
cards.b:
Answer from: Pattern review
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"Stop treating it as an incident and treat it as a project: fix the class, not the instance. One owner, a dated plan, and the pages counted weekly until they go to zero. If the fix is expensive, I make the cost of not fixing it visible — hours of engineer sleep lost per month."

Then they will ask: "What if the fix is in another team's system?" — written escalation with the data, and a temporary mitigation on your side.

cards.f: Describe your approach to a correction of error (COE).
cards.b:
Answer from: Part 11C
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"Blameless: the question is what in the system let a reasonable person do this. Five-whys to multiple contributing factors, not one. Action items with an owner and a date each, audited for completion. And the write-up is shared widely so other teams learn."

Then they will ask: "Tell me about a COE that changed something across teams." — one example.

cards.f: Tell me about a time you had to deliver on a deadline with multiple roadblocks and constraints.
cards.b:
Answer from: S1
Say it (about 60 seconds)

Deadline, the three roadblocks, what you traded, what you refused to trade, and the result. "The migration date was fixed by [what]; the roadblocks were [a], [b], [c]; I cut scope on the redesign, not on correctness, negotiated [what] with [whom], and we landed on [date] with [metric]."

Then they will ask: "What did you cut, and who was unhappy?" — be specific; it shows you made a real trade.

cards.f: Tell me about a program that slipped. What changed in how you planned the next one?
cards.b:
Answer from: S5 or S6
Say it (about 60 seconds)

Own the slip in the first sentence. The cause in one sentence. Then the mechanism: "I added a risk register reviewed weekly and dependency sequencing before dates are promised, and I now give dates as ranges with confidence levels until the design is done."

Then they will ask: "Did the next one ship on time?" — have the number.

cards.f: How do you keep a partner team accountable to a dependency?
cards.b:
Answer from: GitLab partner gates; Cameo upgrade
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"Written commitments with dates, a shared tracker both leaders see, an escalation path agreed before it's needed, and the dependency drawn on the roadmap so slippage is visible to everyone, not just to me."

Then they will ask: "What if they still miss?" — the mitigation you prepared, then the escalation, in that order.

cards.f: Tell me about competing priorities and how you managed the trade-offs.
cards.b:
Answer from: Roadmap negotiation
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"Two senior stakeholders wanted [A] and [B] from the same team in the same quarter. I wrote a one-page comparison — customer impact, cost, risk, what each displaces — proposed [the decision], and got both to agree in the same room so there was no relitigation. [A] shipped in [when]; [B] got a smaller version in [when]."

Then they will ask: "How did you decide which customer mattered more?" — the principle you used, not just the outcome.

cards.f: Describe a time a customer asked for one thing but needed something else.
cards.b:
Answer from: S3; or S6
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"The ask was 'make Cindia work'; after sitting with the users for a week the need was a digital thread between [systems]. I showed them the difference with their own data, delivered the small fix they asked for in [time] to earn trust, then the real thing."

Then they will ask: "How did you convince them?" — their own data, in their own words.

cards.f: Tell me about a conflict with your supervisor and how you resolved it.
cards.b:
Answer from: S6
Say it (about 60 seconds)

Respectful, specific, data-first, and committed afterwards. "I disagreed with [decision] because [data]. I said so in writing, proposed [alternative], and when the decision stood I committed fully and said so to my team. The outcome was [what], and [what you learned]."

Then they will ask: "Were you right?" — honest either way; if you were wrong, say what you learned about your own judgment.

cards.f: Tell me about a conflict with someone. How did you resolve it and what did you learn?
cards.b:
Answer from: S6 or the senior-architect disagreement
Say it (about 60 seconds)

The person, the issue, the conversation — in private, with data, listening first — the resolution, and what changed in you. Avoid conflicts you won by authority.

Then they will ask: "What did the other person say about it afterwards?" — shows whether the relationship survived.

cards.f: Tell me about the most challenging situation in your career and how you handled it.
cards.b:
Answer from: S5
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"Inherited, failing, leaderless, customer-visible." The first month's wrong diagnosis, the correction, the delivery, the learning. This is the story that shows self-awareness plus results.

Then they will ask: "What was the hardest conversation in it?" — have the specific one.

cards.f: Give an example where you failed / failed to do the right thing.
cards.b:
Answer from: S5 "wrong first month"
Say it (about 60 seconds)

It must be your failure, with a real cost, and a change you made. "I treated a requirements problem as a staffing problem for a month; it cost [what]. Since then I diagnose with the customer before I change the team."

Then they will ask: "What did it cost?" — a number or a date slipped; vague costs read as not a real failure.

cards.f: When was the last time you did something innovative?
cards.b:
Answer from: S13 (3B) — the portfolio; S7 for the RheinCoder detail
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"RheinCoder — moving from a fixed pipeline to tool-calling agents so the system could pick its own steps. Simpler to extend, and it cut [metric]. The innovation was removing the pipeline, not adding to it."

Then they will ask: "How did you know it was better?" — the measurement.

cards.f: Tell me about a time you took on something outside your job description.
cards.b:
Answer from: S2 (3B)
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"Vehicle provisioning was failing and it was not my team's system. I took it anyway because the customer impact was ours: [the IMEI story], [the outcome], and the recall it avoided."

Then they will ask: "Did anyone push back on you stepping in?" — how you handled the ownership boundary.

cards.f: Tell me about a decision without enough data.
cards.b:
Answer from: S3
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"I had [what] and needed to decide by [when]. I framed it as a two-way door, set a checkpoint at [when] with the signal that would make me reverse, and went. The signal said [what]; we [kept/reversed]."

Then they will ask: "What would have made you reverse?" — the pre-agreed signal.

cards.f: Tell me about a time you pushed back on a decision and then committed to it.
cards.b:
Answer from: S12 (3B)
Say it (about 60 seconds)

Ford hybrid: the position, the data, the decision that went the other way, and committing visibly — including telling your own team the decision was now yours too.

Then they will ask: "How do you keep your team from hearing 'I disagreed' as 'this is wrong'?" — your exact words to them.

cards.f: What are your main responsibilities in your current position?
cards.b:
Answer from: Part 8 opener
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"Three things. I own the architecture and engineering for [area]: [N] engineers through [N] leads. I own the roadmap and budget for the digital-engineering platform, PLM/MBSE tooling and the on-prem AI platform. And I own the technical bar — design reviews, hiring, and the standards the teams build to." Then stop; let them pick which to dig into.

Then they will ask: "Which of those takes most of your time?" — be honest; a manager who says "architecture" at a manager screen should explain why.
cards.s: Confirmed hiring-manager phone-screen questions (Alexa SDM screen, reported)

cards.f: What is your scope, and which responsibilities matter most? Why?
cards.b:
Answer from: Part 8; S4
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"Scope in numbers: [N] people, [N] systems, [N] internal customer teams, budget [N]. What matters most is the platform the other teams depend on — if it is late or wrong, forty engineers elsewhere are blocked — so operational health of that platform is the responsibility I protect first, ahead of new features." One example of a time you chose it over a feature.

Then they will ask: "What do you deliberately not do?" — name what you delegated and why.
cards.s: Confirmed hiring-manager phone-screen questions (Alexa SDM screen, reported)

cards.f: Describe a time you gave your team goals that proved unrealistic. Why did you set them, how did the team react, how did you respond?
cards.b:
Answer from: S5 first delivery after takeover, or S6
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"When I took over the Cameo program I set a delivery date for [when] based on the plan I inherited, before I had done my own diagnosis. By week [N] the team told me — quietly at first — that the requirements were not stable enough to build to. I was wrong to set a date before I understood the work. I said so to the team in the same meeting, re-planned with them, moved the date to [when] with the customer, and we hit that one. The learning: diagnose before you commit, and give ranges until the design is done."

Then they will ask: "How did the customer take the slip?" — the conversation, and what you offered in exchange (a smaller early deliverable).
cards.s: Confirmed hiring-manager phone-screen questions (Alexa SDM screen, reported)

cards.f: How do you manage your strongest performers?
cards.b:
Answer from: S8; Part 6
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"Three things they need from me: a problem bigger than they are, not more of the same work; visibility — I put them in front of leadership and give them the credit by name; and honest feedback, because strong people are the ones nobody corrects. I also watch for the trap of over-loading them: the strongest person becomes the bottleneck, so I pair them with someone to grow — that is how [S8 name] became a lead."

Then they will ask: "Have you lost a strong performer? Why?" — honest, and what you changed afterwards.
cards.s: Confirmed hiring-manager phone-screen questions (Alexa SDM screen, reported)

cards.f: Describe managing an underperformer whose employment eventually ended. What steps did you follow, what did you learn, what would you change?
cards.b:
Answer from: S10 (3B)
Say it (about 60 seconds)

The S10 story, with the steps numbered: "One, I named the gap in writing with examples. Two, a six-week plan with two concrete deliverables and weekly check-ins. Three, a peer to pair with so it was support, not surveillance. Four, when the deliverables did not land, a dignified exit with HR, references, and a message to the team that respected the person. What I learned: I waited [N] months too long before step one. What I'd change: the first miss gets the conversation."

Then they will ask: "How did the rest of the team react?" — relief plus the trust that came from handling it kindly; have a sentence from a team member if you can.
cards.s: Confirmed hiring-manager phone-screen questions (Alexa SDM screen, reported)

cards.f: Describe an initiative outside your normal responsibilities that produced substantial impact.
cards.b:
Answer from: S2 Stellantis provisioning (3B)
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"Vehicle provisioning was not my team's system, but failures in it were landing on our OTA feature. I took it anyway: traced the IMEI mismatch, ran the 50-person workshop, got the fix prioritized across [N] teams. The outcome was [N] vehicles corrected and a recall avoided — roughly [$]. Ownership at Amazon means the customer problem is yours even when the system isn't."

Then they will ask: "Did the owning team push back?" — how you kept it collaborative rather than a takeover.
cards.s: Confirmed hiring-manager phone-screen questions (Alexa SDM screen, reported)

cards.f: Describe improving your team's processes. How did you identify the inefficiency, and how did the team react?
cards.b:
Answer from: S4 ARV; or the risk-register change in S5
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"I noticed from the data, not from complaints: [metric — e.g., pages per week, review turnaround, cycle time] was [N]. The inefficiency was [what — e.g., every design went through me]. I changed it to [mechanism — written design reviews with two named reviewers and a 48-hour SLA]. The team's first reaction was [honest — more writing]; after a month [metric] went from [N] to [N] and the complaint stopped. The learning: change the mechanism, not the people."

Then they will ask: "What did it cost you personally?" — the control you gave up.
cards.s: Confirmed hiring-manager phone-screen questions (Alexa SDM screen, reported)

cards.f: Describe pursuing a goal and realizing, after you were more than halfway through, that it might be the wrong goal.
cards.b:
Answer from: S12 Ford hybrid; or S3 Cindia
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"At Ford we were [N] months into a lift-and-shift when the data showed the real cost was in [what], not in the move. Halfway in, the honest move was to stop and say the goal was wrong — which I did in writing, with the numbers. Leadership chose [what]; I disagreed, committed, and [outcome]. The learning: put a checkpoint in every plan where you ask whether the goal still holds, and make it safe for the team to say no."

Then they will ask: "What would it have taken for you to stop earlier?" — the signal you now watch for.
cards.s: Peer-SDM first interview and management-screen reports

cards.f: Describe taking an employee through a performance improvement plan.
cards.b:
Answer from: S10 (3B)
Say it (about 60 seconds)

Same S10 story, emphasizing the plan: specific, measurable, time-boxed, with support — "two deliverables, six weeks, weekly check-ins, a pairing partner, and a written record we both signed." Then the outcome, honestly.

Then they will ask: "Have you had a PIP succeed?" — if yes, the one example; if no, say so and what you think that means.
cards.s: Peer-SDM first interview and management-screen reports

cards.f: Describe retaining a high performer who was considering leaving.
cards.b:
Answer from: S8; S5 retention
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"[Name/role] told me they had an offer. I asked what they wanted that they weren't getting — it was scope, not money. I gave them ownership of [what], with the decision rights written down, and a path to [next role] with dates. They stayed [N] years and [what they achieved]. The learning: the retention conversation happens in the 1:1s a year before the offer, not after it."

Then they will ask: "What if it had been money?" — your honest limit and how you handle it.
cards.s: Peer-SDM first interview and management-screen reports

cards.f: How have you helped a strong engineer advance their career?
cards.b:
Answer from: S8 — write it
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"[Name] was a strong individual contributor who [what]. I gave them a scope with its own customers — [what], then [visibility — presenting to leadership], then feedback they did not enjoy about [what]. Today they are [role]." Role, what you gave, where they are now.

Then they will ask: "What did they struggle with in the step up?" — the specific thing and how you coached it.
cards.s: Peer-SDM first interview and management-screen reports

cards.f: How do you establish a project's schedule and milestones?
cards.b:
Answer from: Part 6
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"Backwards from the customer date, forwards from the dependencies. Milestones are demonstrable outcomes — "consumers can read dataset X" — not activities. I give ranges with confidence until the design is done, then a date. Risks ranked and reviewed weekly; the top three have mitigations before I promise anything."

Then they will ask: "How often do your dates hold?" — a number, and what you do when one slips.
cards.s: Peer-SDM first interview and management-screen reports

cards.f: Describe a project failure for which you were accountable.
cards.b:
Answer from: S5 wrong first month; or the goal-you-missed story
Say it (about 60 seconds)

Own it in sentence one. "[Project] missed [date/metric] because of a decision I made: [what]. The cost was [N]. I told [whom] before they found out, re-planned, and changed the mechanism so it would not recur: [what]. Since then [evidence it worked]."

Then they will ask: "Who else was responsible?" — resist; it was you.
cards.s: Peer-SDM first interview and management-screen reports

cards.f: How do you conduct individual management, including one-on-ones?
cards.b:
Answer from: Part 10 peer-SDM block
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"Weekly thirty minutes, their agenda first, a shared running doc so nothing is lost, career explicitly once a quarter, and I ask one question every time: what is getting in your way that I can remove. Skip-levels monthly with my leads' teams."

Then they will ask: "What do you do when a 1:1 has nothing on the agenda?" — that is the signal: ask about career or energy.
cards.s: Peer-SDM first interview and management-screen reports

cards.f: How do you organize your own responsibilities?
cards.b:
Answer from: Part 6
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"A weekly operating rhythm: Monday metrics review, mid-week design and hiring, Friday writing. Anything a lead can do at 80% of my quality is theirs. I keep hiring, firing, budget and the architecture bar. And one hour a week with no meetings to think about the next quarter."

Then they will ask: "What falls through the cracks?" — an honest one and the fix.
cards.s: Peer-SDM first interview and management-screen reports

cards.f: Describe accepting a short-term sacrifice to achieve a longer-term benefit.
cards.b:
Answer from: S1 migration + redesign; S4
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"On the Ford migration I had a fixed date and a tempting shortcut: lift the old reconciliation as-is. I chose to spend [N] weeks re-designing it as event-driven and cut [feature] from the first release instead, because the shortcut would have cost us [on-call/cost] every month after. Result: [metric]. The sacrifice was visible — [who] was unhappy — and I owned that."

Then they will ask: "How did you convince the person who lost the feature?" — the number you showed them.

cards.f: Describe a disagreement and how you resolved it.
cards.b:
Answer from: S6; or the senior-architect disagreement
Say it (about 60 seconds)

Private, specific, data-first, listening first; then the decision; then visible commitment. One story, and what changed in you.

Then they will ask: "What if you had been overruled?" — S12 is the answer.

cards.f: Portray the cycle you have for a programming task, from requirements to delivery.
cards.b:
Answer from: Part 11C / 11D
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"Requirements as a one-page problem statement with the customer and the success metric. A short design doc with alternatives, reviewed by two named people. Work split into slices that each ship behind a flag. Code review and automated tests as the gate. Canary, then waves, with alarms deciding the next step. A dashboard before launch, and a retrospective after. The manager's job is that each step is a mechanism, not a hope."

Then they will ask: "Where does it usually go wrong?" — requirements; say so and what you do about it (the one-pager).

cards.f: What do you do if you have to coach a staff member?
cards.b:
Answer from: S10; S8
Say it (about 60 seconds)

"First understand: is it skill, will, or setup? Then one specific goal, a short timeline, a way to practice with support, and feedback within days not weeks. For skill I pair them; for will I find out what changed; for setup I fix the setup — that is on me." One example from S8 or S10.

Then they will ask: "How do you know when coaching isn't working?" — the timeline and the signal.

decks.title: Leadership Q&A — full answers
decks.blurb: How you build teams, handle stakeholders, delivery and conflict — answered with examples.

cards.f: How do you build high-performing teams?
cards.b:
I think of it as three layers. The foundation is clarity: every engineer knows what they own, what "done" means, and how their work connects to the business. The second layer is standards that are automated rather than enforced by me — code review, tests in CI, documentation as part of the definition of done — so quality doesn't depend on who's paying attention that week. The third layer is growth: people stay and perform when they're learning and when someone is invested in their career.

A concrete example: when I took over the architecture function at Rheinmetall, the team had eight architects with overlapping responsibilities and no shared standards. I started with an ownership map — literally a table of every system and who owned it — and a definition of done that included a design doc and a review. Then I set up a mentorship pyramid: I mentor the two most senior architects directly, and they each mentor two or three others. That's how I scale without being the bottleneck. To give people leverage, I built the tooling — CI/CD with SonarQube, Astrée, and Tessy gates; infrastructure as code; and the RAG assistant so engineers stopped losing hours searching Teamcenter and Confluence. Productivity went up by roughly [30%, measured as X].

At Whisker, I'd start with the same first step — the ownership map — because a team that's been leaderless usually has gaps and overlaps nobody has written down.

cards.f: How would you stabilize a team that has had no leader for a while?
cards.b:
The mistake I've seen new leaders make, and made myself once, is arriving with a plan. A team that's been leaderless has been coping; they've built workarounds and they know where the bodies are. If I show up with an org chart on day one, I've told them their knowledge doesn't matter.

So the first thirty days are listening. I meet every person individually — contractors included, because at Whisker they're a third of the team — and I ask four questions: what's working, what's broken, what would you fix first, and what do you want for yourself in the next year. I read the last six months of postmortems and retros. From that I build three things: an ownership map so nothing falls in a gap, a cadence — weekly 1:1s and a written weekly update so people stop guessing what I think — and a short list of quick wins that signal things are changing. The quick wins matter: killing the noisiest alert or closing the oldest postmortem action item tells the team someone is finally finishing things.

The example is the MBSE team at Rheinmetall. Monthly model deliveries to the Army were failing, the CTO asked me to take ownership, and the systems engineers had been operating without technical leadership under enormous pressure. The temptation was to fix the servers, which were undersized. I did that too — but the real problem was that engineers under pressure were taking modeling shortcuts that created cyclical dependencies. That only became visible from the 1:1s and the defect history. The turnaround came from restoring ownership of model packages, negotiating a delivery extension myself so the engineers weren't absorbing the pressure, and then bringing in a UAF framework and consultancy. We eliminated the recurring failures and [kept the whole team].

cards.f: Tell me about managing an underperformer.
cards.b:
My approach is early, specific, and documented — because vagueness is unfair to the person and to the rest of the team who are carrying the gap.

The shape is: the moment I see a pattern rather than a bad week, I have a direct conversation with two or three specific examples and their impact — "the API change shipped without contract tests twice, and both times mobile found the break in production." I ask what's going on, because sometimes the answer is a scope mismatch or something outside work. Then we agree a written plan: what needs to change, what support I'll provide — pairing, a smaller scope, training — and a date, usually six to eight weeks, with weekly check-ins. Two outcomes are fine: they turn it around, or it becomes clear the role is wrong and we part ways respectfully. The outcome that isn't fine is drifting.

Fill with a real case. Structure: who (role, not name) → the gap and how you noticed → the conversation → the plan → what happened → what you'd do sooner. If the outcome was an exit, say how you handled it with the person and what you told the team.

cards.f: How do you handle a senior architect or engineer who disagrees with your direction?
cards.b:
