cards.s: Amazon, Microsoft, startups — the URL shortener with a body

cards.b:
The one idea: A sliding window counter in a shared Redis, evaluated with one atomic Lua script, with rules pushed to every gateway node without a deploy.

Request hits gateway→Load rule for user+endpoint→Atomic INCR on window key in Redis→Allowed → backend→Over limit → 429 + Retry-After

Clarify

You: Where does the limiter sit — in the gateway, or as a service every backend calls?

Interviewer: Gateway-side, shared across all API servers; it must not add more than 1 ms.

You: What rules: per user, per IP, per endpoint, and how many requests?

Interviewer: Per user and per endpoint, like 1,000 requests a minute; rules change without a deploy.

You: Is a little over-admission acceptable, or must it be exact?

Interviewer: A few percent over during bursts is fine; blocking legitimate users is not.

Size it out loud

10M users, 100K requests a second at peak. A counter per user per endpoint for 50 endpoints is 500M keys worst case, but active in a minute is maybe 1M x 50 = 50M keys at 50 bytes is 2.5 GB — one Redis shard set. Each check is 1 round trip, 0.3 ms inside a region.

Walk through the design

  1. Algorithm: sliding window counter — current minute count plus previous minute weighted by overlap; 2 keys per client, far cheaper than a sliding log.
  2. Atomicity: one Lua script does read, weigh, increment, set expiry; no race between two gateway nodes checking the same user.
  3. Rules: stored in a config table, cached in each gateway node, refreshed every 30 seconds via pub/sub; no deploy to change a limit.
  4. Response: 429 with Retry-After and X-RateLimit-Remaining headers so good clients back off instead of retrying hard.
  5. Failure mode: if Redis is unreachable, fail open with a local token bucket per node; losing some protection beats blocking all traffic.

Deep dive

  • Token bucket vs sliding window: token bucket allows a burst up to bucket size then refills; sliding window smooths the edge spike a fixed window lets through at 59s/01s.
  • Multi-region: counters are per region; a user limit of 1,000 becomes roughly 1,000 per region unless I route users to a home region. I say so rather than pretend global exactness.

Push-backs

They: Why not keep counters in memory on each gateway node?

You: With 50 nodes a user gets 50x the limit. Local memory works only as a pre-filter or as the fail-open fallback.

They: Redis becomes the bottleneck at 100K checks a second.

You: One Redis node handles that; I shard by user id across a cluster anyway, since each user's keys live together and the script touches only one user.

They: A client sends 10,000 requests in the first second of the window.

You: The sliding window counts the previous minute's weight, so the burst is still bounded near 1,000; a token bucket with capacity 100 would be tighter if that matters.

Close

Trade-off: sliding window is approximate by design; I accept 1-2% overshoot for one round trip per request. I'd watch p99 limiter latency and 429 rate per endpoint.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
GatewayAPI Gateway or ALB + Envoy on ECSCloud Load Balancing + Envoy on GKE
CountersElastiCache Redis clusterMemorystore Redis cluster
Rules storeDynamoDBFirestore
Rule pushSNS or Redis pub/subPub/Sub
MetricsCloudWatchCloud Monitoring
Fail-open configAppConfigSecret Manager or Firestore config doc
Trap: Reciting four algorithms without picking one; choose sliding window counter, say why, and spend the time on atomicity and failure behavior.
cards.s: Stripe, Google, Uber — any team that runs a public API

cards.b:
The one idea: Pack timestamp + node id + sequence into 64 bits, minted locally on every node; the only coordination is assigning node ids once at startup.

Node starts: lease node id→Read clock, bump sequence→Pack 41+10+12 bits→Clock goes backwards → wait or refuse

Clarify

You: Must ids be sortable by creation time, and how many per second?

Interviewer: Roughly time-ordered, yes; 10,000 ids a second today, plan for 1 million.

You: Can there be any central service in the path of generation?

Interviewer: No; a node must mint ids with no network call per id.

You: What size is the id?

Interviewer: 64 bits so it fits a bigint column and a JavaScript-safe integer is a bonus but not required.

Size it out loud

64 bits: 41 bits of milliseconds since a custom epoch gives 69 years; 10 bits of node id is 1,024 nodes; 12 bits of sequence is 4,096 ids per millisecond per node, so 4 million a second per node. 1M ids a second needs a single node in theory, 10 nodes in practice for availability.

Walk through the design

  1. Layout: 1 unused sign bit, 41 bits ms timestamp, 10 bits node id, 12 bits sequence; ids from the same node are strictly increasing.
  2. Node id: leased from ZooKeeper or a small table with a 60-second heartbeat; a node that cannot renew stops minting rather than risk a duplicate.
  3. Sequence: reset to 0 each millisecond; if 4,096 are used, spin until the next millisecond — 1 ms stall, never a duplicate.
  4. Clock skew: NTP on every node, and if the clock moves back more than 10 ms, refuse ids until it catches up; small skews just wait.
  5. Library, not service: ship it as a client library so there is no network hop; a thin HTTP service exists only for languages without the library.

Deep dive

  • Why not UUIDv4: 128 bits, random, and not sortable, so B-tree inserts scatter across pages; a Snowflake id lands at the right edge of the index.
  • Why not a database auto-increment: one writer is a bottleneck and a single point of failure; multi-master ranges work but need coordination per block.

Push-backs

They: Two nodes get the same node id.

You: The lease is a conditional write; a second node fails to claim it. If the store is partitioned, a node keeps minting only for its remaining lease time, then stops.

They: The timestamp leaks when a record was created.

You: True — ids reveal creation time to the millisecond. If that matters I encrypt the id at the API boundary or use ULID-style random bits.

They: Ids within a millisecond are not ordered across nodes.

You: Correct; ordering is to the millisecond. Cross-node order inside 1 ms is arbitrary, which every consumer I know can live with.

Close

Trade-off: 69 years of epoch and 1,024 nodes are fixed at design time; I pick the epoch as today and document the layout. I'd watch clock-drift alerts and sequence-exhaustion counts.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
GeneratorLibrary in each service on ECS/EKSLibrary in each service on GKE/Cloud Run
Node id leaseDynamoDB conditional write (or ZooKeeper on EC2)Firestore transaction (or ZooKeeper on GCE)
Time syncAmazon Time Sync ServiceGoogle NTP (metadata server)
Fallback HTTP serviceLambdaCloud Functions
MonitoringCloudWatchCloud Monitoring
Trap: Explaining the bit layout and stopping; the points are in node-id assignment and clock-backwards handling.
cards.s: Twitter, Instagram, Discord — anywhere ids are generated in many places

cards.b:
The one idea: Consistent hashing places keys on N replicas; writes and reads use tunable quorums (W + R > N); vector clocks or last-write-wins resolve conflicts; gossip and hinted handoff handle failures.

Client get/put(key)→Coordinator: hash key → N nodes→Write to W of N replicas→Read R replicas, reconcile→Node down → hinted handoff

Clarify

You: What is the consistency requirement — can a read ever return an older value?

Interviewer: Always writable matters more than always consistent; eventual consistency with a tunable option.

You: Size of the data and the values?

Interviewer: Values under 10 KB; 100 TB total; 100K reads and 20K writes a second.

You: Do we need range scans or transactions?

Interviewer: No; get and put by key, plus delete.

Size it out loud

100 TB with 3 replicas is 300 TB; at 2 TB usable per node that is 150 nodes. 120K ops a second over 150 nodes is 800 ops a second each — easy. One key is 3 replicas; a read at quorum touches 2 of them in parallel, so latency is the slower of 2 disks, about 5 ms.

Walk through the design

  1. Partitioning: consistent hash ring with 256 virtual nodes per server so adding one server moves 1/150 of the data evenly.
  2. Replication: each key goes to the next N=3 distinct servers on the ring; the first is the coordinator for that key.
  3. Quorums: default N=3, W=2, R=2, so a read overlaps a write; W=1, R=1 for a cache-like use, W=3 for a ledger.
  4. Conflicts: version each value with a vector clock; on read, return siblings to the client or apply last-write-wins when the caller opts in.
  5. Failure: hinted handoff writes to a stand-in and replays later; anti-entropy with Merkle trees repairs replicas in the background; gossip spreads membership.

Deep dive

  • Storage engine: an LSM tree per node — append-only write-ahead log, memtable, SSTables with bloom filters; writes are sequential, reads cost 1-3 disk seeks.
  • Sloppy quorum: if a replica is down, the write goes to the next healthy node with a hint; the system stays writable at the cost of a brief window where R=2 can miss it.

Push-backs

They: A client reads its own write and gets the old value.

You: With W=2, R=2 that cannot happen through the same coordinator; across coordinators it can during handoff. For read-your-writes I route a session to one coordinator.

They: Why vector clocks instead of a timestamp?

You: A timestamp silently drops a concurrent write; a vector clock detects it and lets the application merge, like a shopping cart union. If merge is meaningless I use timestamps.

They: A hot key gets 50K reads a second.

You: 3 replicas serve it, so 17K each — near a node's limit. I add a client-side cache with a 1-second TTL or spread reads to all N replicas rather than a quorum.

Close

Trade-off: availability over consistency, by choice. I'd watch quorum-failure rate and hint-queue length; if either climbs, nodes are falling behind and I add capacity.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
Managed equivalentDynamoDBBigtable (or Firestore)
Self-managed nodesEC2 i-family with local NVMeGCE with local SSD
Membership/gossipBuilt in (or ZooKeeper on EC2)Built in (or ZooKeeper on GCE)
BackupsS3 snapshotsCloud Storage snapshots
MonitoringCloudWatch + Prometheus on EKSCloud Monitoring + Prometheus on GKE
Client routingSmart client librarySmart client library
Trap: Drawing a single-leader database with replicas; the whole point is leaderless writes, quorums and conflict handling.
cards.s: Amazon, Apple, LinkedIn — the Dynamo paper in 45 minutes

cards.b:
The one idea: Consistent hashing across a cluster of in-memory nodes, cache-aside from the application, TTLs plus explicit invalidation, and replicas for the hot shards.

App: get(key)→Client lib: hash → node→Hit → return→Miss → DB → set(key, ttl)→Node down → ring reroutes

Clarify

You: What are we caching — database rows, rendered pages, sessions — and how big?

Interviewer: Database rows and small objects, average 1 KB, max 1 MB.

You: What is the target hit rate and what happens on a miss?

Interviewer: 95% or better; a miss goes to the database, which can take 10% of the traffic.

You: Is it acceptable to serve stale data for a few seconds?

Interviewer: Yes, up to 60 seconds for most keys; sessions must not be lost on a node restart.

Size it out loud

1M requests a second at 1 KB is 1 GB a second across the cluster. A node handles 100K ops a second, so 10 nodes for throughput, more for memory: a 200 GB working set with 20% headroom is 240 GB, which is 4 nodes of 64 GB — throughput wins, 10 nodes. At 95% hit rate the database sees 50K a second.

Walk through the design

  1. Placement: consistent hashing with 160 virtual nodes per server in the client library; losing 1 of 10 nodes invalidates 10% of keys, not all.
  2. Pattern: cache-aside — read cache, on miss read DB, then set with a 60-second TTL; writes update the DB then delete the key, never update the cache directly.
  3. Eviction: LRU within a node with a memory limit; a key over 1 MB is refused so one object cannot evict a thousand.
  4. Hot keys: detect keys over 10K reads a second and replicate them to 3 nodes with a suffix, or hold them in a per-app local cache for 1 second.
  5. Stampede: on a miss, one request takes a short lock and recomputes; the rest wait 50 ms or serve the stale value with a probabilistic early refresh.

Deep dive

  • Delete vs update on write: two writers updating the cache can race and leave the older value; delete-then-let-the-next-read-fill cannot, at the cost of one extra miss.
  • Memcached vs Redis: Memcached is multi-threaded and simpler for plain strings; Redis gives data structures, persistence and replication — sessions want Redis.

Push-backs

They: A cache node restarts and the database falls over.

You: Warm it: the ring reroutes 10% of keys to neighbors, and I ramp traffic to the new node over 5 minutes. Replicas for the shard remove the gap entirely for sessions.

They: How do you keep the cache and database consistent?

You: I do not, strictly. Delete on write plus a 60-second TTL bounds staleness; for the few keys that must be exact, I read through the DB and skip the cache.

They: Why consistent hashing instead of a lookup table?

You: A table needs a coordinator and a push on every change; the ring is computed locally and every client agrees with no coordination.

Close

Trade-off: cache-aside means every service duplicates the logic, so I wrap it in a shared client library. I'd watch hit rate, evictions per second and p99 node latency.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
Cache clusterElastiCache Redis (cluster mode) or MemcachedMemorystore Redis Cluster or Memcached
ClientsApplication on ECS/EKS with a smart client libraryApplication on GKE/Cloud Run with a smart client library
Backing storeAurora or DynamoDBCloud SQL or Spanner
Hot-key metricsCloudWatch + custom metricsCloud Monitoring + custom metrics
Config/ring membershipElastiCache cluster endpointMemorystore discovery endpoint
Session persistenceRedis AOF + replicaMemorystore Redis persistence + replica
Trap: Saying 'put Redis in front' and moving on; invalidation, stampedes and hot keys are where the marks are.
cards.s: Meta, Netflix, Amazon — the layer that keeps every other design alive

cards.b:
The one idea: A two-tier cache hierarchy — edge locations in front of regional shields in front of the origin — with anycast DNS routing, and a purge fan-out over pub/sub.

Client DNS → nearest edge→Edge cache hit → serve→Miss → regional shield→Shield miss → origin fetch→Purge → pub/sub → all edges

Clarify

You: What content — static files, video, or dynamic API responses?

Interviewer: Static assets and video segments; dynamic responses pass through but are not cached.

You: How fresh must content be after the origin changes?

Interviewer: Assets are versioned by filename, so forever is fine; a purge must take effect worldwide within 10 seconds.

You: How many edge locations and how much traffic?

Interviewer: Start with 50 locations; 10 Tbps peak, 1 million requests a second.

Size it out loud

1M requests a second over 50 locations is 20K a second per location — a handful of servers each. 10 Tbps over 50 is 200 Gbps per location, which is 10 servers at 25 Gbps NICs. A 90% edge hit rate means the origin sees 100K requests a second, still big, so I add a regional shield tier to push the origin to 1%.

Walk through the design

  1. Routing: anycast IP plus GeoDNS so a request lands at the nearest healthy location; health checks withdraw a location in 30 seconds.
  2. Edge: each server runs an HTTP cache on NVMe keyed by URL plus Vary headers; consistent hashing inside the location so one object lives on one server.
  3. Shield: 5 regional shields collapse 50 edges' misses into one origin fetch per object; request coalescing makes 1,000 simultaneous misses one upstream call.
  4. Freshness: honor Cache-Control max-age; versioned filenames get a 1-year TTL; purge publishes a key or prefix to every location, which marks it stale.
  5. Video: segments of 4 seconds, 2-10 MB each; prefetch the next 3 segments on a hit, since the player will ask for them.

Deep dive

  • Purge at scale: a tag-based index per edge, so purging 'product-123' invalidates 500 URLs without listing them; soft-purge serves stale while revalidating.
  • TLS at the edge: terminate at the edge with the customer's certificate, keep connections to the shield warm with HTTP/2, so a cold client pays 1 round trip not 3.

Push-backs

They: A new 2 GB video is published and 1 million people press play at once.

You: The shield coalesces them into one origin fetch per segment; edges fetch from the shield. The origin sees 500 requests, not 1 million.

They: How is a purge consistent across 50 locations in 10 seconds?

You: Pub/sub fan-out with at-least-once delivery, each edge acks; a location that misses the message catches up on reconnect from a purge log with sequence numbers.

They: Dynamic content is 30% of traffic — can you help?

You: Not with caching, but with the connection: TLS terminates near the user and the edge keeps a warm pool to origin, cutting 100-200 ms off each request.

Close

Trade-off: a shield adds one hop on a miss, about 20 ms, to save the origin. I'd watch edge hit rate, origin requests per second and purge propagation time.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
EdgeCloudFrontCloud CDN
Origin shieldCloudFront Origin ShieldCloud CDN with Media CDN tiering
OriginS3 + ALB for dynamicCloud Storage + Cloud Load Balancing for dynamic
DNS/routingRoute 53 (latency + health checks)Cloud DNS + global anycast load balancer
Purge fan-outCloudFront invalidations / SNSCloud CDN cache invalidation / Pub/Sub
SecurityAWS WAF + ShieldCloud Armor
LogsKinesis Firehose → S3 → AthenaCloud Logging → BigQuery
Trap: Describing a single cache tier; the shield tier, request coalescing and purge propagation are what separates a CDN from a reverse proxy.
cards.s: Akamai, Cloudflare, Netflix — the edge in 45 minutes

cards.b:
The one idea: A horizontally scaled layer-7 proxy tier behind anycast or DNS, with active health checks, weighted least-connections routing and connection draining for deploys.

Client → anycast VIP→L4 tier: ECMP to proxy node→L7: TLS, route by path, pick backend→Backend response → client→Health check fails → eject backend

Clarify

You: Layer 4 or layer 7 — do we route on TCP or on HTTP paths and headers?

Interviewer: Layer 7 for HTTP, with a layer 4 mode for raw TCP; most traffic is HTTPS.

You: How many backends and how much traffic?

Interviewer: Up to 1,000 backends per pool; 500K requests a second, 200K concurrent connections.

You: Must sessions stick to one backend?

Interviewer: Preferably not, but a cookie-based option is required for a few legacy apps.

Size it out loud

500K requests a second at 50K per balancer node is 10 nodes, 15 with headroom. 200K concurrent connections at 10 KB of state each is 2 GB of memory — fine. Health checks every 5 seconds to 1,000 backends from 15 nodes is 3,000 checks a second, trivial.

Walk through the design

  1. Two tiers: a stateless L4 layer spreads packets to L7 nodes with ECMP and consistent hashing on the 5-tuple, so a node loss moves 1/15 of connections.
  2. Algorithm: weighted least-connections by default; round-robin for uniform backends; consistent hashing on a header when the backend has a local cache.
  3. Health: active checks every 5 seconds, eject after 3 failures, readmit after 2 passes; passive checks eject a backend returning 5 consecutive 5xx.
  4. Deploys: a backend set to draining gets no new connections and finishes in-flight ones within 30 seconds; the proxy tier itself drains the same way.
  5. Protection: per-client connection limits, request timeouts of 30 seconds, and a circuit breaker per backend that opens at 50% errors over 10 seconds.

Deep dive

  • Sticky sessions: a cookie carrying the backend id, falling back to consistent hashing when the backend is gone; I warn that stickiness fights autoscaling and ask the app to move state to Redis.
  • Config push: routes and pools live in a control plane; data-plane nodes pull a versioned snapshot every 10 seconds and apply it atomically, so a bad config rolls back by version.

Push-backs

They: The balancer is now the single point of failure.

You: 15 nodes behind anycast; the L4 tier reroutes within one BGP or health-check interval. The control plane can be down for hours and the data plane keeps serving the last config.

They: One backend is slow but not failing health checks.

You: Least-connections already sends it less, since connections pile up there; I add outlier detection — eject a backend whose p99 is 3x its peers.

They: Why terminate TLS at the proxy?

You: One place for certificates and one place to see HTTP for routing and metrics; I re-encrypt to backends with an internal CA so the hop is still private.

Close

Trade-off: L7 costs about 10x the CPU of L4 for the routing and observability it gives. I'd watch backend p99 by pool, ejections per minute and proxy CPU.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
L4 tierNetwork Load BalancerCloud Load Balancing (TCP/UDP, passthrough)
L7 tierApplication Load Balancer (or Envoy on EC2)Cloud Load Balancing (global external HTTPS, Envoy-based)
BackendsEC2 Auto Scaling groups / ECSManaged instance groups / GKE
Health checksALB target group checksBackend service health checks
CertificatesACMGoogle-managed certificates
Control planeRoute 53 + AppConfigCloud DNS + Traffic Director
ProtectionAWS WAF + ShieldCloud Armor
Trap: Listing routing algorithms and stopping; health checking, draining and what happens when the balancer itself dies are the real questions.
cards.s: Google, Cloudflare, HashiCorp — infra and SRE loops

cards.f: Design: Consistent hashing service / sharding layer
cards.b:
The one idea: A routing table of key ranges to shards held by a coordinator and cached in every client, consistent hashing to pick the default home, and an online split-and-move protocol.

Client: tenant id→Router: range table → shard→Shard DB read/write→Split: copy range, dual-write, cut over→Stale route → shard says 'moved' → refresh

Clarify

You: Is this for a stateless cache ring or for a database where moving data is expensive?

Interviewer: A database: 100 TB across 100 shards, and resharding must not take the service down.

You: What is the shard key and are there hot keys?

Interviewer: Tenant id; the top 1% of tenants hold 30% of the data.

You: Do queries ever span tenants?

Interviewer: Rarely; cross-tenant reports go through an offline path.

Size it out loud

100 TB over 100 shards is 1 TB each. A 1% tenant at 30% means the top 10 tenants average 3 TB — bigger than a shard, so the largest tenants need their own shards or further splitting. Moving 1 TB at 200 MB a second takes 90 minutes, so a migration must be online.

Walk through the design

  1. Mapping: hash(tenant) to 4,096 virtual buckets; a small table maps buckets to physical shards. Moving a bucket updates one row, not every client's ring.
  2. Routing: clients cache the table and the version; a shard that receives a key it no longer owns replies 'moved, version N' and the client refreshes.
  3. Hot tenants: a tenant larger than 500 GB gets its own bucket set, and the table can map one tenant to a dedicated shard.
  4. Resharding: snapshot the bucket, stream changes from the source's log, dual-write for 1 minute, then flip the table; writes pause for under 1 second at the flip.
  5. Coordinator: a 3-node consensus group owns the table; it is read on startup and on 'moved' errors, so it is off the request path.

Deep dive

  • Why virtual buckets instead of a raw ring: a raw ring moves data to neighbors only; buckets let me move any slice to any shard and keep the table at 4,096 rows.
  • Secondary indexes across shards: a global index is a separate sharded table keyed by the indexed value; writes become 2 writes, so I use it only for the 3 lookups that need it.

Push-backs

They: A client with a stale table writes to the old shard during a move.

You: The old shard checks bucket ownership per request; after the flip it rejects with 'moved' and the client retries on the new one. Dual-write covers the second before the flip.

They: The coordinator is down — does traffic stop?

You: No; every client and shard has a cached table. Only moves and new shards wait. The coordinator is a 3-node Raft group so this is a rare state anyway.

They: One tenant grows to 5 TB.

You: Its own shard, then split by a second key inside the tenant, like tenant+month. I say up front that tenant-only sharding has a ceiling.

Close

Trade-off: a routing table is a component to run, versus a pure hash ring that needs none; for a database the control it gives is worth it. I'd watch bucket size skew and move duration.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
ShardsAurora clusters or DynamoDB tables per shardCloud SQL instances or Spanner (which shards for you)
Routing tableDynamoDB (strongly consistent reads)Firestore
CoordinatorZooKeeper/etcd on EC2 (or DynamoDB leases)etcd on GKE (or Firestore leases)
Change stream for movesAurora binlog → DMS or KinesisDatastream → Pub/Sub
RouterLibrary in services on EKSLibrary in services on GKE
MonitoringCloudWatchCloud Monitoring
Trap: Drawing the ring and declaring victory; the interviewer wants to hear how 1 TB moves while the service stays up.
cards.s: Amazon, Discord, Pinterest — how data got split and what happens when it moves

cards.b:
The one idea: Partitioned append-only logs on disk, each partition with a leader and 2 followers, consumers tracking their own offsets, and consumer groups for parallelism.

Producer: hash(key) → partition→Leader appends to log segment→Followers replicate; ack at ISR→Consumer group pulls by offset→Broker dies → new leader from ISR

Clarify

You: Is ordering required, and at what granularity?

Interviewer: Ordered within a key, like a user id; global order is not needed.

You: Delivery guarantee — at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once?

Interviewer: At-least-once with consumer-side idempotency; messages must survive a broker crash.

You: Throughput and retention?

Interviewer: 1 million messages a second at 1 KB; keep 7 days; consumers may replay.

Size it out loud

1M messages a second at 1 KB is 1 GB a second in, 3 GB a second with 3 replicas. 7 days is 600 TB raw, 1.8 PB replicated. A broker does 100 MB a second of sequential writes comfortably, so 30 brokers for ingest, 60 with headroom and the replica traffic. 100 partitions per topic keep each under 10 MB a second.

Walk through the design

  1. Storage: each partition is a directory of 1 GB segment files; writes append, reads are sequential, and the OS page cache serves recent data with zero copies.
  2. Replication: 3 replicas, leader takes writes; acks=all waits for the in-sync set, giving durability across 2 broker losses at about 5 ms extra.
  3. Consumers: pull, not push; each group owns offsets per partition in a compacted internal topic; commit after processing for at-least-once.
  4. Ordering: one key always hashes to one partition, and one partition is read by one consumer in a group, so per-key order holds end to end.
  5. Retention: delete segments older than 7 days or beyond a size cap; compaction keeps only the latest value per key for change-log topics.

Deep dive

  • Controller and metadata: a Raft quorum of controllers holds partition assignments and leader epochs; a leader with a stale epoch is fenced so split brain cannot ack writes.
  • Exactly-once: idempotent producers dedupe by sequence number per partition, and transactions commit offsets with outputs atomically; I offer it only inside the system, not to external sinks.

Push-backs

They: A consumer is slow and the lag reaches 100 million messages.

You: Lag is just an offset gap; the data is on disk for 7 days. I add consumers up to the partition count, and if that is the cap I repartition the topic to 200.

They: Why pull instead of push?

You: Consumers set their own pace and batch sizes; push would need per-consumer flow control in the broker, and replay from an old offset is trivial with pull.

They: The leader acked a message and then died before followers copied it.

You: With acks=all it never acked; with acks=1 the message is lost and I said so when I chose it. The default is acks=all for anything that matters.

Close

Trade-off: partitions fix the parallelism ceiling and changing them breaks key-to-partition mapping, so I over-provision to 100 up front. I'd watch consumer lag, under-replicated partitions and disk fill.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
BrokersAmazon MSK (or Kafka on EC2 with EBS gp3)Pub/Sub (or Kafka on GKE with persistent disk)
Controller/metadataMSK KRaft (or ZooKeeper on EC2)Managed by Pub/Sub (or KRaft on GKE)
Producers/consumersServices on EKSServices on GKE
Long-term archiveS3 via MSK tiered storageCloud Storage via Pub/Sub subscription
Stream processingKinesis Data Analytics / Flink on EKSDataflow
MonitoringCloudWatch + PrometheusCloud Monitoring + Prometheus
Schema registryGlue Schema RegistryPub/Sub schemas
Trap: Calling it a queue; a queue deletes on consume and has no replay. The log, offsets and partition-level ordering are the design.
cards.s: LinkedIn, Confluent, Uber — the log that every pipeline sits on

cards.b:
The one idea: Fan-out on write to a per-user feed cache for normal accounts, fan-out on read for celebrity accounts, and merge plus rank at request time.

User posts→Post store + fan-out queue→Workers push post id to 300 follower feeds→GET /feed: cache list + celebrity merge → rank→Celebrity post → skip fan-out

Clarify

You: How many users, and how many posts does each see per day?

Interviewer: 500 million daily users; a user opens the feed 10 times a day and sees 20 posts each time.

You: Is the feed chronological or ranked?

Interviewer: Ranked, but the ranking model is someone else's problem; assume a scoring function I can call.

You: How many people does a typical user follow, and how skewed is it?

Interviewer: Median 300; a few accounts have 50 million followers.

Size it out loud

500M users x 10 opens is 5 billion feed reads a day, 58K a second, 300K at peak. Posts: 1 in 10 users posts a day, so 50M posts a day, 600 a second. Fan-out on write: 50M posts x 300 followers is 15 billion feed inserts a day, 170K a second — fine for a cache cluster at 100 bytes per entry, 1.5 TB a day before trimming.

Walk through the design

  1. Post write: store the post, publish an event; fan-out workers read the follower list and push the post id into each follower's feed list in Redis, capped at 500 ids.
  2. Feed read: fetch the user's cached id list, fetch posts from followed celebrities for the last 24 hours, merge, score with the ranking function, hydrate the top 20.
  3. Hybrid threshold: accounts over 100K followers are not fanned out; their posts are pulled at read time, which keeps one post from causing 50M writes.
  4. Hydration: post ids become post objects through a post cache with a 95% hit rate; authors and media URLs come from the same batch call.
  5. Inactive users: skip fan-out to users who have not opened the feed in 30 days, and rebuild their feed from scratch on their next visit.

Deep dive

  • Data model: Post{id, author, created, text, media}; Feed{user_id → sorted set of post_id by score}; Follow{follower, followee} with an index both ways.
  • Ranking at read: the scorer takes 500 candidates and features per user; 300K reads a second x 500 candidates is a lot, so I pre-score on fan-out and re-rank only the top 100.

Push-backs

They: A celebrity with 50 million followers posts — walk me through it.

You: No fan-out. The post lands in the post store and the author's own timeline; every follower's next feed read pulls the celebrity's recent posts and merges. 300K reads a second each pull 5 celebrity timelines from cache.

They: A user unfollows someone — do old posts vanish from the cache?

You: I filter at read time against the follow list, which is cheaper than scrubbing 500 entries on every unfollow; the next rebuild cleans it fully.

They: Fan-out workers fall 10 minutes behind.

You: Posts appear late for normal accounts; I shard the queue by author and autoscale workers on lag. The feed read still works, so the failure is degraded not down.

Close

Trade-off: fan-out on write spends storage to make reads fast; the hybrid handles the skew. I'd watch fan-out lag, feed cache hit rate and p99 feed latency.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
APIALB + ECSCloud Load Balancing + Cloud Run
Post storeDynamoDBBigtable
Fan-out queueKinesis or SQSPub/Sub
Fan-out workersECS / LambdaGKE / Cloud Functions
Feed cacheElastiCache Redis (sorted sets)Memorystore Redis (sorted sets)
Follow graphDynamoDB with GSIBigtable or Spanner
MediaS3 + CloudFrontCloud Storage + Cloud CDN
Trap: Choosing push or pull as if one is right; the answer is both, with a follower-count threshold you can name.
cards.s: Meta, LinkedIn, Pinterest — the signature social question

cards.b:
The one idea: A timeline cache per user filled by fan-out workers, a celebrity pull path merged at read, and a user timeline served straight from the tweet store by author.

Tweet POST→Tweet store + id (Snowflake)→Fan-out service → 200 follower timelines→Home GET: Redis list + celebrity merge→150M-follower account → pull path

Clarify

You: Home timeline, user timeline, or both?

Interviewer: Both: home is what I follow, user is one account's posts. Search is out of scope.

You: What latency should a home timeline load in?

Interviewer: Under 200 ms at p99, anywhere in the world.

You: Volume?

Interviewer: 300 million daily users; 500 million tweets a day; the most-followed account has 150 million followers.

Size it out loud

500M tweets a day is 6K a second, 20K at peak. Home timeline reads: 300M users x 5 loads is 1.5 billion a day, 17K a second, 100K at peak. Fan-out: average 200 followers x 500M tweets is 100 billion timeline inserts a day, 1.2M a second — a serious Redis fleet; at 20 bytes per entry and 800 entries per user, 300M users is 4.8 TB of timeline cache.

Walk through the design

  1. Ids: Snowflake ids, so sorting a timeline by id is sorting by time, and merging celebrity tweets is a merge of sorted lists.
  2. Fan-out: the service reads the follower list in pages of 10K and pushes tweet ids into each follower's Redis list; 1.2M inserts a second across a 100-node cluster.
  3. Home read: LRANGE the first 800 ids, merge the last 200 ids from each followed celebrity, dedupe, hydrate from the tweet cache, return 50.
  4. User timeline: query the tweet store by author id with a composite key (author, id desc); no cache needed beyond the tweet cache.
  5. Deletes: delete the tweet row and the tweet cache entry; stale ids in timelines hydrate to nothing and are dropped at read.

Deep dive

  • Timeline storage choice: a Redis list capped at 800 per user, pinned in memory with 3 replicas for the 30% of users active each week; cold users are rebuilt from the follow list on demand.
  • Geo: tweets replicate globally, but a user's timeline cache lives in their home region only; a traveler pays one cross-region read, about 100 ms, then is served locally.

Push-backs

They: 1.2 million Redis writes a second — what does that cost and can you cut it?

You: About 100 Redis nodes. I cut it by not fanning out to the 70% of users inactive for 7 days, which drops it to 400K a second, and by the celebrity threshold at 50K followers.

They: Two tweets have the same Snowflake id from different nodes — possible?

You: No; the node id is in the id. Two tweets in the same millisecond from different nodes differ in the node bits and are ordered arbitrarily within that millisecond, which is fine.

They: The fan-out queue has a 10-minute backlog after a World Cup goal.

You: Burst of 100K tweets a second. Queue partitions by author, workers autoscale, and the timeline shows a 'new tweets' banner from the pull path for celebrities, so the goal reactions still appear.

Close

Trade-off: memory for 300M timelines is the price of 200 ms reads. I'd watch fan-out lag, timeline cache miss rate and the celebrity merge cost per read.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
APIALB + EKSCloud Load Balancing + GKE
Tweet storeDynamoDB (author, id) composite keyBigtable (author#id row key)
Id generationSnowflake library on EKSSnowflake library on GKE
Fan-out queueKinesisPub/Sub
Timeline cacheElastiCache Redis clusterMemorystore Redis cluster
Tweet cacheElastiCache MemcachedMemorystore Memcached
Follow graphDynamoDB + GSIBigtable
Trap: Forgetting the user timeline exists, and not putting a number on fan-out writes — the number is what justifies the hybrid.
cards.s: Twitter/X, Meta, Snap — the news feed with a harder tail

cards.b:
The one idea: Upload straight to object storage with a pre-signed URL, async resize pipeline, feed via hybrid fan-out, and stories as a TTL'd list per user with a seen-set.

App: pre-signed PUT → object store→Upload event → resize workers → 4 sizes→Post row + fan-out to followers→Feed/stories read: cache → CDN image URLs→Story TTL 24h → auto-delete

Clarify

You: Photos, videos, or both, and what sizes?

Interviewer: Photos up to 20 MB from the camera, short videos up to 100 MB; serve several resized versions.

You: How do stories differ from posts?

Interviewer: Stories expire 24 hours after posting and show a ring of who has unseen stories.

You: Volume?

Interviewer: 500 million daily users; 100 million photos and 200 million stories a day.

Size it out loud

300M uploads a day is 3,500 a second, 10K at peak. At 2 MB average after client compression that is 600 TB a day in, and 4 resized versions add 1 MB per upload, 300 TB more. Reads: 500M users viewing 100 images a day is 50 billion image loads, 580K a second — this is a CDN problem first.

Walk through the design

  1. Upload: the API hands out a pre-signed URL; the app uploads the original to the bucket; my servers never carry the bytes.
  2. Processing: a bucket event queues a job; workers produce 150, 480, 1080 and 2048 px versions and a blurhash placeholder, then mark the post ready.
  3. Feed: same hybrid fan-out as a news feed, but the cached entry includes image URLs and dimensions so the client can lay out before images arrive.
  4. Stories: per user a Redis list of story ids with a 24-hour TTL per item; the ring is 'any story id in the followed set newer than the viewer's last-seen marker'.
  5. Seen state: a per-viewer per-author marker of the latest story id seen, 16 bytes a pair; 500M viewers x 300 followed is 2.4 TB, so I keep it in a wide-column store, not Redis.

Deep dive

  • Media data model: Media{id, owner, original_key, variants{size → key}, width, height, blurhash, status}; Post{id, owner, media_ids, caption, created}; posts reference media, never embed it.
  • Story expiry: the Redis TTL hides it; a daily lifecycle rule deletes the objects after 25 hours; highlights copy the media id to a permanent list before expiry.

Push-backs

They: A post shows in the feed before the resize finishes.

You: Fan-out happens on 'ready', not on upload; the post row has a status and the feed filters anything not ready, so the worst case is a 5-second delay.

They: Stories ring must load in 100 ms for 300 followed accounts.

You: One Redis MGET for 300 'latest story id' keys plus one batch read of the viewer's seen markers; both are single round trips, about 5 ms each.

They: How do you keep 600 TB a day of originals affordable?

You: Originals go to infrequent-access storage after 30 days and the 2048 px variant becomes the master; I keep a reversible record so I can restore if policy changes.

Close

Trade-off: pre-signed uploads mean the client can upload junk; I validate in the worker and reject before fan-out. I'd watch resize latency, CDN hit rate and story ring load time.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
APIALB + EKSCloud Load Balancing + GKE
Media storageS3 (+ Intelligent-Tiering)Cloud Storage (+ Autoclass)
Resize pipelineS3 events → SQS → Lambda/ECSCloud Storage events → Pub/Sub → Cloud Run
EdgeCloudFrontCloud CDN
Post/feed dataDynamoDB + ElastiCache RedisBigtable + Memorystore Redis
Stories listsElastiCache Redis (TTL)Memorystore Redis (TTL)
Seen markersDynamoDBBigtable
Trap: Spending the hour on the feed and forgetting the media pipeline; the upload path and resized variants are half the question.

The one idea: Long-lived WebSocket connections on a gateway fleet, a session registry mapping user to gateway, and a per-recipient message inbox that holds messages until acked.

Sender's WebSocket → gateway A→Chat service: write to recipient inbox→Lookup recipient's gateway B → push→Recipient acks → delete from inbox, receipt to sender→Recipient offline → inbox + push notification

Clarify

You: Must messages be delivered if the recipient is offline, and for how long?

Interviewer: Yes; store for 30 days until delivered, then drop. Delivered and read receipts are required.

You: End-to-end encryption?

Interviewer: Assume yes; the server stores ciphertext and cannot read it.

You: Scale?

Interviewer: 1 billion users, 500 million online at peak, 100 billion messages a day.

Size it out loud

100 billion messages a day is 1.2M a second, 3M at peak. 500M concurrent connections at 50K per gateway server is 10,000 gateway servers. A message is 200 bytes; 30 days of undelivered at 5% is 150 billion x 200 bytes, 30 TB — small next to the connection fleet.

Walk through the design

  1. Connections: gateways hold WebSockets and nothing else; on connect they write user → gateway id into a registry with a 60-second heartbeat.
  2. Send: the chat service assigns a per-conversation sequence number, writes to the recipient's inbox, then pushes to the recipient's gateway if the registry has one.
  3. Delivery: the client acks each message id; the server deletes it from the inbox and forwards a 'delivered' receipt; 'read' is a client event sent the same way.
  4. Offline: no registry entry means a push notification with no content; on reconnect the client pulls its inbox from its last sequence number.
  5. Ordering: per-conversation sequence numbers from a single partition owner; the client sorts by sequence, and gaps trigger a pull.

Deep dive

  • Inbox store: wide-column keyed (recipient, seq), TTL 30 days, writes 1.2M a second spread over 1B partition keys; the delete-on-ack keeps it small.
  • Gateway failure: 50K users reconnect to other gateways; the registry entries expire in 60 seconds and are overwritten on reconnect, and the inbox makes the window lossless.

Push-backs

They: Both users are on the same gateway — do you still go through the chat service?

You: Yes; the inbox write is the durability step. Skipping it saves 2 ms and loses the message when the gateway dies.

They: How do you get exactly-once delivery to the recipient's screen?

You: At-least-once from the server plus the client deduping on message id. A reconnect may re-deliver 5 messages; the client has seen the ids.

They: 500 million WebSockets — what is the registry doing?

You: 500M small keys, 50 bytes each, 25 GB in a sharded Redis; writes are only on connect, so about 50K a second from churn, reads once per message.

Close

Trade-off: the inbox write adds a hop but makes every other failure recoverable. I'd watch undelivered-inbox size, gateway connection counts and p99 send-to-deliver latency.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
GatewaysEC2/EKS with Network Load Balancer (WebSocket)GKE with Cloud Load Balancing (WebSocket)
Session registryElastiCache Redis clusterMemorystore Redis cluster
Chat serviceEKSGKE
Inbox storeDynamoDB (TTL) or Cassandra on EC2Bigtable (TTL) or Cassandra on GCE
Push notificationsSNS → APNs/FCMFirebase Cloud Messaging
MediaS3 + CloudFrontCloud Storage + Cloud CDN
MonitoringCloudWatchCloud Monitoring
Trap: Treating it as HTTP polling or forgetting the offline case; connections, the registry and the inbox are the whole design.
cards.s: Meta, Discord, Slack — the persistent-connection question

cards.b:
The one idea: A per-group message log that members read, push to online members below a size threshold, and presence as heartbeats with expiry fanned out to contacts on change only.

Sender → gateway → group service→Append to group log (group_id, seq)→Fan-out: push to online members' gateways→Presence: heartbeat → Redis TTL key→Group > 1,000 → members pull on open

Clarify

You: How big can a group be?

Interviewer: Up to 10,000 members, median 20; Discord-style servers with 100K are out of scope.

You: What does presence mean — online/offline, or typing and last-seen too?

Interviewer: Online/offline and last-seen, visible to your contacts; typing indicators are nice to have.

You: Scale?

Interviewer: 200 million daily users, 50 million online at peak, 20 billion messages a day.

Size it out loud

20 billion messages a day is 230K a second, 700K at peak. Median group of 20 means 14M deliveries a second at peak; a 10,000-member group turns one send into 10,000 pushes, so large groups need a pull model. Presence: 50M online users heartbeating every 30 seconds is 1.7M writes a second — the biggest write load in the system.

Walk through the design

  1. Storage: one log per group keyed (group_id, seq); every member reads from their own cursor, so there is one copy per message not one per member.
  2. Fan-out: for groups under 1,000, push the message to each online member's gateway; larger groups get a lightweight 'new message' ping and pull the log.
  3. Cursors: per (user, group) last-read seq; unread count is log head minus cursor, computed at read, not maintained per message.
  4. Presence: heartbeat every 30 seconds sets a key with a 45-second TTL; a key expiring or appearing publishes one change event to that user's contacts.
  5. Typing: fire-and-forget over the WebSocket to online members only, throttled to 1 event per 3 seconds; it is never stored.

Deep dive

  • Presence fan-out math: changes, not heartbeats, are fanned out; 50M users changing state 10 times a day with 200 contacts is 100 billion events a day, so I batch per subscriber into 1-second windows.
  • Membership changes: a user removed from a group loses read access from their removal seq; messages before that remain readable, and the group log is unchanged.

Push-backs

They: A 10,000-member group gets 100 messages a second.

You: No push. Online members have the group open and poll the log every 2 seconds, or get one coalesced ping; that is 5,000 reads a second against one partition, so I replicate the hot log.

They: Presence shows someone online 45 seconds after they lost connectivity.

You: Correct, and it is the trade-off: shorter TTLs multiply heartbeat writes. The gateway also sends an explicit offline on clean disconnect, which covers 90% of cases.

They: How are messages ordered across members in different regions?

You: The group's log lives in one region with a single sequencer; cross-region senders pay 100 ms to append. Order is total per group, which is what users expect.

Close

Trade-off: one log per group makes storage cheap but makes a hot group a hot partition. I'd watch per-group write rate, presence heartbeat write load and fan-out lag.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
GatewaysEKS behind Network Load BalancerGKE behind Cloud Load Balancing
Group serviceEKSGKE
Group logsDynamoDB (group_id, seq) or Cassandra on EC2Bigtable (group_id#seq) or Cassandra on GCE
PresenceElastiCache Redis (TTL keys + pub/sub)Memorystore Redis (TTL keys + pub/sub)
Fan-out queueKinesisPub/Sub
CursorsDynamoDBFirestore or Bigtable
Push notificationsSNS → APNs/FCMFirebase Cloud Messaging
Trap: Copying every message into every member's inbox; at 10,000 members that is the design that falls over, and presence math is the part most candidates skip.
cards.s: Slack, Discord, Meta — the one-to-one chat with fan-out and a heartbeat

cards.b:
The one idea: One ingest API with an idempotency key, a router that applies preferences and templates, one queue per channel with rate-limited workers, and delivery receipts fed back.

Service: notify(event, user, idempotency key)→Dedupe + preferences + template → channel→Per-channel queue (push/email/SMS)→Workers → APNs/FCM/SES/Twilio→Push fails → fallback to SMS; opt-out → drop

Clarify

You: Which channels, and who decides which channel a notification uses?

Interviewer: Push, email and SMS; the user's preferences and the notification type decide, with fallback if push fails.

You: What volume and what latency?

Interviewer: 100 million notifications a day, with bursts of 1 million in a minute; transactional ones within 5 seconds, marketing within an hour.

You: Is a duplicate notification acceptable?

Interviewer: Never twice for the same event; a missed marketing one is acceptable, a missed transactional one is not.

Size it out loud

100M a day is 1,200 a second average; a 1M-in-a-minute burst is 17K a second, so queues must absorb 15x the average. SMS at $0.01 is $1M a day if everything went SMS, which is why channel choice and dedupe matter. Provider rate limits are 1-10K a second, so per-provider workers back off.

Walk through the design

  1. Ingest: callers send an event id as the idempotency key; a conditional insert into a dedupe table with a 7-day TTL rejects repeats before anything is queued.
  2. Routing: load the user's preferences and quiet hours, pick the channel, render the template in the user's language, write the notification row with status 'queued'.
  3. Queues: one per channel with a priority lane for transactional; workers are rate-limited per provider token bucket, and retries use exponential backoff with a dead-letter queue.
  4. Delivery receipts: provider webhooks update the row to delivered, bounced or failed; a failed push for a transactional notification re-enters the router for fallback.
  5. Marketing batches: a campaign of 50M is chunked into 10K-user jobs and trickled at 5K a second so transactional traffic keeps its lane.

Deep dive

  • Data model: Notification{id, user, type, channel, status, attempts, created, delivered_at}; Preference{user, type → channels, quiet_hours}; Device{user, token, platform, last_seen}.
  • Template versioning: templates are versioned and the notification row records the version, so a changed template does not alter history and A/B tests are reproducible.

Push-backs

They: The SMS provider is down for 20 minutes.

You: The SMS queue backs up; the worker's circuit breaker opens; transactional SMS fall back to a second provider, marketing SMS just wait. Nothing is lost because the row is already persisted.

They: A user gets the same order-shipped notification twice.

You: Either the caller sent 2 event ids, which I surface in the dedupe metrics, or a worker crashed after sending and before marking sent; I mark 'sending' first and treat a retry of 'sending' as a manual review for SMS.

They: How do you avoid waking someone at 3 am?

You: Quiet hours in preferences, applied at routing; the notification is scheduled, not dropped, and goes at 8 am local time with a delayed-delivery queue.

Close

Trade-off: at-least-once with dedupe at the entrance means a mid-send crash can double-send; I accept that for push and email and add a 'sending' state check for SMS. I'd watch queue depth per channel and provider error rate.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
Ingest APIAPI Gateway + LambdaCloud Run
Dedupe tableDynamoDB (TTL)Firestore (TTL)
Channel queuesSQS (FIFO for transactional) + DLQPub/Sub (ordered for transactional) + dead-letter topic
WorkersECS FargateCloud Run jobs / GKE
ProvidersSNS (push/SMS) + SES (email)Firebase Cloud Messaging + Twilio/SendGrid via API
Preferences/notificationsDynamoDBFirestore
Delayed deliveryEventBridge SchedulerCloud Tasks (scheduled)
Trap: Drawing one queue to three providers; dedupe, preferences, rate limits per provider and fallback are what the interviewer is waiting for.
cards.s: Uber, Airbnb, Amazon — every product team has one

cards.b:
The one idea: Store each comment with a materialized path and parent id, precompute sorted comment pages per post into a cache, and load collapsed subtrees on demand.

Client GET /post/comments?sort=best→Cache: top 200 tree for (post, sort)→Miss → query by post_id, path prefix→Vote → counter → score recompute (async)→100K-comment post → page by subtree

Clarify

You: How deep can threads go, and how many comments can a post have?

Interviewer: Unlimited depth in theory, show 10 levels and collapse; up to 100K comments on a viral post.

You: How are comments sorted — by time, by votes, or both?

Interviewer: Best (votes with a confidence score), top, new; sort applies at every level.

You: Volume?

Interviewer: 50 million daily users, 10 million comments a day, 1 billion comment views a day.

Size it out loud

10M comments a day is 115 a second — writes are trivial. Reads are 1 billion a day, 12K a second, 50K at peak, mostly the top 200 comments of hot posts. A comment row with its path is 500 bytes; 100K comments on one post is 50 MB, too big to fetch whole, so I page by subtree.

Walk through the design

  1. Model: Comment{id, post_id, parent_id, path, author, body, created, score, replies_count}; path is ancestor ids joined, so a subtree is a prefix query.
  2. Read: for (post, sort) the cache holds the first 200 comments as a nested JSON tree built once; a miss rebuilds from the store in one range query on post_id.
  3. Sort: 'best' uses the Wilson lower bound of up/down votes so a 5-0 comment outranks 50-30; scores are recomputed by a worker on vote, debounced to once a second per comment.
  4. Deep threads: the client gets 10 levels; a 'continue thread' link fetches a subtree by path prefix, limit 200, so one request never returns 100K rows.
  5. Writes: insert the comment, bump parent replies_count, publish an event; the cached tree for that post is invalidated and rebuilt lazily on the next read.

Deep dive

  • Path vs adjacency list vs nested sets: adjacency needs recursive queries; nested sets make inserts rewrite siblings; materialized path makes insert one row and subtree one prefix scan.
  • Vote storage: Vote{comment_id, user_id, dir} so a user can change a vote; counters live on the comment and are the source for score; the vote table is the audit trail.

Push-backs

They: A post gets 1,000 comments a minute and the cache is rebuilt every time.

You: Debounce: invalidate at most once per second and serve the stale tree meanwhile; new comments appear within 1-2 seconds, which Reddit users accept.

They: How do you show a user their own comment immediately after posting?

You: The client inserts it locally, and the API returns the row; the cached tree catches up within a second. No read-your-writes from the cache.

They: A deleted comment has 50 replies.

You: Soft delete: body becomes '[deleted]', author is blanked, the row stays so the subtree is intact; hard delete only when the subtree is empty.

Close

Trade-off: materialized path lengths grow with depth — 10 levels of 12-byte ids is 130 bytes, fine; I cap the path at 50 levels. I'd watch cache rebuild rate per post and p99 read latency.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
APIALB + ECSCloud Load Balancing + Cloud Run
Comment storeAurora PostgreSQL (path index) or DynamoDBCloud SQL PostgreSQL (path index) or Spanner
Tree cacheElastiCache RedisMemorystore Redis
Vote eventsKinesisPub/Sub
Score workersLambdaCloud Functions
Search/moderationOpenSearchElastic on GCE or Vertex AI Search
Trap: Fetching every comment and building the tree in the API server; paging by subtree and caching per (post, sort) is the design.
cards.s: Reddit, Meta, Disqus — tree data under a hot post

cards.b:
The one idea: A stream job that counts in tumbling 10-second buckets per (country, hashtag), a count-min sketch plus a heap for top-K per window, and a merge of recent buckets to serve any window.

Post event → stream→Extract hashtags, key by country→Count per 10-second bucket (sketch + heap)→Merge 30 or 360 buckets → top 10 → cache→Spam bursts → rate-limited per author

Clarify

You: Trending over what window, and how fresh?

Interviewer: Top 10 hashtags over the last 5 minutes and the last hour, refreshed every 10 seconds; by country too.

You: Exact counts or approximate?

Interviewer: Approximate is fine if the top 10 is right; off-by-5% counts are acceptable.

You: Event volume?

Interviewer: 20,000 posts a second with hashtags, 1 billion distinct hashtags over a month, 200 countries.

Size it out loud

20K events a second is 6M per 5 minutes, 72M per hour. Exact per-country per-hashtag counts is 200 x 1B keys worst case — too big; but active hashtags per hour are maybe 10M, 100 bytes each is 1 GB, which fits in memory. A count-min sketch of 4 rows x 100K counters is 1.6 MB per window per country, 320 MB for all.

Walk through the design

  1. Ingest: posts flow through a partitioned stream keyed by country, so one worker owns a country and its counts stay local.
  2. Counting: each worker keeps a count-min sketch and a top-1,000 heap per 10-second bucket; every 10 seconds it emits the bucket's top-1,000 with counts to a store.
  3. Windows: the serving layer sums the last 30 buckets for 5 minutes or 360 for an hour over the union of each bucket's top-1,000 — a 36K-row merge, under 10 ms.
  4. Serving: the result per (country, window) is written to a cache every 10 seconds; the API only reads the cache, so 100K reads a second is trivial.
  5. Trending vs popular: score is count in window divided by the hashtag's 7-day baseline, so 'love' does not trend every day and a new tag spikes correctly.

Deep dive

  • Why top-1,000 per bucket is enough: a hashtag in the hourly top 10 must average 1/360 of its hourly count per bucket; anything below the bucket's 1,000th is noise at this volume. I say the bound, not just 'approximate'.
  • Exact mode: a batch job over the raw event store recomputes exact top-K hourly for the dashboard; the stream result serves the product.

Push-backs

They: A bot network pushes a hashtag 100K times in a minute.

You: Per-author rate cap at 10 hashtag events a minute before counting, dedupe on (author, hashtag, minute), and a spam classifier flag that excludes the event. That cuts 100K to 10K from 10K bots, which I surface as an anomaly.

They: The worker for the United States crashes.

You: The stream retains events; a new worker replays from the last checkpoint 10 seconds back and rebuilds the window from stored buckets. Trending for the US is stale for about 30 seconds.

They: Why not just use a sorted set in Redis per country?

You: ZINCRBY per event is 20K writes a second — fine — but a 1-hour window needs 360 sorted sets and a ZUNIONSTORE over them every 10 seconds, which is heavy; emitting bucket tops is the same idea with bounded cost.

Close

Trade-off: approximate counts for bounded memory; the top-10 ordering is correct in practice. I'd watch stream lag, bucket emit latency and the sketch's error estimate versus the batch job.

Event streamKinesis Data StreamsPub/Sub
Stream jobKinesis Data Analytics (Flink) or Flink on EKSDataflow
Bucket storeDynamoDB (TTL)Bigtable (TTL)
Serving cacheElastiCache RedisMemorystore Redis
APIAPI Gateway + LambdaCloud Run
Exact batchEMR Spark on S3Dataproc Spark on Cloud Storage
DashboardAthena / QuickSightBigQuery / Looker Studio
Trap: Proposing a global exact counter table; the interviewer wants a window, a bounded data structure and the merge step.
cards.s: Twitter/X, Google, TikTok — streaming aggregation under skew

cards.b:
The one idea: An adjacency list in a wide-column store stored in both directions, a bloom filter or cache for edge checks, and an offline friends-of-friends job that writes top-20 suggestions per user.

Follow(A,B)→Write forward (A→B) and reverse (B←A) rows→Edge check: cache → store→Nightly job: 2-hop candidates → score → top 20→Block → remove both edges, exclude from suggestions

Clarify

You: Directed follows or symmetric friendships?

Interviewer: Directed follows; a friendship is a mutual follow. Blocks must hide both directions.

You: What queries must be fast?

Interviewer: Does A follow B, list followers and following with paging, mutual count, and suggestions on profile load.

You: Scale?

Interviewer: 1 billion users, 100 billion edges, 10 million new edges a day; suggestions can be hours stale.

Size it out loud

100 billion edges at 20 bytes each is 2 TB, 6 TB with 3 replicas; stored twice (forward and reverse) is 12 TB. 10M new edges a day is 115 a second — writes are nothing; reads are 'does A follow B' at 500K a second from every feed and profile render. Friends-of-friends for a user with 300 follows is 90K candidates, so suggestions are offline.

Walk through the design

  1. Storage: Following{user_id, followee_id, created} and Followers{user_id, follower_id, created}, partitioned by the first column so listing is one partition scan.
  2. Write: write both rows in a transaction or with an outbox so a crash cannot leave half an edge; counts are maintained in a separate counter with eventual repair.
  3. Edge check: a per-user bloom filter of followees for users with under 10K follows gives a 1% false-positive rate in 12 KB; a positive hits the store to confirm.
  4. Suggestions: a nightly graph job computes friends-of-friends per user, scores by mutual count, shared employer and recent interactions, and writes the top 20 to a table.
  5. Serving: profile load reads the suggestion row, filters out users followed since the job ran and anyone blocked, and returns 10.

Deep dive

  • Celebrity partitions: a user with 100M followers has a 2 GB partition; I bucket the Followers table as (user_id, bucket = hash(follower) % 1,000) so no partition exceeds 2 MB and listing fans across buckets.
  • Graph database or not: a graph DB wins for 3-hop queries online, but the only online query here is 1-hop; a wide-column store at 100B edges is cheaper and I know its limits.

Push-backs

They: A celebrity follows someone — anything special?

You: No; the celebrity's Following partition is tiny. The expensive side is their Followers partition, which the buckets solve.

They: Suggestions recommend someone I just blocked.

You: The serving read filters against the block list, which is small and cached per user; the nightly job also excludes blocks, so the window is a few hours at most and the filter closes it.

They: How do you compute friends-of-friends for a billion users nightly?

You: A 2-hop join on 100B edges is 10 trillion pairs naively; I cap each user at 500 followees sampled by recency, which bounds it to 250K pairs per user, and run it as a Spark job on 500 nodes in about 4 hours.

Close

Trade-off: the double-write costs storage and a transaction; it buys one-partition reads in both directions. I'd watch edge-check cache hit rate, the biggest partition size and suggestion-job duration.

cards.b:
The one idea: Record each like as an idempotent row keyed (object, user), aggregate counts through a stream with sharded counters, and serve counts from a cache with exact per-user like state.

POST /like (object, user)→Conditional insert Like row (idempotent)→Event → stream → aggregator adds per object→Count cache serves reads; store checkpoints→100K/s hot object → sharded counters merge

Clarify

You: What must be exact — the count shown, whether I liked it, or both?

Interviewer: Whether I liked it must be exact; the displayed count can be off by a few percent and catch up within a minute.

You: How hot does one object get?

Interviewer: A viral video can get 100K likes a second for a few minutes; a normal post gets 1 a minute.

You: Scale?

Interviewer: 1 billion likes a day across 10 billion objects; 50 billion count reads a day.

Size it out loud

1B likes a day is 12K a second average, but one object at 100K a second is the problem — a single row cannot take that. 50B count reads a day is 580K a second, so counts must come from cache. Like rows at 30 bytes are 30 GB a day, 11 TB a year; the per-user like set is what 'did I like it' reads.

Walk through the design

  1. Like write: conditional put on (object_id, user_id); a repeat is a no-op, an unlike deletes; this is the truth and it is per-user partitioned so no row is hot.
  2. Counting: the write emits an event; a stream job keyed by object_id sums in 1-second windows and increments the count in cache and store once per second per object.
  3. Hot objects: the aggregator is the shard — 100K events a second become 1 increment a second; if one object exceeds a worker, the key is split into 16 sub-partitions and summed at read.
  4. Reads: count from cache with a 1-second refresh; 'did I like it' from a per-user Redis set or a batch get on the Like table for the 20 objects on screen.
  5. Repair: a nightly job counts Like rows per object and overwrites drifted counters, so any lost event is corrected within a day.

Deep dive

  • Why not INCR in Redis directly: it works to 500K a second per key on one node, but the Like row must be written anyway for idempotency, and a lost INCR drifts forever without the repair path.
  • Display rules: show exact counts under 1,000 and rounded above, '12.3K', which hides the approximation and lets the cache serve a 1-second-old value with no visible flicker.

Push-backs

They: A user double-taps and sends two likes in 50 ms.

You: Same (object, user) key; the second conditional put fails and emits no event. The client shows liked state from the first response.

They: The aggregator falls 5 minutes behind during a viral spike.

You: Counts lag; likes are safe in the Like table. I scale workers on lag; the count catches up and the nightly repair guarantees convergence. Users see 1.2M instead of 1.5M for 5 minutes.

They: Why do you need the stream — write the Like row and INCR the counter in one request?

You: Two writes without a transaction can leave them inconsistent, and the INCR is the hot row again. The event is the outbox; one source of truth and the counter derives from it.

Close

Trade-off: counts are eventually consistent by a second; like state is exact. I'd watch aggregator lag, the hottest object's event rate and nightly repair drift.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
APIALB + ECSCloud Load Balancing + Cloud Run
Like tableDynamoDB (object_id, user_id)Bigtable (object_id#user_id)
Event streamDynamoDB Streams → KinesisPub/Sub
AggregatorKinesis Data Analytics (Flink)Dataflow
Count cacheElastiCache RedisMemorystore Redis
Count storeDynamoDBBigtable
Nightly repairEMR Spark / Athena over S3 exportDataproc Spark / BigQuery over export
Trap: Starting with 'just INCR a counter'; the interviewer wants idempotent likes, the hot-row problem named and the stream that removes it.
cards.s: Meta, YouTube, Reddit — the hot-row problem

cards.b:
The one idea: Upload once, transcode into segments, store in object storage, and serve HLS/DASH chunks from the CDN; metadata lives in a separate small database.

Client: pre-signed multipart upload→Transcode workers: 6 renditions, 4-second segments→Segments + manifests in object store→Player: CDN → manifest → chunks→Failed job → retry queue, author notified

Clarify

You: How many uploads a day, and how many hours watched?

Interviewer: 500 hours uploaded a minute; 1 billion hours watched a day; views are about 1,000x uploads.

You: Which devices and qualities do we serve?

Interviewer: Phones to 4K TVs, so adaptive bitrate from 240p to 2160p; start playback within 2 seconds.

You: Is this public video on demand only, or live too?

Interviewer: On demand only; comments and search are out of scope, recommendations are a separate team.

Size it out loud

500 hours a minute is 720,000 hours a day; at 1 GB per hour raw that is 720 TB a day of ingest, 260 PB a year before transcoding into 6 renditions (about 3x storage after compression). 1 billion watch-hours a day at 1.5 Mbps average is 675 PB a day of egress, roughly 60 Tbps sustained — only a CDN can serve that; origin sees under 5% of it.

Walk through the design

  1. Upload: the client gets a pre-signed URL and uploads directly to object storage in 10 MB parts; my API servers never touch video bytes.
  2. Transcode: a job per video fans out to one task per rendition; workers write 4-second fMP4 segments plus an HLS and DASH manifest; a video is 'ready' once 360p lands, other renditions follow.
  3. Serving: the player fetches the manifest, picks a rendition from measured bandwidth, and pulls chunks from the CDN; cache keys are video id + rendition + segment number.
  4. Metadata: Video{id, owner, title, status, duration, renditions[]} in a relational store with a read cache; views counted via a stream, flushed every 10 seconds.
  5. Cold tail: 80% of views hit 5% of videos; keep popular segments in CDN, move videos unwatched for 1 year to cold storage with a 30-second rehydrate on first request.

Deep dive

  • Adaptive bitrate: each rendition is a ladder rung (240p 300 Kbps up to 2160p 15 Mbps); the player switches at segment boundaries, so 4-second segments bound how fast it can react.
  • Transcode scheduling: a 1-hour 4K upload is about 4 CPU-hours per rendition; I split by time range into 2-minute chunks so 30 workers finish it in 8 minutes instead of 4 hours.

Push-backs

They: A video goes viral — 10 million views in an hour.

You: The CDN serves it; the origin sees one miss per edge per segment, about 2,000 requests total. I set long cache TTLs because segments are immutable.

They: Why segments instead of one big file with range requests?

You: Segments let the player switch quality mid-stream, give the CDN small cacheable objects, and let transcoding run in parallel on chunks.

They: Transcoding is 10 hours behind after a big event.

You: Priority queues: new uploads from large channels first, and only the 360p rendition is on the critical path; the rest drain overnight on spot capacity.

Close

Trade-off: 6 renditions triple storage but cut egress, which costs 10x more. I'd watch time-to-first-frame, rebuffer ratio and CDN hit rate; at 10x I'd push per-title encoding to shave 20% off bitrate.

Segment storageS3 + Glacier for cold tailCloud Storage + Archive class for cold tail
DeliveryCloudFrontMedia CDN
MetadataAurora + ElastiCacheCloud SQL + Memorystore
Job queueSQS + Step FunctionsPub/Sub + Workflows
View countsKinesis → Flink → DynamoDBPub/Sub → Dataflow → Bigtable
Trap: Designing the recommendation feed or comments; the interviewer wants the byte path — upload, transcode, segment, CDN.
cards.s: Google, Meta, Amazon — the big one for media teams

cards.b:
The one idea: A small, pre-encoded catalog pushed to CDN edges ahead of demand, a precomputed home page per user refreshed by batch and nudged by a stream, and a playback service that hands out DRM licenses.

Ingest: studio master → encode ladder→Catalog + segments pre-pushed to edges→Home: precomputed rows + real-time rerank→Play: license + manifest → CDN chunks→Play events → stream → feature store

Clarify

You: Is the catalog licensed and curated, or user-uploaded?

Interviewer: Curated: about 20,000 titles, a few hundred new a week; no user uploads.

You: How personal should the home page be, and how fresh?

Interviewer: Rows ranked per user; recomputed at least daily, with recent plays reflected within minutes.

You: How many subscribers and concurrent streams?

Interviewer: 200 million subscribers, 30 million concurrent at peak; every stream must be DRM protected.

Size it out loud

20,000 titles x 2 hours x 8 renditions x 1 GB per hour is 320 TB of encoded catalog — small. 30 million streams at 5 Mbps is 150 Tbps at peak, so delivery is the problem, not storage. Recommendations: 200M users x 20 rows x 30 titles x 4 bytes is 480 GB of precomputed rows; a daily batch over 1 billion play events is a few hundred machine-hours.

Walk through the design

  1. Catalog: every title is encoded once into the full ladder and pre-positioned to CDN edges overnight by predicted popularity; 95% of plays never touch origin.
  2. Home page: a nightly batch scores titles per user with collaborative filtering, writes 20 rows x 30 titles to a key-value row store; the API reads one key per user in 5 ms.
  3. Freshness: play and browse events go through a stream; a real-time reranker reorders the precomputed rows with the last hour's signals, no new candidates.
  4. Playback: the client asks for a session; I check entitlement, issue a 4-hour DRM license, return the manifest and a CDN token; chunks come from the CDN.
  5. Resilience: if the recommender is down, serve the last computed rows or a popularity fallback; a degraded home page beats an empty one.

Deep dive

  • Two-stage recommender: candidate generation picks 500 titles from 20,000 by embedding similarity, then a ranker scores those 500 with user and context features; cheap first, expensive second.
  • Artwork personalization: 10 thumbnails per title, pick per user by predicted click rate; a few hundred KB more per title, and a 10-20% lift in play starts.

Push-backs

They: A new season drops at midnight and 20 million people press play.

You: Pre-pushed to every edge the day before, so it is a CDN hit from the first second; the licensing service is the one thing that scales linearly, so I pre-warm it and cache entitlements.

They: Why precompute the home page instead of ranking at request time?

You: 200M users x 20,000 titles is 4 trillion scores; batch makes that affordable. Request-time I only rerank 600 already-chosen titles.

They: A user watches 3 episodes; the home page still shows them.

You: The stream path updates a per-user 'recently played' set within seconds; the reranker filters it on every read.

Close

Trade-off: nightly batch means a brand-new title reaches home pages up to 24 hours late; an editorial row covers that. I'd watch play-start latency, rebuffer rate and the recommender's offline-online gap.

Implementation

EncodingMediaConvertTranscoder API

DeliveryCloudFront (or own edge appliances)Media CDN
Recommender batchEMR Spark + SageMakerDataproc Spark + Vertex AI
Home rows storeDynamoDBBigtable
Event streamKinesis → FlinkPub/Sub → Dataflow
Playback/DRMECS + MediaPackage DRMGKE + third-party DRM on GKE
Trap: Spending 30 minutes on the ML model; the interviewer wants the serving path — how 200 million home pages are computed, stored and kept fresh.
cards.s: Netflix, Disney, Amazon Prime — catalog, playback and the home row

cards.b:
The one idea: Encrypted tracks served from the CDN in small chunks, a player that prefetches the next track's first 15 seconds, and playlist and library data in a key-value store sharded by user.

Tap play: client checks local cache→Track service: license + chunk URLs→CDN: first 2 chunks fast, rest paced→Prefetch next track head→Play events → stream → royalties + recs

Clarify

You: How big is the catalog and how many listeners?

Interviewer: 100 million tracks; 500 million users, 100 million concurrent at peak hour.

You: Do we need offline downloads and playlists?

Interviewer: Yes to both; playlists can have 10,000 tracks and are shared and collaborative.

You: Latency target for play?

Interviewer: First audio within 300 ms on tap; that is the headline metric.

Size it out loud

100M tracks x 4 MB at 320 Kbps x 3 qualities is about 1 PB — manageable. 100M concurrent streams at 160 Kbps average is 16 Tbps peak egress. Playlists: 4 billion playlists x 200 tracks x 16 bytes is 13 TB of ids. Play events: 100M listeners x 15 tracks an hour is 400K events a second at peak.

Walk through the design

  1. Audio: each track is stored as 1 MB encrypted chunks per quality; the client fetches chunk 0 at full speed, then paces the rest to the bitrate, so one tap costs 1 round trip plus 1 chunk.
  2. 300 ms start: the client keeps the first 15 seconds of the next 3 likely tracks on disk; on a known device most plays never hit the network for the first chunk.
  3. Playlists: Playlist{id, owner, version, tracks[]} in a key-value store, edited with version checks; a 10,000-track playlist is pages of 500 so the app does not load 160 KB on open.
  4. Offline: downloads are the same encrypted chunks plus a 30-day license; the client refreshes licenses when online, and plays are logged locally and uploaded later.
  5. Events: every play, skip and seek goes to a stream; one consumer settles royalties per track daily, another feeds recommendations, with at-least-once delivery and dedupe by event id.

Deep dive

  • Why not stream over HTTP byte ranges from one file: chunks are CDN-cacheable units and let me switch quality under poor networks; one file per quality would also break my prefetch math.
  • Royalty counting: a play counts after 30 seconds, so the client emits a 'qualified play' event; dedupe on (user, track, timestamp bucket) catches offline replays uploaded twice.

Push-backs

They: An artist releases an album and 50 million people play it at once.

You: Chunks are already on every CDN edge from the pre-release window; the track service only hands out URLs, which I cache per track for 1 hour.

They: Two people edit a collaborative playlist at the same time.

You: Each edit carries the version it read; the store rejects stale writes and the client retries with a merge — add/remove by track id resolves cleanly, reorder uses last-writer-wins.

They: Why not keep everything in one relational database?

You: Catalog and metadata fit a relational store fine; playlists and libraries are user-sharded key-value because 4 billion rows with 500M writers wants horizontal scale, not joins.

Close

Trade-off: prefetching costs bandwidth for tracks never played, about 10% waste, for a 300 ms start. I'd watch time-to-first-audio, skip-rate after start, and CDN hit rate by region.

Audio storageS3Cloud Storage
