cards.b:
The one idea: A mutually authenticated MQTT edge that accepts batched, compressed frames, a stream backbone with the raw frames kept as-is, and three consumers: a hot store for the live view, a rules engine, and a columnar lake for analytics.

Vehicle: mTLS MQTT, 10-s batch, store-and-forward→Ingest brokers: auth, decode, validate VIN→Stream partitioned by VIN→Live store (last state) + rules + lake→Bad cert / schema → reject, quarantine topic

Clarify

You: How many vehicles, what do they send, and how often?

Interviewer: 5 million vehicles; 50 signals every second while driving, batched every 10 seconds; 1 hour average driving a day.

You: What consumes it — live dashboards, alerts, or analytics and ML later?

Interviewer: All three: live view per vehicle, rules like 'engine temp over threshold', and long-term analytics.

You: Connectivity and security constraints?

Interviewer: Cellular with gaps of minutes to days; each vehicle has a certificate; data must be attributable to a VIN.

Size it out loud

5M vehicles x 1 hour a day is 5M vehicle-hours; at 50 signals a second that is 900 billion samples a day. Batched every 10 seconds in a compact binary of 2 KB, that is 1.8 billion messages a day, 21,000 a second average and about 100,000 at the commute peak. 2 KB x 1.8B is 3.6 TB a day raw; compressed and columnar, 500 GB a day, 180 TB a year.

Walk through the design

  1. Device side: a buffer on the vehicle holds up to 7 days when offline; frames carry a monotonic sequence and vehicle time, so late data is ordered and gaps are visible.
  2. Edge: brokers terminate mTLS with a per-vehicle certificate; the VIN comes from the certificate, never from the payload, so a vehicle cannot spoof another.
  3. Stream: partition by VIN so one vehicle's frames are ordered; retain 7 days so a consumer can be rebuilt; schema registry with a version in every frame.
  4. Consumers: a stateful job keeps last-known state per VIN for the live view; a rules job evaluates thresholds and windows; a batch job writes hourly Parquet partitioned by date and model.
  5. Late data: the lake accepts frames with vehicle time days old into their proper partition; the live view ignores anything older than its current state.

Deep dive

  • OTA adjacency: the same mTLS channel carries campaign commands down; update status comes up as telemetry, so rollout dashboards use this pipeline. Commands are signed separately.
  • Privacy: location at 1 Hz is sensitive; raw location is retained 30 days, then aggregated to trips; access is per purpose and audited, and a driver can request deletion that is honored in the lake by rewriting partitions.

Push-backs

They: A software bug makes 1 million vehicles send 10x data.

You: Per-vehicle rate limits at the broker and a quota by firmware version; over-limit frames are sampled, not dropped entirely, and the firmware team gets an alert in 5 minutes.

They: A million vehicles reconnect after an outage and dump 2 days of buffer.

You: The brokers accept at their rate and vehicles back off with jitter; the stream absorbs the burst over hours; the live view is unaffected because it only takes the newest frame.

They: Someone extracts a certificate from a vehicle.

You: Certificates are per vehicle in a hardware secure element; a leaked one is revoked and the VIN quarantined; anomaly detection flags a VIN reporting from two places.

Close

Trade-off: keeping raw frames for 7 days in the stream is expensive but lets me replay into any new consumer. I'd watch ingest lag per broker, rejected-frame rate by reason and lake partition completeness.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
EdgeIoT Core (MQTT, mTLS) or EKS MQTT brokers behind NLBGKE MQTT brokers behind Cloud Load Balancing (mTLS)
StreamMSK (Kafka) partitioned by VINPub/Sub keyed by VIN (or Kafka on GKE)
Stream processingManaged Service for Apache FlinkDataflow
Live stateDynamoDBBigtable
LakeS3 Parquet + Glue + AthenaCloud Storage Parquet + BigQuery
Device identityIoT Core registry + ACM Private CACertificate Authority Service
MonitoringCloudWatchCloud Monitoring
Trap: Treating it as a logging pipeline; device identity, offline buffering and late data are what the automotive interviewer wants to hear.
cards.s: Tesla, Ford, Uber Freight, Samsara — IoT ingestion with a strong device identity story

cards.f: Design: Real-time location sharing / driver tracking
cards.b:
The one idea: Ingest over a persistent connection to a sharded location service, keep last-known position in memory, and push to viewers through subscription-based fan-out on the same connection layer, with the trail written asynchronously.

Sender: WebSocket, point every 3 s→Location shard by sender id: update + publish→Pub/sub topic per sender → viewer connections→Trail writer: batch to time-series store→Viewer offline → last-known on reconnect

Clarify

You: Who watches whom — one rider watching one driver, or a family of 5 watching each other?

Interviewer: Both: 1-to-1 driver tracking, and small groups up to 20 members.

You: Update frequency and acceptable lag?

Interviewer: Sender every 3 seconds; viewers should see it within 2 seconds of that.

You: Scale and retention?

Interviewer: 10 million active sharers at peak; keep a 24-hour trail, longer trip history is a separate service.

Size it out loud

10M sharers every 3 seconds is 3.3M location updates a second in, and with 1 to 5 viewers each, up to 10M pushes a second out. Each update is 50 bytes, 165 MB a second in. Last-known state: 10M x 100 bytes is 1 GB. A 24-hour trail at 1 point per 3 seconds is 28,800 points x 20 bytes, 576 KB per sharer, 5.8 TB for everyone — stored compressed and sampled.

Walk through the design

  1. Connections: a gateway tier holds WebSockets for senders and viewers; 10M senders plus 20M viewers at 50K connections per node is 600 nodes; the gateway knows which topics each connection subscribes to.
  2. Location shard: in-memory map sender → last point and list of subscribed gateways; an update writes the map and publishes to those gateways only, so fan-out is targeted.
  3. Subscription: a viewer opens the trip or group, the gateway subscribes to the sender's topic on the right shard, and gets the last-known point immediately.
  4. Trail: updates are batched per sender into a time-series store every 30 seconds, 24-hour TTL; the live path never waits for it.
  5. Smoothing: the client interpolates between points and snaps to roads for drivers, so a 3-second cadence looks continuous.

Deep dive

  • Pub/sub choice: a broker topic per sender is 10M topics, which most brokers hate; I use in-process pub/sub inside the shard with gateway addresses as subscribers, and a broker only for cross-region.
  • Privacy controls: sharing has an explicit end time or trip end; the server stops publishing at that moment regardless of client state, and the trail is deleted with the TTL.

Push-backs

They: A celebrity driver has 1 million viewers.

You: That is a broadcast, not sharing; the shard publishes once to each gateway and the gateway fans out locally, or I cap viewers per sender at 100 and route the rest to a 10-second CDN snapshot.

They: The sender's phone sends points out of order after a tunnel.

You: Each point carries a device timestamp; the shard keeps the newest timestamp, not the newest arrival, and the trail sorts by timestamp.

They: Battery: 3-second GPS drains the phone.

You: Adaptive cadence: 3 seconds while moving fast, 15 seconds when slow, 60 seconds when stationary; the server sends the cadence to the client based on viewers present.

Close

Trade-off: in-memory shards lose state on crash, but it rebuilds in 3 seconds from the next updates; I keep it cheap instead of durable. I'd watch end-to-end lag p95 and connections per gateway.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
Connection gatewayNLB + EKS (WebSockets)Cloud Load Balancing + GKE (WebSockets)
Location shardsEKS in-memory, or ElastiCache RedisGKE in-memory, or Memorystore Redis
Cross-region pub/subMSKPub/Sub
Trail storeTimestream or DynamoDB (TTL)Bigtable (TTL)
Map snappingLocation ServiceMaps Platform Roads API
Push for backgrounded appsSNS mobile pushFirebase Cloud Messaging
MetricsCloudWatchCloud Monitoring
Trap: Writing every point to a database and polling it; the design is connections, in-memory state and targeted fan-out.
cards.s: Uber, Find My, Life360, DoorDash — fan-out of a moving point

cards.f: Design: Airline check-in and seat assignment
cards.b:
The one idea: A flight seat map as the unit of consistency with a conditional seat claim, a rules engine for eligibility evaluated before offering seats, and a boarding pass issued as a signed document once the PNR system confirms.

Passenger: open check-in (PNR, name)→Load PNR + seat map, apply eligibility rules→Claim seat: conditional update on (flight, seat)→Sync to PNR system → issue boarding pass→Seat taken / rule fails → offer alternatives

Clarify

You: Scope: check-in opening 24 hours before departure, seat selection, boarding pass; or also booking and pricing?

Interviewer: Check-in, seat selection and boarding pass; the reservation already exists in a PNR system we read from.

You: Scale?

Interviewer: 5,000 flights a day, 180 seats each, 900,000 passengers a day; check-in opens at exactly T-24h and 30% check in within the first hour.

You: Seat rules?

Interviewer: Exit rows need an adult, some seats are paid, families with children should sit together, and airport staff can override anything.

Size it out loud

900K passengers a day is 10 a second average; the T-24h wave is 30% of a flight's 180 passengers in an hour, and with flights opening around the clock that is about 50 check-ins a second with spikes of 500 when many flights open together. Seat maps: 5,000 flights x 180 seats x 100 bytes is 90 MB — tiny. The whole thing is about correctness and integration, not scale.

Walk through the design

  1. Seat map: per flight, one row per seat {flight_id, seat, state: free|held|assigned|blocked, passenger_id, attrs: exit|paid|preferred}; cached in Redis, source of truth in the database.
  2. Eligibility: rules take the passenger (age, fare class, status, infant) and the seat attrs; the map shown is already filtered, so most rule failures never reach the claim.
  3. Claim: 'UPDATE seat SET state=assigned, passenger=? WHERE flight=? AND seat=? AND state=free'; group seating holds several seats in one transaction or none.
  4. PNR sync: the reservation system is the airline's system of record; the assignment is written there synchronously with a retry queue, and the boarding pass is only issued after it acknowledges.
  5. Boarding pass: a signed barcode (IATA BCBP) stored with the check-in; the gate scanner validates the signature offline and the status online when it can.

Deep dive

  • Opening at T-24h: a scheduler flips the flight to 'check-in open' and pre-warms the seat map cache; the spike is predictable to the second, so I scale ahead rather than react.
  • Irregular operations: an aircraft swap changes the seat map; a job remaps seats by priority and notifies passengers; staff overrides use the same claim path with a 'force' flag and audit entry.

Push-backs

They: Two passengers pick 12C at the same moment.

You: The conditional update lets one through; the other sees 'just taken' and the refreshed map. The cache is updated on the write path so the second person rarely even sees it free.

They: The PNR system is down for 20 minutes.

You: Seat claims continue locally; boarding passes are issued with a 'pending sync' marker and the retry queue drains when it returns. Gate agents can see the local assignment.

They: A family of 4 and only 2 adjacent pairs remain.

You: The group claim tries adjacency first, then same row, then nearest rows, all in one transaction so they never end up with 3 of 4; failing that, offer to hold until staff resolve at the gate.

Close

Trade-off: syncing to the legacy PNR system synchronously adds 500 ms to check-in; the alternative is divergence between our map and theirs, which is worse. I'd watch claim conflict rate, PNR sync lag and boarding-pass issue failures.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
APIAPI Gateway + ECS FargateAPI Gateway + Cloud Run
Seat maps + check-insAurora PostgreSQLCloud SQL PostgreSQL
Seat map cacheElastiCache RedisMemorystore Redis
PNR sync queueSQS + LambdaCloud Tasks + Cloud Functions
Check-in openingEventBridge SchedulerCloud Scheduler
Boarding pass signingKMSCloud KMS
NotificationsSNS + SESFirebase Cloud Messaging + SendGrid
Trap: Designing for internet scale; the interviewer wants the seat race, the rules and the dependency on an external system of record.
cards.s: Amazon, Expedia, airline tech teams — booking rules plus a seat-level race

cards.b:
The one idea: Agents push samples to a sharded in-memory time-series store for the last 2 hours, flushed to object storage as compressed blocks; alerts evaluate on the hot tier and rollups serve long ranges.

Agent scrapes host every 10 s→Ingest: hash series id → shard→Hot tier: 2 h in RAM, compressed→Flush 2 h blocks to object store + rollups→Query/alert: hot tier, then blocks

Clarify

You: How many hosts and how many time series, and how often do they report?

Interviewer: 50,000 hosts, about 100 million active series, one sample every 10 seconds.

You: What do people do with it — dashboards, alerts, ad-hoc queries over a year?

Interviewer: Alerts on the last 5 minutes, dashboards over hours; a year of history at lower resolution.

You: How fresh must an alert be, and can we lose a few samples?

Interviewer: Alert within 30 seconds of the condition; losing 0.1% of samples is fine, losing alerts is not.

Size it out loud

100M series every 10 s is 10M samples a second. Raw at 16 bytes is 160 MB/s, 14 TB a day; Gorilla-style compression gets a sample to about 1.5 bytes, so 1.3 TB a day. 30 days of raw is 40 TB; rolled up to 1-minute and 1-hour averages, a year adds about 10 TB. Query side: 20,000 alert rules every 30 s is 700 evaluations a second over hot in-memory data.

Walk through the design

  1. Series identity: hash of metric name plus sorted labels is the series id; an index maps label values to series ids so a query like host=~'web.*' resolves to ids first.
  2. Ingest: stateless receivers hash the series id to 1 of 256 shards, each shard replicated 2x in memory; a shard holds about 400K series and 24K samples a second.
  3. Hot storage: delta-of-delta timestamps and XOR floats, 1.5 bytes a sample; 2 hours of 100M series is about 100 GB across the cluster.
  4. Cold storage: every 2 hours a shard writes an immutable block with its own index to object storage; a compactor merges blocks and produces 1-minute and 1-hour rollups.
  5. Alerting: rules evaluate every 30 s against the hot tier only, fan out by shard, and fire through a dedupe-and-group service so one outage is one page, not 500.

Deep dive

  • Cardinality: a label like request_id creates millions of series; I enforce a per-metric series cap of 100K at ingest and reject beyond it, since a cardinality bomb takes the whole shard.
  • Query engine: push-down to shards, each returns pre-aggregated series for its range; the frontend merges and applies rate() and sum by(). Long ranges hit rollups automatically above 7 days.

Push-backs

They: A shard node dies — do we lose 2 hours of data?

You: Each shard has 2 in-memory replicas plus a write-ahead log on local disk; a replacement replays the log, about 2 minutes. Alerts keep evaluating off the surviving replica.

They: A dashboard queries a year of one metric across 50,000 hosts.

You: That is 1.5 billion raw points; the engine picks the 1-hour rollup, 8,760 points per host, and sum-by-shard returns 8,760 points. Under a second.

They: Why push instead of Prometheus-style pull?

You: Pull needs discovery and open ports on every host; at 50,000 hosts behind NATs and in batch jobs, push through a local agent with retry is simpler. I keep pull for Kubernetes targets.

Close

Trade-off: 0.1% sample loss is accepted in exchange for no backpressure on ingest. I'd watch series count per shard, ingest lag, and alert-evaluation lag; if lag passes 15 s, I split shards.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
AgentsCloudWatch agent / OpenTelemetry collectorOps Agent / OpenTelemetry collector
Ingest + hot tierEKS (Prometheus/Mimir/M3) or Amazon Managed PrometheusGKE (Prometheus/Mimir/M3) or Managed Service for Prometheus
Block storageS3Cloud Storage
Rollups/compactionEMR on EKS or compactor on EKSDataproc Serverless or compactor on GKE
AlertingManaged Prometheus alert manager + SNSCloud Monitoring alerting + Pub/Sub
DashboardsManaged GrafanaCloud Monitoring dashboards / Grafana
Platform metricsCloudWatchCloud Monitoring
Trap: Designing a generic database; the marks are in compression, cardinality limits and keeping alerts alive when storage is sick.
cards.s: Datadog, Google (Monarch), Meta (Gorilla), Uber (M3) — the on-call question

cards.b:
The one idea: Agents ship lines into a durable log buffer; indexers write time-and-service partitioned compressed chunks with a small inverted index and bloom filters to object storage; one year of raw stays in cheap storage.

Agent tails files, batches 1 MB→Streaming buffer, partition by service→Indexer: parse, chunk, index, compress→Chunks + index → object store→Search: index → chunks → merge

Clarify

You: What is the volume and the retention — searchable for how long, kept for how long?

Interviewer: 1 GB a second sustained, 3x at peak; searchable 14 days, kept 1 year for audit.

You: How fast must a line be searchable after it is written?

Interviewer: Under 60 seconds; engineers tail logs during incidents.

You: What queries: free text, structured filters, or both?

Interviewer: Mostly service plus time range plus a keyword; some full-text; a few aggregations.

Size it out loud

1 GB/s is 86 TB a day, 1.2 PB for 14 days; compressed 10:1 that is 120 TB searchable and 3 PB a year in cold storage. At 300 bytes a line that is 3.3 million lines a second. A buffer of 1 hour at peak is 10 TB — a 30-broker streaming cluster at 100 MB/s each with headroom.

Walk through the design

  1. Collection: a per-host agent tails files, parses JSON, batches 1 MB or 1 second, and retries with a local 1 GB disk buffer so a backend stall does not drop lines.
  2. Buffer: a streaming log keyed by service with 512 partitions and 1-hour retention at peak absorbs a 3x burst and lets indexers restart without loss.
  3. Indexing: indexers cut 256 MB chunks per service per 15 minutes, build a bloom filter per field value and a sparse inverted index, zstd-compress, and write to object storage.
  4. Query: the planner prunes by service and time, then by bloom filter, then streams only the surviving chunks through a scan fleet; most incident queries touch under 10 chunks.
  5. Tiering: 14 days hot with index; after that only compressed raw stays for a year, searchable by a slow batch scan when audit asks.

Deep dive

  • Schema-on-read vs full index: indexing every token like Elasticsearch costs 1-2x raw in index size; bloom filters plus columnar scan give 10:1 compression and 2-5 s queries, which engineers accept.
  • Multi-tenancy: a noisy service logging 300 MB/s gets its own partitions and a per-service quota; over quota it is sampled at ingest rather than starving others.

Push-backs

They: An incident triples log volume at the exact moment people need search.

You: The buffer absorbs 3x for an hour; indexers autoscale on lag; search prefers the last 15 minutes which are indexed in memory before flush. Freshness degrades to 2-3 minutes, not zero.

They: Someone logs a credit card number.

You: Agents run a redaction rule set at the edge for PAN and token patterns; what gets past is deleted by chunk rewrite with an audit entry. Prevention beats deletion at 1 GB/s.

They: Why not Elasticsearch for all of it?

You: 1.2 PB with a full inverted index is 300-plus hot nodes. I use object storage plus bloom filters and keep a small Elasticsearch only for the 1% of services that need sub-second full-text.

Close

Trade-off: queries take seconds instead of milliseconds to make storage 10x cheaper. I'd watch end-to-end latency from write to searchable, buffer lag, and cost per GB a month.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
AgentsFluent Bit / OpenTelemetry on hostsFluent Bit / Ops Agent on hosts
BufferMSK (or Kinesis)Pub/Sub
IndexersEKS workers (Loki / OpenSearch ingest)GKE workers (Loki / Dataflow)
Chunk + index storeS3 (Intelligent-Tiering, Glacier after 14 d)Cloud Storage (Autoclass, Archive after 14 d)
Query fleetEKS or Athena for cold scansGKE or BigQuery external tables for cold scans
Hot full-textOpenSearch (subset)Elasticsearch on GKE (subset)
Pipeline metricsCloudWatchCloud Monitoring/Logging
Trap: Putting everything in a search engine and never doing the storage math; 1 GB/s is a cost question first.
cards.s: Splunk, Datadog, Netflix, Uber — any company whose logs outgrew grep

cards.f: Design: Distributed job scheduler (millions of cron jobs)
cards.b:
The one idea: Store each schedule with a precomputed next_fire_at, partition schedules across shards that lease their partition, and poll the due set every second into a durable work queue so firing and executing are separate.

API: create schedule (cron, target)→Store row with next_fire_at, shard id→Shard leader polls due rows every 1 s→Enqueue fire event, bump next_fire_at→Workers execute, retry, record history

Clarify

You: How many jobs, how often do they fire, and what does a job actually run?

Interviewer: 10 million schedules; most hourly or daily; a job is an HTTP call or a container launch owned by the caller.

You: What are the guarantees — exactly once, at least once, on time to the second?

Interviewer: At least once, fire within 60 seconds of the scheduled time, never miss a run entirely.

You: Do jobs have dependencies on each other?

Interviewer: No; that is the workflow engine's job. Just schedules, retries and history.

Size it out loud

10M schedules, average once an hour, is 2,800 fires a second, peaking 10x at the top of the hour: 28,000 a second for a minute. Each fire is a 1 KB row; a year of history at 2,800 a second is 90 billion rows, 90 TB — keep 30 days hot, 7 TB. The next-fire index is 10M rows, 1 GB, cached in memory on each scheduler shard.

Walk through the design

  1. Data model: Schedule{id, owner, cron, tz, target, next_fire_at, shard}; a secondary index on (shard, next_fire_at) makes the due query a range scan of a few thousand rows.
  2. Sharding: 64 shards by hash of schedule id; each shard has a leader elected with a 10-second lease in a coordination store, so one process polls each shard and no job fires twice per tick.
  3. Firing: the leader reads rows with next_fire_at <= now, writes a fire event to the queue and advances next_fire_at in one transaction; the queue, not the scheduler, holds the work.
  4. Execution: a worker pool consumes the queue, calls the target with a fire id, retries with exponential backoff up to 5 times, and writes a history row with status and duration.
  5. Top-of-hour spike: jitter new schedules by up to 59 seconds unless the owner opts out; the 28,000-a-second peak becomes about 3,000 a second steady.

Deep dive

  • Clock and timezones: next_fire_at is computed in UTC from the cron plus the owner's timezone at write time, and recomputed on DST changes by a nightly job; the scheduler never parses cron in the hot loop.
  • Missed runs: if a shard was down for 10 minutes, the leader finds rows with next_fire_at in the past and fires them once each with a late flag rather than firing 10 times; owners choose catch-up or skip.

Push-backs

They: Two leaders think they own the same shard.

You: The lease is a compare-and-set with a fencing token; the queue rejects fire events carrying a stale token. Worst case a duplicate fire, which at-least-once already allows.

They: A target is down and 50,000 jobs retry at once.

You: Retries are per-target with a circuit breaker; after 20% failures for a target, its fires park in a delay queue for 5 minutes and retry gradually.

They: Why not just use the database as the queue?

You: Polling 28,000 due rows a second with updates on the same table causes lock contention; writing to a queue is one append and lets executors scale separately from schedulers.

Close

Trade-off: at-least-once with idempotent fire ids rather than exactly once. I'd watch fire lag (scheduled time to enqueue), queue depth, and per-target failure rate; at 10x I go to 512 shards.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
APIAPI Gateway + ECSAPI Gateway + Cloud Run
Schedule storeDynamoDB (GSI on shard, next_fire_at)Spanner (index on shard, next_fire_at)
Leader leasesDynamoDB conditional writes (or ZooKeeper on EC2)Spanner transactions (or ZooKeeper on GCE)
Fire queueSQS (plus delay queue)Pub/Sub (plus Cloud Tasks for delays)
WorkersECS Fargate / LambdaCloud Run / GKE
HistoryDynamoDB → S3 after 30 dBigtable → Cloud Storage after 30 d
Managed alternativeEventBridge SchedulerCloud Scheduler/Tasks
Trap: Scanning 10 million rows every second; precompute next_fire_at and index it, then spend the time on leases and the top-of-hour spike.
cards.s: Google (Borg cron), Amazon, Dropbox, Airbnb — the cron-at-scale question

cards.b:
The one idea: A control plane that owns state transitions and a data plane of workers that only execute steps; every transition is an event-sourced history record, so recovery is replay, and a step is a task on a queue with a lease.

Submit DAG + inputs→Planner: ready steps → task queue→Worker leases task, runs, heartbeats→Result event appended to history→Decider advances DAG, retries or completes

Clarify

You: What runs in a step — a container, a function, a call to another service — and how long can a step take?

Interviewer: Any of those; steps run from 1 second to 12 hours.

You: How many workflows run concurrently, and how big is a DAG?

Interviewer: 100,000 active workflows; DAGs up to 500 steps; 1 million step executions a day.

You: What guarantees on step execution and on state if the orchestrator crashes?

Interviewer: Every step runs at least once; a crash must not lose progress or re-run completed steps.

Size it out loud

1M steps a day is 12 a second average, maybe 200 a second at peak — tiny for the control plane. State: 100,000 active workflows x 500 steps x 1 KB of history is 50 GB, fine in one database. The data plane is the hard part: 12-hour steps mean up to 100,000 containers alive at once, so the orchestrator must never hold a thread per step.

Walk through the design

  1. Representation: a DAG is a JSON of steps with upstream ids, retry policy, timeout and compensating step; stored versioned so a running workflow keeps its own version.
  2. Control plane: a decider per workflow shard reads history, computes which steps are ready, and enqueues tasks; it is stateless apart from the history table and can restart anywhere.
  3. Execution: workers pull tasks from per-queue partitions, hold a 60-second lease with heartbeats, and report success or failure with an idempotency key; a lost heartbeat requeues the task.
  4. Retries and timeouts: per-step policy, exponential backoff 10 s to 10 min, max attempts 5; a timer service fires timeouts as events, so a 12-hour step costs one timer row.
  5. History: append-only events (scheduled, started, completed, failed) per workflow; state is a fold over events, which gives replay, audit and exactly-once decisions.

Deep dive

  • Exactly-once decisions, at-least-once steps: the decider is serialized per workflow by a shard lock; a step may run twice after a lost heartbeat, so step authors get an attempt id and must be idempotent.
  • Backfills and fan-out: a map step over 10,000 items expands into child tasks with a concurrency cap per workflow (say 100) so one backfill cannot starve 99,999 other workflows.

Push-backs

They: The orchestrator database is down for 5 minutes.

You: Workers keep running their current steps and buffer results locally; deciders pause. On recovery, results are appended and deciders replay. Nothing completed is re-run because the result event carries the attempt id.

They: How is this different from the cron scheduler?

You: Cron fires things on time; this manages dependencies, state and retries between steps. The scheduler is a trigger source into this; I would not merge them.

They: A workflow of 500 steps with a hot history — does replay get slow?

You: History grows to 2,000 events; the decider checkpoints a snapshot every 100 events and replays only the tail, so recovery is under 50 ms.

Close

Trade-off: event sourcing is more code than a status column but makes crash recovery and audit free. I'd watch task-queue age, decider lag per shard, and retry rate per step type.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
Control planeEKS (Temporal/Cadence or Airflow scheduler)GKE (Temporal/Cadence or Airflow scheduler)
History storeAurora PostgreSQL (or DynamoDB)Cloud SQL (or Spanner)
Task queuesSQS per queuePub/Sub per queue
TimersDynamoDB TTL + EventBridge SchedulerCloud Tasks scheduled delivery
WorkersEKS / ECS Fargate / LambdaGKE / Cloud Run / Cloud Functions
ArtifactsS3Cloud Storage
Managed alternativeStep Functions + MWAAWorkflows + Cloud Composer
Trap: Drawing Airflow and describing the UI; the marks are in the state machine, leases and what happens when the orchestrator dies mid-step.

cards.f: Design: Distributed lock / leader election service
cards.b:
The one idea: A small replicated state machine over Raft holds locks and leases; a lock is a session-bound lease with a fencing token, and watchers get notified on release, so clients do not poll.

Client opens session, heartbeats→Leader proposes 'acquire lock X'→Raft log replicated to 3 of 5→Grant: lease + monotonically increasing token→Session expires → lock released, watchers notified

Clarify

You: What do clients use it for — short locks on a resource, or long-lived leadership for a service?

Interviewer: Both: leader election for about 1,000 services and short locks held for seconds by maybe 10,000 clients.

You: How many lock operations a second and how fast must they be?

Interviewer: A few thousand a second; 10 ms is fine. Correctness beats speed.

You: Must a lock be strictly exclusive even if a client pauses or partitions?

Interviewer: Yes; two holders at once must be impossible for the protected resource.

Size it out loud

10,000 locks at 200 bytes is 2 MB of state — tiny. 5,000 ops a second through a 5-node consensus group with 2 ms replication is fine; one group does 10,000-plus writes a second. Sessions: 11,000 clients heartbeating every 2 seconds is 5,500 heartbeats a second, served by followers. 99.99% availability needs 5 nodes across 3 zones; losing 2 keeps quorum.

Walk through the design

  1. Consensus: 5 nodes, Raft, every write through the leader and committed at majority; reads served from the leader or with a read index so a client never sees a revoked lock as held.
  2. Sessions: a client holds a session with a 10-second TTL kept alive by heartbeats; all its locks are tied to the session and vanish together when it expires.
  3. Fencing: every grant carries a token from a counter that only increases; the protected resource (database, storage) rejects writes with a token lower than the last seen.
  4. Leader election for apps: candidates create an ephemeral sequential node under /election/service; the lowest number leads and watches only its predecessor, so a release wakes 1 client, not 999.
  5. Client library: retries with backoff, re-establishes sessions, and surfaces 'lock lost' as a callback; most bugs in these systems are client bugs.

Deep dive

  • Why fencing tokens: a client can hold a lock, pause for 15 seconds in GC, lose the session, and resume thinking it still holds it. The token lets the resource refuse the stale writer; nothing else does.
  • Lease length trade-off: a 10-second TTL means up to 10 seconds of no leader after a crash; a 2-second TTL fails over faster but false-expires under load. I make it per-lock, default 10.

Push-backs

They: The network partitions and the old leader is on the minority side.

You: It cannot commit, so it steps down after one election timeout; the majority elects a new leader. Clients on the minority side get errors, not stale grants.

They: Can I use Redis SETNX instead?

You: For a best-effort lock, yes. For strict exclusivity across a failover, no: an asynchronous replica can lose the key, and there is no fencing. The question said two holders must be impossible.

They: 10,000 clients watch the same lock.

You: Thundering herd on release; I give out a queue position so each client watches the one ahead of it, and the service coalesces notifications per client.

Close

Trade-off: a consensus group is slower and smaller than a sharded store, so I keep only coordination state in it, never application data. I'd watch leader changes per hour, proposal latency and session expirations.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
Consensus clusteretcd / ZooKeeper on EC2 across 3 AZs (or EKS)etcd / ZooKeeper on GCE across 3 zones (or GKE)
Client discoveryRoute 53 private zoneCloud DNS private zone
Snapshots/backupS3Cloud Storage
Managed near-equivalentDynamoDB conditional writes + TTLSpanner / Firestore transactions with TTL
MonitoringCloudWatch + PrometheusCloud Monitoring + Prometheus
Trap: Hand-waving 'use ZooKeeper'; be ready to explain sessions, ephemeral nodes and why a lock without a fencing token is not a lock.
cards.s: Google (Chubby), Apache ZooKeeper users, HashiCorp, Amazon — the consensus-in-practice question

cards.b:
The one idea: Evaluate flags locally in an SDK against a full ruleset cached in memory; a control plane stores versioned rules and streams changes to servers while mobile clients pull a signed snapshot from a CDN.

Operator edits flag in UI/API→Store versioned rule, audit row→Publish change event (version n)→Server SDKs stream updates; mobile pulls from CDN→Evaluate locally: hash(user) % 100 < pct

Clarify

You: How many flags, how many services evaluate them, and how often does a flag change?

Interviewer: 20,000 flags; 5,000 service instances plus 100 million mobile clients; a few hundred changes a day.

You: What does a flag decide on — just on/off, percentage rollouts, user segments?

Interviewer: All three: boolean, percentage by user id, and rules over attributes like country and plan.

You: How fast must a change reach every evaluator, and what if the service is down?

Interviewer: Under 10 seconds for servers, minutes for mobile; evaluation must keep working with the last known rules.

Size it out loud

20,000 flags at 2 KB of rules is 40 MB total, 10 MB compressed — small enough for every server to hold in memory. Evaluations: 5,000 servers at 1,000 a second each is 5M evaluations a second, all local, zero network. Change fan-out: 300 changes a day to 5,000 servers is 1.5M small pushes a day; mobile pulls a delta on app start, 100M a day at 2 KB is 200 GB a day through the CDN.

Walk through the design

  1. Rule model: Flag{key, variations, rules[attribute matchers], percentage rollout, default}; evaluation order is explicit, first match wins, and the whole thing is a JSON document per environment.
  2. Server SDK: loads the full snapshot at start, keeps a long-lived stream for deltas, evaluates in-process in microseconds; if the stream drops it keeps serving the last snapshot and reconnects.
  3. Mobile: on app start fetch a per-user evaluated bundle (not the rules) from the CDN, signed and with ETag; the device never sees other users' segments.
  4. Consistency of rollouts: percentage buckets use hash(flag key + user id) mod 10,000, so a user stays in the same bucket across services and a 10% to 20% ramp keeps the first 10%.
  5. Safety: every change is a new version with who, when and a diff; kill switch flips bypass approval; staged rollout with auto-revert if an error-rate metric crosses a threshold.

Deep dive

  • Push vs poll: server streaming via SSE gives sub-second fan-out and the relay layer holds 5,000 connections easily; mobile at 100M devices polls with ETags, because 100M open sockets is a different product.
  • Flag debt: every flag records last-evaluated time; a flag unevaluated for 30 days or at 100% for 60 days is flagged for removal, since stale flags are where outages hide.

Push-backs

They: The flag service is completely down for an hour.

You: Nothing changes; every SDK serves its cached rules and mobile uses the last bundle. New deploys start from a snapshot baked at build time plus the CDN copy.

They: Someone flips a flag to 100% and takes down checkout.

You: Changes to flags tagged critical require two approvals and a 5% to 25% to 100% ramp; an automated guard watches checkout error rate and reverts within 60 seconds.

They: Why evaluate in the SDK instead of calling a flag API?

You: 5M evaluations a second as network calls is a new tier 1 dependency with its own outages. Local evaluation adds no latency and fails safe.

Close

Trade-off: local evaluation means a change takes up to 10 seconds, not instant, and every SDK must agree on hashing. I'd watch snapshot age per instance and time from change to 99% of instances.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
Control plane APIECS + API GatewayCloud Run + API Gateway
Rule storeDynamoDB (versioned items)Firestore (versioned docs)
Change fan-outAppSync / SNS → SSE relay on ECSPub/Sub → SSE relay on Cloud Run
Mobile bundlesS3 + CloudFront (signed)Cloud Storage + Cloud CDN (signed)
Audit logDynamoDB Streams → S3Firestore export → BigQuery
Guardrail metricsCloudWatch alarmsCloud Monitoring alerts
Managed alternativeAppConfigFirebase Remote Config
Trap: Designing a lookup API with a cache; the point is that evaluation is local, rollouts are deterministic, and the service being down changes nothing.
cards.s: LaunchDarkly, Meta (Gatekeeper), Netflix, Uber — the 'ship dark, flip later' question

cards.b:
The one idea: A stateless proxy fleet behind an L4 balancer with routing and policies pushed from a control plane; auth and rate limiting decided locally with a shared counter store only for global limits.

Client HTTPS request→L4 balancer → proxy node (TLS end)→Auth: JWT verify or key cache→Rate limit (local + shared Redis)→Route by path/version → backend; 401/429 on deny

Clarify

You: What traffic — public API with keys, internal service-to-service, or both — and how much?

Interviewer: Public and partner APIs, 200,000 requests a second at peak across 300 backend services.

You: What must the gateway do versus leave to services?

Interviewer: Terminate TLS, authenticate, route by path and version, rate limit, and emit metrics; no business logic.

You: Latency budget for the gateway itself?

Interviewer: Under 5 ms added at p99; it is in front of everything.

Size it out loud

200K requests a second at 2 KB in and out is 400 MB/s each way. A proxy node handles about 20K requests a second with TLS and auth, so 10 nodes, 20 for headroom across 3 zones. Auth: JWT verification is a local signature check in 50 microseconds; API-key lookups hit a local cache with a 60-second TTL, so the key store sees 1,000 reads a second, not 200K.

Walk through the design

  1. Data plane: Envoy-class proxies, stateless, 20 nodes; config is a versioned snapshot of routes and policies pushed by the control plane within 5 seconds of a change, applied atomically.
  2. Auth: JWTs verified locally with cached public keys rotated hourly; API keys resolved through an in-memory cache then the key store; a revoked key propagates through a push within 10 seconds.
  3. Routing: longest-prefix match on path plus header-based version; canary weights per route; per-route timeouts, retries (idempotent methods only) and a circuit breaker per backend.
  4. Throttling: two layers — a local token bucket per node for abuse (cheap, approximate) and a sliding window in shared Redis for per-customer plan limits with one round trip.
  5. Observability: one access log line per request with request id, route, status and latency to a stream; metrics per route to monitoring; a trace header injected for backends.

Deep dive

  • Why not put this in the load balancer: L7 balancers do routing but not plan-based quotas, key management or request transformation; a proxy fleet does, and stays vendor neutral.
  • Control plane separation: the UI and API that manage routes can be down for a day and the data plane keeps serving the last snapshot; the gateway must never depend on its own admin service.

Push-backs

They: A backend is slow and ties up gateway connections.

You: Per-route concurrency limits and a 2-second timeout; the circuit breaker opens after 50% failures in 10 seconds and returns 503 fast. Other routes are unaffected because limits are per backend.

They: The Redis used for rate limits dies.

You: Local token buckets keep abuse protection; plan quotas fail open for up to 5 minutes and I log the gap. Blocking all customers because a counter store died is the worse failure.

They: How do you roll out a gateway change safely?

You: Config changes canary to 1 node for 5 minutes with automatic rollback on 5xx rise; binary upgrades roll one zone at a time. The gateway is tier 0.

Close

Trade-off: local rate limits are approximate and shared ones cost a round trip; I split them by purpose. I'd watch added latency p99, 5xx by route, and config propagation time.

Implementation

Edge/L4NLB (+ CloudFront + WAF)Cloud Load Balancing (+ Cloud CDN + Cloud Armor)
Proxy fleetEnvoy on EKS / ECSEnvoy on GKE / Cloud Service Mesh gateways
Control planeECS service + DynamoDB routesCloud Run service + Firestore routes
Auth keys/JWKSCognito or KMS-signed keys; API keys in DynamoDBIdentity Platform or Cloud KMS-signed keys; API keys in Firestore
Rate-limit countersElastiCache RedisMemorystore Redis
Access logsKinesis → S3 → AthenaPub/Sub → BigQuery
Managed alternativeAPI GatewayApigee/API Gateway
Trap: Listing features for 20 minutes; pick auth, routing and throttling, then show the data plane surviving a control plane outage.
cards.s: Amazon, Kong, Google (Apigee), Netflix (Zuul) — every microservices shop

cards.b:
The one idea: An AP registry with heartbeat leases: instances register and renew, clients cache the full catalog with deltas, and health is a mix of liveness heartbeat and active probes, with staleness bounded by the lease.

Instance starts: register(name, ip, port, meta)→Registry stores lease, 30 s TTL→Instance heartbeats every 5 s; prober checks /health→Clients pull deltas every 10 s, cache catalog→Missed 3 heartbeats or failed probe → removed

Clarify

You: How many services and instances, and how often do instances come and go?

Interviewer: 2,000 services, 100,000 instances; autoscaling churns about 1,000 instances an hour, 10,000 during a deploy wave.

You: Who resolves — clients in-process, a sidecar, or DNS?

Interviewer: Clients and sidecars; DNS is a fallback for things we do not control.

You: What is the tolerance for routing to a dead instance?

Interviewer: Under 10 seconds of staleness; a few failed requests are OK, a black hole for a minute is not.

Size it out loud

100,000 instances at 300 bytes is 30 MB for the full registry — every client can hold it. Heartbeats every 5 seconds is 20,000 a second, served by a fleet of registry nodes. Clients: 100,000 instances each pulling a delta every 10 seconds is 10,000 reads a second, trivial. Health checks from a central prober: 100,000 every 10 seconds is 10,000 checks a second across 20 prober nodes.

Walk through the design

  1. Registry: 5 to 9 nodes replicating registrations by gossip or peer sync; availability matters more than a perfectly consistent view, so no quorum on the read path.
  2. Leases: registration carries a 30-second TTL renewed every 5 seconds; 3 missed heartbeats evicts; clients also get 'last seen' so they can prefer fresher entries.
  3. Health: liveness is the heartbeat; readiness is an active HTTP probe of /health every 10 seconds from 2 probers; failing either removes the instance from the healthy set, not the registry.
  4. Client side: SDK or sidecar caches the catalog, applies zone-aware load balancing, and marks an instance bad after 3 consecutive connection failures without waiting for the registry.
  5. Deploy waves: a draining state lets an instance deregister 30 seconds before shutdown so clients stop sending; new instances must pass the readiness probe before they appear.

Deep dive

  • AP vs CP: a Raft-backed registry refuses registrations during a partition, which is exactly when autoscaling needs it; I take gossip plus eventual consistency and bound staleness at 10 seconds.
  • Self-preservation: if the registry suddenly loses heartbeats from 50% of instances, that is a network problem, not 50,000 crashes; it stops evicting and keeps the last known set until heartbeats return.

Push-backs

They: The registry is down for 10 minutes.

You: Clients serve from their cached catalog; new instances cannot register, so a deploy wave pauses. I alert on registry unreachability and freeze deploys automatically.

They: Why not just DNS?

You: DNS TTLs are honored badly, clients cache for minutes, and it carries no health or metadata. I publish DNS from the registry for legacy consumers, but SDK clients use the catalog.

They: A healthy instance returns errors to one client only.

You: The registry cannot see that; the client-side outlier detection ejects it locally for 30 seconds and retries elsewhere. Discovery gives candidates; the client decides.

Close

Trade-off: eventual consistency means up to 10 seconds of stale routes, which I pay for a registry that never blocks registration. I'd watch heartbeat miss rate, catalog delta size, and eviction spikes.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
RegistryConsul / Eureka on EKS (or AWS Cloud Map)Consul / Eureka on GKE (or Service Directory)
ProbersECS tasks per AZCloud Run jobs per zone
Client SDK / sidecarEnvoy sidecars (App Mesh) or libraryEnvoy sidecars (Traffic Director/Cloud Service Mesh) or library
DNS fallbackRoute 53 private zoneCloud DNS private zone
MetricsCloudWatchCloud Monitoring
Registry snapshotsS3Cloud Storage
Trap: Making the registry strongly consistent; the question is about staying available during churn and keeping clients working when the registry is not.
cards.s: Netflix (Eureka), HashiCorp (Consul), Google, Uber — the 'how do services find each other' question

cards.b:
The one idea: Envelope encryption: a hardware-backed root key wraps per-secret data keys; access is by workload identity, not passwords; dynamic short-lived credentials make rotation routine; every access is an audit event.

Service presents workload identity token→Auth: identity → policy → allowed paths→Fetch ciphertext + wrapped data key→KMS unwraps data key (HSM); decrypt, return→Audit event appended; lease timer for dynamic creds

Clarify

You: What secrets — database passwords, API tokens, TLS keys, encryption keys — and how many?

Interviewer: All of them; 200,000 secrets, read by 50,000 service instances, mostly at startup.

You: What does rotation mean here: we generate new credentials, or just store what someone uploads?

Interviewer: Both: static secrets uploaded by owners, and dynamic database credentials we create and expire.

You: Who can read what, and what is the audit requirement?

Interviewer: Per-service identity with least privilege; every read logged with who, what, when, kept 7 years.

Size it out loud

200,000 secrets at 4 KB encrypted is 800 MB. Reads: 50,000 instances reading 10 secrets at startup, with 1,000 restarts an hour, is 3 reads a second steady and 30 a second during a deploy wave — tiny. Dynamic credentials with a 24-hour TTL for 50,000 instances is 50,000 issues a day. Audit: 1M reads a day at 500 bytes is 180 GB a year.

Walk through the design

  1. Encryption: each secret has its own data key; data keys are wrapped by a root key that never leaves the HSM; the store holds only ciphertext, so a database dump is useless.
  2. Identity: no master passwords; a service proves who it is with a platform identity token (instance or pod identity), mapped to a policy of path globs and read/write verbs.
  3. Dynamic secrets: for databases the service creates a user with a 24-hour TTL, hands it out with a lease, and revokes on expiry; rotation is just not renewing.
  4. Static rotation: owners register a rotation function; the service invokes it on a schedule, writes version n+1, keeps n readable for 24 hours so in-flight clients are not broken, then retires n.
  5. Audit: every request writes an immutable event with identity, path, version and outcome to an append-only log shipped to write-once storage with a 7-year retention lock.

Deep dive

  • Unsealing and availability: 3 to 5 replicas on a Raft store auto-unseal from KMS; a KMS outage stops new decrypts, so clients cache secrets in memory and I run in 2 regions.
  • Key rotation vs re-encryption: rotating the root key only re-wraps data keys (200,000 small operations); data keys rotate when a secret is written; I never bulk re-encrypt 800 MB on a schedule.

Push-backs

They: A service instance is compromised — what did the attacker get?

You: Only the secrets its identity is allowed, with the audit log showing exactly which; dynamic creds expire in 24 hours anyway, and I revoke the identity, which kills its leases immediately.

They: A database password rotates and 2,000 instances have the old one.

You: Dual validity: n and n+1 both work for 24 hours; clients re-fetch on an auth failure and on a 1-hour cache TTL. Rotation never breaks a healthy client.

They: Why not store secrets as environment variables set at deploy time?

You: They leak into logs, crash dumps and child processes, and rotating them means a redeploy of everything. Fetch at startup with identity, keep in memory only.

Close

Trade-off: a central secrets service is a hard dependency at startup, so clients cache and the service runs multi-region. I'd watch decrypt latency, failed auth attempts by identity, and secrets past their rotation deadline.

Implementation

Secrets serviceVault on EKS (or Secrets Manager)Vault on GKE (or Secret Manager)
Root key / HSMKMS (CloudHSM-backed)Cloud KMS (Cloud HSM-backed)
Workload identityIAM roles for pods/tasksGKE Workload Identity / service accounts
Encrypted storeRaft on EBS (or DynamoDB)Raft on Persistent Disk (or Firestore)
Audit logCloudWatch Logs → S3 Object LockCloud Logging → Cloud Storage with retention lock
Rotation functionsLambdaCloud Functions
Dynamic DB credsRDS/Aurora IAM authCloud SQL IAM auth
Trap: Saying 'encrypt it and put it in a database'; the question is identity, envelope encryption, and rotating without breaking anyone.
cards.s: HashiCorp (Vault), Amazon, Google, Stripe — the security-flavored design question

cards.f: Design: CI/CD build and deploy platform (canary, rollback)
cards.b:
The one idea: A build service with remote cache produces signed, immutable artifacts; a deploy controller runs a canary state machine per region, judged by metrics, with rollback as a first-class, fast path.

Commit → webhook → pipeline queued→Builder: fetch, cache hit?, test, build image→Sign + push artifact, record provenance→Deploy controller: canary 1% → 10% → 50% → 100% per region→Metric judge fails → automatic rollback

Clarify

You: How many services, commits a day, and how long does a typical build take?

Interviewer: 2,000 services, 20,000 commits a day, builds from 2 to 30 minutes, median 8.

You: What is the deploy target and what is the safety bar?

Interviewer: Kubernetes in 3 regions; a bad deploy must be caught within 10 minutes and rolled back without a human.

You: Do we need hermetic, reproducible builds and artifact provenance?

Interviewer: Reproducible builds and a signed artifact per deploy, yes; supply-chain audits ask for it.

Size it out loud

20,000 builds a day at 8 minutes median is 160,000 build-minutes, about 110 builds running at once on average, 500 at the 10 a.m. peak; 4 cores each is 2,000 cores, autoscaled. Artifacts: 20,000 images at 200 MB is 4 TB a day, dedup by layer brings it to 400 GB. Deploys: 2,000 services deploying 5 times a day is 10,000 deploys, each a 3-region canary of about 30 minutes.

Walk through the design

  1. Build: ephemeral containers from a pinned toolchain image, inputs hashed; a remote cache keyed by input hash skips 60% of steps; tests shard across workers so a 30-minute suite runs in 5.
  2. Artifacts: every build emits an image plus an attestation (source commit, builder, dependencies) signed by the build service; deploys refuse unsigned or non-main artifacts.
  3. Deploy state machine: per region, shift 1%, 10%, 50%, 100% with a 5-minute bake each; regions go one at a time; state lives in a database so a controller restart resumes mid-rollout.
  4. Judgment: compare canary vs baseline on error rate, p99 latency and a service-specific metric; fail if error rate is 2x baseline with 99% confidence; rollback is a pointer flip to the previous artifact.
  5. Rollback: previous artifact and config are kept warm; rollback is the same state machine run in reverse at 100% immediately, under 2 minutes, and it never needs a build.

Deep dive

  • Config and schema: config ships as a versioned artifact deployed by the same canary path; database migrations are expand-then-contract so a rollback of code never needs a rollback of schema.
  • Isolation and cost: builds run in sandboxed pods with no cluster credentials; cache is content-addressed so a poisoned cache entry cannot be injected without the matching input hash.

Push-backs

They: A bad deploy only shows up at 100% under full load.

You: The 50% stage with a 5-minute bake catches most; for the rest, post-deploy monitoring keeps the judge running for 30 minutes at 100% with the same automatic rollback.

They: Two deploys of the same service collide.

You: A per-service deploy lock; the second queues. A hotfix can cancel the first rollout, which rolls back to the last good artifact before the hotfix proceeds.

They: The build queue is 500 deep at 10 a.m.

You: Autoscale builders on queue age with a 2-minute target; prioritize main-branch and hotfix builds over PR builds; cache hits drain the queue faster than new cores do.

Close

Trade-off: 30-minute canaries slow each deploy to make the fleet safe; services opt into faster ramps with better metrics. I'd watch build p50, deploy lead time, rollback rate and change failure rate.

Implementation

Source + triggersCodeCommit/GitHub webhooks → EventBridgeCloud Source Repos/GitHub webhooks → Eventarc
BuildersEKS autoscaled pods (or CodeBuild)GKE autoscaled pods (or Cloud Build)
Remote cacheS3 + ElastiCache indexCloud Storage + Memorystore index
Artifact registryECR (immutable tags, signed)Artifact Registry (immutable tags, signed)
Deploy controllerArgo Rollouts / Spinnaker on EKS (or CodeDeploy)Argo Rollouts / Spinnaker on GKE (or Cloud Deploy)
Canary metricsCloudWatch + Managed PrometheusCloud Monitoring + Managed Prometheus
Pipeline stateAurora PostgreSQLCloud SQL
Trap: Describing a YAML pipeline; the points are in artifact immutability, the canary judge and a rollback that needs no build.
cards.s: Google, Meta, Netflix (Spinnaker), Amazon (CodeDeploy), Uber — the developer-platform question

cards.f: Design: Multi-tenant data lake for thousands of teams
cards.b:
The one idea: One object store with a central catalog as the source of truth, table-format metadata for atomic commits, schema contracts enforced at publish, and policy-based access evaluated by every engine the same way.

Producer registers dataset + contract→Write: engine commits table snapshot→Catalog validates schema vs contract, updates pointer→Policy service: grants, masks, row filters→Consumers query via any engine, same rules

Clarify

You: How many teams and datasets, and what is the total size and growth?

Interviewer: 3,000 teams, 200,000 datasets, 50 PB today growing 2 PB a month.

You: Who reads what — do teams share freely, or is access per dataset with approvals?

Interviewer: Shared by default inside the company, but PII and finance datasets need approval and row or column masking.

You: What stops a producer from breaking 50 downstream consumers with a schema change?

Interviewer: Nothing today; that is the problem. We want contracts.

Size it out loud

50 PB on object storage at about 20 dollars a TB a month is 1M dollars a month before tiering; 40% cold after 90 days halves that. 200,000 datasets with 100 partitions each is 20M partitions in the catalog — a metadata store sized for 10,000 lookups a second. Queries: 3,000 teams running 10,000 jobs a day is 100 jobs a minute, each scanning 1 GB to 10 TB.

Walk through the design

  1. Layout: one bucket per domain, dataset as a table-format table (Iceberg) under a path; the catalog, not the path, is the identity, so moves and compactions never break readers.
  2. Catalog: dataset name, owner, schema versions, contract, SLA, partitions, lineage; backed by a database with a cache; every engine (Spark, Trino, warehouse) resolves tables through it.
  3. Contracts: a producer declares schema, allowed evolution (add nullable columns yes, drop or rename no), freshness SLA and quality checks; a commit that violates it is rejected at publish time.
  4. Access: tags on columns (pii, finance) drive policies; a grant is per dataset per team with an approver; engines fetch a policy bundle and apply row filters and column masks consistently.
  5. Tenancy and cost: per-team compute quotas and a cost ledger attributing storage and scans to the team; a dataset nobody read in 180 days gets a deletion ticket to its owner.

Deep dive

  • Why a table format: without atomic snapshots, a reader mid-write sees half a partition; Iceberg gives atomic commits, schema evolution with column ids, and time travel, which makes contracts enforceable.
  • Catalog scale: 20M partitions do not live in the database; the table format keeps partition manifests in object storage and the catalog holds one pointer per table, so planning scales with the table, not the lake.

Push-backs

They: A producer needs to rename a column that 80 teams read.

You: A rename is a contract violation; they add the new column, dual-write for 30 days, and the catalog shows who still reads the old one; then they deprecate with a date.

They: A team wants to query PII without the masking.

You: They request a grant with a justification; the approver is the dataset owner plus privacy; the grant is time-boxed and every query is logged with the policy version applied.

They: 3,000 teams and one catalog — is it a bottleneck?

You: 10,000 metadata reads a second with a cache in front of the database is fine; writes are 100 commits a second at most. The catalog is small; the data is big.

Close

Trade-off: contracts slow producers down at publish time to save consumers from surprise breakage. I'd watch contract rejections, time-to-grant, and cost per team per month.

Implementation

StorageS3 (Intelligent-Tiering)Cloud Storage (Autoclass)
Table format + catalogIceberg on Glue Data CatalogIceberg via BigLake metastore / Dataplex
Access policyLake Formation (row/column policies)Dataplex + BigQuery policy tags
ComputeEMR on EKS, Athena, Redshift SpectrumDataproc Serverless, BigQuery
Contract validationLambda on catalog eventsCloud Functions on Eventarc
Lineage/metadataDataZone or OpenMetadata on EKSDataplex Data Catalog or OpenMetadata on GKE
Cost ledgerCost and Usage Reports → AthenaBilling export → BigQuery
Trap: Talking about buckets and folders; the lake is the catalog, contracts and policy, and the storage is the easy part.
cards.s: Amazon (BDT), Netflix, Uber, LinkedIn — the platform-level data question

cards.f: Design: Streaming ingestion at 1M events/s, 5-minute freshness
cards.b:
The one idea: A partitioned durable stream with a schema registry at the door, stream processors that dedupe and validate, micro-batched commits to table-format tables every minute, and compaction behind the readers.

Producers → ingest gateway, schema check→Stream: 1,000 partitions by source→Processor: dedupe (24 h key TTL), validate, route→Sink: 1-min micro-batch → Iceberg commit→Readers query tables; quarantine for bad records

Clarify

You: What are the events, how big, and how many distinct sources?

Interviewer: App and service events, 1 KB average, from 500 producers; 1 million a second sustained, 3 million at peak.

You: Where do they land and who reads them — only batch tables, or real-time consumers too?

Interviewer: Both: query-able tables with 5-minute freshness, and a stream other teams can subscribe to.

You: What about duplicates, late events and bad records?

Interviewer: Producers retry, so duplicates exist; late by up to 24 hours; bad records must not block the pipeline.

Size it out loud

1M events a second at 1 KB is 1 GB/s, 86 TB a day raw; columnar compression 5:1 gives 17 TB a day, 6 PB a year. The stream needs 3 GB/s at peak: 60 brokers at 50 MB/s each with 3x replication, or 1,000 partitions. A 5-minute window at 1 GB/s is 300 GB in flight; sink workers write 256 MB files, so about 1,200 files per 5 minutes before compaction.

Walk through the design

  1. Ingest gateway: validates against the schema registry, stamps event time and ingest time, batches 1 MB, and acknowledges only after the stream has replicated to 2 of 3 brokers.
  2. Stream: 1,000 partitions keyed by source and event key, 7-day retention so any consumer can replay; producers get a quota per source so one bad client cannot flood.
  3. Processing: stateful workers dedupe on event id with a 24-hour keyed state, validate fields, and route by event type; invalid records go to a quarantine table with the reason, never dropped silently.
  4. Sink: each worker buffers 60 seconds per table and partition, writes a Parquet file, and a single committer appends files to the Iceberg table in one atomic snapshot; freshness is 1-2 minutes, under the 5-minute SLA.
  5. Compaction: a background job rewrites small files into 512 MB files hourly and expires old snapshots; readers never see the difference because the commit swaps manifests atomically.

Deep dive

  • Exactly-once to the table: the sink uses checkpointed stream offsets and Iceberg commit ids together; on restart it re-reads from the checkpoint and the commit of already-written files is idempotent by file name.
  • Late data: tables are partitioned by event hour; a late event writes into its own hour's partition, and downstream aggregates re-process partitions touched in the last 24 hours rather than only the latest.

Push-backs

They: Peak is 3M a second and the processors fall behind.

You: The stream buffers 7 days, so nothing is lost; freshness degrades. Workers autoscale on consumer lag, and the partition count already supports 3x. I alert when lag passes 3 minutes.

They: A producer changes a field type without telling anyone.

You: The gateway rejects events that fail schema compatibility; the producer gets a 400 and a page; nothing reaches the stream. Compatible changes register automatically.

They: Why micro-batch files instead of writing rows to a database?

You: 1M rows a second into a transactional database is 50-plus nodes for nothing; columnar files on object storage cost 100x less and every engine can read them.

Close

Trade-off: 1-2 minute freshness rather than seconds, which buys exactly-once table commits and cheap storage. I'd watch consumer lag, commit latency, small-file count and quarantine rate.

cards.f: Design: CDC from hundreds of databases
cards.b:
The one idea: Read each database's replication log with a connector that writes ordered change events per table to a stream; an interleaved chunked snapshot bootstraps without locks; sinks upsert into table-format tables by primary key.

Source DB write-ahead/binlog→Connector: read log, decode, stamp LSN→Stream: topic per table, key = PK→Snapshot chunks interleaved with log→Sink: merge-on-PK into Iceberg; consumers subscribe

Clarify

You: How many databases, which engines, and what change rate?

Interviewer: 400 databases, mostly MySQL and PostgreSQL, a few hundred tables each; about 200,000 row changes a second in total.

You: What do consumers need — the latest row state, or every change in order?

Interviewer: Both: an ordered change stream per table, and query-able tables that mirror current state within 10 minutes.

You: How do we get the initial copy of a 5 TB table without stopping writes?

Interviewer: That is for you to design; no locking the source for more than seconds.

Size it out loud

200,000 changes a second at 2 KB (before and after image) is 400 MB/s, 35 TB a day of change log; 7 days of retention is 245 TB on the stream. Connectors: 400 databases, one connector each, 500 changes a second average, 20,000 on the busiest. Initial snapshots: 400 databases at 2 TB average is 800 TB, done in chunks over weeks.

Walk through the design

  1. Capture: a connector per database tails binlog or logical replication slot, converts to a standard envelope {op, before, after, source, lsn, ts_ms}, and commits its offset only after the stream acknowledges.
  2. Ordering: one topic per table partitioned by primary key, so all changes to a row are in order on one partition; cross-table order is not promised and I say so.
  3. Snapshot without locks: read primary-key chunks of 10,000 rows between a low and high watermark written to the log; log events inside the watermarks override the chunk's rows, so the result stays consistent.
  4. Sink: a merge job applies changes to the mirror table by primary key every 5 minutes using Iceberg row-level upserts; deletes become tombstones so late consumers see them.
  5. Schema changes: DDL in the log emits a schema event; the registry evolves the topic schema if compatible, and the connector pauses with an alert if not, rather than writing garbage.

Deep dive

  • Replication slot risk: a paused PostgreSQL connector makes the source retain WAL until disk fills; I alert at 50 GB of slot lag and have a kill switch that drops the slot and re-snapshots rather than taking down the source.
  • Exactly-once semantics: connector restarts re-emit from the last committed LSN, so duplicates appear; every event carries LSN plus table, and sinks apply with 'if LSN greater than stored' so a replay is harmless.

Push-backs

They: A 5 TB table needs re-snapshotting while production is live.

You: Chunked snapshot at 10,000 rows per query with 20 ms sleeps costs the source about 5% CPU and takes 2 days; the watermark trick keeps it consistent with concurrent writes.

They: A consumer wants transactions, not rows.

You: The envelope carries transaction id and a 'last event in txn' marker; a consumer can buffer by txn id. Most do not need it, so I do not pay for it in the default path.

They: The source database fails over to a replica.

You: The connector reconnects, finds the new primary, and resumes from the last LSN that exists on it; events between failover and the last committed offset may replay, which the sinks tolerate.

Close

Trade-off: per-row order only, not global order, to keep the stream partitionable. I'd watch connector lag in seconds, slot or binlog retention on sources, and sink merge latency.

Trap: Proposing 'select where updated_at > last_run'; it misses deletes and in-flight updates. The log is the only honest source.
cards.s: Amazon, Netflix (DBLog), Airbnb (SpinalTap), Stripe — the 'replicate the OLTP world' question

cards.f: Design: Data warehouse / lakehouse with Iceberg
cards.b:
The one idea: Tables as immutable data files plus a tree of metadata; every write is a new snapshot committed by an atomic pointer swap in the catalog, which gives readers isolation, time travel for free, and lets many engines share one table.

Writer produces Parquet files→Build manifest listing new files + stats→Commit: CAS metadata pointer in catalog→Readers plan from snapshot: prune by stats→Maintenance: compact, expire snapshots

Clarify

You: Who writes and who reads — many writers to one table, many engines?

Interviewer: Hourly batch writers plus a streaming writer on the same tables; readers from Spark, Trino and a warehouse engine.

You: What correctness do readers need: can they see a half-written partition?

Interviewer: Never; a read sees a complete snapshot, and we need to query 'as of yesterday' for audits.

You: Size and shape of the big tables?

Interviewer: The largest is 2 PB, partitioned by day, 10 billion rows added daily; most tables are under 1 TB.

Size it out loud

2 PB at 512 MB per file is 4M data files; manifests at 200 bytes a file is 800 MB of metadata, split into manifests per partition so a one-day query reads 1 manifest of 10,000 files. 10 billion rows a day at 100 bytes compressed is 1 TB a day, 2,000 new files. Snapshots: 24 hourly commits plus 1,440 streaming commits a day; keeping 7 days is 10,000 snapshots.

Walk through the design

  1. Metadata tree: catalog pointer → table metadata JSON → manifest list → manifests → data files with column min/max and null counts; a query prunes files by partition and stats before touching data.
  2. Atomic publish: a writer stages files, writes a new metadata JSON, and does a compare-and-swap on the catalog pointer; if another writer committed first, it retries by re-applying its manifest on the new base.
  3. Concurrency: the hourly batch and the streaming writer append to the same table; appends never conflict; a compaction that rewrites files conflicts only with a delete touching the same files and retries.
  4. Time travel: snapshots are retained 7 days with ids and timestamps; 'as of yesterday' is a read of an older pointer; rollback is setting the pointer back, no data copied.
  5. Maintenance: hourly compaction of files under 128 MB into 512 MB, manifest rewrite when manifests exceed 100, snapshot expiry at 7 days, and orphan-file cleanup weekly.

Deep dive

  • Hidden partitioning: partition on day(ts) is stored as a transform, so a reader filtering on ts gets pruning without knowing the layout, and I can change the partition spec without rewriting old data.
  • Row-level changes: copy-on-write rewrites a whole file for one updated row, cheap to read; merge-on-read writes a delete file and defers the cost to readers, cheap to write. Streaming upserts use merge-on-read with compaction every hour.

Push-backs

They: Two writers commit at the same time; who wins?

You: Whoever swaps the pointer first; the other sees the CAS fail, reloads the new metadata, checks for conflicts with its files, and retries. Appends always succeed on retry; overlapping deletes abort.

They: A streaming writer commits every minute — 1,440 snapshots a day. Does planning slow down?

You: Planning reads the current snapshot only; the count matters for the metadata file size, which manifest rewrites keep small. Snapshot expiry keeps the history bounded.

They: Why not just a warehouse engine with its own storage?

You: Lock-in and copies: Spark, Trino and the warehouse all reading one open table removes the 3 copies of 2 PB I would otherwise maintain. The warehouse engine still runs on top of it.

Close

Trade-off: metadata management is now my job, and small-file pressure from streaming writers never goes away. I'd watch files per partition, commit retry rate, and planning time per query.

Trap: Comparing Iceberg, Delta and Hudi for 10 minutes; pick one and explain the atomic commit and the metadata tree.
cards.s: Netflix, Apple, Amazon, Databricks — the table-format question in disguise

cards.f: Design: Managed Spark job platform (control plane vs data plane, fairness)
cards.b:
The one idea: A thin control plane that accepts, queues and tracks jobs, and a data plane of Kubernetes pools that runs drivers and executors; hierarchical fair-share queues with quotas decide who runs next, and every container is tagged for cost.

Submit job (jar/notebook, resources, queue)→Control plane: validate, persist, enqueue→Scheduler: fair-share pick → place driver on pool→Driver requests executors; autoscaler adds nodes→Logs, metrics, lineage → platform stores

Clarify

You: How many jobs a day, how big, and how many teams share the compute?

Interviewer: 50,000 jobs a day from 1,000 teams; from 1 to 2,000 executors; 20% are scheduled, the rest ad hoc or notebooks.

You: What isolation do teams need — separate clusters, or shared with quotas?

Interviewer: Shared pools with per-team quotas and cost attribution; some teams need dedicated capacity for SLAs.

You: What is the bar on job start latency and on fairness?

Interviewer: Under 60 seconds to start; no team can starve another, and a small team must still get its share during a big team's backfill.

Size it out loud

50,000 jobs a day at an average of 20 executors for 30 minutes is 500,000 executor-hours a day, about 21,000 executors live on average, 60,000 at peak — 60,000 nodes of 4 cores if one executor each, or 15,000 16-core nodes. Start latency: pre-warmed pools of 500 nodes per region cover the 60-second target; the rest autoscale in 3 minutes.

Walk through the design

  1. Control plane: an API and a job database with states (queued, scheduling, running, done); it holds no job data, only metadata, so it stays small and multi-tenant; one per region.
  2. Data plane: Kubernetes clusters per environment with node pools (on-demand, spot, dedicated); each job runs as a driver pod plus executor pods in a team namespace with network and secret isolation.
  3. Fair-share scheduling: queues form a tree (org → team → user) with weights and guaranteed minimums; the scheduler picks the queue furthest below its fair share; a backfill can use idle capacity but is preempted back to its guarantee.
  4. Autoscaling and spot: executors run on spot by default with the driver on on-demand; a 500-node warm pool per region hides the 3-minute node start for the 60-second goal.
  5. Cost and observability: every pod carries team and job labels; a nightly job joins node cost with pod runtime into a per-team ledger; logs and the Spark history server are per job in object storage.

Deep dive

  • Shuffle: executors on spot lose local shuffle files when reclaimed; an external shuffle service or remote shuffle on object storage makes executors stateless and keeps spot usable for 80% of the fleet.
  • Preemption policy: only executors are preempted, never drivers; a job gives back executors over 2 minutes, and the Spark dynamic allocation requests them again, so a preempted stage reruns rather than the whole job.

Push-backs

They: A team's backfill asks for 10,000 executors at 9 a.m.

You: They get up to their queue's share immediately and idle capacity beyond it; as other teams submit, their executors above guarantee are preempted over minutes. The backfill finishes slower, nobody else waits.

They: Why Kubernetes instead of YARN on fixed clusters?

You: Per-job isolation, mixed workloads on the same nodes, and autoscaling with spot are native; YARN clusters sit idle at 40% because sizing is per cluster.

They: Job start takes 4 minutes — where did the 60 seconds go?

You: Image pull and node start. I pre-pull the base image on warm nodes, keep 500 warm per region, and cap job image size; p50 start lands at 30 seconds, p99 at 2 minutes.

Close

Trade-off: shared pools with fair share give 70% utilization but weaker tail-latency guarantees than dedicated clusters, which I keep for 10% of teams. I'd watch queue wait by team, preemption rate and cost per executor-hour.

Implementation

SchedulerYunikorn / Volcano on EKSYunikorn / Volcano on GKE

cards.s: Amazon (EMR), Databricks, Netflix, Uber — the 'run everyone's jobs on shared compute' question

cards.b:
The one idea: An entity graph with versioned aspects fed by an event stream from every engine and orchestrator; a search index for discovery and a graph store for lineage traversal, both derived from the same log.

Engines emit metadata/lineage events (OpenLineage)→Stream: metadata change log→Ingest: upsert entity aspects, extract edges→Derive: search index + graph store→UI/API: search, impact analysis, ownership

Clarify

You: What do we catalog — tables only, or also dashboards, pipelines, ML models?

Interviewer: All of them: 200,000 tables, 50,000 pipelines, 10,000 dashboards, 2,000 models.

You: How is lineage captured — people type it in, or we observe it?

Interviewer: Observed from the engines; manual lineage is always stale.

You: What are the main uses: search, impact analysis, or compliance?

Interviewer: All three; an engineer must answer 'what breaks if I drop this column' in seconds.

Size it out loud

260,000 entities with 5 KB of metadata each is 1.3 GB — small. Lineage edges: each pipeline reads 5 tables and writes 1, so 300,000 edges at table level; column level is 20x, 6 million edges. Ingestion: 50,000 pipeline runs a day emit lineage events, under 1 a second. Search: 2,000 users, 20,000 queries a day. Impact queries traverse a graph with a depth of 10, touching up to 10,000 nodes.

Walk through the design

  1. Model: entity URN (dataset, pipeline, dashboard, model, column) with aspects (schema, ownership, tags, docs, stats); each aspect is versioned so the UI shows who changed what and when.
  2. Capture: Spark and warehouse query hooks, the orchestrator, and the BI tool emit run events with inputs and outputs, including column-level mappings when the planner can give them; nothing depends on humans typing lineage.
  3. Storage: the metadata log is the source of truth; a document store holds the latest aspects, a search index is built for discovery, and a graph store holds edges for traversal; all three rebuild from the log.
  4. Impact analysis: downstream traversal from a column with depth 10, deduped, ranked by usage count and owner; results in under 2 seconds from the graph store with edges in memory.
  5. Quality signals: freshness from pipeline runs, usage from query logs, and test results are aspects too, so search ranks a table that is fresh, used by 300 people and owned above one that is stale and orphaned.

Deep dive

  • Column-level lineage from SQL: use the engine's logical plan, not the text, so a star select or CTE chain resolves to exact column mappings; when that fails I fall back to table-level and mark it.
  • Why an event log instead of crawling: crawlers see a table but not who produced it or when; run events carry inputs, outputs, code version and timing, which is what impact analysis and freshness need.

Push-backs

They: Lineage is wrong because a job reads a table it does not declare.

You: Observed lineage comes from the engine's actual reads, not declarations; a hidden read in a UDF is the one gap, and I surface 'lineage confidence' on edges so users know.

They: 200 teams want their own tags and ownership rules.

You: Aspects are extensible: a team registers a new aspect type with a schema; the core model stays small, and search indexes the custom fields generically.

They: Someone needs 'every dashboard that uses PII' for an audit.

You: A tag on a column plus downstream traversal to dashboard entities; it is a graph query of about 10,000 nodes, answered in a few seconds and exportable.

Close

Trade-off: observed lineage is complete only where engines emit it, so coverage is a metric I publish per engine. I'd watch ingestion lag, lineage coverage percent, and search-to-click rate.

Implementation
