cards.f: Design: A/B testing and experimentation platform
cards.b:
The one idea: Deterministic hash-based assignment in an SDK with layers to keep conflicting experiments orthogonal; exposure logging as the join key; a stats engine computing variance-reduced, sequential-safe results daily plus hourly guardrails.

SDK: hash(user, layer salt) → bucket → variant→Log exposure event (user, exp, variant, ts)→Metric events from product pipelines→Stats job: join, compute lift, CI, SRM→Results UI + guardrail auto-stop

Clarify

You: How many experiments run at once, how many users, and where is assignment made?

Interviewer: 500 concurrent experiments, 100 million users; assignment in services and on mobile clients.

You: What metrics, and how fresh must results be?

Interviewer: Conversion, revenue, retention and latency; a daily readout is fine, plus a same-hour guardrail to stop harmful tests.

You: Do experiments interact — can a user be in several?

Interviewer: Yes, many at once, as long as the ones that conflict are kept apart.

Size it out loud

100M users at 10 sessions a day with 500 experiments is up to 5 billion assignment lookups a day, all computed locally by hashing — no service call. Exposure events: 1 per user per experiment per day when actually exposed, maybe 2 billion a day at 200 bytes, 400 GB a day. Daily stats: join 2 billion exposures to metric events for 500 experiments, a 2-hour batch job on 200 executors.

Walk through the design

  1. Assignment: each experiment lives in a layer; hash(user id + layer salt) mod 10,000 gives a bucket; experiments in the same layer split the buckets, experiments in different layers overlap orthogonally.
  2. Config: experiment definitions (layer, buckets, variants, targeting, metrics) are versioned and pushed to SDKs like feature flags; the SDK logs an exposure only when the variant actually changes behavior.
  3. Metrics: a metrics catalog defines each metric once as SQL over the event tables; the stats job computes per-user aggregates, then per-variant means, variance, CI and p-value with CUPED using pre-period data.
  4. Guardrails: an hourly job checks sample-ratio mismatch and crash rate, latency, and error-rate deltas; a breach pauses the experiment through the config service automatically.
  5. Analysis integrity: pre-registered primary metric, minimum run of 1 week, sequential testing so peeking does not inflate false positives, and a readout page that shows power and SRM status first.

Deep dive

  • Sample-ratio mismatch: if a 50/50 test shows 51/49 over a million users, assignment or logging is broken, not the product; the platform refuses to show results on SRM and that catches more bugs than any stats fix.
  • Why log exposures rather than compute assignment in the warehouse: the SDK can decide not to expose (targeting failed, feature not reached); only logged exposures are in the analysis, which keeps the denominator honest.

Push-backs

They: Two experiments change the same checkout button.

You: Same layer, so they split buckets and never overlap on a user. The platform makes conflicts explicit by surface tag so owners pick the layer deliberately.

They: A PM wants results after 2 days.

You: The sequential test gives a valid always-on boundary; it will usually say 'not yet'. I show the expected days to power so the conversation is about waiting, not hacking the stats.

They: A metric is defined differently by two teams.

You: One definition in the metrics catalog with an owner; teams can add a metric but not redefine a shared one; the readout labels which version it used.

Close

Trade-off: a daily batch readout instead of real-time stats to keep the computation cheap and correct; guardrails cover the urgent case. I'd watch SRM rate, exposure log loss and time-to-readout.

cards.b:
The one idea: Two paths over one immutable click log: a streaming aggregator with watermarks and dedupe for the 1-minute dashboard, and a batch recount that produces the exact billing numbers and overwrites the streaming ones.

Click → gateway: validate, stamp, click id→Append to stream, partition by ad id→Stream job: dedupe 1 h, window 1 min, watermark 1 h→Upsert minute counts → serving store→Nightly batch: exact recount from log → billing, overwrite

Clarify

You: How many clicks a second, and what do we count — per ad per minute, per advertiser per day?

Interviewer: 100,000 clicks a second peak, 1 billion a day; counts per ad per minute, rolled up to campaign and day.

You: How accurate and how fresh must the numbers be, and who uses them?

Interviewer: Real-time dashboards within 1 minute can be 1% off; billing at end of day must be exact and auditable.

You: How late can a click arrive, and how do we treat duplicates and fraud?

Interviewer: Up to 1 hour late from mobile; duplicates by click id must count once; fraud is filtered by a separate model whose output we apply.

Size it out loud

100K clicks a second at 300 bytes is 30 MB/s, 26 TB a month raw. Aggregates: 10M active ads x 1,440 minutes is 14 billion rows a day if every ad clicks every minute; in practice 500M rows a day at 50 bytes, 25 GB. Dedupe state: 1 hour of click ids at 100K a second is 360M ids, 16 bytes each is 6 GB across the stream workers.

Walk through the design

  1. Ingest: the gateway assigns a click id (or validates the client's), stamps event time and ingest time, and appends to a stream partitioned by ad id, 7-day retention, so the raw log is the system of record.
  2. Streaming aggregation: keyed by ad id, 1-minute tumbling windows on event time, a 1-hour allowed lateness with a watermark, and a keyed dedupe set of click ids with a 1-hour TTL; late events update the already-emitted window.
  3. Serving: minute counts upsert into a wide-column store keyed by (ad id, minute) with the window version; dashboards read the last 24 hours and roll up to campaign in the query layer.
  4. Reconciliation: a nightly batch reads the raw log for the day, applies the fraud model output, dedupes globally, counts exactly, writes billing tables, and overwrites the streaming numbers for that day.
  5. Checkpointing: the stream job checkpoints state and offsets every 30 seconds; sink upserts are idempotent by (ad id, minute, version), so a restart replays without double counting.

Deep dive

  • Why 'exactly-once-ish': the stream job is exactly-once inside its own state, but the serving store write is at-least-once made safe by idempotent upserts; the batch recount is the only truly exact number, and billing waits for it.
  • Hot ads: one ad gets 20K clicks a second during a Super Bowl spot; the key is pre-aggregated per partition with a random salt of 0 to 9, then merged, so one key never lands on one worker.

Push-backs

They: A click arrives 2 hours late, after the window closed.

You: The streaming path drops it with a counter; the nightly recount includes it because the log kept it. Billing is exact; the dashboard was 1 click off for a day, within the 1% bar.

They: The stream job is down for 30 minutes.

You: The log holds everything; on restart it replays from the checkpoint and catches up at 3x speed in 15 minutes. Dashboards show a gap that fills in; nothing is lost.

They: Why keep both paths — is batch not enough?

You: Batch alone gives advertisers yesterday's numbers; streaming alone cannot be audited or recomputed after a fraud-model change. The log makes both cheap.

Close

Trade-off: two implementations of the same count, which I accept because billing must be re-derivable. I'd watch watermark lag, dedupe-state size, late-drop rate and the stream-vs-batch daily delta.

Trap: Claiming exactly-once end to end; say where it holds, where it is idempotence, and why billing comes from the batch recount.
cards.s: Google, Meta, Amazon Ads, The Trade Desk — the counting-money-at-scale question

cards.b:
The one idea: A columnar OLAP store with real-time and historical segments: events stream into memory segments, get flushed to immutable sorted columns with inverted and star-tree indexes; pre-aggregated rollups serve the common dashboards and raw segments serve the long tail.

Events → stream (partition by time)→Real-time nodes ingest into in-memory segments→Flush: immutable columnar segments → deep store→Broker: scatter query to real-time + historical nodes→Dashboard: merged result in < 1 s

Clarify

You: What are the queries — fixed dashboards with filters, or free-form SQL over raw events?

Interviewer: Mostly fixed dashboards: time series and top-N by a few dimensions, with filters; a little ad hoc.

You: How much data, how fresh, and how fast?

Interviewer: 5 billion events a day; visible within 30 seconds; p95 query under 1 second with 500 concurrent users.

You: How many dimensions and how high is their cardinality?

Interviewer: About 20 dimensions; city and merchant go into the millions, the rest are small.

Size it out loud

5 billion events a day is 58,000 a second, 170,000 at peak. Raw at 200 bytes is 1 TB a day; columnar with dictionary encoding is 150 GB a day, 4.5 TB for 30 days hot. Pre-aggregated to 1-minute by 5 common dimensions cuts 5 billion rows to about 50M a day, a 100x reduction, so a day-range dashboard scans 50M rows in 200 ms on 10 nodes. 500 users at 5 queries a minute is 40 queries a second.

Walk through the design

  1. Ingestion: real-time servers consume stream partitions, build a mutable segment with dictionaries and bitmaps, and serve queries from it immediately; the 30-second freshness is the consumer lag.
  2. Segments: every 15 minutes or 500 MB the segment is sealed, sorted by time then a chosen dimension, compressed, uploaded to deep storage, and handed to historical servers; a segment is replicated 2x.
  3. Indexes: inverted bitmap indexes on the small dimensions, range index on time, and a star-tree index that stores pre-aggregated counts and sums for combinations of the 5 most-used dimensions.
  4. Query path: a broker parses SQL, prunes segments by time, scatters to the servers holding them, merges partial aggregates and applies top-N; a per-query budget of 2 seconds and 1,000 segments.
  5. Rollups and retention: a daily batch rewrites 30-day-old segments to 1-hour granularity (10x smaller) and drops raw at 90 days; dashboards switch granularity by range automatically.

Deep dive

  • Star-tree vs materialized views: a star-tree pre-aggregates inside the segment for any subset of chosen dimensions, so adding a filter does not require a new view; it costs 2 to 5x segment size, which is fine on 4.5 TB.
  • High-cardinality dimensions: merchant with 2M values gets a dictionary and a sorted column, no bitmap; a top-N merchants query scans the column with a filter in 300 ms, and the query layer caps top-N at 1,000.

Push-backs

They: A dashboard filters on a dimension nobody pre-aggregated.

You: It falls back to the raw columnar segments; 1 day is 5 billion rows scanned across 10 nodes, about 3 seconds. I watch which filters are slow and promote them into the star-tree weekly.

They: 500 users hit the same dashboard at 9 a.m.

You: A result cache keyed by query plus segment versions serves identical queries for 30 seconds; the store sees 40 distinct queries a second, well under its 500 a second capacity.

They: Why not just a warehouse like Redshift or BigQuery?

You: They give seconds to minutes, not sub-second with 30-second freshness at 40 queries a second. I keep the warehouse for ad hoc and history and use the OLAP store for the live dashboards.

Close

Trade-off: pre-aggregation makes the designed dashboards fast and everything else ordinary. I'd watch consumer lag, query p95 by dashboard, segment count per server, and the slow-filter list.

Implementation

DashboardsManaged Grafana / QuickSightGrafana / Looker

MonitoringCloudWatchCloud Monitoring
Trap: Answering 'put it in a warehouse'; the question is about segment design, indexes and which aggregates to precompute.
cards.s: Uber, LinkedIn (Pinot), Netflix (Druid), Amazon — the sub-second-over-billions question

cards.f: Design: ML feature store (online + offline, point-in-time correctness)
cards.b:
The one idea: A feature registry defines each feature once; pipelines write timestamped values to an offline table-format store and the latest value to an online key-value store; training joins labels to features with an as-of join so no value from the future leaks in.

Define feature in registry (entity, type, source, TTL)→Batch/stream job computes values with event timestamps→Offline: append (entity, ts, value) to Iceberg table→Online: upsert latest to KV, TTL→Serve: multi-get at inference; as-of join for training

Clarify

You: How many features and entities, and what is the online read load?

Interviewer: 10,000 features across 50 entity types; 100 million users; 500,000 feature lookups a second at p99 under 10 ms.

You: How are features computed — batch daily, streaming, or both?

Interviewer: Both; some update daily, some from a stream within seconds; training uses up to 2 years of history.

You: What is the correctness bar for training data?

Interviewer: A training row must only use feature values that were known at the time of the label; leakage has burned us before.

Size it out loud

100M users x 200 features at 8 bytes is 160 GB online, 480 GB with 3 replicas, fits a 10-node key-value cluster; 500K lookups a second as 50K multi-get calls of 10 entities each. Offline: 10,000 features with daily snapshots for 2 years is 730 snapshots; at 100M rows x 8 bytes a feature that is 800 MB per feature-day, 6 PB if naive, 600 TB with change-only storage and compression.

Walk through the design

  1. Registry: Feature{name, entity, dtype, owner, freshness SLA, source pipeline, online TTL}; one definition feeds both stores, so training and serving cannot drift in meaning.
  2. Offline store: one Iceberg table per feature group partitioned by day, rows (entity id, event ts, values); append-only so every historical value is kept with the time it became known.
  3. Online store: wide-column key-value keyed by entity id with a column per feature and a TTL equal to the feature's freshness SLA; a stale feature returns null, not an old value, by design.
  4. Materialization: batch features are written to offline then copied to online once a day; streaming features are written to online by the stream job and appended to offline by the same job with the same timestamp.
  5. Training data generation: given labels (entity, label ts), an as-of join picks for each feature the latest value with event ts less than label ts; the job runs on Spark and emits a dataset with the registry versions used.

Deep dive

  • Point-in-time correctness: joining on entity id alone gives a 2023 label today's value — leakage. The as-of join sorts both sides by (entity, ts) and merges, 10x cheaper than a window function over 600 TB.
  • Training-serving skew: the same transformation code runs in the batch job and the stream job via a shared library, and a daily check samples 10,000 entities and compares offline latest to online values; a 1% mismatch pages the owner.

Push-backs

They: A model at inference reads a feature that updated 5 minutes ago in the stream — what did training see?

You: The same semantics: offline has the value with its 5-minute-old timestamp, so training rows with labels after that time see it, earlier ones do not. The timestamp is the contract.

They: 500K lookups a second with p99 under 10 ms — one KV cluster?

You: Multi-get batches 10 entities into one call, so 50K calls a second across 10 nodes; local SSD-backed wide-column stores do 5K to 10K calls a second a node at 5 ms p99. I add a 1-second in-process cache for the hottest entities.

They: Why not compute features at request time from raw data?

You: A 30-day count over raw events per request is 100 ms and 1,000x the read load; precomputed features are the whole point, and request-time features stay for the few that must be instant.

Close

Trade-off: the online store returns null past TTL rather than a stale value, which models must handle; that is safer than silent staleness. I'd watch online p99, materialization lag per feature, and the daily skew-check mismatch rate.

Implementation

RegistryDynamoDB + ECS API (or SageMaker Feature Store catalog)Firestore + Cloud Run API (or Vertex AI Feature Store registry)
Offline storeS3 + Iceberg via Glue CatalogCloud Storage + Iceberg via BigLake / BigQuery
Online storeDynamoDB (TTL) or ElastiCacheBigtable (GC policy) or Memorystore
Batch materializationEMR on EKS (Spark), scheduled by Step FunctionsDataproc Serverless (Spark), scheduled by Cloud Composer
Streaming featuresManaged Service for Apache Flink (MSF) from KinesisDataflow from Pub/Sub
Training data jobsEMR on EKS / SageMaker ProcessingDataproc Serverless / Vertex AI Pipelines
Managed alternativeSageMaker Feature StoreVertex AI Feature Store
Trap: Describing two databases and a copy job; the question is the as-of join, timestamps as the contract, and keeping training and serving transformations identical.
cards.s: Uber (Michelangelo), Airbnb (Zipline), Amazon, LinkedIn — the ML-platform data question

cards.b:
The one idea: Route each user to a home region with anycast DNS, replicate data asynchronously to the others, and fail over by changing routing, not by changing code.

User → anycast / latency DNS→Nearest healthy region→Home-region write + async replicate→Read served locally→Region fails → DNS shifts traffic

Clarify

You: Is the goal latency for global users, or surviving a whole region going down, or both?

Interviewer: Both: users get a nearby region, and losing one region must not take us down.

You: What is the consistency need on writes — can two regions accept writes to the same record?

Interviewer: Mostly single-owner data; a user's data is written from one region at a time, but we cannot lose writes.

You: How many regions, and what traffic?

Interviewer: 3 regions, 50,000 requests a second total, 10% writes.

Size it out loud

50K requests a second across 3 regions is about 17K each; if one fails the other two take 25K each, so I size every region for 2x its share. 5K writes a second replicated to 2 peers is 10K cross-region writes a second; at 1 KB each that is 10 MB a second of replication. Cross-region round trip is 70-150 ms, so sync replication on every write would cost more than the request.

Walk through the design

  1. Routing: latency-based DNS with health checks and a 30-second TTL; a global accelerator or anycast IP removes even the TTL wait for most clients.
  2. Data: a global table with async replication, under 1 second lag; each record has a home region and conflicts resolve last-writer-wins on a hybrid clock.
  3. Stateless compute in every region behind its own load balancer; configuration and secrets replicated so a region can run alone.
  4. Failover: health checks fail 3 times in 30 seconds, DNS pulls the region, sessions re-home to the next region; writes made in the last second may replay.
  5. Capacity: every region runs at under 50% so losing 1 of 3 regions leaves headroom; I test this with a quarterly region evacuation drill.

Deep dive

  • Write conflicts: with one home region per user, conflicts only happen during failover; I keep a version vector so the merge is explicit rather than silent.
  • Why not synchronous multi-region: 3 round trips of 100 ms each per write kills p99; Spanner-style systems do it with TrueTime, and I'd name that as the alternative at a cost.

Push-backs

They: A user writes in region A, A dies, the user reads from region B before replication caught up.

You: They see data up to 1 second stale. I bound it: show the client a version token, and B serves 'retry' for a request whose token is newer than its replica.

They: Two regions both think they own a user after a partition.

You: Ownership is a lease in the global table with a 10-second TTL; a region that cannot renew stops writing for that user. Split brain costs me availability for a few users, not corruption.

They: How do you deploy without breaking all 3 regions at once?

You: One region at a time, 1 hour apart, with automatic rollback on error rate; a bad build never reaches region 2.

Close

Trade-off: async replication means a failover can lose up to 1 second of writes; I say that number out loud and get it signed off. I'd watch replication lag and per-region error rate; at 10 regions I'd cell-partition users rather than replicate everything everywhere.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
Global routingRoute 53 latency routing + Global AcceleratorCloud DNS + global Cloud Load Balancing (anycast)
ComputeECS/EKS per region behind ALBGKE/Cloud Run per region
DataDynamoDB Global Tables (or Aurora Global Database)Spanner multi-region (or Firestore multi-region)
CacheElastiCache per regionMemorystore per region
Config/secretsSecrets Manager replicatedSecret Manager automatic replication
Health and failoverRoute 53 health checks + CloudWatchLoad balancer health checks + Cloud Monitoring
Trap: Promising strong consistency across 3 regions with no latency cost; pick async with a stated RPO or sync with a stated latency, and defend one.
cards.s: Netflix, Google, Amazon — any team that has lived through a regional outage

cards.f: Design: Disaster recovery for a stateful system (RTO/RPO tiers)
cards.b:
The one idea: Tier the systems by RTO and RPO, pay for a live replica only where the 15-minute target demands it, and rehearse the failover so the runbook is real.

Primary region serves writes→Tier 1: streaming replica in region B→Tier 2/3: snapshots to cross-region storage→Disaster → promote replica, flip DNS→Tier 2 restore from snapshot

Clarify

You: What are the RTO and RPO targets, and are they the same for every system?

Interviewer: Tier 1 payments: RTO 15 minutes, RPO near zero. Tier 2 reporting: RTO 4 hours, RPO 1 hour. Tier 3: next day.

You: What kind of disaster — a region, a bad deploy, or a deleted table?

Interviewer: All three; the region loss is the one the auditor cares about, the deleted table is the one that actually happens.

You: What is the data size and write rate for Tier 1?

Interviewer: 2 TB in a relational database, 3,000 writes a second.

Size it out loud

2 TB restored from a snapshot at 500 MB a second is about 70 minutes — too slow for a 15-minute RTO, so Tier 1 needs a live replica. 3,000 writes a second at 1 KB is 3 MB a second of log shipping, trivial for a cross-region link. Tier 2 at RPO 1 hour means hourly snapshots; 24 a day of 500 GB incremental is cheap. A warm standby costs about 60% of production; a pilot light about 10%.

Walk through the design

  1. Tier 1: a cross-region read replica with under 1 second lag, promotion scripted; DNS flip and app config pointing at the new writer in under 10 minutes.
  2. Tier 2: hourly snapshots copied to another region with a 35-day retention; restore is a scripted job tested monthly, measured at 90 minutes.
  3. Tier 3: nightly backups to cold storage, restore on request; cost is dominated by storage, about 3 cents a GB a month.
  4. Point-in-time recovery: continuous log backup so a deleted table at 14:03 can be restored to 14:02; this covers the disaster that actually happens.
  5. Runbook and drills: one named person, one command, a quarterly game day with the real database, and the measured RTO on a dashboard.

Deep dive

  • RPO near zero vs zero: zero needs synchronous commit to the second region, costing 50-100 ms per write; 'near zero' with async replication loses the last second. I ask which one the auditor wrote down.
  • Backups that are never restored are not backups: restore time must be measured, and the restore must land in a clean account so ransomware on the primary cannot touch it.

Push-backs

They: The replica was corrupted by the same bad write that corrupted the primary.

You: Replication copies the bug. That is why point-in-time recovery from logs exists alongside the replica; I rewind to before the bad write, which costs RPO but saves the data.

They: Failover happened; how do you fail back?

You: I do not rush it. The old primary becomes a replica of the new one, catches up, and I flip back during a maintenance window. Failing back under pressure is how you lose data twice.

They: How do you know the standby still works after 6 months?

You: Automated: every week the pipeline restores a snapshot, runs a row-count and checksum against production, and alerts on drift. A drill that nobody runs is a wish.

Close

Trade-off: a warm standby for Tier 1 roughly doubles that database's cost; I spend it only on the 15-minute tier. I'd watch replica lag, last successful restore test, and backup age per system.

Implementation

Tier 1 replicaAurora Global Database or RDS cross-region replicaCloud SQL cross-region replica or Spanner
SnapshotsRDS automated snapshots copied cross-regionCloud SQL backups to another region
Cold backupsS3 Glacier with Object LockCloud Storage Archive with retention lock
Point-in-timeRDS PITR / DynamoDB PITRCloud SQL PITR / Firestore PITR
Failover routingRoute 53 health-check failoverCloud DNS + load balancer failover
RunbooksSystems Manager AutomationWorkflows
Drill alertsCloudWatch + EventBridgeCloud Monitoring + Cloud Scheduler
Trap: Treating one DR plan as right for everything; the interviewer wants to hear you price each tier and admit backups are useless until restored.
cards.s: Banks, Amazon, Microsoft — the question behind every compliance audit

cards.f: Design: Zero-downtime database migration (dual-write, backfill, cutover)
cards.b:
The one idea: Dual-write behind a flag, backfill history underneath it, verify the two stores agree, then flip reads and finally writes — each step reversible.

App writes old store (flag off)→Flag: write old + new→Backfill job copies history→Verifier compares chunks→Reads → new, then writes → new only

Clarify

You: What are we moving from and to, and why?

Interviewer: From a single Postgres with 5 TB to a sharded store; the old one is at 80% CPU and cannot be upgraded further.

You: Can we tolerate any read-only window or data loss?

Interviewer: No downtime; a few seconds of elevated latency is fine. Zero lost writes.

You: Does the schema change, or only the engine?

Interviewer: Both: the new store is keyed by customer id and drops two columns.

Size it out loud

5 TB backfilled at 100 MB a second is about 14 hours; I throttle to 50 MB a second to spare the old database, so 28 hours. 2,000 writes a second dual-written adds 2,000 writes to the new store, which it is sized for 10x. Verification compares 1 billion rows by hashed chunks of 10,000 rows, 100,000 chunk comparisons, done in an hour.

Walk through the design

  1. Step 1 dual-write: the app writes the old store, then the new one; a failure on the new side is logged and queued for repair, never surfaced to the user.
  2. Step 2 backfill: a job walks the old table by primary key in 10,000-row pages, upserting into the new store; dual-writes that arrive later win on a version column.
  3. Step 3 verify: hash each 10,000-row chunk in both stores and compare; mismatches go to a repair queue and I do not proceed until drift is 0 for 24 hours.
  4. Step 4 shadow reads: read from both, serve old, log differences at 1% sampling; then flip reads to new by percentage, 1, 10, 50, 100.
  5. Step 5 cutover writes: stop writing old, keep it as a read-only fallback for 2 weeks, then drop it. Every step is a flag I can flip back in seconds.

Deep dive

  • Ordering problem: a dual-write and a backfill of the same row can race; a monotonic version per row (updated_at or a sequence) makes the upsert last-write-wins safe.
  • Why not change-data-capture instead of app dual-write: CDC avoids touching app code and is my choice when the schema is the same; with a reshape, app-level dual-write keeps the transform in one place.

Push-backs

They: The write to the new store succeeds and the write to the old store fails.

You: I write old first because it is the source of truth until cutover; if old fails the request fails and new was never written. Old-then-new, never the reverse.

They: The backfill is hammering the old database.

You: It is throttled to a target of 20% extra CPU and backs off on replica lag; 28 hours instead of 14 is fine. I never run it against the primary if a replica can serve it.

They: Two columns are dropped; what if someone still needs them?

You: I keep them in a side table keyed by the same id for 90 days. A migration that destroys data on day 1 has no undo.

Close

Trade-off: dual-writing doubles write cost and adds code for weeks; the price of zero downtime. I'd watch drift count, backfill lag, and the shadow-read mismatch rate, and I would not flip writes until all are zero.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
Old storeRDS PostgresCloud SQL Postgres
New storeDynamoDB or Aurora shardedSpanner or Bigtable
Backfill jobAWS Batch or GlueDataflow
CDC optionDMSDatastream
Repair queueSQSPub/Sub
FlagsAppConfigFirestore config doc or Cloud Deploy params
Verification metricsCloudWatchCloud Monitoring
Trap: Describing a one-shot copy and a weekend cutover; the question is the reversible step list and how you prove the two stores agree.
cards.s: Stripe, Shopify, Uber — every company that outgrew its first database

cards.f: Design: Deployment system with canary and automatic rollback
cards.b:
The one idea: Immutable builds rolled out in stages, with a canary compared to a baseline of the same size, and an automatic rollback when the comparison fails.

Merge → build image, tag by commit→Deploy 1% canary + 1% fresh baseline→Compare error, latency, saturation for 10 min→Pass → 10/25/50/100%→Fail → route back to old image

Clarify

You: How many services and deploys a day, and what is the fleet size per service?

Interviewer: 500 services, about 2,000 deploys a day; typical service runs 20 to 500 instances.

You: Who decides a deploy is bad — a human, or the system?

Interviewer: The system within 15 minutes; a human can always override.

You: Stateless services only, or schema changes too?

Interviewer: Stateless here; schema changes have their own process and must be backward compatible.

Size it out loud

2,000 deploys a day is about 1 every 40 seconds in business hours. A 500-instance service canaried at 1% is 5 instances; at 1,000 requests a second per instance the canary sees 5,000 a second, so a 1% error rate difference is visible in under 1 minute at 99% confidence. Full rollout in 5 steps of 1, 10, 25, 50, 100% at 10 minutes each is about 50 minutes; a rollback is a redirect to the old image in under 2 minutes.

Walk through the design

  1. Artifacts: one immutable image per commit, signed; deploy means pointing a target group at a new image, rollback means pointing it back.
  2. Canary vs baseline: I deploy the new build to 1% and the old build to a fresh 1% at the same time, so I compare like with like and not against warmed-up instances.
  3. Analysis: error rate, p99 latency, CPU and memory, plus 2 service-owned metrics; each must stay within a tolerance; 10 minutes per stage; a failed stage triggers rollback with no human.
  4. Rollout: 1, 10, 25, 50, 100% with a bake at each; per-region order, never two regions at once; a freeze window before major events.
  5. Rollback: traffic shift to the previous image first, then instance replacement; config and feature flags roll back together with the image to avoid a half-state.

Deep dive

  • Statistical honesty: with 5 canary instances I use a Mann-Whitney style comparison across instances, not a single aggregate; one noisy host should not fail or pass the whole deploy.
  • Backward compatibility: during the 50 minutes both versions run; APIs, message formats and database reads must work on both, which is why schema changes are separate and expand-then-contract.

Push-backs

They: A bug only shows up at 100% because it is a cache-key change that interacts across instances.

You: The canary cannot catch every bug; the 100% stage still bakes for 10 minutes with the same checks and rolls back. I'd also add a shadow-traffic stage for services that touch shared caches.

They: Rollback itself fails because the old image was garbage-collected.

You: Images are retained for 30 days and the last 10 known-good versions are pinned; rollback that depends on a rebuild is not rollback.

They: 2,000 deploys a day; the analysis service becomes the bottleneck.

You: It is stateless, reads metrics from the time-series store, and runs one evaluation per minute per deploy; 200 concurrent deploys is 200 queries a minute, nothing.

Close

Trade-off: 50 minutes to full rollout slows urgent fixes; I give a break-glass fast path that skips bakes with a named approver. I'd watch rollback rate per service and time-to-detect; a canary that never fails is not measuring anything.

Implementation

Traffic shiftingALB weighted target groupsCloud Run revisions / GKE Gateway weighted routing
MetricsCloudWatchCloud Monitoring
Canary analysisLambda or Step Functions against CloudWatchCloud Functions or Workflows against Cloud Monitoring

Trap: Describing blue-green and stopping; the points are the baseline-vs-canary comparison and what makes rollback actually work at 2 a.m.
cards.s: Google, Meta, Netflix — the infrastructure interview for platform teams

cards.f: Design: DDoS protection and edge rate limiting
cards.b:
The one idea: Absorb volumetric attacks at a provider's anycast edge, then score HTTP requests at the edge with per-IP, per-ASN and per-fingerprint limits, and protect origin with a hard admission cap.

Traffic → anycast edge network→L3/L4 scrubbing: SYN cookies, drop junk→L7 rules: WAF, rate limit, bot score→Challenge or block suspects→Clean traffic → origin behind cap

Clarify

You: What layer are the attacks — volumetric packets, or HTTP floods that look like users?

Interviewer: Both: 500 Gbps SYN floods happen a few times a year; 1 million requests a second HTTP floods happen monthly.

You: What is normal traffic, and how much of it is logged-in users?

Interviewer: 20,000 requests a second normal, 100,000 at peak; 70% are logged in.

You: How much false positive can we take?

Interviewer: Blocking 0.1% of real users during an attack is acceptable; blocking 5% is not.

Size it out loud

A 1M requests a second flood is 10x our peak, so origin cannot absorb it; the edge must drop 90%+ before it reaches us. 500 Gbps volumetric needs a network with at least 10x that capacity, which means a provider, not me. Per-IP state for 10 million distinct IPs at 100 bytes each is 1 GB per edge location, fine. A challenge page costs the edge 1 ms of CPU; 1M a second across 50 edge locations is 20K a second each.

Walk through the design

  1. Network layer: anycast spreads 500 Gbps across 50+ locations; SYN cookies and packet signatures drop floods without state; origin IPs are never public.
  2. Edge rate limits: sliding windows per IP (100 a second), per ASN, per JA3 TLS fingerprint and per path; logged-in users get per-account limits that are more generous.
  3. Bot scoring: cheap signals first — missing headers, impossible user agents, request timing — then a JavaScript or managed challenge for mid scores; block only high scores.
  4. Origin protection: a token bucket at the load balancer capped at 150K a second; above that the edge serves cached or static responses rather than letting origin fall over.
  5. Playbook: attack mode flips the challenge threshold lower and caches more aggressively; it is a one-click switch, tested quarterly against a traffic generator.

Deep dive

  • Why per-IP alone fails: a 10,000-node botnet sends 100 a second each and sits under every per-IP limit; the ASN, fingerprint and path dimensions catch the shape, not the source.
  • Logged-in users as the safe set: sessions established before the attack get a signed cookie and a higher budget; new anonymous sessions bear the challenge, which keeps the 0.1% false-positive target.

Push-backs

They: The attacker targets an expensive endpoint like search with 5,000 real-looking requests a second.

You: Per-path limits and cost-weighted budgets: search costs 50 tokens, a static page 1. I also cache search for anonymous users for 60 seconds, so the expensive path is served from the edge.

They: Residential proxies make every IP look like a home user.

You: Then IP is a weak signal and I lean on fingerprint, behavior and the challenge; a human can solve one challenge per session, a bot cannot solve 1M a second at any price I care about.

They: Origin falls over anyway.

You: Load shedding: the load balancer admits 150K a second, the rest get a cached page or a 503 with Retry-After; a half-working site beats a dead one.

Close

Trade-off: challenges annoy some real users during an attack; I accept it for anonymous traffic only. I'd watch edge block rate, challenge solve rate, and origin saturation; a solve rate under 50% means I am blocking people.

Implementation

Volumetric scrubbingAWS Shield AdvancedCloud Armor Adaptive Protection
Edge and cachingCloudFrontCloud CDN
L7 rules and bot scoringAWS WAF with Bot ControlCloud Armor rate limiting + reCAPTCHA Enterprise
Origin capALB + target-group limitsCloud Load Balancing + backend capacity
Origin hidingOrigin access + security groupsPrivate backends + IAP
Attack dashboardsCloudWatch + Shield metricsCloud Monitoring + Cloud Armor logs
DNSRoute 53Cloud DNS
Trap: Saying 'put it behind Cloudflare' and stopping; name the layers, the signals beyond IP, and what protects origin when the edge lets something through.
cards.s: Cloudflare, Akamai, AWS — and any consumer company that was taken down once

cards.f: Design: Cache stampede and hot-key handling
cards.b:
The one idea: Only one request rebuilds a key (a lock or single-flight), others serve stale; refresh hot keys early; and replicate hot keys across shards and local memory.

Request → local in-process cache→Miss → Redis shard (key + replica suffix)→Miss + lock won → rebuild from DB→Lock lost → serve stale or wait 50 ms→Hot-key detector promotes keys

Clarify

You: What is the cache in front of, and how expensive is a miss?

Interviewer: A product page built from 5 database queries, 50 ms per miss; 200,000 reads a second at peak with a 98% hit rate.

You: What is the hot-key situation — a few keys with most traffic?

Interviewer: A flash sale puts 30% of traffic on one product id for 10 minutes.

You: Can we serve slightly stale data?

Interviewer: Up to 30 seconds stale is fine.

Size it out loud

200K reads a second at 98% hit is 4K misses a second, each 50 ms, so 200 concurrent database queries — fine. A stampede when a hot key expires: 60K requests a second for one key all miss at once; 60K x 50 ms is 3,000 concurrent queries, which takes the database down. One Redis shard does about 100K reads a second; a 60K-a-second key on one shard eats 60% of it.

Walk through the design

  1. Single-flight: on a miss, SET NX a lock key with a 5-second TTL; the winner rebuilds and writes; losers return the stale value if present or wait up to 50 ms and retry.
  2. Stale-while-revalidate: store value plus a soft TTL of 30 seconds and a hard TTL of 5 minutes; after the soft TTL, serve stale and trigger a background refresh.
  3. Probabilistic early refresh: each read refreshes with probability that rises as expiry nears, so popular keys never actually expire; cold keys expire normally.
  4. Hot-key replication: a sampler counts keys per second in each server; a key over 5,000 a second is written under 10 suffixed copies spread across shards, and reads pick one at random.
  5. Local cache: a 1-second in-process cache per app server for keys flagged hot cuts Redis load for the top 100 keys by 100x.

Deep dive

  • TTL jitter: set TTLs to 300 plus or minus 30 seconds so a deploy that warms 1 million keys at once does not expire them all at once 5 minutes later.
  • Cache warming on deploy: new instances start with empty local caches; I warm the top 10,000 keys from a list before taking traffic, or roll out slowly enough that Redis absorbs it.

Push-backs

They: The lock holder crashes mid-rebuild.

You: The lock TTL of 5 seconds expires and the next miss wins the lock; meanwhile everyone serves stale. Nobody blocks longer than the TTL.

They: Redis itself goes down.

You: The local 1-second cache keeps the hottest keys alive; everything else goes to the database with a per-server concurrency cap of 20 queries, so the database degrades instead of dying.

They: A key must be invalidated immediately on a price change.

You: Publish an invalidation; every app server drops its local copy and Redis deletes the key and its 10 replicas. The 30-second staleness budget is a ceiling, not a promise to be slow.

Close

Trade-off: serving stale means a user can see a price 30 seconds old during a sale; the product owner signed that. I'd watch miss rate per key, lock wait time, and the hot-key list; at 10x I'd move the top keys to the CDN.

Implementation

CacheElastiCache Redis clusterMemorystore Redis cluster
App servers with local cacheECS/EKSGKE/Cloud Run
DatabaseAurora with read replicasCloud SQL with read replicas
Invalidation busSNS or Redis pub/subPub/Sub
Hot-key metricsCloudWatch + custom samplerCloud Monitoring + custom sampler
Edge for top keysCloudFrontCloud CDN
Trap: Talking only about hit rate; the interviewer wants the miss storm math and the three mechanisms that keep one key from killing the database.
cards.s: Meta, Twitter, Shopify — the question after you say 'just add a cache'

cards.f: Design: Idempotent retries and exactly-once-ish processing
cards.b:
The one idea: Clients send an idempotency key; the server stores the result under that key in the same transaction as the side effect; consumers dedupe by message id and make every step a conditional write.

Client POST with Idempotency-Key→Lookup key: hit → replay stored response→Miss → do work + store result atomically→Publish event with same key→Consumer: processed-ids table, conditional write

Clarify

You: Where do retries come from — clients, our own queue consumers, or both?

Interviewer: Both: mobile clients retry on timeout, and the order pipeline is at-least-once from a queue.

You: What is the cost of a duplicate?

Interviewer: A double charge or a double shipment; both are unacceptable. A duplicate email is annoying but survivable.

You: What volume and how long must we remember a request?

Interviewer: 5,000 requests a second; a client may retry for up to 24 hours.

Size it out loud

5,000 a second for 24 hours is 432 million idempotency keys; at 100 bytes each that is 43 GB in a key-value store with TTL, cheap. A write that checks-then-inserts costs 1 extra round trip of 1 ms. Queue redelivery under normal operation is under 0.1%, but after a consumer crash a batch of 1,000 messages replays at once, so dedupe must be per message, not per batch.

Walk through the design

  1. API: Idempotency-Key header, scoped to the account; first request inserts key with state 'in progress', does the work, then stores the response; a retry returns the stored response.
  2. Atomicity: the key row and the business write live in the same database transaction, so I never charge without recording the key or record without charging.
  3. Concurrent duplicates: the 'in progress' row makes the second request wait or get a 409 for up to 30 seconds, instead of both doing the work.
  4. Consumers: each message carries the key; the consumer inserts into a processed table with 'only if absent' before side effects; outbox pattern so publish and commit cannot diverge.
  5. External calls: pass the same key downstream to the payment provider, which has its own idempotency; retries all the way down carry one identity.

Deep dive

  • Exactly-once is a lie across systems; what I build is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent effects, which looks exactly-once from the outside. I say that sentence in the interview.
  • Key mismatch: the same key with a different request body is a client bug; I return 422 rather than replay, because replaying the wrong operation silently is worse.

Push-backs

They: The client never sends a key.

You: Then I derive one from account plus a hash of the body plus a 5-minute bucket; weaker, but it catches the double-tap, which is 90% of the problem.

They: The transaction commits, then the server crashes before responding; the client retries.

You: The key row is committed with the result, so the retry gets the stored response. The commit is the point of no return, which is why the response is stored inside it.

They: A consumer processes a message, crashes before acking, the message redelivers to another consumer.

You: The processed table rejects the insert and the second consumer acks without doing the work. The table is the truth, the ack is just housekeeping.

Close

Trade-off: storing keys and responses for 24 hours costs 43 GB and 1 ms per request; cheap insurance against a double charge. I'd watch duplicate-hit rate and 'in progress' timeouts, which point at slow downstreams.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
APIALB + ECSCloud Load Balancing + Cloud Run
Idempotency keysDynamoDB with TTL (conditional writes)Firestore with TTL (transactions)
Business dataAurora Postgres (same transaction via outbox)Cloud SQL Postgres (same transaction via outbox)
QueueSQS FIFO with deduplication idPub/Sub with ordering keys + dedupe table
ConsumersECS or LambdaCloud Run or Cloud Functions
Outbox relayDynamoDB Streams / Debezium on EC2Datastream / Debezium on GKE
Trap: Claiming 'exactly-once' from the queue's checkbox; the interviewer wants the key, the transaction boundary, and the crash-between-commit-and-reply case.
cards.s: Stripe, Square, Uber — the question hiding inside every payments design

cards.f: Design: Backpressure and load shedding under overload
cards.b:
The one idea: Bound every queue, reject early by priority when a bound is hit, and let pressure flow upstream as fast 503s with Retry-After so clients back off instead of piling on.

Requests tagged with priority→Admission: concurrency limit per service→Over limit → shed lowest priority, 503→Downstream signals: latency, queue depth→Clients back off with jitter

Clarify

You: What happens today when traffic exceeds capacity?

Interviewer: Latency climbs, queues grow, everything times out, and we serve nothing to anyone for 20 minutes.

You: Are some requests more important than others?

Interviewer: Yes: checkout beats browsing, logged-in beats anonymous, and health checks must always pass.

You: Is the overload at the edge or in a deep dependency?

Interviewer: Usually a database or a downstream service; the edge is fine.

Size it out loud

Capacity 50,000 requests a second at p99 of 200 ms; a 2x spike means 100K arriving. With a queue and no shedding, 50K a second pile up; in 10 seconds the queue holds 500K requests, each waiting 10 seconds and timing out at 5 — 100% failure. Shedding the lowest 50% keeps the top 50K a second at 200 ms. A bounded queue of 2x concurrency, say 400 slots, adds at most 1 extra p99.

Walk through the design

  1. Priority tagging at the edge: 4 classes — critical, high, default, sheddable — carried as a header; checkout is critical, recommendations are sheddable.
  2. Adaptive concurrency: each service measures its own p99 and queue wait, lowers its concurrency limit when latency rises (gradient or AIMD), raises it when healthy; no fixed numbers to tune.
  3. Shedding order: when the limit is hit, drop sheddable first, then default; critical is dropped only when the process itself is unhealthy. Reject in under 1 ms, do not queue.
  4. Backpressure upstream: a 503 with Retry-After and a quota header; the gateway converts bursts of 503s into per-client throttling so the retry storm never forms.
  5. Deadline propagation: every request carries a deadline; a service that cannot finish in time drops the work instead of doing it for a client that already gave up.

Deep dive

  • Why unbounded queues kill you: a queue is a promise to do the work later; under sustained overload it only turns a capacity problem into a latency problem and then a total outage.
  • Retries make overload worse: 3 retries turn a 2x spike into 6x; I budget retries at 10% of traffic per client and use exponential backoff with full jitter.

Push-backs

They: The database is the thing that is overloaded, not the service.

You: Each service holds a bounded pool to the database, say 20 connections; when all are busy, the service sheds instead of queuing, and the database sees constant load, not a cliff.

They: A critical request depends on a sheddable downstream call.

You: The downstream call inherits the caller's priority; recommendations called from checkout are critical, called from the homepage are sheddable.

They: How do you know shedding is working and not just breaking things?

You: A dashboard of admitted vs shed per priority class and a load test that pushes 3x and shows checkout success staying above 99% while browsing degrades.

Close

Trade-off: shedding means deliberately failing some users; I'd rather fail 30% of browsers than 100% of everyone. I'd watch shed rate per class and p99 under load; and I would run the 3x load test every month.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
Edge priority taggingCloudFront Functions + ALBCloud Load Balancing + Cloud Armor headers
Services with adaptive limitsECS/EKS with Envoy (or Netflix concurrency-limits)GKE with Envoy / Istio
Queues (bounded)SQS with max in-flight + visibility timeoutPub/Sub with flow control + Cloud Tasks rate limits
Database poolsRDS ProxyCloud SQL Auth Proxy + pgbouncer
Metrics and alarmsCloudWatchCloud Monitoring
AutoscalingApplication Auto ScalingGKE HPA / Cloud Run concurrency
Trap: Answering 'autoscale'; autoscaling takes minutes and the spike takes seconds. The points are bounded queues, priority, and killing retry storms.
cards.s: Google, Netflix, Amazon — the SRE round

cards.f: Design: Global leaderboard / ranking with millions of players
cards.b:
The one idea: A Redis sorted set per leaderboard holds score and rank in one structure; the database is the source of truth, and rank is a cache I can rebuild.

Score event → stream→Validate + write to DB→ZADD leaderboard:{season} player score→Top 100 cached 1 s; my rank via ZREVRANK→Nightly rebuild from DB

Clarify

You: How many players, and how often do scores change?

Interviewer: 20 million players; 10,000 score updates a second at peak.

You: What queries: top N, my rank, players near me?

Interviewer: All three; top 100, my exact rank, and the 10 above and below me.

You: Does rank need to be exact and instant?

Interviewer: Top 100 exact and instant; my rank can be 5 seconds stale and approximate past the top 10,000.

Size it out loud

20M entries in a Redis sorted set at about 100 bytes each is 2 GB on one node. ZADD and ZRANK are O(log N), 25 steps at 20M, so 10K updates a second and 50K rank reads a second is well within one node's 100K ops a second. A daily leaderboard reset is a new key per day; 365 keys of 2 GB is 730 GB, so old ones move to cold storage after 7 days.

Walk through the design

  1. Write path: score events go to a stream; a consumer writes the durable score to the database, then ZADD with the max of old and new; idempotent by event id.
  2. Reads: top 100 is ZREVRANGE cached for 1 second at the API tier; my rank is ZREVRANK, neighbors are ZREVRANGE by rank offset — all single calls.
  3. Scoping: one sorted set per season, per region and per friend group; the global one is 20M entries, a friends board is 200.
  4. Ties: score is a float with the timestamp packed into the low bits so earlier achievers rank higher; deterministic and no second lookup.
  5. Durability: Redis is a cache; a nightly job rebuilds the set from the database in 5 minutes, and AOF persistence covers restarts in between.

Deep dive

  • Beyond one node: shard by score range — 10 shards of 2M players each; my rank is my rank within my shard plus the counts of all higher shards, which I keep as 10 counters.
  • Approximate rank for the long tail: past the top 10,000 I can answer from a histogram of 1,000 score buckets refreshed every 5 seconds; nobody at rank 14,203,117 needs it exact.

Push-backs

They: A cheater posts a score of 1 billion.

You: Validation before the write: a score must be reachable from the game session's telemetry; suspicious scores go to a quarantine set and appear only after review.

They: Redis loses the sorted set.

You: The database has every score; the rebuild job repopulates 20M entries in 5 minutes with pipelined ZADDs, and the top 100 comes from a 1-second database query meanwhile.

They: Players want rank across 50 regions combined with real-time updates.

You: That is the 20M global set I already have; regional boards are separate sets fed by the same stream. Each update is 1 global ZADD plus 1 regional, 20K a second.

Close

Trade-off: exact rank for everyone costs O(log N) per read on one node; I give exactness to the top 10K and buckets to the rest. I'd watch Redis memory and ZADD latency; at 200M players I shard by score range.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
Score ingestKinesisPub/Sub
ConsumerLambda or ECSCloud Run or Cloud Functions
Durable scoresDynamoDBFirestore or Bigtable
LeaderboardElastiCache Redis (sorted sets)Memorystore Redis (sorted sets)
APIAPI Gateway + LambdaCloud Run
Rebuild jobEventBridge Scheduler + ECS taskCloud Scheduler + Cloud Run job
Cold boardsS3Cloud Storage
Trap: Designing a SQL ORDER BY with an index and calling it done; 'my rank' on 20M rows is a COUNT(*) WHERE score > mine, and that is the whole question.
cards.s: Riot, Zynga, Epic — and Amazon as a Redis question in disguise

cards.b:
The one idea: Partition by series id and time, keep the last 2 hours in memory with delta-of-delta compression, flush immutable blocks to object storage, and downsample by age.

Agents push batches→Ingest: series id = hash(name+tags)→In-memory head block per shard, WAL→Every 2 h → compressed block → object store→Query: index → head + blocks → merge

Clarify

You: What is the ingest rate and the shape of a data point?

Interviewer: 10 million points a second; a point is a metric name, a set of tags, a timestamp and a float.

You: What queries: recent raw data, or long aggregates?

Interviewer: 90% of queries are the last 1 hour at full resolution; the rest are 30-day rollups. Retention 1 year.

You: How many distinct series?

Interviewer: About 100 million active series, and tags churn with every deploy.

Size it out loud

10M points a second at 16 bytes raw is 160 MB a second, 14 TB a day, 5 PB a year — too much. Gorilla-style compression gets a point to about 1.5 bytes: 15 MB a second, 1.3 TB a day. Rollups to 1-minute after 7 days cut another 60x. 100M series at 1 KB of index each is 100 GB of inverted index, which must be sharded in memory.

Walk through the design

  1. Series id: hash of metric name plus sorted tags; an inverted index maps each tag=value to a posting list of series ids, so 'cpu where host=~web.*' is a posting-list intersection.
  2. Head block: per shard, the last 2 hours in memory with timestamp delta-of-delta and XOR float compression, written to a write-ahead log first; a crash replays the WAL.
  3. Blocks: every 2 hours the head is flushed as an immutable block with its own index; a compactor merges 2-hour blocks into 1-day blocks and drops old ones per retention.
  4. Downsampling: blocks older than 7 days are rewritten at 1-minute resolution with min, max, sum, count; older than 90 days at 1 hour; raw is deleted.
  5. Sharding: 100 shards by series id hash; a query fans out to all shards for a tag match, each answers from memory for the 1-hour case in under 50 ms.

Deep dive

  • Cardinality is the enemy: a tag like request_id creates a new series per point and blows the index; I enforce a per-metric series cap of 100,000 and reject above it with a clear error.
  • Why not a relational table (ts, series, value): a B-tree per point is 50 bytes and random inserts; the time-series layout gets 1.5 bytes and append-only writes, 30x cheaper.

Push-backs

They: A deploy changes a tag on every series; 100M new series appear at once.

You: Churned series age out of the head after 2 hours and live in old blocks only; the index per block is bounded. I alert on series churn rate so the team fixes the tag.

They: A query asks for 30 days of raw data across 1 million series.

You: I refuse it, or answer from the 1-minute rollup — 30 days x 1,440 points x 1M series is 43 billion points. The query planner picks the resolution for the time range.

They: A shard's node dies.

You: The WAL and blocks are on durable storage; a replacement node replays the last 2 hours of WAL in under a minute, and queries serve from the replica shard meanwhile.

Close

Trade-off: raw data lives only 7 days; a question about a 2-second spike from last month cannot be answered. I'd watch active series count, head memory, and compaction lag; at 10x I'd push the index to a separate tier.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
IngestKinesis or NLB → ingest service on EKSPub/Sub or NLB → ingest service on GKE
Hot storageEKS stateful nodes with EBS (WAL + head)GKE stateful nodes with Persistent Disk (WAL + head)
Block storageS3Cloud Storage
Managed alternativeAmazon TimestreamBigtable (or Cloud Monitoring)
Compaction jobsECS tasksCloud Run jobs
Query serviceEKSGKE
DashboardsManaged GrafanaManaged Grafana / Cloud Monitoring
Trap: Starting with 'use InfluxDB'; the interviewer wants the compression math, the series index, and what you do about cardinality.
cards.s: Datadog, InfluxData, Google (Monarch) — the storage-engine interview

cards.f: Design: Online chess / turn-based game server
cards.b:
The one idea: Each game lives on one node (a single-writer actor), moves are validated there and appended to a durable log, and spectators get a fan-out stream separate from the players.

Players connect via WebSocket gateway→Route game id → owning game node→Validate move, update clock, append to log→Push state to both players→Spectator fan-out via pub/sub + 1 s batch

Clarify

You: How many concurrent games, and what is the move rate?

Interviewer: 500,000 concurrent games; a move every 10 seconds per game on average.

You: Do we need real-time clocks and spectators?

Interviewer: Yes: clocks to the tenth of a second, and popular games can have 50,000 spectators.

You: Must games survive a server crash?

Interviewer: Yes; a game in progress must never be lost, and a disconnected player gets 60 seconds to reconnect.

Size it out loud

500K games at 1 move per 10 seconds is 50K moves a second. 1M players on WebSockets at 50K connections per server is 20 servers. A game state is about 2 KB; 500K games is 1 GB, so all live games fit in memory on a few nodes. A 50K-spectator game fans out 1 move into 50K messages; 5 moves a second is 250K messages a second, which is a pub/sub job, not a game-server job.

Walk through the design

  1. Game actor: the game id hashes to one node that holds the state in memory, validates legality server-side, and updates the clock; no locks because one writer.
  2. Durability: every move is appended to a per-game event log before the ack; a crashed node's games are rebuilt on another node by replaying the log in milliseconds.
  3. Clocks: server-authoritative; the clock stops on move receipt and the client gets the remaining time with each state push; a client clock is only a display.
  4. Reconnect: the gateway holds a session token; on reconnect within 60 seconds the player rejoins the same game, otherwise the clock runs out and they lose on time.
  5. Spectators: the game node publishes each move to a topic; a fan-out tier batches at 1 second and pushes to 50K viewers via the CDN-friendly WebSocket layer.

Deep dive

  • Data model: Game{id, white, black, state_fen, clock_w, clock_b, status}, Move{game_id, seq, san, ts}; the move log is the truth and the state is a cache of it.
  • Why not peer-to-peer validation: a cheating client could send an illegal move; the server has the only legal-move generator that matters, and it costs 10 microseconds per move.

Push-backs

They: Both players make a move at the same instant after a lag spike.

You: Only the player on turn can move; the actor processes messages in order, accepts the first legal one, and rejects the other with the current state so the client resyncs.

They: A game node dies holding 10,000 games.

You: The cluster's consistent hash reassigns those ids; new owners replay logs from the store, 2 KB each, 20 MB total, under 2 seconds. Players see a brief 'reconnecting'.

They: Matchmaking at 1,000 queue entries a second.

You: A separate service buckets players by rating in 50-point bands and pairs within a band every 2 seconds, widening the band the longer someone waits.

Close

Trade-off: one node per game caps a single game's write rate, which for chess is irrelevant; for 100K-player battle royale it is not. I'd watch move ack latency and log append latency; spectator load is the thing that scales independently.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
WebSocket gatewayALB (WebSocket) + ECSCloud Load Balancing + GKE
Game nodesEKS (stateful set with consistent hashing)GKE (stateful set with consistent hashing)
Move logDynamoDB (game_id, seq) + StreamsBigtable (game_id, seq) or Firestore
Spectator fan-outSNS/Kinesis → fan-out tier on ECSPub/Sub → fan-out tier on GKE
Matchmaking stateElastiCache RedisMemorystore Redis
Game archiveS3 + AthenaCloud Storage + BigQuery
Trap: Spending the time on chess rules or a REST API for moves; the points are single-writer ownership, durable move logs, clocks, and spectator fan-out.
cards.s: Lichess-style questions at Google, Amazon, and game studios

cards.f: Design: Real-time multiplayer game state sync
cards.b:
The one idea: Authoritative server simulation on a fixed tick, clients send inputs not positions, and client-side prediction with reconciliation plus delta snapshots hide the 100 ms.

Client sends input + tick number (UDP)→Server simulates tick 30x/s→Delta snapshot per client, interest-managed→Client predicts, reconciles on snapshot→Match ends → results to backend

Clarify

You: What kind of game — a 10-player shooter at 60 ticks, or a 100-player world at 10 ticks?

Interviewer: A 16-player action game; 30 ticks a second; players are within 100 ms of the server.

You: Is the server authoritative, and how much cheating do we care about?

Interviewer: Fully authoritative; cheating is a top-3 problem.

You: How many concurrent matches?

Interviewer: 100,000 concurrent matches globally.

Size it out loud

16 players x 30 ticks is 480 inbound inputs a second per match; outbound is 16 x 30 state snapshots, at 500 bytes delta-compressed is 240 KB a second per match. 100K matches is 24 GB a second outbound globally, about 200 Gbps, spread over 20 regions. One game server core runs about 10 matches, so 10,000 cores globally; at 100 ms RTT a player sees the world 50 ms old, which client prediction hides.

Walk through the design

  1. Transport: UDP with a thin reliability layer; inputs are sent redundantly 3 ticks in a row so a lost packet does not stall; TCP head-of-line blocking is unacceptable at 30 Hz.
  2. Server tick: a fixed 33 ms loop applies all inputs received, runs physics and hit detection, and writes a snapshot; players are never trusted with positions.
  3. Snapshots: per-client deltas against the last acked snapshot, quantized positions, and interest management so each client gets only the 8 or so entities near it.
  4. Client prediction: the client applies its own input immediately, keeps a buffer of unacked inputs, and on each server snapshot rewinds and replays — misprediction shows as a small correction.
  5. Lag compensation: the server keeps 200 ms of position history and rewinds to the shooter's view time to judge a hit, so a 100 ms player can still hit what they saw.

Deep dive

  • Match placement: a matchmaker picks a region where all 16 players are under 80 ms and allocates a server from a warm pool; cold-starting a game server takes 5 seconds, so I keep 5% spare.
  • Anti-cheat on the server: validate input rates, movement speed and impossible actions per tick; a client claiming 50 inputs in a tick is dropped. Client-side anti-cheat is extra, not instead.

Push-backs

They: A player with 300 ms latency joins.

You: Matchmaking should have refused; if they are in, lag compensation caps at 200 ms so they get worse hit registration rather than everyone else getting shot around corners.

They: The game server process crashes mid-match.

You: A 16-player match is 2 minutes of someone's evening; I checkpoint state every 5 seconds to local disk and restart in place, and if the host died the match is lost and players get credit. Full state replication is not worth 30 Hz of cost.

They: Bandwidth per client must stay under 50 KB a second on mobile.

You: Interest management and quantization get a snapshot to 300 bytes; 30 a second is 9 KB a second. If still too much, drop to 20 Hz snapshots with interpolation on the client.

Close

Trade-off: prediction shows corrections under packet loss, which players call 'rubber-banding'; the alternative is 100 ms input delay, which is worse. I'd watch tick time, which must stay under 33 ms, and per-match packet loss.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
Game serversGameLift (or EC2 with Agones on EKS)GKE with Agones
MatchmakingGameLift FlexMatch or custom on ECSOpen Match on GKE
Match results and profilesDynamoDBFirestore or Spanner
Low-latency routingGlobal AcceleratorPremium Tier networking + Cloud Load Balancing
TelemetryKinesis → S3Pub/Sub → Cloud Storage
Anti-cheat analysisEMR or Athena over telemetryDataproc or BigQuery over telemetry
Trap: Proposing WebSockets and JSON over TCP at 30 Hz; the question is UDP, ticks, prediction, and interest management.
cards.s: Riot, Epic, Roblox — the networking round for game infrastructure

cards.b:
The one idea: Model each car as a state machine (idle, moving up, moving down, doors open) and a dispatcher that assigns hall calls by estimated cost, with the car then serving stops in its direction (SCAN).

Hall button or cabin button event→Dispatcher scores each car for the call→Assign to lowest-cost car→Car serves stops in direction, then reverses→Safety controller overrides all

Clarify

You: How many elevators and floors, and how is this used — a single building controller, or a fleet across buildings?

Interviewer: A 40-floor building with 6 elevators; one controller, but the same design should carry to a campus.

You: What is optimized — wait time, travel time, or energy?

Interviewer: Average wait time first, then energy; nobody should wait more than 60 seconds.

You: What inputs exist — only hall up/down buttons, or destination entry in the lobby?

Interviewer: Hall buttons on every floor, destination buttons inside; destination dispatch is a nice-to-have.

Size it out loud

40 floors at 3 seconds a floor plus 10 seconds per stop; a full traverse with 10 stops is 220 seconds. Morning peak: 2,000 people in 30 minutes, about 1 a second, 16 per car trip; 6 cars doing a 90-second lobby round trip move 64 a minute, which is just enough. Control loop ticks every 100 ms; 6 cars and 80 hall buttons is trivial compute — the problem is the algorithm, not the hardware.

Walk through the design

  1. Entities: Building, Floor, Elevator{current_floor, direction, state, stops: up-set and down-set, capacity, load}, HallCall{floor, direction, ts}, CabinCall{car, floor}; the dispatcher owns hall calls, cars own cabin calls.
  2. Car algorithm: SCAN — keep moving in the current direction while any stop lies ahead; stop at floors in the ordered set; reverse when none remain. Simple, fair, no starvation.
  3. Dispatch cost: for each car, estimated time to reach the call = travel plus 10 seconds per stop in between, plus a penalty if full or moving away; assign the lowest; re-evaluate unassigned calls every tick.
  4. Peak modes: morning up-peak parks idle cars at the lobby; evening down-peak favors top floors; a schedule or a load sensor switches modes.
  5. Safety and hardware: door sensors, overload, and emergency stop are a separate controller that can halt a car regardless of software; the scheduler only suggests.

Deep dive

  • Why SCAN over shortest-seek-first: SSF starves far floors during busy periods; SCAN bounds every wait at one traverse, about 220 seconds worst case, better with 6 cars.
  • Destination dispatch: if the lobby panel takes a destination, the dispatcher groups people by floor into the same car, cutting stops by about 30%; it changes the data model to Passenger{origin, dest}.

Push-backs

They: All 6 cars are at the top and 50 people are in the lobby.

You: Up-peak mode sends idle cars down; the dispatcher also notices the lobby call age exceeding 30 seconds and raises its priority. The 60-second bound is a hard rule in the cost function.

They: A car breaks down mid-shaft.

You: Its state becomes out-of-service; its assigned hall calls return to the dispatcher and are reassigned in the next tick; cabin passengers are a safety-controller matter, not the scheduler's.

They: Make it work for a campus with 20 buildings.

You: One dispatcher per building, since cars never cross buildings; a fleet service collects telemetry and pushes mode schedules. The per-building design does not change.

Close

Trade-off: SCAN is simple and fair but not optimal; a learned dispatcher could beat it by 10-20% on wait time at the cost of explainability. I'd watch p95 wait per floor and stops per trip.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
Building controllerEdge device with IoT GreengrassEdge device with a local controller (ClearBlade Edge)
Device messagingIoT CorePub/Sub (via ClearBlade IoT Core)
Telemetry storeTimestreamBigtable
Fleet analyticsKinesis → S3 → AthenaPub/Sub → Cloud Storage → BigQuery
Mode schedulesDynamoDB + EventBridge SchedulerFirestore + Cloud Scheduler
AlertsCloudWatch + SNSCloud Monitoring + Pub/Sub
Trap: Drawing a class diagram for 30 minutes; name the classes in 2 minutes and spend the rest on the dispatch algorithm and its failure modes.
cards.s: Amazon, Microsoft, Bloomberg — the object-modeling question that is secretly a scheduler

cards.b:
The one idea: One single-threaded engine per symbol shard consuming a sequenced input log; the order book is in memory, every event is journaled before it is acted on, and replaying the log reproduces the book.

Gateway validates, assigns sequence number→Sequencer: total order of events→Engine thread: match against book→Trades + book updates → outbound log→Market data and clearing consume log

Clarify

You: What order types and what throughput and latency?

Interviewer: Limit and market orders, cancels; 1 million orders a second at peak; under 100 microseconds inside the engine.

You: Is price-time priority required, and is fairness audited?

Interviewer: Yes to both; the sequence of events must be reproducible to the regulator.

You: How many instruments?

Interviewer: 5,000 symbols; the top 100 take 80% of volume.

Size it out loud

1M orders a second at 100 microseconds each means no network call, no lock, no disk in the hot path. A single core does about 5-10M simple operations a second, so one core per shard of symbols handles 1M if the data structure is tight. Order book memory: 5,000 symbols x 100,000 resting orders x 64 bytes is 32 GB, fine. The journal at 1M events x 64 bytes is 64 MB a second, sequential writes.

Walk through the design

  1. Sequencer: all inbound events pass through one sequencer per shard that stamps a monotonic number and writes to a replicated log; the engine reads the log, so it is deterministic.
  2. Order book: per symbol, two price-level maps (bids descending, asks ascending), each level a FIFO of orders; a limit order walks the opposite side while prices cross, then rests.
  3. Matching: price-time priority — best price first, oldest order first at that price; partial fills update quantity in place; a market order walks until filled or the book is empty.
  4. Cancel: an order id hash map points into the level's list for O(1) removal; a cancel for an already-filled order returns 'too late' with the sequence number as proof.
  5. Hot path discipline: pre-allocated arrays, no garbage collection, pinned cores, kernel bypass networking; nothing in the loop touches a disk or another thread.

Deep dive

  • Failover: a hot standby engine consumes the same sequenced log and holds an identical book; on primary failure it takes over at the next sequence number with zero state transfer.
  • Why single-threaded: the book for one symbol is a shared structure; a lock per order at 1M a second costs more than the matching, and determinism dies with threads. Parallelism is across symbols.

Push-backs

They: One symbol gets 500K orders a second on earnings day.

You: That symbol gets its own shard and core; 500K at 100 microseconds is 50 seconds of CPU per second — too much, so it is actually 500K at 1 microsecond of matching, which a tight loop does. Validation moved to the gateway.

They: How do you prove to a regulator that order A was matched before order B?

You: The sequence number from the sequencer, journaled before the engine saw either; replaying the journal yields the same trades byte for byte.

They: A self-trade: the same account on both sides.

You: A check at match time against the resting order's account; the policy is cancel-newest by default; it costs one integer compare in the loop.

Close

Trade-off: one engine per shard means a symbol's throughput is bounded by one core; it is also what makes it correct. I'd watch engine loop time per event and journal fsync lag; the day loop time hits 50 microseconds I re-shard.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
Engine hostsEC2 bare-metal with enhanced networking (cluster placement group)Compute Engine C3 bare-metal, compact placement
Sequenced logAeron/Chronicle on EC2 (or MSK for non-hot-path)Aeron/Chronicle on GCE (or Pub/Sub for non-hot-path)
Order gatewayEC2 with Nitro + kernel bypassGCE with gVNIC + kernel bypass
Market data fan-outMSK → consumersPub/Sub → consumers
Journal archiveS3Cloud Storage
Clearing and reportsAurora + AthenaSpanner + BigQuery
Trap: Proposing a database table with a SELECT for the best price; the engine is an in-memory data structure on one thread with a journal, and the interviewer wants to hear why.
cards.s: Jane Street, Citadel, Coinbase, Nasdaq — the low-latency round

cards.f: Design: Calendar and meeting scheduler (free/busy, recurrence, invites)
cards.b:
The one idea: Store recurrence as a rule plus exceptions, expand instances only for a time window on read, keep an attendee-indexed copy for fast calendar views, and compute free/busy as an interval merge.

Create event with RRULE + attendees→Write master event + attendee rows→Fan out invites, notifications→View: expand rules for window → merge exceptions→Find-a-time: free/busy intervals → gaps

Clarify

You: How many users, and what is the read/write mix?

Interviewer: 100 million users; 20 events created per user per week; calendar views are 50x more common than writes.

You: Do we need recurring events with exceptions, and across time zones?

Interviewer: Yes: 'every Tuesday except next week, moved to Wednesday', across any time zone and DST.

You: What about find-a-time across 10 people?

Interviewer: Yes; it must answer in under 500 ms.

Size it out loud

100M users x 20 events a week is 2 billion events a week, about 3,300 writes a second; reads at 50x is 165K a second. An event row is about 500 bytes; 2B a week is 1 TB a week, 52 TB a year, sharded by user. A free/busy query across 10 people for 2 weeks reads 10 calendars x maybe 100 events each, 1,000 rows, one round trip each in parallel.

Walk through the design

  1. Data model: Event{id, owner, start, end, tz, rrule, title}, EventException{event_id, original_date, replacement or cancelled}, Attendee{user_id, event_id, status}; the Attendee table is sharded by user so 'my week' is one range scan.
  2. Recurrence: store the RRULE (RFC 5545) and the original time zone; expansion for a 2-week window happens at read time and is cached per user per week; never materialize 'forever'.
  3. Exceptions: editing one occurrence writes an EventException keyed by the original date; 'this and following' splits the series by setting an UNTIL and creating a new master.
  4. Invites: an event write enqueues a fan-out job that creates Attendee rows and sends notifications; the organizer's write returns in 50 ms, the attendees see it within seconds.
  5. Free/busy: for each attendee fetch the window, expand, merge intervals, then intersect the free sets; 10 people in parallel is under 100 ms; results are cached for 1 minute.

Deep dive

  • Time zones and DST: 'every Tuesday at 9 a.m. New York' must stay 9 a.m. local after the clocks change; I store the rule in local time with the zone and compute UTC at expansion, which is why I never store expanded UTC instances.
  • External calendars: iCal feeds and CalDAV sync pull every 10 minutes; a sync token per feed avoids re-reading the whole calendar, and external events are marked read-only in the model.

Push-backs

They: The organizer changes the time of a 500-person recurring meeting.

You: One master row update plus a fan-out job that touches 500 Attendee rows and sends 500 notifications in the background; the attendee views read the master, so they are correct before the fan-out finishes.

They: Two assistants book the same room at the same time.

You: Rooms are resources with a conditional insert on (room, slot) in a bookings table; the second write fails and the UI offers the next slot. Optimistic, not a lock.

They: Find-a-time across 10 people is slow for someone with 2,000 recurring rules.

You: Expansion is cached per user per week; the first expansion of 2,000 rules takes 200 ms, every later query reads the cache. I also cap rules per user at 5,000 with an error.

Close

Trade-off: expanding recurrence on read costs CPU per view; the alternative, materializing instances, breaks on every DST rule change. I'd watch expansion time p99 and fan-out lag for large invites.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
APIALB + ECSCloud Load Balancing + Cloud Run
Events and attendeesDynamoDB (sharded by user) or AuroraSpanner or Firestore (sharded by user)
Fan-out queueSQS + LambdaPub/Sub + Cloud Functions
Expansion cacheElastiCache RedisMemorystore Redis
NotificationsSNS / SESPub/Sub + SendGrid or FCM
External syncEventBridge Scheduler + LambdaCloud Scheduler + Cloud Run jobs
Trap: Modeling a recurring meeting as 1,000 rows; the recurrence rule plus exceptions, and DST, are the whole question.
cards.s: Google, Microsoft, Calendly — a data-modeling question with a nasty corner

cards.f: Design: Web analytics (Google Analytics: pageviews, sessions, funnels)
cards.b:
The one idea: A collector that writes to a stream, a streaming layer for real-time counters and sketches, and a columnar warehouse partitioned by site and day for funnels and ad-hoc reports.

JS tag / SDK → collector endpoint→Stream, partitioned by site id→Stream job: sessionize, counters, HLL per minute→Batch: raw → columnar, partition site/day→Dashboards: counters for real-time, warehouse for reports

Clarify

You: What event volume, and how fresh must dashboards be?

Interviewer: 1 million events a second across all customers; real-time counts within 10 seconds, deep reports can lag an hour.

You: What queries: simple counts, or funnels and unique users over 30 days?

Interviewer: Both; funnels over arbitrary steps and uniques over any date range are the hard ones.
