You: Data retention and privacy constraints?

Interviewer: 13 months of raw; must honor deletion requests per user within 30 days.

Size it out loud

1M events a second at 300 bytes is 300 MB a second, 26 TB a day, about 10 PB over 13 months raw; compressed columnar at 10x is 1 PB. A real-time counter per (site, metric, minute) for 1M sites is 1M increments a minute, trivial. A 30-day unique-users query over 1B events per site must not scan raw; HyperLogLog sketches at 12 KB per (site, day) give 2% error and merge in milliseconds.

Walk through the design

  1. Collection: a 1x1 pixel or POST to an edge endpoint that validates, adds server timestamp and geo, and writes to the stream; no processing in the request path; 202 in 5 ms.
  2. Sessionization: a stream job keyed by (site, visitor id) holds the last event time; a gap over 30 minutes starts a new session; session rows are emitted on close.
  3. Real-time: per (site, metric, minute) counters and HLL sketches in a key-value store with a 48-hour TTL; a dashboard sums 60 minutes in one multi-get.
  4. Warehouse: hourly batch compacts raw events into columnar files partitioned by site and day, clustered by visitor id, so funnels and uniques scan one site's partitions only.
  5. Funnels: a query over sessions ordered by time per visitor, with window functions checking step order within a window; pre-aggregated for saved funnels nightly, ad hoc on demand.

Deep dive

  • Uniques at scale: exact distinct counts over 30 days need every visitor id; HLL sketches per day merge into any range with 2% error, 12 KB each, 365 x 1M sites is 4 TB of sketches, acceptable.
  • Deletion requests: raw partitions clustered by visitor id let me rewrite only the affected files; a deletion queue batches requests and rewrites once a day; sketches cannot forget, so they are rebuilt from raw monthly.

Push-backs

They: A customer's site goes viral and sends 200K events a second.

You: The stream partitions by site id with a salt for hot sites — site id plus a 0-15 suffix — so one site spreads over 16 partitions; the counters are sharded the same way and summed on read.

They: Bot traffic inflates every number.

You: A known-bot filter at the collector using user-agent lists and an IP reputation feed, plus a daily model that flags sessions with no mouse or scroll events; flagged events get a column, not a delete, so customers can toggle.

They: The funnel query over 90 days for a big site takes 10 minutes.

You: Pre-aggregate: a nightly job computes step counts for every saved funnel; ad hoc 90-day funnels run on a sample of 10% of visitors with an error bar.

Close

Trade-off: real-time counters are approximate and sketches have 2% error; exact numbers come from the hourly batch. I'd watch collector p99, stream lag, and batch compaction delay; at 10x I'd move raw landing to a cheaper tier.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
CollectorCloudFront + ALB + ECSCloud CDN + Cloud Load Balancing + Cloud Run
StreamKinesis (sharded by site)Pub/Sub (keyed by site)
Stream processingKinesis Data Analytics (Flink)Dataflow
Real-time countersDynamoDB with TTL (or ElastiCache)Bigtable (or Memorystore)
Raw and columnar storageS3 (Parquet)Cloud Storage (Parquet)
Warehouse queriesAthena or RedshiftBigQuery
Batch jobsEMR SparkDataproc Spark
Trap: Designing only the ingest pipeline; the interviewer wants to hear how uniques and funnels are answered without scanning 10 PB.
cards.s: Google, Amplitude, Mixpanel — the batch-plus-stream pipeline interview

cards.f: Design: Ad serving and real-time bidding
cards.b:
The one idea: Fan out a compact bid request to bidders in parallel with a hard 50 ms timeout, run a second-price auction in memory, and keep budgets and frequency caps in a fast key-value store with async reconciliation.

Page → ad request with user id, slot→Profile + frequency cap lookup (5 ms)→Fan out to 20 bidders, 50 ms timeout→Auction: filter, rank, second price→Return creative, log impression, debit budget

Clarify

You: Are we the exchange running the auction, or a bidder responding to it?

Interviewer: The exchange: a page loads, we ask bidders, pick a winner and return the ad.

You: What is the latency budget and request rate?

Interviewer: The whole thing in 100 ms, bidders get 50 ms; 2 million ad requests a second at peak.

You: How accurate must budgets and frequency caps be?

Interviewer: Overspend under 1% per campaign per day; a user should not see the same ad more than 3 times an hour.

Size it out loud

2M requests a second x 20 bidders each is 40M bid requests a second outbound; at 1 KB each that is 40 GB a second — this is why bid requests are compact and bidders are co-located. A user profile read of 2 KB at 2M a second is 4 GB a second from a cache; per-user frequency counters are 2M increments a second. A 100 ms budget: 5 ms profile, 50 ms bidders in parallel, 5 ms auction, 10 ms creative lookup, 30 ms of network.

Walk through the design

  1. Request path: the ad server reads the user profile and frequency counters from a cache, builds an OpenRTB request without the raw user id, and fans out to eligible bidders in parallel.
  2. Timeouts: bidders that miss 50 ms are excluded from that auction; a bidder that misses 10% of auctions in a minute is throttled to half its traffic until it recovers.
  3. Auction: drop bids under floor price, drop campaigns over budget or over frequency cap, rank by bid x predicted quality, charge the second price plus 1 cent.
  4. Budgets: per-campaign spend counters in the cache are debited per impression; pacing spreads a daily budget over the day; an hourly batch reconciles against the impression log and corrects drift.
  5. Logging: every request, bid and impression goes to a stream; billing, reporting and model training read from there; the serving path never waits for it.

Deep dive

  • Overspend bound: with counters in one region and async reconciliation, a campaign can overspend by its spend rate x reconciliation lag; at 1,000 dollars an hour and 1 minute lag that is 17 dollars, under 1%. I stop a campaign at 99% of budget to be safe.
  • Frequency caps across regions: counters are per user and the user is routed to a home region, so the counter is exact in the common case; cross-region users get an approximate cap with a 5-second sync.

Push-backs

They: A bidder is slow for everyone and drags p99 past 100 ms.

You: Timeouts are per bidder, so a slow bidder only loses its own bids; the auction runs at 50 ms with whoever answered. The circuit breaker halves its traffic automatically.

They: A campaign with a 10,000-dollar budget wins every auction for 2 seconds because 50 servers each think there is budget left.

You: Pacing: each server gets a lease of a slice of the budget, say 1% per minute, and bids only against its slice; 50 servers x 1% can overspend by at most 50% of a minute's pace, well within 1% of the day.

They: How do you prevent click fraud?

You: A separate pipeline scores impressions and clicks after the fact — IP velocity, click-to-impression timing under 100 ms, known bot nets — and refunds advertisers; serving stays fast, billing is corrected within 24 hours.

Close

Trade-off: the 1% overspend is the price of not locking a global counter at 2M a second; I would not trade it for exactness. I'd watch bidder timeout rate, auction p99, and budget drift per reconciliation.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
Ad serverEKS with Envoy, cluster placement for biddersGKE with Envoy, compact placement
Profile and countersElastiCache Redis (or DynamoDB DAX)Memorystore Redis (or Bigtable)
Bidder fan-outgRPC over VPC peering / PrivateLinkgRPC over VPC peering / Private Service Connect
Event logsKinesis → S3Pub/Sub → Cloud Storage
Reconciliation and billingEMR + RedshiftDataflow + BigQuery
CreativesS3 + CloudFrontCloud Storage + Cloud CDN
ModelsSageMakerVertex AI
Trap: Describing the auction theory; the points are the 100 ms budget breakdown, timeouts per bidder, and how budgets stay within 1% without a global lock.
cards.s: Google, Meta, The Trade Desk — the 100-millisecond budget question

cards.b:
The one idea: Shard checks across stateless workers by time slot, write results to a stream, and decide 'down' in a separate evaluator that needs agreement across regions and consecutive failures.

Scheduler: checks due this second → queue→Workers in 3 regions run HTTP checks→Results → stream→Evaluator: 2 of 3 regions x 2 in a row → incident→Alerts + rollups to time-series store

Clarify

You: How many checks, how often, and from where?

Interviewer: 5 million monitored URLs; each checked every 60 seconds from 3 regions; alerts within 2 minutes of an outage.

You: What counts as down, and how do we avoid false alarms?

Interviewer: Down means 2 of 3 regions fail twice in a row; alerting a customer about our own network blip is the worst outcome.

You: What do customers see?

Interviewer: Uptime percentage per month, response time charts, and incident history for a year.

Size it out loud

5M checks a minute per region is 83K a second per region, 250K a second across 3; each is an HTTP request averaging 300 ms, so about 25,000 in flight per region, which is 50 workers at 500 concurrent connections each. Results: 250K a second x 100 bytes is 25 MB a second, 2 TB a day; rolled up to 1-minute per check per region, 1 year is 5M x 3 x 525,600 minutes — too much raw, so I keep 1-minute for 30 days and hourly after.

Walk through the design

  1. Scheduling: each check has a slot of 0-59 seconds assigned by hashing its id; the scheduler each second emits the 83K checks for that slot to a queue; no cron, no drift.
  2. Workers: stateless, asynchronous HTTP clients with 10-second timeouts, 500 concurrent each; they record status code, latency, TLS expiry and body match; a worker crash just means its queue messages are redelivered.
  3. Evaluation: a stream job keeps the last 3 results per (check, region); an incident opens when 2 of 3 regions show 2 consecutive failures, closes on 2 consecutive successes; that is a 2-minute detection floor.
  4. Alerting: an incident open event goes to a notifier that dedupes per check, escalates by the customer's policy, and backs off repeats to every 30 minutes.
  5. Storage: raw results for 7 days in the stream and object storage; 1-minute aggregates per check per region in a time-series store for 30 days; hourly for 13 months for the uptime report.

Deep dive

  • Our own outage vs theirs: if a region's failure rate across all checks jumps from 1% to 30% in a minute, that region is quarantined and its votes are ignored; the 2-of-3 rule then needs the other two.
  • Check fairness: a customer with 100,000 URLs on one slow host could hog a worker; per-target concurrency is capped at 10 and slots are spread by hash so no second is heavy.

Push-backs

They: A customer wants 10-second checks.

You: 10-second checks cost 6x; I offer them as a tier with their own slot ring of 0-9 seconds and the same evaluator; the math scales linearly with the worker pool.

They: The queue backs up and checks run 40 seconds late.

You: A late check is marked with its scheduled time, so the evaluator still compares like with like; I autoscale workers on queue age and alert myself when lateness exceeds 15 seconds.

They: A customer's site blocks our IPs as a bot.

You: Published IP ranges and a documented user agent; and a per-check option to send a custom header. If they block us anyway, the check reports 403 and the customer sees why.

Close

Trade-off: requiring 2 consecutive failures from 2 regions means detection takes at least 2 minutes; the alternative is paging customers for our own blips. I'd watch check lateness, per-region failure rate, and false-alarm reports.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
SchedulerECS service + DynamoDB check tableCloud Run service + Firestore check table
Check queueSQS (per region)Pub/Sub or Cloud Tasks (per region)
WorkersECS Fargate in 3 regionsCloud Run in 3 regions
Results streamKinesisPub/Sub
EvaluatorKinesis Data Analytics (Flink) or LambdaDataflow or Cloud Functions
Time-series storeTimestreamBigtable
AlertingSNS + SES + LambdaPub/Sub + SendGrid + Cloud Functions
Trap: Building a cron loop and an HTTP client; the points are the slot ring, multi-region agreement, and quarantining your own bad region.
cards.s: Datadog, Pingdom, PagerDuty — a scheduler question that hides a false-alarm problem

cards.f: Design: Email sender for 100 million emails on 5 machines
cards.b:
The one idea: Partition the list by id range into 10,000 chunks of 10,000, let 5 workers claim chunks from a shared table, and make each send idempotent with a per-recipient sent marker.

Split 100M ids into 10,000 chunks→Worker claims chunk (conditional update)→Render + send batch via relay API→Mark recipient sent, chunk done→Bounces / complaints → suppression list

Clarify

You: What is the deadline, and are the 5 machines a hard constraint?

Interviewer: All 100 million within 24 hours; 5 machines is the budget, but we can use a managed email relay.

You: Is it one campaign or many, and can a recipient get the email twice?

Interviewer: One campaign with light personalization; a duplicate is a visible failure, a missed one is a smaller failure.

You: Where is the recipient list?

Interviewer: A database table of 100 million rows with id, email, name and a few fields.

Size it out loud

100M in 24 hours is about 1,160 emails a second, 232 a second per machine. SMTP to a relay takes about 50 ms per message, so 232 a second needs 12 concurrent connections per machine, trivial. Reading 100M rows at 200 bytes is 20 GB, 4 GB per machine, or streamed in pages of 10,000. The relay's rate limit is the real cap: many relays allow 1,000-5,000 a second per account; I confirm before I promise 24 hours.

Walk through the design

  1. Chunking: a chunk table with (chunk_id, id_from, id_to, status, worker, claimed_at); 10,000 rows; a worker claims with 'update where status = pending' and processes ids in order.
  2. Sending: batch 50 recipients per relay API call with the template and per-recipient merge fields; 1 call every 200 ms per connection keeps a machine at 250 a second.
  3. Idempotency: before sending, check a sent marker per recipient keyed by (campaign, recipient id) with a conditional write; after a crash, the retried chunk skips what was already marked.
  4. Rate control: a token bucket per machine at 250 a second plus a global cap read from the relay's quota, and exponential backoff on 429 or 5xx from the relay.
  5. Failure handling: a chunk claimed more than 10 minutes ago with no heartbeat returns to pending; bounces and complaints from the relay's webhook go to a suppression list applied before every send.

Deep dive

  • Why not a queue of 100M messages: enqueuing 100M items takes longer than the job and costs more; 10,000 chunk rows give the same work distribution with 10,000 writes.
  • Duplicates vs misses: the sent marker is written before the relay call, so a crash between marker and call means a miss, not a duplicate; a sweep at the end re-sends markers without a relay message id.

Push-backs

They: Machine 3 dies at hour 6.

You: Its in-flight chunk times out after 10 minutes and another worker claims it; the sent markers skip the already-sent recipients. The other 4 machines finish at 290 a second each, still inside 24 hours.

They: The relay rate-limits us to 500 a second.

You: Then 100M takes 55 hours on any number of machines; I report that, and ask for a second relay account or a warmed dedicated IP pool, which doubles the cap.

They: Spam complaints spike after the first million.

You: I stop the campaign automatically if complaints exceed 0.1%, apply the suppression list, and resume in smaller batches; getting the sending domain blacklisted is the worst outcome, worse than a day's delay.

Close

Trade-off: the marker-before-send rule means a crash causes misses, which a final sweep fixes; duplicates are the thing I refuse to risk. I'd watch sends per second per worker, relay error rate, and the complaint rate.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
Workers5 EC2 instances (or ECS tasks)5 Compute Engine instances (or Cloud Run jobs)
Chunk and marker tablesDynamoDB (conditional writes)Firestore (transactions)
Recipient listRDS or S3 exportCloud SQL or Cloud Storage export
Email relaySES (batch API, dedicated IPs)SendGrid via Google Cloud Marketplace
Bounce webhooksSNS → Lambda → suppression tableCloud Functions → suppression table
Progress metricsCloudWatchCloud Monitoring
Trap: Answering 'put them in a queue'; the interviewer wants the chunk-claim coordination, the idempotency marker, and the relay rate limit as the real bottleneck.
cards.s: Amazon, Mailchimp, SendGrid — a throughput-and-coordination puzzle

cards.f: Design: Firmware / OTA update delivery to millions of devices (campaigns, cohorts, rollback)
cards.b:
The one idea: Devices pull, never push: a check-in service answers 'is there an update for my cohort and version', the image comes from a CDN as a signed delta, and the device boots the new slot and reports back before the old slot is forgotten.

Device check-in: id, version, cohort→Campaign service: eligible? → manifest + signed URL→Device downloads delta from CDN, verifies signature→Install to B slot, reboot, health check→Report success → fleet state; fail → auto-rollback to A

Clarify

You: How many devices, how big is an update, and how are they connected?

Interviewer: 10 million devices; a full image is 500 MB, deltas are about 20 MB; devices are on home Wi-Fi or cellular and may be offline for weeks.

You: How is a rollout controlled, and what if a build bricks devices?

Interviewer: Campaigns by cohort — 1%, 10%, 100% — with automatic halt if failures exceed a threshold; a device must be able to roll back on its own.

You: Security requirements?

Interviewer: Images are signed; a device must refuse anything unsigned, and we must prove which version each device runs.

Size it out loud

10M devices x 20 MB delta is 200 TB per campaign; at 100% in a week that is 330 MB a second average from the CDN, with peaks at 10x when devices wake at night. 10M devices checking in every hour is 2,800 check-ins a second, 10 KB of state each is 100 GB of fleet state. A 1% cohort is 100,000 devices; with a 0.5% failure threshold that is 500 failures before auto-halt.

Walk through the design

  1. Campaign model: Campaign{build, from_versions, cohorts, stage, halt_threshold}, with stages 1%, 10%, 50%, 100%; a device's cohort is a stable hash of its id plus optional tags like region and hardware revision.
  2. Check-in: every hour with jitter the device sends version and health; the service returns the manifest only if the campaign stage includes its cohort, so rollout is controlled entirely server-side.
  3. Delivery: deltas are generated per (from, to) version pair, stored in object storage, served by a CDN with signed URLs that expire in 24 hours; devices download resumably and verify the signature and hash before install.
  4. A/B slots on the device: install to the inactive slot, reboot into it, run a health check for 10 minutes; only after a successful report does the device mark the slot good, otherwise the bootloader falls back.
  5. Auto-halt: the campaign service tracks success and failure per stage; if failures exceed 0.5% or reports go silent for 5% of the cohort, the stage halts and pages a human; advancing a stage is a manual click.

Deep dive

  • Fleet state and proof: a device report is signed by the device key and stored as the last known version; a BigQuery-style table of (device, version, ts) answers 'how many run 4.2.1' and audits.
  • Delta explosion: 20 supported from-versions x each new build is 20 deltas; I cap support at the last 5 versions and send a full image otherwise, keeping the matrix at 5 x 500 MB of generation work per release.

Push-backs

They: 1 million devices wake at 2 a.m. and all check in.

You: Check-in is cheap, 2,800 a second average and 30K at the peak; the CDN serves the bytes. I also spread the hour by device-id hash so the peak is 10x, not 100x.

They: A build passes the 1% stage and bricks a hardware revision at 10%.

You: Cohorts include hardware revision, so the 1% stage samples every revision; the auto-halt catches the 10% stage at 500 failures; bricked devices booted back to slot A on their own and report the failure.

They: Devices offline for 3 months come back to a version we no longer support deltas for.

You: The manifest says 'full image'; 500 MB over cellular is a user prompt to wait for Wi-Fi. The check-in logic is the same, only the artifact differs.

Close

Trade-off: a device decides when to install, so a campaign is never 'done' — 95% in a week, 99% in a month, and the last 1% may be in a drawer. I'd watch per-stage failure rate, CDN egress, and devices silent for more than 7 days.

Implementation

ComponentAWSGCP
Device check-in and jobsIoT Core + IoT JobsPub/Sub + ClearBlade IoT Core (or Cloud Run HTTPS check-in)
Campaign serviceECS + DynamoDBCloud Run + Firestore
Image and delta storageS3Cloud Storage
DeliveryCloudFront with signed URLsCloud CDN with signed URLs
SigningKMS + SignerCloud KMS
Fleet state and reportsIoT Device Shadow → Kinesis → S3 → AthenaPub/Sub → Dataflow → BigQuery
Delta generationAWS BatchCloud Run jobs or Dataproc
Trap: Describing a push from the server to 10 million devices; devices pull on their own schedule, and the design is cohorts, A/B slots, and the auto-halt.
cards.s: Tesla, Apple, Amazon (Alexa), automotive OEMs — the device-fleet question

decks.title: Data-platform theory — 14 ideas
decks.blurb: Lakehouse, columnar files, snapshots, watermarks, idempotency, backpressure, control vs data plane, SLOs, cost per unit.

cards.b: A warehouse is one big SQL database you load data into in a fixed shape: fast and tidy, but expensive and rigid. A lake is files on cheap storage in any shape: store first, decide later — flexible, but it becomes a swamp without discipline. A lakehouse adds a table layer (Iceberg) over the lake files so they behave like database tables: transactions, versions, schema. Andes is a lakehouse. Say: "cheap files underneath, warehouse guarantees on top".

In an old warehouse the disks and the CPUs were the same machine, so you bought both together. In a lake, data sits in S3 and any number of engines (Spark, Athena, Redshift) read it; you pay for compute only while a job runs and can scale either side alone. This is why one dataset can be read by ten teams with ten engines. Say: "storage is shared and cheap; compute is rented by the minute".

A dataset is a product with a producer (the team that makes it) and consumers (teams that read it). The contract is the schema, the freshness promise (SLA), the owner, and the subscription list. The platform's job is to make the contract explicit and enforce it: no schema, no listing; break the schema, notify subscribers. Say: "consumers bind to the catalog contract, not to a bucket path".

Thousands of teams share one platform. Tenancy means: isolation (one team's failure or secret never touches another), quotas (a fair share of compute), fairness (idle share is lent out; nobody starves), and attribution (every byte and CPU-second has a team name on it for the bill). The noisy-neighbor problem — one tenant degrading everyone — is the classic failure. Say: "quota per tenant, weighted fair queueing, cost tagged per tenant".

Analytics queries touch a few columns of billions of rows. Storing by column means reading only those columns, and similar values side by side compress 5–10×. Parquet is the standard. The practical rules: files of 128 MB to 1 GB (small files make every query slow — the "small-file problem"), partitioned by the column you filter on most (usually date). Say: "Parquet, big files, partition by date, compact the small ones".

A pile of Parquet files does not know which files belong to version 7 of a table. Iceberg adds a small metadata layer: a snapshot is a list of files that together form the table at one moment; a commit swaps the current-snapshot pointer. That gives you atomic writes (readers see a whole snapshot or none), time travel (read snapshot 6), schema evolution (add a column without rewriting), and safe concurrent writers. Say: "a table is a pointer to a snapshot; a write is a new snapshot and a pointer swap".

The deep reason behind Q5. Object storage makes each file atomic but not a set of files, so a job that writes 300 files can be seen half-done. Fix: write everywhere nobody looks, then write one manifest, then flip one pointer. Readers follow the pointer. Iceberg does this for you; without Iceberg you must build it. Say: "many files, one manifest, one pointer flip".

Data is read a lot when new and almost never when old. Storage classes charge less for slower access, so move files by age or last access: hot (S3 Standard) → infrequent (30 days) → archive (a year). Keep the metadata hot so old data is still findable. The restore path of archive storage takes hours and costs money — say so before promising it. Say: "tier by last access, metadata never goes cold".

Batch: collect for an hour or a day, process the pile, publish. Simple, efficient, late by the batch interval. Streaming: process each event within seconds as it arrives, using a stream (Kinesis/Kafka) as the buffer and a processor (Flink/Spark Streaming) that keeps state and checkpoints. Streaming costs more and is harder to get right; use it only when the freshness requirement demands it. Say: "batch by default; streaming where the SLA needs minutes".

Events carry the time they happened (event time) and arrive later (processing time), sometimes out of order. If you count by arrival you get wrong answers when a phone was offline. Count by event time, and use a watermark — a running estimate of "nothing older than X will still arrive" — to decide when a time window can be published. Late events after the watermark become corrections or are dropped, by policy. Say: "window by event time, publish at the watermark, corrections for stragglers".

Networks and retries mean every event may be delivered more than once (at-least-once). "Exactly-once" across systems is not really achievable; what you build is effectively once: give every event an id, de-duplicate within a window, make every write safe to repeat (idempotent), and make publication atomic. Then duplicates do no harm. Say: "at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing equals effectively-once".

Producers can send faster than consumers can process. Without a plan, buffers grow until something dies. The plan: a bounded buffer (the stream) that absorbs bursts; a lag metric that alarms; scale consumers first; then shed low-priority producers deliberately and count what you dropped. Never drop silently. Say: "buffer, measure lag, scale, then shed by tier — visibly".

A Spark job has a driver (plans the work, tracks progress) and executors (do the work). Data is split into partitions (~128 MB each); each partition is a task. Joins and group-bys move data between executors — the shuffle — which is the expensive part. One huge partition (skew) makes one task run forever while the rest sit idle. Executors on cheap Spot instances can vanish; Spark reruns their tasks, so keep the driver on reliable capacity. Say: "driver plans, executors work, shuffle and skew are where the time goes".

The control plane is the small set of services that decide and remember: accept the job, queue it, schedule it, track its state, hold the lease. It must never lose a job, so it is tiny, durable and boring. The data plane is the big fleet that does the work — Spark clusters — and it is disposable: lose a cluster and the control plane simply reschedules. Keep them separate so the big fleet can be cheap and replaceable. Say: "small durable brain, big disposable muscle".

Users of a data platform feel three things: freshness (is today's data here by 6am?), correctness (does it reconcile with the source?), and query latency. Set objectives on those, derive the internal metrics that explain them (queue delay, failure rate), and alert on error-budget burn rate rather than on CPU. Say: "SLOs on what the customer feels, alerts on burn rate".

cards.f: Governance: catalog, lineage, classification, authorization, audit
cards.b: Catalog: what exists, who owns it, what shape it has. Lineage: which job read what and wrote what, so you can answer "who breaks if I change this". Classification: tags like PII on columns, ideally automatic. Authorization: rules on tags, decided centrally, enforced in every engine. Audit: every access decision in a log nobody can edit. These five are what makes a lake not a swamp. Say: "catalog, lineage, tags, central policy, immutable audit".

A platform's cost conversation is about the unit: dollars per terabyte processed, per query, per tenant. Levers in order of payoff: compact small files (queries scan less), right-size and use Spot for executors, tier storage by age, delete datasets nobody reads, then make waste visible to teams (showback) before charging them (chargeback). Say: "name the unit, then the three biggest levers".

Data in S3 is already copied across availability zones; the risk is a region or a bad deploy. Replicate the catalog and manifests (the table of contents) to a second region asynchronously with a published lag; replicate only the datasets whose recovery-time requirement justifies the cost; keep rollback a pointer flip to a previous snapshot. Say: "replicate the table of contents, tier the datasets by RTO, rollback is a pointer".

decks.title: Data-platform design questions (50)
decks.blurb: Lakes, ingestion, CDC, Spark platforms, scheduling, catalogs, governance, query, SLOs, cost.

cards.f: Q1 Multi-tenant enterprise data lake for thousands of teams
cards.b:
In one sentence: Six layers — ingest, store, process, describe, guard, use — with the catalog as the only thing consumers bind to and one policy service enforced in every engine.

In plain words: Think of the lake as a library. Ingestion is the loading dock (nothing enters without a catalog card — the schema and owner). Storage is the shelves (S3 files, organized into tables by Iceberg). Processing is the staff who make new books from old ones (Spark jobs). The catalog is the card index — the only thing readers search. Access control is the librarian who checks your card before handing over a restricted book, and writes down that she did.

Numbers to remember 38K datasets · 900K jobs/day · 80K users Andes today  ·  3,500 PUT/s per S3 prefix why one bucket per domain  ·  128 MB–1 GB target Parquet file size  ·  60 s policy-decision cache TTL
Say it like this (about 90 seconds)
  1. "Assume Andes scale: tens of thousands of datasets, a million jobs a day, a hundred thousand users."
  2. "Ingestion is a set of adapters behind one onboarding API — a dataset must have a schema and an owner before any byte lands."
  3. "Storage is S3, Parquet inside Iceberg tables, published atomically through manifests."
  4. "Processing is multi-tenant managed Spark with quotas and a control plane that never loses a job."
  5. "The catalog holds schema, owner, version, contract and lineage; consumers subscribe to the catalog, never to a bucket path."
  6. "Access control is decided in one service and enforced in every engine, with an immutable audit log."
Trap: Drawing a pile of AWS logos. Draw layers and say what each layer promises the one above it.
▸ Depth — follow-ups, how to build it on AWS, push-backs (open only if you want it)

If they dig deeper

  • Data model: Dataset, Version, Schema, Contract, Subscription, Policy, LineageEdge, Job. APIs: registerDataset, publishVersion, subscribe, query.
  • Isolation: IAM role per tenant, KMS key per domain, compute quota per tenant, cost tagged per tenant.
  • Failures: idempotent jobs keyed by (dataset, version, partition); consumer never sees a partial version; malformed data goes to quarantine.
  • Rollout: one domain first, with a dual-run against its existing reports, then expand by domain.

How I would actually build it

  1. Storage: one S3 bucket per domain, prefix {dataset}/v={n}/dt=YYYY-MM-DD/; Iceberg tables in the Glue Data Catalog; bucket policy denies any principal except the engines' roles.
  2. Catalog service: Lambda/ECS behind API Gateway; records in DynamoDB (PK = dataset id, SK = version); every write emits an EventBridge event.
  3. Ingestion: Kinesis Firehose for streams, DMS for CDC, S3 drop zone for files; a registration check rejects data with no catalog entry.
  4. Processing: EMR on EKS with one Kubernetes namespace per tenant; jobs submitted through our control plane, never directly.
  5. Access: Lake Formation LF-Tags on columns; policy decisions cached in ElastiCache for 60 s; decisions streamed to an audit table in S3 with Object Lock.
  6. Cost: cost allocation tag tenant= on every job, bucket and query; a nightly job joins Cost Explorer export to the catalog.

They will push back with…

  • Why not one bucket for everything? — Blast radius, per-domain KMS keys, and bucket-level throttles — 3,500 writes/s per prefix adds up across tenants.
  • What breaks first at 10×? — The catalog's partition listing and the scheduler's dependency graph; both move to Iceberg metadata and a partitioned DynamoDB table.
  • How does a consumer know a dataset changed shape? — Schema registry compatibility check at publish; subscribers get an event; breaking changes require a new major version.
  • Who owns a bad dataset? — The registered owner — no owner, no listing. The platform owns freshness of the mechanism, not of the content.

Ask them first / ask back

  • Are we building for one business unit or company-wide? (decides how strict tenancy must be)
  • Is there an existing catalog I must integrate with, or am I the catalog?
  • Batch-first or streaming-first? What freshness do the top ten consumers actually need?
  • Is there a regulatory boundary (PII, export control, region residency)?

In one sentence: A workflow — register, gate, list, request, grant — where the producer owns the contract and access auto-expires.

In plain words: A marketplace is an app store for datasets. A producer lists a dataset the way a developer lists an app: it must pass review (the quality gate) and declare what it contains (classification). A consumer finds it by searching, asks for access with a reason, and the access expires unless renewed. The producer can see everyone who depends on the dataset before changing it — that is the "subscription".

Numbers to remember time to first query the metric for the marketplace  ·  auto-approve non-PII human approval only for tagged data  ·  7 days warning before a grant expires  ·  30-day usage count the main ranking signal
Say it like this (about 90 seconds)
  1. "The producer registers a dataset with a schema, an owner and an SLA; nothing is listed without a quality gate and a classification."
  2. "Discovery is a search index over the catalog: name, columns, owner, freshness, quality score, who else uses it."
  3. "Access is a request with a purpose and a duration; approval can be automatic for non-sensitive data, human for PII."
  4. "The grant is a policy record — enforced by the engines, auto-expired, fully audited."
Trap: Talking about the UI. The hard part is the contract between producer and consumer, not the portal.
▸ Depth — follow-ups, how to build it on AWS, push-backs (open only if you want it)

If they dig deeper

  • Subscription is the contract: the producer sees who depends on them before changing a schema.
  • Ranking: usage count, freshness, quality score, and whether the user can already read it.
  • Metrics: time from request to first query; percent of datasets with an owner and SLA.

How I would actually build it

  1. Registration API writes a Dataset record; a Step-Functions-style workflow runs the quality gate (row count, nulls, PII scan) and sets status=listed.
  2. Discovery: OpenSearch index rebuilt from catalog events; document = name, columns, owner, tags, freshness, 30-day query count.
  3. Access request = a row in an AccessRequest table with purpose, duration, approver; non-PII auto-approves via a rule; PII routes to the owner via a ticket/Slack approval.
  4. Grant = a Lake Formation permission with an expiry; a nightly job revokes expired grants and emails the requester a week before.
  5. Subscription table (dataset → consumers) is what the producer sees before any schema change.

They will push back with…

  • What stops a team listing junk? — The gate: no owner, no schema, no sample rows → no listing. Quality score shown on the card.
  • How do you rank search results? — Usage, freshness, quality score, and whether the user can already read it — in that order.
  • Approvals will become a bottleneck. — Auto-approve by classification; owners get a weekly digest; SLA on approvals is a metric I publish.

Ask them first / ask back

  • Who approves access today, and how long does it take? (that number is the thing to beat)
  • Is the problem discovery (can't find) or trust (can't rely)? They need different fixes.
  • Do consumers need the data in place, or copied into their account?

cards.f: Q3 — Storage layout for a petabyte lake
cards.b: Partition by the filter you query most (usually date), target 128 MB–1 GB files, Parquet + Zstd, lifecycle to Infrequent Access at 30 days and Glacier at 1 year, keep raw separate from curated.

cards.f: Q4 — Lakehouse with updates and time travel
cards.b: Plain Parquet cannot update a row; a table format (Iceberg) gives transactions, upserts, schema evolution and snapshots. Choose Iceberg when you have updates, deletes or many writers.

cards.f: Q6 — Small-file compaction without disrupting readers
cards.b: Write compacted files to new names, then commit a new snapshot; readers on the old snapshot finish unharmed; delete old files after a grace period.

cards.f: Q7 — Partition management for skewed datasets
cards.b: Measure partition size; bucket the hot keys, coarsen partitions that are tiny, and let Iceberg do partition evolution without rewriting history.
Tier on last-access, not age; keep metadata hot so archived data is still discoverable; test the restore path and its cost before you promise it.
Replicate the manifest and catalog, not random files; async with a published lag; residency decides which datasets may leave the region; pay for it only where the RTO demands it.

cards.f: Q10 — Migrate a legacy warehouse to the lake
cards.b: Dual-run: load both, compare report outputs row by row, flip readers one at a time, keep the warehouse until the last report matches for a full cycle.

cards.f: Q5 Atomic dataset publication (and Q14 idempotent pipelines)
cards.b:
In one sentence: Write many files, write one manifest, flip one pointer; readers follow the pointer so they see all-or-nothing.

In plain words: A big job writes hundreds of files. If a reader looks while the job is half done, it sees half a dataset. The fix is a two-step: write all the files somewhere nobody looks, then write one small "table of contents" file (the manifest), then move a single pointer to say "the current version is this manifest". Readers only follow the pointer, so they see the whole old version or the whole new one. Iceberg does this trick for you.

Numbers to remember 1 manifest · 1 pointer the whole trick  ·  conditional PutItem exactly one attempt wins  ·  24 h staging prefix cleanup window  ·  S3 = atomic per object not per set of objects
Say it like this (about 90 seconds)
  1. "A distributed job writes hundreds of files; S3 makes each file atomic but not the set."
  2. "So the job writes to a temporary prefix, then writes a single manifest listing the files, then the catalog pointer flips to that manifest in one write."
  3. "Readers only ever read through the pointer — they see version 7 or version 8, never a mix."
  4. "Retries are safe because the job is keyed by dataset, version and partition: rerun it and you get the same manifest, not a duplicate (that is Q14)."
Trap: "We use _SUCCESS files." A marker file is a convention, not a guarantee; the pointer is the guarantee.
▸ Depth — follow-ups, how to build it on AWS, push-backs (open only if you want it)

If they dig deeper

  • Iceberg does exactly this for you: snapshot = manifest list, commit = pointer swap with optimistic concurrency.
  • Duplicate records inside a file: dedupe on an event id within the window; publish-level idempotency handles duplicate outputs.
  • A failed commit leaves orphan files — a cleanup job deletes anything not referenced by any snapshot.

How I would actually build it

  1. Job writes Parquet files to s3://lake/ds/_staging/{job-id}/; each file named with the attempt id.
  2. On success the driver writes manifest-{version}.json listing files, row counts and a checksum; then a conditional write to DynamoDB: PutItem(dataset, version) IF attribute_not_exists.
  3. Readers call getLatestVersion(dataset) and read only the files in that manifest. With Iceberg this is the snapshot commit — the same idea, done for you.
  4. A cleaner deletes staging prefixes older than 24 h that no manifest references.

They will push back with…

  • Two attempts finish at the same time? — The conditional write loses for one of them; its files are orphaned and cleaned. Exactly one version wins.
  • What about a consumer mid-read when the pointer flips? — It keeps reading the old manifest — the files still exist until the retention window passes.
  • How does this work for streaming output? — Micro-batch commits every minute; each commit is a snapshot; readers see whole minutes.

Ask them first / ask back

  • Do consumers read via a table format or raw paths? (raw paths means I must own the manifest discipline)
  • How long must old versions stay readable? (sets the retention window and the storage bill)

cards.f: Q11 One million events per second, analytics within five minutes
cards.b:
In one sentence: Buffer in Kinesis or MSK, process in Flink by event time, land 1–2 minute micro-batches into Iceberg, compact later.

In plain words: A million events a second cannot be written to a database one at a time. So: a stream (Kinesis) acts as a wide, durable conveyor belt that absorbs the flood; a stream processor (Flink) rides the belt, cleans and groups the events by the time they actually happened; every minute or two it drops a neat batch of files into the lake. A later tidy-up job merges small files into big ones. The five-minute promise is met because the belt-to-lake trip takes two minutes.

Numbers to remember 1M events/s ≈ 1 GB/s ≈ 86 TB/day say this first  ·  1 MB/s per Kinesis shard → ~1,000 shards the scale knob  ·  60 s checkpoints · 60 s commits Flink cadence  ·  2 min allowed lateness event-time window  ·  256 MB compaction target
Say it like this (about 90 seconds)
  1. "Scale check: one million events at about a kilobyte each is a gigabyte per second, 86 terabytes a day raw."
  2. "Producers batch and sign events with an id so retries are safe; the stream is the shock absorber — shards are the scale knob."
  3. "Flink parses, dedupes by id, and windows by event time with watermarks; it checkpoints every minute so a crash loses nothing."
  4. "Output lands in Iceberg every one to two minutes, which gives a five-minute freshness SLA with margin; a compaction job fixes the small files behind the scenes."
Trap: Writing to S3 per event. A million tiny objects a second is a bill, not an architecture.
▸ Depth — follow-ups, how to build it on AWS, push-backs (open only if you want it)

If they dig deeper

  • Backpressure: when a consumer lags, the stream fills; alarm on consumer lag, scale consumers, then throttle the lowest-tier producers.
  • Hot partition: if one key gets most traffic, add a random suffix to the partition key and aggregate downstream.
  • Cost: Spot executors for Flink, compress on the wire, tier raw stream archives to cheap storage after a day.
  • Freshness SLO is measured as "max event time landed vs now" — that is the number the dashboard shows.

How I would actually build it

  1. Producers use a thin SDK: batch 500 events, gzip, sign each with event_id = hash(producer, seq); retry with backoff to Kinesis PutRecords.
  2. Kinesis: 1,000+ shards (1 MB/s each) or MSK with ~200 partitions; partition key = producer id with a salt for hot producers.
  3. Flink on Kinesis Data Analytics (or EKS): parse → dedupe on event_id in a 10-minute RocksDB state window → event-time windows with a 2-minute allowed lateness → Iceberg sink committing every 60 s.
  4. Checkpoints to S3 every 60 s; on crash the job restarts from the last checkpoint and the Iceberg sink de-duplicates the in-flight commit.
  5. Compaction job every 15 min rewrites small files to 256 MB targets; Athena/Spark read through Glue.

They will push back with…

  • 1 GB/s into one Flink job? — It is parallel: ~100 task slots at ~10 MB/s each; scale by adding slots; shards are the back-pressure buffer.
  • Five-minute SLA during a backfill? — Backfill runs as a separate job in a separate pool reading from the stream archive, never sharing live slots.
  • Exactly-once? — Effectively-once: idempotent event ids + checkpointed offsets + atomic Iceberg commits. I say that phrase, not "exactly-once".
  • Cost? — Roughly: streaming ingest + compute is the big line; archive raw to S3 IA after a day; Spot for Flink task managers with checkpoint-based recovery.

Ask them first / ask back

  • Event size and whether the million is peak or average? (10× difference in cost)
  • Is five minutes end-to-end, or from arrival at the platform?
  • Can producers be changed (SDK, ids), or must I accept what they send?
  • Does analytics need raw events, or aggregates are fine? (aggregates cut everything by 100×)

cards.f: Q12 CDC from hundreds of databases
cards.b:
In one sentence: Start the change stream first, take the snapshot second, and merge on log position so overlap is harmless and gaps are impossible.

In plain words: CDC means copying every change from a database by reading its transaction log, like reading the bank's ledger instead of asking for a balance. For a new database you need the "balance" (a full snapshot) and the "ledger from then on" (the change stream). Start recording the ledger first, then take the snapshot, then replay only ledger entries newer than the snapshot. Overlap is harmless because applying the same change twice gives the same result.

Numbers to remember stream first, snapshot second order that cannot lose data  ·  lsn > snapshot_lsn the merge rule  ·  hourly count + hash reconciliation cadence  ·  no primary key → daily snapshot say the limitation
Say it like this (about 90 seconds)
  1. "Each database gets a connector — Debezium or DMS — that reads the transaction log and publishes changes to a topic."
  2. "For a new source I start the change stream, note the log position, then take a full snapshot to S3."
  3. "Merge applies only changes with a log position after the snapshot; the overlap is replayed harmlessly because upserts by primary key are idempotent."
  4. "Landed data is an Iceberg table that supports updates and deletes, with a freshness lag metric per source."
Trap: Snapshot first, stream later — the gap between them is data you lost.
▸ Depth — follow-ups, how to build it on AWS, push-backs (open only if you want it)

If they dig deeper

  • Schema change on a source: the connector emits a schema event; compatible changes flow, incompatible ones quarantine that table and page the owner (Q18).
  • Hundreds of sources means fleet management: a connector registry, health per connector, and a rate limiter so one busy database cannot starve others.
  • Deletes: capture tombstones; keep them for a retention window so late consumers see them.

How I would actually build it

  1. Connector fleet: one Debezium/DMS task per source database, config in a Source table (host, tables, credentials in Secrets Manager, status, lag).
  2. Steps per source: (1) create the task and record the start LSN, (2) snapshot tables to S3 with the LSN in the file name, (3) stream changes to a Kafka/Kinesis topic per table, (4) a Spark MERGE job applies changes with lsn > snapshot_lsn into Iceberg by primary key.
  3. Schema events go to a schema registry; incompatible = quarantine that table, open a ticket to the owner, keep other tables flowing.
  4. Reconciliation: hourly count-and-hash per table vs source; mismatch auto-reloads that partition.

They will push back with…

  • Hundreds of connectors — who watches them? — A connector health table with lag per source; alarms on lag > SLA; auto-restart with backoff; a dashboard per source owner.
  • Source DB is overloaded by log reading. — Read from a replica; cap connector throughput per source; schedule snapshots off-peak.
  • Primary key missing on a table? — No PK, no CDC — it becomes a daily full snapshot with a diff; I say that limitation out loud.

Ask them first / ask back

  • Which engines (Postgres, MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server)? Oracle changes the tool choice and cost.
  • Do we need the history of every change, or just the current state? (append log vs upsert table)
  • Who owns the source schema — can they be made to announce changes?

cards.f: Q13 — One onboarding interface for files, CDC and streams
cards.b: One registration API (schema, owner, cadence, classification); three adapters behind it; everything lands in the same layout with the same metadata.
Process by event time; a watermark says "nothing older than X will arrive"; emit a provisional result at the watermark and a correction for stragglers, with a final close after N hours.

cards.f: Q16 — Replay and backfill without hurting live traffic
cards.b: Separate replay lane with its own quota and lower priority; write to a new version and swap the pointer; never let backfill share the live stream's shards.
Buffer absorbs bursts; measure consumer lag; scale consumers first; then shed by tier (free-tier producers first); never drop silently — count what you dropped.

cards.f: Q18 — Schema evolution across thousands of teams
cards.b: Schema registry with compatibility rules (add nullable column = fine; rename or type change = breaking); breaking changes require a new version and a consumer notice from the subscription list.
Bad records go to a quarantine table with the reason; the good records keep flowing; the owner gets a count and a fix-and-replay button.
Compare counts, sums and hashes per partition per day between source and lake; alert on drift; auto-reload the partition that disagrees.

cards.f: Q21 Managed Spark platform (with Q23 fairness and Q24 control plane)
cards.b:
In one sentence: A small, durable control plane that owns jobs, queues and leases, and a big, disposable data plane of Spark on EMR/EKS that can be thrown away.

In plain words: A managed Spark platform is a taxi dispatcher. Customers say where they want to go (a job); they never drive. The dispatcher (control plane) keeps the list of rides, who is waiting, who is driving, and must never lose it — so it is small and stored in a durable database. The cars (data plane — Spark clusters) are many, cheap and replaceable; if one breaks, the dispatcher sends another. A "lease" is the driver radioing in every thirty seconds; silence means the ride is reassigned.

Numbers to remember 2 min lease · 30 s heartbeat liveness  ·  5 Spot instance types diversification  ·  drivers On-Demand, executors Spot the split  ·  cost per job returned to every tenant
Say it like this (about 90 seconds)
  1. "Customers submit SQL, Python or Scala with a dataset in and a dataset out; they never see a cluster."
  2. "The control plane is small and boring: a submit API, a job record in DynamoDB, a queue per tenant, a scheduler, and a lease with heartbeat per running job."
  3. "The data plane is EMR on EKS: a pod per job, Spot for executors, warm pools so start-up is seconds not minutes."
  4. "Fairness is quotas plus weighted fair queuing: every tenant gets a guaranteed share, idle share is lent out, and an aging rule prevents starvation."
Trap: Letting the control plane run on the same cluster as the jobs. When the cluster dies, you must not lose the list of what was running.
▸ Depth — follow-ups, how to build it on AWS, push-backs (open only if you want it)

If they dig deeper

  • Job states: submitted → queued → scheduled → running → succeeded/failed/cancelled; every transition is an event, so status and metrics are free.
  • Lease expiry: if heartbeats stop, the job is re-queued with attempt+1; outputs are idempotent so a double run is harmless.
  • Urgent work: a small reserved "express" pool; preempt only Spot executors, never drivers.
  • Cost: Graviton, Spot, right-sizing from the Spark history server, and a cost line per job returned to the tenant.

How I would actually build it

  1. Submit API (API Gateway → Lambda) validates the job spec, writes Job{id, tenant, spec, state=SUBMITTED, attempt=0} to DynamoDB, pushes id to an SQS FIFO queue per tenant.
  2. Scheduler (ECS service, stateless, several replicas) pulls from tenant queues in weighted round-robin, checks quota in a TenantUsage table, and submits a SparkApplication to EMR on EKS in the tenant's namespace.
  3. Lease: scheduler sets lease_until = now+2min; the Spark driver sidecar heartbeats every 30 s extending it; a sweeper re-queues jobs whose lease expired with attempt+1.
  4. Warm pool: a Karpenter/cluster-autoscaler node group kept at N nodes; executors on Spot with 5 instance types; drivers on On-Demand.
  5. Logs to CloudWatch/S3, Spark history server per tenant, metrics (queue wait, run time, cost) emitted per job to a metrics table the tenant can query.

They will push back with…

  • Why DynamoDB and not Postgres for job state? — Millions of rows a day, key-value access, conditional writes for leases, no schema migrations in my hot path. Postgres would work until it doesn't.
  • Spot kills your executors mid-job. — Spark re-executes lost tasks; checkpoints for long jobs; drivers never on Spot; diversify instance types so a single pool reclaim does not take everything.
  • A tenant submits 10,000 jobs at once. — Per-tenant queue and quota: they wait on their own queue, nobody else notices. Aging prevents starvation of small tenants.
  • What does the customer see when it fails? — State, attempt count, last error, a link to logs and the Spark UI — and a cost line even for failures.

Ask them first / ask back

  • Are customers submitting SQL mostly, or code? (SQL lets me add a query layer and optimize for them)
  • Latency expectation: minutes-to-start is fine, or do they need seconds?
  • Is there a shared cluster today? What hurts most — cost, fairness, or reliability?
  • Who pays — a central budget or chargeback per tenant?

cards.f: Q22 Scheduler for millions of daily jobs
cards.b:
In one sentence: A DAG store, a ready queue, a quota gate, and a state store — triggered by time or by data arrival.

In plain words: A scheduler decides when jobs run. Most jobs depend on other jobs' outputs ("run the sales report after the orders table is updated"). So each job declares what it needs; when all its inputs are published, it becomes "ready" and goes into a queue sorted by importance and deadline; a dispatcher hands ready jobs to the Spark platform as long as the team has not used up its quota. State lives in a database so a scheduler crash loses nothing.

Numbers to remember 1M jobs/day ≈ 12/s throughput is easy  ·  min(2^attempt × 30 s, 30 min) retry backoff  ·  deadline − p95 − margin when to alarm  ·  topological check on every dependency write
Say it like this (about 90 seconds)
  1. "Scale check: a million jobs a day is about twelve a second — the throughput is easy, the dependencies are the hard part."
  2. "Each job declares what it reads and writes; a job becomes ready when every upstream dataset version it needs is published."
  3. "The ready queue is ordered by priority and deadline; dispatch is gated by tenant quota; state lives in DynamoDB with a lease per attempt."
  4. "Retries use exponential backoff with a cap; cancellation sets a flag the worker checks on every heartbeat."
Trap: Cron everywhere. Time-based schedules silently run on incomplete upstream data; data triggers do not.
▸ Depth — follow-ups, how to build it on AWS, push-backs (open only if you want it)

If they dig deeper

  • Deadline scheduling: start time = deadline − p95 duration − margin; alert before the deadline is missed, not after.
  • Data triggers come from catalog publish events, which makes dependency-aware scheduling (Q29) the same mechanism.
  • Scheduler itself is stateless and horizontally scaled; it reads the state store, it never holds the truth in memory.

How I would actually build it

  1. Tables: Job (spec, owner, priority, deadline), Dependency (job → upstream dataset + version rule), Run (job, attempt, state, lease), Trigger (cron or dataset event).
  2. Catalog publish events hit an SQS queue; a resolver marks dependents whose inputs are now satisfied as READY and inserts them into a priority queue (DynamoDB sorted by priority#deadline or Redis sorted set).
  3. Dispatchers pop READY runs, check quota, hand to the execution platform (Q21), move state to SCHEDULED.
  4. Retries: attempt < max → re-queue after min(2^attempt × 30 s, 30 min); cancellation sets cancel_requested, worker checks it on every heartbeat.
  5. Deadline alarm: a sweeper computes deadline − p95_duration − now and alerts the owner while there is still time.

They will push back with…

  • Cycles in the DAG? — Rejected at registration — a topological check on every dependency write.
  • A million jobs, how big is the ready queue? — Peak is tens of thousands; priority queue in Redis handles that trivially; persistence is in DynamoDB, Redis can be rebuilt.
  • Clock skew and cron? — Cron triggers only create a run; dependencies still gate it. Time is a hint, data is the truth.
  • Upstream published a bad version? — Downstream pinned the version it consumed; republish creates a new version; dependents re-run from the pin rule (latest vs exact).

Ask them first / ask back

  • How many jobs are time-triggered versus data-triggered today? (tells me how much silent staleness exists)
  • Do deadlines mean "alert me" or "cancel it"?
  • Is there an existing orchestrator (Airflow) I must keep compatible with?

cards.f: Q25 — Shared platform for batch and streaming
cards.b: Share the control plane, catalog, auth, metrics; isolate the compute pools (streaming is long-lived, batch is bursty); one output format (Iceberg) so both land the same way.

Streaming: Flink checkpoints to S3 every minute, restart from last one. Batch: stage-level outputs are idempotent partitions, rerun only the failed stage; whole-cluster loss = re-queue from the control plane.

cards.f: Q27 — Optimization service for expensive jobs
cards.b: Read the Spark event log: skew = one task 10× the median, shuffle too big = repartition hint, bad join = broadcast the small side; show cost per job and the top three fixes.
Warm pool for the first minute, autoscale on queue depth, Spot with diversification across instance types, fall back to on-demand for drivers and deadline jobs.
A job pins the upstream version it consumed; it starts only on a publish event for a compatible schema; lineage is recorded for free.

cards.f: Q30 — Publishing lake data to DynamoDB / Redis / search
cards.b: Build the new copy off to the side, swap an alias/pointer, keep the old copy for rollback; partial failure = alias never moves; rebuild = rerun from the lake version.

cards.f: Q31 Scalable metadata catalog (with Q33 lineage)
cards.b:
In one sentence: A hot key-value store for lookups, a search index for discovery, and a lineage graph — all fed by change events from one write path.

In plain words: A catalog answers three different questions: "give me the details of table X" (a fast lookup by key — DynamoDB), "find tables about customers" (a text search — OpenSearch), and "what depends on table X" (a graph walk — lineage). One write path records every change and emits an event; the search index and the graph are built from those events, so they can always be rebuilt.

Numbers to remember PK = dataset id, SK = meta | v#0007 | schema#3 DynamoDB key design  ·  reads ≫ writes so cache + DAX  ·  partition lists from Iceberg metadata keep the catalog small  ·  catalog SLO > every engine's SLO it is on every path
Say it like this (about 90 seconds)
  1. "Scale: millions of tables and tens of millions of partitions, read far more than written."
  2. "Writes go through one versioned API into DynamoDB keyed by dataset id; every write emits an event."
  3. "From the events I build OpenSearch for discovery and a graph of job → reads → writes edges for lineage; both can be rebuilt from the event log."
  4. "Lineage is captured where it is cheapest: the Spark listener and the SQL parser record inputs and outputs automatically — no one fills in a form."
Trap: Making the catalog a relational table with a billion rows and a search box. Separate lookup, search and graph.
▸ Depth — follow-ups, how to build it on AWS, push-backs (open only if you want it)

If they dig deeper

  • Partition listing is the hot path — cache it, and let Iceberg metadata carry partition lists so the catalog stays small.
  • Impact analysis is a graph walk: "who breaks if I change this column" answered in seconds.
  • Catalog availability must exceed every engine's, since every query starts here — multi-AZ, read replicas, and a stale-read fallback.

How I would actually build it

  1. Write path: POST /datasets, POST /datasets/{id}/versions, PUT /datasets/{id}/schema — all go through one service that validates and writes DynamoDB (PK dataset id, SK meta | v#0007 | schema#3).
  2. DynamoDB Streams → Lambda → OpenSearch index (search) and a lineage edge table (src_dataset, job, dst_dataset, version).
  3. Lineage capture: a Spark listener in the platform image records inputs/outputs per job automatically; a SQL parser does the same for Athena/Redshift queries through the gateway.
  4. Reads: getDataset served from DynamoDB with DAX cache; partition lists come from Iceberg metadata files, not the catalog.
  5. Backfill/rebuild: replay the change stream from S3 to rebuild OpenSearch or the graph from scratch.

They will push back with…

  • Why not just Glue Data Catalog? — I use Glue as the engine-facing view, but ownership, contracts, quality and lineage live in my catalog; Glue is a projection of it.
  • Lineage at the column level? — Phase two: the SQL parser already sees columns; store column edges only for tagged (PII) datasets first.
  • Catalog goes down? — Engines keep a cached last-known-good; writes queue; catalog is multi-AZ with a read replica — its SLO is higher than any engine's.

Ask them first / ask back

  • Is lineage for compliance (must be complete) or for impact analysis (good enough is fine)?
  • How many catalogs exist today? Am I replacing or federating?
  • Who are the readers — humans searching, or engines looking up ten thousand times a second?

In one sentence: Policies on tags (not table names) at dataset, column and row level, decided in one service, enforced in every engine, with every decision logged.

In plain words: Authorization answers "may this person read these columns of this table?" The rules are written against tags ("PII", "Finance") rather than table names, so a new PII column is protected automatically. One service makes the decision; every query engine asks it (or receives its compiled rules) and enforces the answer; every decision is written to a log nobody can edit.

Numbers to remember tags, not table names policy scope  ·  60 s decision cache  ·  allow AND deny logged audit completeness  ·  bucket policy trusts engine roles only no bypass
Say it like this (about 90 seconds)
  1. "Policies attach to tags like PII or Finance, so a new column tagged PII is protected the day it appears."
  2. "A decision service answers: may user U read columns C of dataset D under row filter F — cached for seconds, logged forever."
  3. "Enforcement is in the engines: Lake Formation for Athena and Redshift Spectrum, a Spark plug-in for Cradle — the same answer everywhere."
  4. "Row-level rules are injected as filters; column rules as masking; the user never sees the raw table."
Trap: Enforcing in the gateway only. Anyone with a direct S3 path or a notebook bypasses you; enforce at the engine and the bucket policy.
▸ Depth — follow-ups, how to build it on AWS, push-backs (open only if you want it)

If they dig deeper

  • Break-glass access: time-boxed, approved by the dataset owner, flagged in the audit log.
  • Cross-account (Q35): grants are time-limited, revocable, and expressed as the same policy records.
  • Performance: decisions are pre-computed per (user, dataset) into a small cache; policy changes invalidate it.

How I would actually build it

  1. Policies as records: Policy{tag, principal_group, columns_allowed, row_filter, expiry}; tags attached to datasets and columns in the catalog.
  2. Lake Formation gets the compiled grants (LF-Tags → IAM principals) for Athena/Redshift Spectrum; Cradle Spark uses a plug-in that calls the same decision API and rewrites the query plan to drop columns and inject the row filter.
  3. Decision API: can(user, dataset, columns, purpose) → cached 60 s in ElastiCache; cache invalidated by policy-change events.
  4. Every decision (allow or deny) is written to Kinesis → S3 Object Lock bucket, partitioned by day, queryable in Athena.
  5. Break-glass: a time-boxed policy created through a workflow, flagged in the audit log, auto-expired.

They will push back with…

  • Someone reads the S3 bucket directly. — Bucket policy only trusts the engine roles; humans have no S3 path; LF-registered locations enforce that.
  • Row filters are slow. — They are predicates pushed to Parquet row groups; partition the data by the filter column where possible; measure the overhead per engine.
  • Policy by tag — who tags? — Auto-classification at registration plus owner confirmation; untagged columns default to the most restrictive class.

Ask them first / ask back

  • Which engines must be covered on day one? (each one is a different enforcement path)
  • Do we need row-level, or is column masking enough for the next year?
  • Is there a central identity (groups) I can bind to, or do I have to own principals too?
Index name, columns, owner, tags; rank by usage, freshness, quality score; show only what the user may request; show "who else uses this".
Share by policy record with purpose, expiry, revocation; data never copied, access granted in place (Lake Formation / S3 access points); every read audited.
Scan on registration (Macie-style classifiers + column names); auto-tag PII; tokenize or mask at publish; raw stays in a restricted zone.

cards.f: Q37 — Customer deletion across the lake
cards.b: Deletion is a dataset too: a stream of ids every job must honor; lineage finds derived copies; Iceberg delete + snapshot expiry removes history; backups expire on their retention clock; prove it with a report.
Rules per dataset (nulls, ranges, counts vs yesterday); publication gate blocks the pointer flip on failure; anomalies open an exception the owner must clear.
Every decision → Kinesis → S3 (object lock) → Athena; sample the successes, keep every denial; partition by day so queries stay cheap.
Pin data snapshot id + code commit + config together as a version record; ML training reads the snapshot, never "latest".

cards.f: Q41 Query gateway over Athena, Redshift and Spark (with Q42–Q44)
cards.b:
In one sentence: One front door that authenticates, classifies, routes by query shape, and logs cost — three engines behind it.

In plain words: A query gateway is one front door in front of three engines. It checks who you are, reads your SQL, applies the authorization rules, guesses how big the query is, and sends it to the engine that fits: small and rare to Athena, repeated dashboards to Redshift, huge transformations to Spark. It also records what every query cost, which is how teams get a bill.

Numbers to remember route by query shape not by team  ·  concurrency + daily bytes budget per tenant  ·  cache key = SQL + snapshot ids + policy version stale impossible by construction  ·  engine, bytes, seconds, dollars logged per query
Say it like this (about 90 seconds)
  1. "Every query comes through one endpoint; I parse it, apply policy, estimate its size and route: ad-hoc and small to Athena, repeated BI to Redshift, heavy transformations to Spark."
  2. "Admission control is per tenant: a concurrency limit and a bytes-scanned budget, so one bad query queues instead of degrading everyone (Q43)."
  3. "Results are cached by (normalized SQL, dataset versions, user's policy version) — any of those change and the entry is invalid (Q44)."
  4. "The gateway records engine, bytes, seconds and dollars per query, which is the input to showback."
Trap: Routing by team name. Route by what the query needs; let a team use all three.
▸ Depth — follow-ups, how to build it on AWS, push-backs (open only if you want it)

If they dig deeper

  • Predictable latency (Q42): Redshift for the dashboards with reserved concurrency; Athena for the long tail; pre-aggregate the ten most common queries.
  • Cancellation: the gateway owns a query id and can kill it in any engine.
  • Failover: if an engine is unhealthy, route to the next-best one and tell the user it may be slower.

How I would actually build it

  1. Gateway: ECS service behind an ALB; POST /query returns a query id; GET /query/{id} returns status/results location.
  2. Pipeline inside: authenticate (IAM/SSO) → parse (SQL parser) → policy rewrite (Q34) → cost estimate (bytes from table stats) → router → engine adapter → result to S3 with a signed URL.
  3. Admission: per-tenant concurrency and daily bytes budget in a TenantQuota table; over budget → queued, not rejected; user sees position in queue.
  4. Result cache: key = hash(normalized SQL + input snapshot ids + policy version); stored in S3 with TTL; a hit is returned in milliseconds.
  5. Every query row: engine, bytes, seconds, dollars → a usage table that feeds showback.

They will push back with…

  • Why not let people use Athena directly? — They can — through the gateway, which is where auth, cost and cancel live. Direct access is a bypass of all three.
  • How do you decide Athena vs Redshift? — Estimated bytes and repeat frequency: small/rare → Athena; repeated dashboard → Redshift; huge transformations → Spark. The rule lives in config, not code.
  • Cache returns stale data. — The key includes snapshot ids, so a new publish is a new key automatically. Stale is impossible by construction, not by TTL.

Ask them first / ask back

  • What is the mix today — interactive dashboards or ad-hoc exploration?
  • What is "predictable" in numbers? p95 of 5 seconds and p95 of 60 seconds are different systems.
  • Do I own the BI tool connection, or do I expose JDBC?

In one sentence: Measure what customers feel — freshness, job success, query latency — set SLOs on those, and alert on error-budget burn, not on CPU.

In plain words: Observability means knowing, from numbers, whether customers are happy. The top of the pyramid is what they feel: "is my dataset ready by 6am?" Below that are the platform numbers that explain it (queue delays, failure rates), and below that the machine numbers (CPU, disk). Alerts fire when you are burning through your allowed failures too fast — not when a CPU is busy.

Numbers to remember 1 h fast burn pages · 6 h slow burn tickets alert windows  ·  freshness lag = now − max(event time) the SLI  ·  fresh_by stored next to the dataset SLO lives in the catalog  ·  impacted datasets + tenants every incident record
Say it like this (about 90 seconds)
  1. "Top of the stack are customer SLOs: dataset X is fresh by 06:00, p95 query under ten seconds, 99.9% of jobs succeed."
  2. "Underneath are the platform indicators that explain them: scheduling delay, freshness lag per dataset, error rate per engine."
  3. "I alert on burn rate — spending the monthly budget in a few hours pages a human, slow burn makes a ticket."
  4. "Customer impact is a first-class field: every incident says how many datasets and tenants were late, and by how long."
Trap: A wall of infrastructure graphs. Start from the customer promise and work down.
▸ Depth — follow-ups, how to build it on AWS, push-backs (open only if you want it)

If they dig deeper

  • Correctness SLI: reconciliation pass rate and quarantine rate per dataset.
  • One dashboard per persona: producer (my datasets), consumer (my subscriptions), operator (the platform).
  • Every SLO has an owner and a review cadence; an SLO nobody reviews is a number.

How I would actually build it

  1. SLIs computed by a metrics job from the control-plane tables: job success rate per tenant, scheduling delay p95, freshness lag = now − max(event time) per dataset.
  2. SLOs stored next to the dataset in the catalog (fresh_by=06:00); a sweeper compares and emits a late event with the number of downstream subscribers affected.
  3. Alerting: CloudWatch alarms on burn rate (two windows: 1 h fast burn pages, 6 h slow burn tickets); PagerDuty routes to the owning team by catalog ownership.
  4. Dashboards: one per persona; incidents tagged with impacted datasets and tenants so the COE has numbers, not adjectives.

They will push back with…

  • Who gets paged — platform or dataset owner? — Platform for mechanism failures (scheduler down), owner for content failures (their job crashed). The catalog ownership field routes it.
  • Alert fatigue? — Only burn-rate alerts page; everything else is a ticket; I review the page list monthly and delete alerts that never led to action.
  • How do you know correctness, not just arrival? — Reconciliation and quality-gate pass rate per dataset are SLIs too.

Ask them first / ask back

  • What do customers complain about most today — late data, wrong data, or slow queries?
  • Do we have an on-call rotation and a COE process, or am I building that too?
  • Which ten datasets, if late, would the business notice?

cards.f: Q46 — Regional outage: contain and recover
cards.b: Freeze non-essential jobs; run the tier-1 datasets in the second region from replicated manifests; drain the backlog by deadline, then priority, with a cap so recovery does not overload the catalog.

Tag everything by tenant at submit time; compute cost = job seconds × instance rate, storage = bytes × days, queries = bytes scanned; showback first, chargeback second, soft budgets that warn, hard quotas that queue.
Canary a few jobs, run old and new side by side, diff the outputs row-level, keep rollback a pointer flip, move tenants in waves by risk, never force a date.

cards.f: Q48 Workload doubles, budget stays flat
cards.b:
In one sentence: Say the unit cost first — dollars per terabyte processed — then measure, cut waste, make waste visible, and defer on purpose.

In plain words: The workload doubles, the money does not. The only way out is to halve the cost of each unit of work. First measure (cost per terabyte, per team, and how much capacity sits idle). Then cut waste with engineering (merge small files, cheaper instance types, Spot pricing, move cold data to cheap storage). Then make waste visible so teams fix their own. Then name what you will not do this year.

Numbers to remember cost per TB processed the unit  ·  30–50% from compaction + right-sizing  ·  60–70% Spot saving on executors  ·  showback → chargeback one month apart
Say it like this (about 90 seconds)
  1. "If work doubles and money does not, I need to halve the cost per unit; so first I measure cost per terabyte and per tenant, and how much capacity sits idle."
  2. "Then the engineering cuts: compaction so queries scan less, Graviton and Spot for compute, lifecycle tiering for storage, kill zombie jobs nobody reads."
  3. "Then the behavior cuts: quotas and showback make waste visible to the team that causes it."
  4. "And I say out loud what I will defer — a new engine, exotic features — and get agreement on that list."
Trap: Promising it all with "optimization". Name the unit, the three biggest levers, and the things you will not do.
▸ Depth — follow-ups, how to build it on AWS, push-backs (open only if you want it)

If they dig deeper

  • Typical wins: 30–50% from small-file compaction and right-sizing alone; Spot another 60–70% on executor cost.
  • Measure weekly, publish the trend, celebrate the teams that cut the most.
  • The thing not to cut: the control plane's durability and the audit log.

How I would actually build it

  1. Week 1: a cost report per tenant per job from the usage table and the Cost Explorer export — cost per TB processed, idle capacity, top 20 jobs by dollars.
  2. Weeks 2–6: compaction service on the most-read tables, Graviton instance types, Spot for executors, S3 lifecycle policies, Spark config right-sizing from the history server.
  3. Weeks 6–10: showback dashboards per tenant; soft budgets that warn; kill switch for jobs with zero downstream readers in 30 days.
  4. Ongoing: weekly cost review with the three biggest tenants; a deferred-list published and agreed with leadership.

They will push back with…

  • Which lever first? — The one with the biggest number on my report — usually small files and idle clusters. I will not guess; I measure first.
  • Teams will resist quotas. — Showback before chargeback; show them their own waste; quotas only after the data is visible for a month.
  • What do you refuse to cut? — Control-plane durability, the audit log, and on-call sanity.

Ask them first / ask back

  • Is the budget flat in dollars or in headcount too?
  • Which costs are mine to control — compute, storage, or data transfer too?
  • Is there a date, or is it a trend to bend?

cards.f: Q50 MVP and evolution for a Cradle-like platform with ten engineers
cards.b:
In one sentence: Build one job type end to end in the first quarter, adopt managed services for everything that is not the differentiator, and name a separate owner for each boundary.

In plain words: With ten engineers, build the narrow path first: a customer can submit one Spark job, it reads and writes S3 safely, and they can see whether it worked. Everything that is not the special sauce (catalog, Kubernetes, identity) is adopted, not built. The scheduler comes second, streaming third. Two teams: one owns the dispatcher, one owns the cars.

Numbers to remember time to first successful job < 1 day MVP metric  ·  10 tenants weekly, > 99% success six-month bar  ·  2 teams of 5 control plane / data plane  ·  adopt: catalog, auth, Kubernetes build: job model + fairness
Say it like this (about 90 seconds)
  1. "Quarter one: submit a Spark job, read from S3, write to S3 with atomic publication, see status and logs — one path that works every time."
  2. "I adopt EMR on EKS, the Glue catalog, DynamoDB and IAM rather than build them; the differentiator is the job model, scheduling and fairness, so that is what we write."
  3. "Quarter two: scheduler with dependencies, retries and quotas; quarter three and four: streaming, lineage, cost per tenant."
  4. "Ten engineers is two teams: one owns the control plane, one owns the data plane; the catalog and auth are consumed from the platform teams that already own them."
Trap: Building the catalog and the scheduler before a single job runs end to end.
▸ Depth — follow-ups, how to build it on AWS, push-backs (open only if you want it)
