If they dig deeper

  • Defer: multi-region, a custom query engine, a UI beyond a status page.
  • Metrics from day one: time to first successful job, job success rate, cost per job.
  • Risk: scope creep from the first big customer — write the MVP contract and hold it.

How I would actually build it

  1. Q1: submit API + DynamoDB job table + one SQS queue + EMR on EKS + S3 in/out with manifests + a status page. One job type (Spark SQL). Two engineers on control plane, four on data plane and onboarding, two on tooling, two floating.
  2. Q2: scheduler with dependencies, retries, per-tenant quotas; Glue catalog hook; first three customers in production.
  3. Q3: streaming (Flink), cost per tenant, Spark history server, warm pools, on-call rotation and runbooks.
  4. Q4: lineage capture, result caching, canary deploys for platform versions; hand the catalog and auth to their owning teams via interfaces.

They will push back with…

  • Why not build the catalog first? — Nothing to catalog until a job runs. Customers pay for the job path, not the catalog.
  • Ten engineers is not enough. — Then I adopt more: managed Flink, managed Airflow if needed; I write only the fairness and job model, which is the differentiator.
  • How do you know the MVP worked? — Time to first successful job under a day; ten tenants running weekly; success rate > 99%.

Ask them first / ask back

  • Who are the first three customers and what one job must work for them?
  • What exists already that I can adopt — catalog, auth, Kubernetes platform?
  • What does success look like at six months in a number?

decks.title: Worked designs & scalability Q&A
decks.blurb: Telemetry pipelines, lakehouse, OTA, multi-tenant APIs, and short scalability answers.

cards.f: D1. Backend platform for a fleet of connected home robots
cards.b:
Clarify

2M devices today, 5M in three years; one telemetry message per 5 minutes plus events; commands must round-trip in under 3 s p99; AWS primary; core robot function must not depend on the cloud.

Architecture

App (iOS/Android/Web)
   │ OIDC/PKCE
   ▼
API Gateway ─▶ BFF (GraphQL) ─▶ Accounts │ Devices │ Commands │ Telemetry-read │ Notifications │ Entitlements
                                     │         │            │                        ▲
                                  Aurora   DynamoDB    SQS/EventBridge               │
                                                         │                            │
Devices ═MQTT/mTLS═▶ IoT Core ──rules──▶ Kinesis ──▶ Flink ──▶ Timestream (hot) / S3 Parquet (raw) / Redshift (gold)
   ▲   shadow, jobs      │                                └──▶ SNS/APNs/FCM notifications
   └─────── commands ◀───┘

Key decisions

  • Managed broker (IoT Core) for a 9–15 person team; revisit EMQX on EKS only if message cost dominates at 5M devices.
  • Control path isolated from analytics: commands and acks use their own topics and a dedicated consumer; telemetry goes through Kinesis.
  • Shadow for config, commands for actions; command records in DynamoDB with TTL; state exposed to the app.
  • Schema registry with additive-only evolution; adapter at ingest; golden fixtures in CI.
  • BFF in GraphQL with persisted queries; domain services REST/gRPC; N−2 app support.

Failure modes

  • Broker restart → reconnect storm: device jittered backoff, connection rate limits, warm capacity. Robots keep cleaning.
  • Region outage: control-path active/passive in a second region with DNS failover; device certs valid in both; telemetry buffered on device.
  • Bad firmware build spamming errors: per-device rate limit at broker; DLQ alert; OTA stage halts automatically.
  • Entitlement service down: fail open for a short TTL, then closed.
  • Notification storm: queue with dedup and rate caps per user.

Operations and cost

SLOs: command round-trip 99.5% < 3 s; connectivity 99%; API 99.9%. Dashboards by firmware × hardware rev. Cost per active device tracked monthly; first lever is batching telemetry on device. Rough messaging cost at 1M devices and 288 msgs/day is on the order of $9–10K/month; batching hourly cuts it roughly 12×.

cards.f: D2. Telemetry ingestion and real-time analytics
cards.b:
Requirements

Ingest 5–50K events/s with bursts; per-source ordering; queryable within 60 s; replay for a month; feed dashboards, alerts, and ML; cost proportional to volume.

Architecture (Kappa)

Sources ─▶ Stream (Kinesis / Kafka)  keyed by source id, 2–7 day retention
             ├─▶ Validator (schema registry, DLQ) ─▶ Enricher (device/account context from cache)
             │        └─▶ Flink: dedup(source,seq) → event-time windows / sessions → alerts
             ├─▶ Raw sink: S3 Parquet partitioned dt=/cohort=/  (system of record, replay)
             ├─▶ Hot store: Timestream / ClickHouse (7–30 days, dashboards, app history)
             └─▶ Warehouse: Redshift / BigQuery via dbt (aggregates, joins, BI, feature tables)

Decisions

  • Kappa over Lambda architecture: one code path; replay from the raw archive when logic changes.
  • Event time with watermarks; late data to a side output and reconciled nightly.
  • At-least-once plus idempotent writes; exactly-once only where a sink needs it (billing).
  • Partition by source hash; monitor skew; a per-source quota upstream.
  • Hot/warm/cold tiering; downsample after 30 days.

Operations

Consumer lag and DLQ rate are the two pages. Backfill runbook from S3. Schema changes go through the registry's compatibility check. Cost reported per million events and per source.

Trap: proposing Kafka Streams and Flink and Spark together. Pick one processor and say why.

Requirements

Push signed firmware to 2M devices in cohorts; halt automatically on regression; roll back safely; support devices offline for months; audit every campaign.

Components

  • Artifact service: images in S3, signed with a KMS-held key, SBOM attached, immutable version metadata (hardware compatibility, minimum-from version).
  • Campaign service: target definition (hardware rev, region, current firmware, opt-in), stages with gate metrics, schedule windows (not during a cycle, not at night), approvals.
  • Fleet state: per-device firmware version, last seen, update eligibility — from shadow/registry.
  • Job dispatcher: IoT Jobs (or a topic per device) delivering a job document with a pre-signed URL and expiry; progress reported to job topics.
  • Gate evaluator: per stage, compares boot-success, connect-rate, cycle-success, and error-code rates for updated vs control cohort; auto-halts on regression.
  • Device side: verify signature, write to inactive slot, reboot, confirm health, commit; bootloader rolls back after N failed boots.

Edge cases

Device comes online after a campaign ended → eligible for the latest completed campaign, not the halted one. Power loss mid-write → slot integrity check. Partial fleets stuck on old versions → dashboard of the tail with reasons (offline, ineligible, opted out).

Metrics

Rollout velocity, per-stage failure rate, rollback count, time to majority, tail size.

cards.f: D4. Vehicle feature management at 11M vehicles
cards.b:
This is S1 as a design. Requirements: return the feature set for a vehicle in <100 ms p99 at 30M+ req/month growing to hundreds of millions; correctness within minutes of a configuration change; resilience to downstream outages.

Architecture

Manufacturing / config / entitlement events ─▶ Event bus ─▶ Capability engine (rules × 15 params)
                                                                    │
                                                          Document DB (capability per VIN)  ◀── nightly/15-day reconciliation
                                                                    │
                                                          Redis cache ◀── Read API (serverless) ◀── FordPass / vehicle / dealer
  • Compute on change, not on read. Reads are a cache hit; the read path has zero synchronous downstream dependencies.
  • Reconciliation catches missed events; versioned rules so a rule change triggers targeted recomputation.
  • Cache invalidation by VIN on capability update; TTL as backstop.
  • Regional read replicas for latency; the event path can be single-region.

Result in practice: sub-100 ms, horizontal scale, lower compute, and capability visible before sale. Generalizes to any "derived state read far more than it changes" problem — entitlements, device capabilities, pricing.

• Inputs: device events, account events, marketing (separate pipeline and consent). Output: push, email, SMS, in-app inbox.
  • Flow: event → rules (which users, which template, priority) → preference and quiet-hours filter → dedup window per (user, event type) → per-channel queues → senders with retries and provider failover → delivery receipts → analytics.
  • Store: user preferences and device tokens (multi-device), notification log with TTL.
  • Latency budget: p95 under 10 s from device event; trace end to end with the device correlation ID.
  • Protections: per-user rate caps, global circuit breaker on provider errors, a kill switch per template, and a canary user cohort for template changes.
  • Localization from day one for Canada (French) and Germany.

Requirements

Dozens of plants, several ERPs by acquisition, historians and MES per site, OEM reporting obligations; support BI, advanced analytics, and ML; multi-cloud by inheritance; governance and cost control.

Architecture

Plant edge: OPC-UA → edge gateway (buffer, contextualize with ISA-95 ids) → MQTT/Kafka
Enterprise: ERP/MES/PLM/CRM → CDC (Debezium/DMS) or batch → landing
                     │
              Bronze (raw, immutable, Parquet/Iceberg on S3/ADLS)
                     │  dbt + Spark, tests, contracts
              Silver (conformed: asset, part, order, work order, quality result, downtime)
                     │
              Gold data products (OEE, scrap, warranty, inventory, energy) → warehouse / semantic layer → Power BI
                     │
              Feature store → MLOps (registry, pipelines, monitoring) → models (batch + edge)
Catalog + lineage + access policy across all layers; single orchestration (Airflow/Dagster)

Decisions

  • Iceberg tables so Spark, Trino, Redshift Spectrum, BigQuery, and Databricks all read the same data — this is the anti-lock-in move.
  • Conformed dimensions for asset, part, and plant are the hardest and most valuable work; fund a data-modeling effort explicitly.
  • Semantic layer (dbt metrics / Power BI datasets) so OEE means one thing company-wide.
  • Edge buffering and contextualization so plant data arrives with the work order and part it belongs to; otherwise it's unusable.
  • Domain ownership with platform standards; data contracts with quality SLAs.

Sequencing

Quarter 1: catalog, landing, two gold products (OEE, scrap) for two plants. Quarter 2–3: warranty and inventory products; first ML use case. Year 2: scale plants, energy, engineering data. Measure freshness SLAs, certified products, adoption, and cost per product.

cards.f: D7. Real-time SPC on the floor plus strategic AI research on the same data
cards.b:
• Two speeds, one source: an edge/streaming path for operations and a lakehouse path for research, both fed from the same bronze events.
  • Edge: gateway computes control charts (X-bar/R, EWMA, CUSUM) and Western Electric rule violations locally within seconds; alerts to HMI/andon; works with the WAN down.
  • Stream: events to Kafka/Kinesis with part genealogy; Flink computes multi-station correlations and feeds a live quality dashboard; alerts into the MES.
  • Lakehouse: full history for capability studies, root-cause analytics, and predictive quality models; models trained centrally, deployed to the edge as scoring containers with version control.
  • Governance: one definition of each measurement; calibration metadata; model changes go through the same change control as process changes (IATF expects it).
  • Metric: first-pass yield, scrap $, time from deviation to intervention.

cards.f: D8. Enterprise RAG / agentic assistant, IP-sensitive, on-prem or VPC
cards.b:
You've built this (RheinMan, RheinCoder). Present it as a design.

Sources (PLM, Confluence, work instructions, quality records, code) ─▶ Ingestion (connectors, chunking, PII/CUI scrubbing via Presidio)
     ─▶ Embeddings ─▶ Vector store (Qdrant) + metadata/ACL index
User ─▶ Gateway (SSO, input filtering, rate limits) ─▶ Orchestrator (n8n / LangGraph)
     ─▶ Retrieval (hybrid: vector + keyword, ACL-filtered, reranked) ─▶ LLM (on-prem or private endpoint)
     ─▶ Tools (Teamcenter query, MES lookup, code actions with approval) ─▶ Response with citations
Evaluation harness (golden Q&A set, faithfulness, retrieval recall) · Flight recorder / audit log · Cost and latency telemetry
  • Access control enforced at retrieval, not by prompt; the index carries document ACLs.
  • Hybrid retrieval and reranking beat bigger models for accuracy on enterprise docs.
  • Evaluation set before rollout; regression tests on every prompt or model change.
  • Agentic actions: tool scopes, human approval for side effects (per-hunk diff approval), full audit trail.
  • Model choice by data classification: on-prem for CUI/IP; private cloud endpoints for the rest. You evaluated several open models and rejected one for the secured slot — say why.
  • Measure: task time saved, answer acceptance rate, cost per query.

cards.f: D9. Multi-region consumer backend with GDPR residency
cards.b:
• Regions: US (primary), EU (Frankfurt) for German customers, possibly Canada. Account and PII data pinned to the home region; a global directory maps account → region.
  • Routing: geo-DNS to nearest edge; the gateway looks up the home region and proxies if the user travels.
  • Devices connect to the home region's broker; certs valid in all regions; telemetry pseudonymized (device key, not account) if centralized for analytics.
  • Data lifecycle: retention schedule per data class; deletion cascades (account, devices, telemetry keys, backups within the policy window); subject-access export.
  • Consent and DPIA for camera/AI features; processor agreements with vendors; breach process meeting 72-hour notification.
  • Infrastructure: region rebuilt from Terraform; per-region dashboards and on-call; per-region cost.
  • Tradeoff to state: active/active for the control path is expensive and rarely needed; active/passive with buffered devices is usually enough.

• Data: OEM warranty claims (often EDI or portals, inconsistent codes), returned-part analysis, production genealogy (which lot, machine, shift, supplier lot), quality results, field telemetry where available, supplier data.
  • Join key is the hard part: serial or lot traceability from claim back to the production record. Fund traceability gaps first.
  • Analytics: claim rate by build month/plant/line/supplier lot (Weibull and hazard curves), early-warning detection (claims trending above expected for a cohort), text mining of claim narratives, cost attribution.
  • Actions: engineering change, supplier containment, field campaign decisions, negotiation with OEMs on responsibility.
  • Metrics: warranty cost per unit, time from first field signal to containment, recovery from suppliers.
  • Sequencing: one product family with the highest warranty spend; a monthly early-warning report in a quarter; a model later.

cards.f: D11. Modernizing a monolith without downtime
cards.b:
1. Observability first: traces, metrics, and a dependency map of the monolith so you know what you're cutting.
  2. Identify bounded contexts by change frequency and team ownership, not by table.
  3. Strangler pattern: an API gateway in front; extract the highest-change, lowest-coupling context first; route traffic gradually; contract tests between old and new.
  4. Data: expand/contract migrations; CDC or an outbox to keep the monolith's database and the new service in sync during transition; never share a database long-term.
  5. Platform in parallel: CI/CD, containers, IaC, so each extracted service lands on a paved road.
  6. Stop when the remaining monolith is stable and rarely changes; a modular monolith is a valid end state.

Measure with DORA and incident trends. Avoid big-bang rewrites; they fail on the data migration and the second-system effect.

cards.f: D12. API gateway and distributed rate limiter
cards.b:
• Gateway responsibilities: TLS, JWT validation, routing, per-client and per-user limits, request validation, WAF, canary weights, observability.
  • Rate limiting algorithms: token bucket (bursty-friendly, the default), sliding window log (accurate, memory-heavy), sliding window counter (good compromise), leaky bucket (smooth output).
  • Distributed: counters in Redis with Lua for atomic check-and-decrement; key = client/user × window; local in-memory pre-limits at each gateway node to shed load before hitting Redis; accept slight over-admission during Redis failover (fail open with a local cap).
  • Tiers: per app version, per user, per device, per endpoint; higher limits for the control path than for analytics reads.
  • Responses: 429 with Retry-After; clients back off with jitter.

• Data: ERP purchase orders and inventory, supplier portals/EDI (ASNs, confirmations), MES consumption, logistics tracking, supplier quality (SCARs), demand from OEM releases.
  • Model: a control-tower view of material availability by plant/part/day; exception-based alerts (late ASN, short shipment, quality hold) rather than dashboards nobody reads.
  • Analytics: safety-stock optimization from demand variability and lead-time variability; supplier risk scoring; what-if on schedule changes.
  • Your Plex Supplier Portal and Power BI Mfg S&C dashboard with Supplier OTD, SCARs, and Material Availability drill-downs are exactly this — cite it.
  • Metrics: OTD, days of inventory, expedite spend, working capital freed.

cards.f: D14. Multi-agent coding platform for a regulated engineering org
cards.b: RheinCoder as a design: VS Code extension; LangGraph tool-calling loop; tools for read/edit/build/semantic search/impact analysis/plan context; repository intelligence via a code graph; project rules file; per-hunk approval; flight recorder for audit; on-prem models only; automated test suite; targets Spring Boot and embedded C. Decisions to highlight: migrating from a classifier/lane pipeline to a tool-calling loop (why: composability and fewer brittle heuristics), keeping humans in the approval loop, and evaluating models for the secured slot. Metrics: acceptance rate of proposed changes, build-pass rate, time to complete tasks, and incidents caused (zero tolerance).

cards.f: What's the difference between scalability and performance?
cards.b: Performance is how fast one request is; scalability is whether throughput grows roughly linearly with resources. A system can be fast and unscalable (a single big database) or scalable and slow (a wide batch system). Ask which the customer needs; for a data platform it's usually throughput per dollar with a latency floor per tier.

cards.f: Horizontal vs vertical scaling — when each?
cards.b: Vertical (a bigger box) is simplest and often right until you hit the largest instance or need redundancy; it has a ceiling and a single point of failure. Horizontal (more boxes) needs stateless services or partitioned state, a load balancer, and coordination — but has no ceiling and gives fault tolerance. Databases are the usual holdout: read replicas first, then sharding when writes saturate.

cards.f: How do you scale a stateful component like a database?
cards.b: In order: query and index tuning (most "scale" problems are one bad query), caching reads, read replicas, vertical headroom, then partitioning by a key that matches the access pattern (tenant, customer, date). Sharding is irreversible-ish and complicates joins and transactions, so it comes last. For analytic workloads, move to a columnar store or the lake instead of sharding an OLTP database.

cards.f: What breaks at 10× traffic in a system you've owned?
cards.b: Feature Management at Ford: per-request computation made CPU scale with reads and four synchronous dependencies made availability the product of theirs. At 10×, compute cost and tail latency would have been the first to break, then downstream rate limits. The redesign made reads a cache hit and moved compute to configuration events, so 10× reads cost almost nothing. The general lesson: find the resource that scales with the wrong variable.

cards.f: How do you choose a partition key, and what's a hot partition ?
cards.b: Choose the key consumers filter or join on, with enough cardinality to spread load and enough locality to keep related data together — device ID for per-device ordering, date for time-range scans. A hot partition is one key taking a disproportionate share (a single chatty producer, a celebrity user, today's date in a date-keyed table). Mitigations: hash a suffix onto the key, write sharding, rate limits upstream, and monitoring that shows per-key skew before customers do.

cards.f: Caching: where, what, and the two classic failures.
cards.b: Cache at the edge (CDN) for static, at the service for computed reads (Redis), at the database for query results. Cache what's read far more than written and tolerates staleness. Failures: the stampede when a hot key expires and thousands of requests recompute at once (fix: request coalescing, jittered TTLs, refresh-ahead), and stale-after-permission-change (fix: include the policy version in the cache key).

cards.f: Synchronous vs asynchronous — how do you decide?
cards.b: Synchronous when the caller needs the answer to proceed and latency is tight. Asynchronous when work can be deferred, fans out, or crosses a team boundary — queues absorb bursts and decouple failure. The structural rule from every system I've run: the latency-critical path and the batch/analytics path never share a queue, a cluster, or a database.

cards.f: How do you handle a thundering herd ?
cards.b: Jittered exponential backoff on clients, rate limiting at the edge, warm capacity before a known event, request coalescing, and queues that smooth the spike into sustainable throughput. For a data platform the herd is a hub dataset publishing and five hundred downstream jobs waking at once — rate-limit the fan-out and prioritize by tier.

Under a partition you choose one (CAP); without one you trade latency for consistency (PACELC). Control-plane state (job leases, catalog commits) needs strong consistency — DynamoDB conditional writes or a transactional store. Analytics outputs tolerate eventual consistency with versioning so readers always see a complete version. Say which part of the system is which; that's the senior answer.

Parallelism is the partition count, so plan it ahead (Kafka partitions can't shrink; Kinesis shards split/merge). Consumer lag is the health metric; autoscale consumers on it. Keep keyed state bounded (TTL, windows). Separate hot aggregates from the archival sink. Back-of-envelope every time: events/s × bytes = MB/s → shards/partitions at 1–5 MB/s each.

cards.f: Scaling Spark jobs — the five things that matter.
cards.b: Input file size and format (small files and JSON kill it), partition count vs executor count, shuffle volume (joins and group-bys — broadcast the small side), skew (one key with 40% of rows — salt it), and memory spill. Adaptive query execution handles some automatically; an advisor service on event logs finds the rest. Most "we need a bigger cluster" requests are one of these five.

cards.f: How do you scale an organization, not just a system?
cards.b: Team boundaries aligned to service boundaries with API contracts (Conway's law, used deliberately); a platform team providing paved roads so product teams don't each build CI, observability, and infra; written standards and decision records so coordination doesn't require meetings; and operational ownership — the team that builds it runs it. Amazon's two-pizza team is this idea; my version at Rheinmetall was domain-aligned pods on shared CI/CD and a reference architecture.

cards.f: How do you know when you're over-engineering for scale?
cards.b: When the design handles 100× and the roadmap says 3×. Design for roughly 5× current with a documented path to 50×: stateless services, a partitionable data model, and no shared queues between critical and batch paths. Spanner-class global databases, active/active multi-region, and custom schedulers are earned, not assumed — say so, and say what signal would trigger the next step.

A system that scales linearly in cost with usage is only scalable if the business scales too. The metric is unit cost — per request, per TB processed, per active device — and the design goal is sub-linear: caching, batching, columnar formats, Spot, and compute that scales with change rather than with reads. The Andes migration is the public example: higher load, 40–90% lower cost.

cards.f: Give a back-of-envelope estimate for a lake ingesting 50 TB a day.
cards.b: 50 TB/day raw ≈ 580 MB/s sustained; as Parquet at ~8:1, ~6 TB/day stored, ~2.2 PB/year before tiering; S3 Standard at ~$23/TB-month → ~$50K/month by year end, halved with tiering. Processing: if every byte is read twice a day by Spark, ~12 TB/day scanned; at Spot EMR pricing that's a few hundred dollars a day. The point isn't the exact numbers; it's that you can produce them in thirty seconds and know which one dominates.

decks.title: Cloud architecture & system design book
decks.blurb: Architecture, microservices, cloud, reliability, DevOps, data, security, observability, leadership, trade-offs.

cards.b: System architecture is the backbone of any scalable software product. This chapter covers the fundamental design patterns, decisions, and tradeoffs that define how modern large-scale systems are built and operated.

System architecture defines the high-level structure of a software system — its components, how they interact, and the principles guiding their design. At scale, architecture decisions can mean the difference between a product that thrives under millions of users and one that collapses under load.

When designing systems, always start by clarifying requirements before jumping into solutions.

Requirements Framework
Functional Requirements Non-Functional Requirements
User registration and authentication Availability: 99.99% uptime
Real-time data processing Latency: < 200ms p99
Search and retrieval Throughput: 100k requests/sec
Notifications and alerts Durability: no data loss
Admin and reporting dashboards Scalability: 10x growth in 2 years

A typical large-scale architecture separates concerns into distinct layers: the client tier, the API/gateway tier, the service tier, the data tier, and the infrastructure tier.

  • Client Tier: Web, mobile, and third-party consumers

  • API Gateway / Load Balancer: Single entry point, routing, rate limiting, auth

  • Service Tier: Business logic implemented as microservices or a modular monolith

  • Data Tier: Databases, caches, object stores, message queues

  • Infrastructure Tier: Compute, networking, security, observability

Scaling is not just about adding more servers. It requires careful planning at every layer.

Horizontal vs. Vertical Scaling
Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out) Vertical Scaling (Scale Up)
Add more instances behind a load balancer Add more CPU, RAM, storage to existing machine
Better fault tolerance — no single point of failure Simpler to implement — no code changes needed
Preferred for stateless services Limited by hardware ceiling
Requires session externalization (Redis) Suitable for databases short-term
AWS: Auto Scaling Groups, EKS node pools AWS: EC2 instance type upgrade (t3 → m5 → c5)
GCP: Managed Instance Groups, GKE node auto-provisioner GCP: Custom machine types in Compute Engine
Load Balancing

Load balancers distribute incoming traffic across multiple backend instances. They are essential to eliminate single points of failure and improve throughput.

AWS Elastic Load Balancer (ELB) comes in three flavors: Application Load Balancer (ALB) for HTTP/HTTPS Layer 7 routing, Network Load Balancer (NLB) for ultra-high performance TCP/UDP, and Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) for inline virtual appliances. ALB supports path-based and host-based routing, WebSockets, and deep health checks.
GCP Google Cloud Load Balancing is a globally distributed, anycast-based service. The HTTP(S) Load Balancer provides global routing with Cloud Armor (DDoS and WAF), while the Internal TCP/UDP Load Balancer handles east-west traffic within a VPC. GCP’s Premium Tier routes traffic over Google’s private backbone for lower latency.

A reliable system is designed with the assumption that failures will occur. The goal is to contain failures, recover quickly, and degrade gracefully.

  • Redundancy: Deploy across multiple Availability Zones (AZs) and regions

  • Health Checks: Regular liveness and readiness probes to remove unhealthy nodes

  • Circuit Breakers: Stop cascading failures by short-circuiting calls to failing services

  • Retries with Exponential Backoff: Avoid thundering herds during recovery

  • Bulkheads: Isolate resource pools so one failure does not consume all capacity

  • Timeout Policies: Every external call must have a configured timeout

Active-Active Active-Passive
Both regions serve live traffic simultaneously One region is standby, promoted on failure
Better performance and utilization Simpler configuration and data consistency
Complex data synchronization required RPO/RTO higher — switch takes time
AWS: Route 53 latency-based routing across two regions GCP: Cloud DNS failover with health check policies
GCP: Global Load Balancer with multi-region backends AWS: Route 53 failover routing policy

You cannot improve what you cannot measure. Observability is the ability to infer the internal state of a system from its external outputs.

Pillar What It Answers Tools
Metrics Is the system healthy? What is the load? Prometheus, CloudWatch, Cloud Monitoring
Logs What happened and when? ELK Stack, CloudWatch Logs, Cloud Logging
Traces Where is the latency in a request? Jaeger, OpenTelemetry, AWS X-Ray, Cloud Trace

Chaos engineering is the practice of deliberately injecting failures into your system in a controlled way to verify that it behaves as expected when real failures occur. Netflix pioneered this with their Chaos Monkey tool.

Key Principle Run chaos experiments in production — with blast radius controls — because staging environments rarely mirror production conditions accurately. Start with low-risk experiments (kill one instance) before escalating to AZ failures.

The choice between microservices and a monolith is one of the most consequential architectural decisions a team makes. Both have legitimate use cases; the wrong choice leads to unnecessary complexity or inflexibility.

A monolithic architecture packages all application components — UI, business logic, data access — into a single deployable unit.

When to Use a Monolith

  • Early-stage product with small team (< 10 engineers)

  • Domain is not yet well understood — boundaries are unclear

  • Speed of development matters more than scale

  • Low operational budget — fewer moving parts

Monolith Pitfalls at Scale

  • A single bug can take down the entire application

  • Long build and deployment cycles as codebase grows

  • Technology lock-in — hard to introduce a new language or framework for a subsystem

  • Database becomes a bottleneck — one schema for all features

Microservices decompose an application into small, independently deployable services, each owning its own data and business logic. Each service communicates with others over well-defined APIs.

Core Principles

  • Single Responsibility: Each service does one thing well

  • Loose Coupling, High Cohesion: Services are independent; related logic lives together

  • Own Your Data: Each service has its own database (no shared schema)

  • Design for Failure: Assume services will fail; build resilience in

  • Automated Deployment: Each service has its own CI/CD pipeline

When NOT to Use Microservices

  • Team is too small to own multiple services independently

  • Domain boundaries are unclear — premature decomposition leads to ‘distributed monolith’

  • Your team lacks operational maturity for Kubernetes, service mesh, distributed tracing

  • Startup with an unproven product — adds operational overhead too early

Synchronous (Request/Response) Asynchronous (Event-Driven)
Direct call; caller waits for response Producer emits event; consumer processes independently
Simpler to reason about Better decoupling; higher resilience
Risk: cascading failures if downstream is slow Risk: eventual consistency; harder to debug
Use for: user-facing APIs, real-time queries Use for: order processing, notifications, data pipelines
Protocols: REST, gRPC, GraphQL Protocols: Kafka, SQS/SNS, Pub/Sub, RabbitMQ
AWS: API Gateway → Lambda → RDS AWS: SNS → SQS → Lambda fan-out pattern
GCP: Cloud Endpoints → Cloud Run → Cloud SQL GCP: Pub/Sub → Dataflow → BigQuery

A service mesh is a dedicated infrastructure layer that handles service-to-service communication, providing observability, traffic management, and security without modifying application code.

Istio on AWS EKS Deploy Istio on Amazon EKS to manage mTLS between services, enforce traffic policies (circuit breaking, retries, timeouts), and generate distributed traces via Envoy sidecars. AWS also provides AWS App Mesh as a managed alternative.
Istio on GCP GKE Google Kubernetes Engine natively integrates with Anthos Service Mesh (ASM), which is a managed, enterprise-grade Istio distribution. It provides pre-built dashboards in Cloud Monitoring and integrates with Traffic Director for global load balancing.

In a microservices world, a single business transaction may span multiple services and databases. Traditional ACID transactions across service boundaries are not viable.

The Saga Pattern

A Saga is a sequence of local transactions, each publishing an event or message that triggers the next step. If a step fails, compensating transactions undo previous steps.

Choreography-Based Saga Orchestration-Based Saga
Services react to events — no central coordinator A central orchestrator directs all steps
Loosely coupled; easy to add new services Easier to understand and debug flow
Hard to track overall state across services Orchestrator can become a bottleneck/SPOF
Good for: high-throughput async flows Good for: complex, long-running business processes
AWS: EventBridge routing events between Lambda functions AWS: Step Functions as the orchestrator
GCP: Pub/Sub events between Cloud Run services GCP: Workflows orchestrating Cloud Run tasks

A circuit breaker prevents a service from repeatedly calling a failing downstream dependency, allowing the system to fail fast rather than queue up blocking calls.

State Behavior Transition
Closed Calls pass through normally; failure count tracked Opens when failure threshold exceeded
Open Calls fail immediately without reaching downstream Transitions to Half-Open after timeout
Half-Open Limited calls pass through as a probe Closes if probe succeeds; re-opens if fails

Libraries: Resilience4j (Java), Polly (.NET), Hystrix (legacy). In Kubernetes, Istio’s Envoy proxy provides circuit breaking at the network layer.

An API Gateway acts as the single entry point for all client traffic. It handles cross-cutting concerns so that individual services do not need to implement them.

  • Authentication and authorization (JWT, OAuth 2.0)

  • Rate limiting and throttling

  • Request routing and path rewriting

  • Protocol translation (REST to gRPC)

  • Caching and response compression

  • SSL termination and TLS offloading

☁ AWS API Gateway
• REST API, HTTP API (lighter, lower cost), and WebSocket APIs
• Native integration with Lambda, ECS, EKS, and private VPC resources via VPC Link
• Usage Plans and API Keys for partner/external access
• WAF integration for Layer 7 protection
☁ GCP API Gateway / Apigee
• Cloud Endpoints: lightweight, OpenAPI-based gateway for Cloud Run and GKE
• Apigee: enterprise-grade API management with analytics, developer portal, and monetization
• Supports gRPC transcoding — expose gRPC services as REST
• Integrated with Cloud Armor and Identity-Aware Proxy

Cloud architecture is the application of cloud computing principles — on-demand resources, managed services, and global distribution — to design systems that are scalable, cost-efficient, and resilient.

Deploying across multiple regions provides disaster recovery, lower latency for geographically distributed users, and compliance with data residency requirements.

AWS Multi-Region Design

  • Route 53 with latency-based or geolocation routing

  • S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) for object storage

  • DynamoDB Global Tables — multi-region, multi-master

  • Aurora Global Database — sub-second cross-region replication

  • CloudFront as global CDN fronting all regions

  • AWS Global Accelerator for TCP/UDP acceleration over AWS backbone

GCP Multi-Region Design

  • Global Load Balancer with backends in multiple regions

  • Spanner — globally distributed relational database

  • Cloud Storage multi-region buckets with automatic geo-replication

  • Cloud CDN integrated with the global Load Balancer

  • Cloud DNS geo-routing policies

Key Insight Multi-region adds significant cost and complexity. Before committing, define your RTO (Recovery Time Objective) and RPO (Recovery Point Objective). Many systems do not need active-active multi-region — a warm standby with automated failover often satisfies the requirements at a fraction of the cost.

Both Kubernetes and serverless platforms solve the problem of running workloads at scale, but they make very different tradeoffs.

Kubernetes Serverless
Full control over runtime environment Zero infrastructure management
Predictable performance and resource allocation Auto-scales to zero — pay only when invoked
Long-running services, stateful workloads Event-driven, short-duration tasks
Complex to operate — requires SRE expertise Simple to deploy — focus on function code
Multi-tenant cluster efficiency at high scale Cold start latency can be problematic
AWS: EKS (managed Kubernetes) AWS: Lambda + API Gateway
GCP: GKE Autopilot (managed nodes) GCP: Cloud Functions / Cloud Run
When to Choose Kubernetes

  • Complex microservices with long-running processes

  • Stateful workloads requiring persistent volumes

  • Custom runtimes or GPU workloads (ML inference)

  • Predictable, high-throughput traffic where per-invocation pricing becomes expensive

When to Choose Serverless

  • Event-driven processing: file uploads, API callbacks, scheduled jobs

  • Unpredictable or spiky traffic patterns

  • Small teams that cannot afford Kubernetes operational overhead

  • Rapid prototyping — deploy in minutes

Infrastructure as Code means managing and provisioning infrastructure through machine-readable definition files rather than manual configuration. IaC is the foundation of repeatable, auditable, and scalable cloud operations.

Terraform

Terraform by HashiCorp is the industry-standard IaC tool. It is cloud-agnostic, uses a declarative HCL language, and maintains a state file representing the real-world infrastructure.

  • Supports AWS, GCP, Azure, and 1000+ providers

  • Plan → Apply workflow prevents unintended changes

  • Remote state with locking (S3 + DynamoDB on AWS, GCS + Firestore on GCP)

  • Modules enable reusable, composable infrastructure templates

AWS-Native IaC

  • AWS CloudFormation: declarative YAML/JSON templates, native integration, no separate state file

  • AWS CDK: define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, or Java — compiles to CloudFormation

GCP-Native IaC

  • Google Cloud Deployment Manager: YAML or Python templates for GCP resources

  • Config Connector: manage GCP resources as Kubernetes custom resources (GitOps friendly)

Autoscaling automatically adjusts compute capacity in response to real-time demand, ensuring performance during peaks and cost savings during quiet periods.

Scaling Type AWS Implementation GCP Implementation
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) EKS with custom CloudWatch metrics GKE HPA with Stackdriver metrics
Cluster Autoscaler EKS Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter GKE Autopilot or Cluster Autoscaler
Scheduled Scaling EC2 Auto Scaling scheduled actions Managed Instance Group autoscaling schedules
VMs / Instances EC2 Auto Scaling Groups (target tracking) Managed Instance Groups (MIG autoscaling)
Serverless Lambda concurrent execution scales automatically Cloud Functions auto-scales to 0

Strategy Characteristics
Backup & Restore (RTO: hours, RPO: hours) Lowest cost. Restore from snapshots. Suitable for non-critical data.
Pilot Light (RTO: tens of mins, RPO: minutes) Core services run at minimal scale in DR region. Scale up on activation.
Warm Standby (RTO: minutes, RPO: seconds) Scaled-down but fully functional copy always running.
Active-Active (RTO: ~0, RPO: ~0) Highest cost. Full capacity in both regions. Requires conflict resolution.

Vendor lock-in occurs when switching cloud providers would require significant rewrites. Preventing it requires deliberate architectural choices.

  • Use open standards: Kubernetes (not ECS), PostgreSQL (not DynamoDB), Kafka (not Kinesis) wherever possible

  • Abstract provider-specific APIs behind internal interfaces

  • Adopt OpenTelemetry for observability — vendor-neutral instrumentation

  • Store data in open formats (Parquet, Avro) in object storage

  • Use Terraform for IaC — the same workflow works across AWS and GCP

Trade-off Warning Avoiding lock-in has a cost: you sacrifice managed service optimizations and native integrations. Be pragmatic — accept some lock-in for commodity services (object storage, DNS), but abstract mission-critical differentiators like data storage and event streaming.

Technique AWS GCP
Reserved / Committed Capacity Reserved Instances (1–3 yr) Committed Use Discounts (1–3 yr)
Spot / Preemptible VMs EC2 Spot Instances (up to 90% off) Preemptible / Spot VMs (60–91% off)
Right-sizing Compute Optimizer recommendations Active Assist Recommender
Data Transfer Costs Use VPC endpoints, S3 Transfer Acceleration Premium vs Standard Network tier
Auto-scaling to zero Lambda, Fargate Spot Cloud Run (scales to 0)

Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) is a discipline that applies software engineering practices to operations. It originated at Google and defines a rigorous, data-driven approach to running production systems.

Metric Definition Example
SLI (Indicator) A quantitative measure of a service’s behavior % of requests served < 200ms
SLO (Objective) A target range for an SLI 99.9% of requests < 200ms over 30 days
SLA (Agreement) A contractual commitment to customers with penalties 99.9% availability; credit if breached
Error Budget 1 - SLO = allowed downtime/errors 0.1% of 30 days = ~43 minutes/month

Error budgets are the key innovation of SRE. If the error budget is healthy, the team can move fast. If it is nearly exhausted, reliability work takes priority over new features.

The Four Golden Signals (from the Google SRE Book)

  • Latency: How long does it take to serve a request? Track p50, p95, p99, p999 separately.

  • Traffic: How much demand is the system handling? (requests/sec, events/sec)

  • Errors: What fraction of requests are failing? (5xx rate, exception rate)

  • Saturation: How full is the service? (CPU, memory, queue depth, disk I/O)

☁ AWS CloudWatch
• CloudWatch Metrics with EMF (Embedded Metric Format) for custom application metrics
• CloudWatch Synthetics — canary scripts that continuously probe endpoints
• CloudWatch Contributor Insights for top-N analysis
• AWS X-Ray for request tracing with sampling rules
• Container Insights for EKS/ECS workload observability
☁ GCP Cloud Operations Suite
• Cloud Monitoring with Metrics Explorer and custom dashboards
• Cloud Trace with sampling and automatically tracked Google client libraries
• Cloud Profiler — continuous production CPU/memory profiling with zero overhead
• Error Reporting — automatic grouping and alerting on production exceptions
• Uptime Checks — synthetic monitoring from 6+ global locations

Cascading failures occur when a failure in one service overloads others, spreading like a wave across the system. Prevention requires defense in depth.

  • Load Shedding: Deliberately reject low-priority requests when capacity is near full

  • Graceful Degradation: Return cached or partial results instead of failing completely

  • Circuit Breakers: Short-circuit calls to services that are already failing

  • Timeouts on All Calls: Never let an upstream call block indefinitely

  • Retry Budgets: Cap total retries system-wide; do not let clients amplify load

  • Bulkheads: Separate thread pools per dependency — one slow service cannot starve others

A well-defined incident management process minimizes mean time to resolution (MTTR) and prevents the same incidents from recurring.

Phase Actions Tools
Detection Alert fires; on-call notified via PagerDuty CloudWatch Alarms, GCP Alerting, PagerDuty
Triage Establish severity; assemble incident team; open war room Slack, Zoom, PagerDuty
Mitigation Rollback, feature flag off, redirect traffic Spinnaker, LaunchDarkly, Route 53
Resolution Root cause identified; fix deployed CI/CD pipeline, Terraform
Post-Mortem Blameless review; 5 Whys; action items Confluence, Jira
Blameless Post-Mortems Google’s SRE culture mandates blameless post-mortems. The goal is to identify systemic failures, not punish individuals. A culture of psychological safety is a prerequisite for honest incident retrospectives — and for improving reliability over time.

Chaos engineering deliberately introduces failures to validate that a system’s reliability mechanisms work as intended.

Principles

  • Define steady state before you inject chaos

  • Vary real-world events (latency, packet loss, CPU stress, AZ failure)

  • Run experiments in production — with proper blast radius controls

  • Automate continuously, not just one-off experiments

AWS Fault Injection Simulator (FIS)

  • Native AWS service — inject failures into EC2, EKS, RDS, ECS, and more

  • Pre-built experiment templates for common failure scenarios

  • Stop conditions halt experiments automatically if SLOs breach

GCP Fault Injection

  • Cloud Load Balancing fault injection — inject delays and abort percentages at the LB layer

  • Istio/ASM traffic management — inject faults per route without code changes

  • Chaos Monkey principles apply: run Chaos Toolkit on GKE workloads

Platform engineering is the practice of building internal developer platforms (IDPs) that abstract infrastructure complexity, enabling product engineers to self-serve. DevOps is the cultural and technical foundation.

A modern CI/CD pipeline enables teams to ship software reliably, frequently, and with low risk. At scale, the pipeline itself is a product that the platform team owns.

Pipeline Stages

  • Source: Developer commits to feature branch; pull request opened

  • Build: Compile, lint, static analysis (SAST), dependency scanning

  • Test: Unit tests, integration tests, contract tests

  • Artifact: Publish Docker image to registry with immutable tag

  • Deploy to Staging: Automated deployment; smoke tests

  • Quality Gates: Performance tests, DAST, coverage thresholds

  • Deploy to Production: Blue/green or canary deployment

  • Post-Deploy: Health checks, SLO validation, rollback trigger if needed

☁ AWS CI/CD Stack
• CodeCommit (Git) → CodeBuild (build/test) → CodePipeline (orchestration)
• ECR (Elastic Container Registry) for Docker image storage
• CodeDeploy for EC2, ECS, Lambda, and EKS deployments
• Integration with GitHub Actions via OIDC — no long-lived AWS credentials in CI
☁ GCP CI/CD Stack
• Cloud Source Repositories or GitHub → Cloud Build (build/test)
• Artifact Registry for Docker images and language packages
• Cloud Deploy for progressive delivery to GKE and Cloud Run
• Binary Authorization — enforce signed images in production GKE clusters

GitOps treats Git as the single source of truth for both application code and infrastructure state. All changes go through Git pull requests, providing a full audit trail and easy rollbacks.

  • Declarative configuration stored in Git

  • Automated reconciliation: an agent continuously compares desired state (Git) to actual state (cluster)

  • Rollback = git revert — simple and auditable

  • Tools: ArgoCD, Flux, and Jenkins X are the primary GitOps platforms for Kubernetes

Strategy Description &** Use Case**
Recreate Stop old version, start new. Downtime acceptable. Rarely used in production.
Rolling Update Replace instances one at a time. Zero downtime but mixed versions coexist briefly.
Blue/Green Two identical environments; flip traffic instantly. Easy rollback; expensive (2x infra).
Canary Route a small % of traffic to new version. Validate before full rollout. Best for risk control.
Shadow / Dark Launch Mirror live traffic to new version without serving responses. Test under real load.
Feature Flags Toggle features at runtime without deployment. Decouple deploy from release.

Quality gates are automated checkpoints in the CI/CD pipeline that prevent low-quality or insecure code from reaching production.

  • Code Coverage Threshold: e.g., fail if unit test coverage drops below 80%

  • SAST (Static Analysis): SonarQube, Checkmarx — catch bugs and security issues pre-build

  • DAST (Dynamic Analysis): OWASP ZAP — run against a live staging environment

  • Dependency Scanning: Snyk, Dependabot — detect vulnerable third-party libraries

  • Performance Regression Gate: Block if p99 latency regresses by > 10% vs. baseline

  • Infrastructure Policy as Code: OPA/Gatekeeper — block non-compliant Kubernetes manifests

An Internal Developer Platform abstracts infrastructure concerns and provides self-service capabilities so that product engineers can provision environments, deploy services, and access observability without filing tickets.

Capability AWS IDP Pattern GCP IDP Pattern
Self-service environments Service Catalog + CloudFormation StackSets Cloud Foundation Toolkit + Terraform
Secrets management AWS Secrets Manager + Parameter Store Secret Manager + Workload Identity
Service deployment EKS + ArgoCD + Helm GKE + Config Sync + Kustomize
Developer portal Backstage.io (self-hosted) Backstage.io + Cloud Run
Cost visibility AWS Cost Explorer + tagging Cloud Billing export to BigQuery
Data architecture governs how data is stored, organized, processed, and accessed across the organization. At scale, poor data architecture is one of the most common causes of system bottlenecks.

Database Type Best Suited For
Relational (PostgreSQL, MySQL) Structured data, complex joins, ACID transactions
Document (MongoDB) Flexible schema, nested objects, content management
Wide-Column (Cassandra) High write throughput, time-series, IoT, audit logs
Key-Value (Redis, DynamoDB) Low-latency lookups, caching, sessions, leaderboards
Graph (Neo4j) Highly connected data, social graphs, fraud detection
Time-Series (InfluxDB, TimescaleDB) Metrics, events, financial ticks, IoT sensor data
Search (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch) Full-text search, faceted navigation, log analysis
Columnar OLAP (BigQuery, Redshift, Snowflake) Analytics, aggregations, reporting over billions of rows

Cassandra MongoDB
Wide-column store — row key + column families Document store — JSON-like BSON documents
Designed for extreme write throughput Better for read-heavy, flexible-schema workloads
Linear horizontal scalability (consistent hash ring) Horizontal scaling via sharding
Tunable consistency per operation Strong consistency within a replica set
No joins — denormalize for access patterns Rich query language with joins via $lookup
Best: IoT, audit logs, messaging inboxes Best: catalogs, CMS, user profiles
AWS: Amazon Keyspaces (managed Cassandra) AWS: DocumentDB (MongoDB-compatible API)
GCP: Use self-managed on GKE or Bigtable for similar patterns GCP: Atlas for MongoDB or self-managed on GKE

A real-time analytics platform ingests streaming data and makes it queryable with low latency — typically sub-second to a few seconds from event to insight.

Lambda Architecture (Batch + Speed)

  • Batch Layer: Process all historical data in a distributed compute job (Spark, Flink)

  • Speed Layer: Process real-time data stream for low-latency recent results

  • Serving Layer: Merge batch and real-time views for queries

Kappa Architecture (Stream-Only)

  • A simplification of Lambda — only one streaming pipeline

  • Historical reprocessing done by replaying the event stream (Kafka retention)

  • Preferred when simplicity is more valuable than absolute reprocessing performance

☁ AWS Real-Time Analytics Stack
• Kinesis Data Streams — ingestion of real-time events at scale
• Kinesis Data Firehose — delivery to S3, Redshift, or OpenSearch
• Apache Kafka on MSK (Managed Streaming for Kafka)
• Redshift Streaming Ingestion — query Kinesis data directly in Redshift
• Amazon Athena — serverless SQL on S3 for ad-hoc analysis
☁ GCP Real-Time Analytics Stack
• Pub/Sub — globally distributed, low-latency event ingestion
• Dataflow — managed Apache Beam for batch and stream processing
• BigQuery — serverless OLAP with streaming inserts and real-time analysis
• Bigtable — sub-10ms latency wide-column store for time-series at petabyte scale
• Looker — BI and data exploration layer on top of BigQuery

At petabyte scale, traditional RDBMS architectures break down. Successful large-scale data systems are built on a few key principles.

  • Data Lake First: Land raw data in object storage (S3, GCS) before transforming

  • Schema-on-Read: Defer schema enforcement to query time for maximum flexibility

  • Columnar Formats: Use Parquet or ORC — 10x compression, 100x faster analytical queries

  • Partitioning: Partition data by date, region, or tenant to enable partition pruning

  • Compute Separation: Decouple storage (S3/GCS) from compute (Spark, Presto, BigQuery)

  • Data Catalog: Maintain a metadata catalog (AWS Glue, GCP Data Catalog, Apache Atlas)

Cache Layer Use Case &** Pattern**
Client-Side Cache (browser, mobile) Static assets, API responses. Use ETags and Cache-Control headers.
CDN Cache (CloudFront, Cloud CDN) Images, JS/CSS, publicly cacheable API responses. Edge caching.
API Gateway Cache Cache responses per route/user. Reduce backend load.
Application Cache (Redis, Memcached) Session data, computed results, expensive DB queries.
Database Query Cache Database-level result caching. Avoid for write-heavy tables.
Read-Through Cache App checks cache first; on miss, loads from DB and populates cache.
Write-Through Cache Writes go to both cache and DB atomically. Strong consistency.
Write-Behind / Lazy Write Write to cache; async flush to DB. High write throughput; risk of data loss.
Cache Invalidation Cache invalidation is one of the two hard problems in computer science. Prefer TTL-based expiry for simplicity. For strong consistency requirements, use an event-driven invalidation approach: on write, publish an event that clears the relevant cache keys.
Security must be designed in from the start — not bolted on as an afterthought. A layered security model (defense in depth) ensures that no single control failure leads to a breach.

Zero Trust replaces the perimeter-based ‘castle and moat’ model with the principle: never trust, always verify. Every request — whether from inside or outside the network — must be authenticated, authorized, and encrypted.

  • Identity-centric: Authenticate every user and service, every request

  • Least Privilege: Grant the minimum permissions required for a task

  • Micro-segmentation: Limit lateral movement with network policies

  • Continuous Verification: Re-evaluate trust at every access request

☁ AWS Zero Trust
• IAM Identity Center (SSO) — centralized identity for all AWS accounts
• VPC Security Groups and NACLs — micro-segment network traffic
• AWS PrivateLink — access services privately without traversing the public internet
• Amazon Verified Access — Zero Trust access to corporate applications without VPN
• GuardDuty — ML-powered threat detection across accounts and workloads
☁ GCP Zero Trust (BeyondCorp)
• BeyondCorp Enterprise — context-aware access replacing traditional VPN
• Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) — HTTP-level Zero Trust for web apps and SSH
• VPC Service Controls — prevent data exfiltration from managed services
• Binary Authorization — only signed, attested container images run in GKE
• Security Command Center Premium — centralized threat intelligence and risk dashboard

• Apply the Principle of Least Privilege: never grant wildcards like *

  • Use roles (not users) for service-to-service authentication — no long-lived credentials

  • Enable MFA for all human accounts — mandatory for production access

  • Rotate keys and secrets regularly; prefer short-lived tokens over long-lived keys

  • Use attribute-based access control (ABAC) for dynamic, context-aware permissions

AWS IAM Pattern GCP IAM Pattern
IAM Roles for EC2/Lambda/EKS via instance profiles Workload Identity Federation for GKE pods
Service Control Policies (SCP) for org-wide guardrails Org policies for org-wide constraints
Permission Boundaries to limit max permission scope Conditions in IAM bindings for context-based access
AWS Organizations for multi-account isolation GCP Resource Hierarchy: Org → Folder → Project

Secrets (database passwords, API keys, TLS certificates) must never appear in code, environment variable files, or Docker images. A secrets management system provides secure storage, automatic rotation, and audit logging.

AWS Secrets Manager GCP Secret Manager
Stores and auto-rotates RDS, Redshift, and custom secrets Stores any secret as versioned binary or string
Native Lambda rotation functions Manual rotation or Cloud Functions trigger
IAM-based access with fine-grained policies IAM-based access; Workload Identity for GKE
Audit via CloudTrail Audit via Cloud Audit Logs
Cost: ~$0.40/secret/month + $0.05 per 10k API calls Cost: ~$0.06/version/month + $0.03 per 10k ops

For Kubernetes: External Secrets Operator syncs secrets from AWS Secrets Manager or GCP Secret Manager into Kubernetes Secrets, keeping sensitive values out of Git repositories.

• mTLS Between Services: Mutual TLS ensures every service call is authenticated and encrypted — Istio/Envoy can handle this transparently

  • API Security: Validate JWTs at the gateway; never pass raw credentials between services

  • Container Security: Use minimal base images (distroless), run as non-root, read-only filesystems

  • Network Policies: Kubernetes NetworkPolicy or Cilium to restrict pod-to-pod traffic

  • Runtime Security: Falco for anomaly detection on kernel syscalls in containers

  • Image Scanning: Trivy, ECR Enhanced Scanning, or Artifact Analysis (GCP) in CI pipeline

Encryption Type Implementation
Encryption at Rest AWS KMS / GCP Cloud KMS — managed key lifecycle; customer-managed keys for compliance
Encryption in Transit TLS 1.2+ everywhere; enforce via security policies on load balancers
End-to-End Encryption Client-side encryption before upload; server never sees plaintext
Database Encryption RDS/Aurora TDE; Cloud SQL encryption with CMEK
Field-Level Encryption Encrypt specific sensitive fields (PII) at the application layer
Observability is the capacity to understand the internal state of a distributed system from its external outputs — metrics, logs, and traces — collectively called the three pillars.

Pillar Characteristics Primary Tools
Metrics Numeric, time-series data. High cardinality kills performance. Pre-aggregate where possible. Prometheus, Grafana, CloudWatch, Cloud Monitoring
Logs Timestamped text events. Rich context but expensive to store and query at scale. ELK / EFK Stack, Loki, CloudWatch Logs, Cloud Logging
Traces Correlated request journey across services. Essential for microservices latency debugging. Jaeger, Zipkin, AWS X-Ray, Cloud Trace, Tempo

Modern observability platforms like Honeycomb, Grafana Cloud, and Datadog unify all three pillars with high-cardinality event storage, enabling arbitrary slicing and dicing of production data.

At large scale, ad-hoc observability breaks down. Observability must be designed as a platform with standards, automation, and self-service.

Standardization

  • Mandate OpenTelemetry (OTel) SDK across all services — vendor-neutral instrumentation

  • Define a common log schema (JSON with trace_id, span_id, service, severity)

  • Enforce metric naming conventions: _

  • Require health endpoints: /healthz (liveness), /readyz (readiness) on every service

Centralized Collection

  • OpenTelemetry Collector deployed as a DaemonSet on every Kubernetes node

  • Collector handles batching, retry, and fan-out to multiple backends

  • Tail-based sampling: sample 100% of error traces, 1% of healthy traces

☁ AWS Observability Stack
• Prometheus + Grafana on EKS via Amazon Managed Grafana / Amazon Managed Prometheus
• AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) — OTel Collector configured for AWS backends
• CloudWatch Container Insights for EKS/ECS resource metrics and log aggregation
• AWS X-Ray for distributed tracing — integrated with Lambda, API Gateway, ECS
• CloudWatch Synthetics — canary scripts checking external endpoints from multiple regions
☁ GCP Observability Stack
• Cloud Monitoring with pre-built GKE dashboards and SLO monitoring
• Cloud Logging with log-based metrics and BigQuery export for long-term analysis
• Cloud Trace with automatic instrumentation for App Engine, Cloud Run, and GKE
• Cloud Profiler — continuous, always-on production profiler with flame graphs
• OpenTelemetry Operator on GKE — auto-instrument workloads without code changes

Traditional threshold-based alerting (CPU > 80%: alert!) generates enormous noise. SLO-based alerting fires only when you are at risk of missing a customer commitment.

Burn Rate Alerting

A burn rate alert fires when you are consuming your error budget faster than the sustainable rate. A burn rate of 1x depletes the budget exactly at the end of the SLO window. A burn rate of 10x means you will exhaust the budget 10x faster.

Alert Window Burn Rate Threshold
1 hour (page now — critical) 14.4x burn rate
6 hours (page soon — high severity) 6x burn rate
3 days (ticket — low severity) 1x burn rate

• Alert on symptoms (SLO burn rate), not causes (high CPU)

  • Every alert must have a runbook — if you cannot write a runbook, the alert is not actionable

  • Use inhibition rules: suppress lower-priority alerts when a higher-priority one is firing

  • Regularly review alert signal-to-noise ratio: aim for < 5 alerts per on-call shift

  • Implement dead man’s switch alerts: alert if you stop receiving heartbeats from critical jobs

Statistical anomaly detection identifies unexpected behavior without requiring hard thresholds.

  • Seasonal decomposition: separate trend, seasonality, and residual; alert on residual spikes

  • Z-score alerting: alert when a metric exceeds N standard deviations from rolling mean

  • Percentile comparison: alert when p99 diverges significantly from p50

AWS Anomaly Detection CloudWatch Anomaly Detection uses ML to model expected metric ranges based on historical patterns, accounting for time-of-day and day-of-week seasonality. Set alarms that fire when a metric falls outside the predicted band.
GCP Anomaly Detection Cloud Monitoring supports metric-based alerting with rolling window conditions. Combine with BigQuery ML for more sophisticated anomaly detection on exported metrics, or use Vertex AI Forecast for production workload prediction.

Technical leaders at the CTO and principal engineer level are responsible not just for technical decisions, but for creating the conditions under which large engineering organizations can produce high-quality systems consistently.

As organizations grow, maintaining architectural consistency across many teams and services becomes a major challenge. Teams make independent decisions that accumulate into incompatible, fragmented systems.

Architecture Review Board (ARB)

  • A forum where proposed architectural changes are reviewed by senior engineers

  • Operates on a lightweight RFC (Request for Comments) process

  • Approves or requests changes for decisions above a defined impact threshold

  • Publishes decisions as Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) in a shared repository

RFC Process

  • Author writes a structured proposal: context, problem, considered options, recommendation

  • RFC posted to a shared channel for async review with a deadline (typically 1–2 weeks)

  • Stakeholders comment; author revises

  • ARB approves, rejects, or escalates

  • Approved RFC becomes a binding ADR — linked from the service that implements it

Microservice sprawl occurs when teams create too many services — each too small to justify its own operational overhead. A healthy microservices ecosystem requires governance.

Problem Prevention
Too many tiny services (nanoservices) Enforce service size guidelines: a service should map to a bounded context
Duplicated functionality across teams Shared platform services for cross-cutting concerns (auth, payments, notifications)
Inconsistent tech stacks Define a curated technology radar: adopt, trial, assess, hold
No discoverability of existing services Maintain a service catalog (Backstage) with ownership, APIs, and runbooks
Unowned services with no clear team Enforce service ownership; tie services to on-call rotations

Technical debt is the accumulated cost of design shortcuts and deferred improvements. Left unmanaged, it slows down all future development.

Types of Technical Debt

  • Deliberate: Conscious shortcuts taken for speed — acceptable if tracked and repaid

  • Accidental: Poor decisions made without full information — discovered in maintenance

  • Bit Rot: Correct code that becomes outdated as dependencies and platforms evolve

Managing Debt Systematically

  • Allocate 20% of each sprint explicitly to tech debt reduction

  • Maintain a technical debt register with business impact assessments

  • Enforce no new debt policies: any new debt requires ARB approval and a repayment plan

  • Measure debt leading indicators: deployment frequency, change failure rate, MTTR

DORA Metrics Google DORA research identifies four key metrics that predict engineering performance: Deployment Frequency, Lead Time for Changes, Change Failure Rate, and Mean Time to Recovery. High-performing organizations deploy on demand with < 1 hour lead time, < 5% change failure rate, and < 1 hour MTTR.

Conway’s Law states that systems mirror the communication structures of the organizations that create them. To change your architecture, you may need to change your team structure.

Team Topologies
Team Type Responsibility
Stream-Aligned Team Owns a product domain end-to-end; fastest path to value delivery
Platform Team Builds the IDP; reduces cognitive load for stream-aligned teams
Enabling Team Short-term coaching; helps stream-aligned teams adopt new practices
Complicated Subsystem Team Owns a specialist component requiring deep expertise (e.g., ML platform, payments)
Cognitive Load Management

  • Limit team service ownership to what fits in the team’s cognitive capacity

  • Platform teams must reduce — not transfer — cognitive load

  • Thick platforms with poor DX are worse than no platform

An ADR is a short document capturing a significant architectural decision, its context, the options considered, and the rationale for the choice made.

ADRs should be: short (1 page maximum), version-controlled alongside code, immutable once approved, and linked from the service or component they affect.

ADR Template

  • Title: Short noun phrase describing the decision

  • Status: Proposed | Accepted | Deprecated | Superseded by [ADR-NNN]

  • Context: What is the situation, the forces at play, and the problem statement

  • Decision: What we chose to do

  • Consequences: What becomes easier, harder, or newly required as a result

Senior engineering leaders are not evaluated on knowing the right answers — they are evaluated on asking the right questions, making decisions with incomplete information, and articulating the tradeoffs clearly.

Every architectural decision involves trade-offs along at least two dimensions. A disciplined framework helps avoid cargo-culting (adopting technology because it is popular) and bikeshedding (over-discussing low-impact decisions).

  • Understand the problem: What are the actual requirements? What does failure look like?

  • Identify options: What are the realistic choices? (Usually 2–4 options.)

  • Evaluate on dimensions: Performance, cost, complexity, operational maturity, vendor risk, team familiarity

  • Document the decision: Write an ADR; capture what you rejected and why

  • Set a review trigger: Under what conditions should this decision be revisited?

Choose Kubernetes When… Choose Serverless When…
Long-running, stateful workloads Event-driven, stateless, short-duration tasks
Custom runtimes or binary dependencies Standard language runtimes suffice
Predictable high traffic where Lambda costs would explode Spiky, unpredictable, or low-traffic workloads
Need GPU, specialized hardware, or NUMA topology Zero infrastructure operations desired
Multi-tenancy and resource isolation at pod level Extreme simplicity and rapid deployment
AWS: EKS for complex, production workloads AWS: Lambda for automation, data processing, APIs
GCP: GKE for orchestrated microservices GCP: Cloud Run for containerized services at any scale

cards.f: 10.3 When is Cassandra the Wrong Choice?
cards.b:
• You need complex queries with joins: Cassandra has no join support — every access pattern requires a dedicated table

  • Your write volume is not high: the operational complexity of managing a Cassandra cluster is not justified for moderate workloads

  • You need strong consistency: Cassandra is eventually consistent by default; tuning to strong consistency reduces availability and performance

  • Your team is small: Cassandra requires operational expertise — compaction, repairs, monitoring — that small teams cannot sustain

  • Your schema is still evolving: adding new access patterns to Cassandra requires schema changes and data migrations

Better Alternatives For time-series data on AWS, consider DynamoDB with a time-based partition key or Amazon Timestream. On GCP, Cloud Bigtable provides similar wide-column semantics with managed operations. For moderate workloads with complex queries, PostgreSQL with partitioning is almost always easier to operate.

Premature decomposition is as dangerous as excessive coupling. Break the monolith only when you have clear evidence that it is limiting you.

Signals That You Should Break the Monolith

  • Independent deployment: teams cannot deploy their changes without coordinating with others

  • Scaling bottleneck: one module needs 10x the resources of others, but you cannot scale it independently

  • Technology mismatch: one module would benefit greatly from a different language or runtime

  • Team size: the codebase is too large for a single team to own and understand

  • Distinct SLOs: different parts of the system have very different reliability requirements

How to Break the Monolith Safely

  • Identify bounded contexts using Domain-Driven Design (DDD) event storming

  • Introduce an anti-corruption layer: facade that proxies calls to the future service

  • Extract the service: move logic and data ownership incrementally

  • Run in parallel: shadow the new service against the monolith; compare outputs

  • Cut over: redirect traffic; monitor; do not delete the monolith code for 30+ days

Choose SQL (Relational) When… Choose NoSQL When…
Data is highly structured and normalized Data is semi-structured, nested, or schema-flexible
You need complex queries, aggregations, joins You need simple, high-volume, low-latency access
ACID transactions are required Horizontal scale is the primary constraint
Team is more familiar with SQL You have a specific access pattern that maps well to NoSQL
AWS: RDS (PostgreSQL/MySQL), Aurora AWS: DynamoDB, ElastiCache, DocumentDB, Keyspaces
GCP: Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, Spanner GCP: Bigtable, Firestore, Memorystore

Every integration between services requires a choice between synchronous and asynchronous communication, each with distinct characteristics.

Event-Driven (Async) Request-Response (Sync)
Producer and consumer are decoupled in time and space Caller waits for an immediate response
Better resilience: consumer failure does not block producer Simpler error handling and debugging
Natural fit for audit logs, notifications, analytics fanout Natural fit for user-facing APIs, real-time queries
Harder to guarantee ordering without partitioning Easy to test and reason about
AWS: Kinesis, SQS, SNS, EventBridge AWS: API Gateway, ALB, AppSync
GCP: Pub/Sub, Eventarc, Workflows GCP: Cloud Endpoints, Load Balancer, gRPC

cards.f: A.2 The Five Most Important Trade-off Questions
cards.b:
• Monolith vs. microservices — what is our team and domain maturity?

  • Kubernetes vs. serverless — what is our traffic pattern and operational capability?

  • SQL vs. NoSQL — what are our access patterns and consistency requirements?

  • Event-driven vs. request-response — what is our tolerance for eventual consistency?

  • Multi-region vs. single-region — what are our real RTO and RPO requirements?

• SLOs defined for every customer-facing service

  • Error budgets tracked and reviewed weekly

  • All single points of failure eliminated or mitigated

  • Runbooks written and linked from every alert

  • Automated rollback on deployment health check failure

  • Load testing completed against peak 3x traffic projection

  • Chaos experiments run quarterly in production

  • DR plan tested with RTO/RPO validation annually

Cloud Architecture & System Design

© Cloud Architecture Reference — For Senior Engineers & CTOs

decks.title: Deployments, DR, DevOps, SRE (cards)
decks.blurb: Deployment strategies, disaster recovery, DevOps/DORA, SLOs and error budgets, incident command, resilience, security, delivery.

cards.b:
What it is. Replace instances a few at a time behind a load balancer. Old and new versions run side by side for a while.

When you use it. The default for stateless services where the new version is backward compatible with the old one.

Number or rule to remember. Set max surge and max unavailable (Kubernetes) or batch size (CodeDeploy) so capacity never dips.

Gotcha. Mixed versions means the database and the API contract must work with both at once. Rollback is a second roll, not instant.

What it is. Two identical environments. Deploy to the idle one, test it, then switch all traffic at the load balancer or DNS.

When you use it. Changes you want to validate fully in a real environment before anyone sees them; instant rollback matters.

Number or rule to remember. Flip-back takes seconds. Keep the old environment alive until you're sure.

Gotcha. Costs double capacity during the switch. The database can't be blue/green'd — schema must work for both. DNS-based switching is slow because of TTLs; use the load balancer.

What it is. Route a small slice of traffic — 1%, then 10%, 50%, 100% — to the new version, watching error rate and latency at each step. Automate the rollback on an SLO breach.

When you use it. Risky changes at high traffic; the standard for services with real users. Firmware and data-platform engine migrations use cohorts instead of traffic percentages.

Number or rule to remember. Gate on error rate, p99 latency, and a business metric, updated cohort vs control, with a soak time per stage.

Gotcha. A canary that only watches CPU catches nothing. Sticky sessions can keep a user on a bad canary.

What it is. Deploy code disabled; turn it on per user, cohort, or percentage at runtime. Separates deploy from release.

When you use it. Every risky feature. Product experiments. Kill switches. Trunk-based development depends on them.

Number or rule to remember. Turning a flag off takes seconds and needs no deploy — the fastest rollback there is.

Gotcha. Flags that never get cleaned up become permanent branches in the code. Flag state must be observable in logs and traces.

What it is. Send a copy of real traffic to the new version and throw away its responses. Compare outputs offline.

When you use it. Validating a rewrite, a new query engine, or a new ML model before it affects anyone (design question Q49).

Number or rule to remember. Zero customer risk; doubles load on dependencies unless they're stubbed.

Gotcha. Side effects — the shadow must not write, send emails, or charge cards.

What it is. Two versions to two cohorts; compare a business metric with statistics.

When you use it. Product decisions, not reliability.

Number or rule to remember. Randomize at the right unit (household, not device); pre-register the metric and sample size; don't stop early.

Gotcha. Peeking inflates false positives. Novelty effects fade.

What it is. Add the new column nullable → deploy code that writes both → backfill → switch reads → drop the old column in a later release.

When you use it. Any schema change on a live system.

Number or rule to remember. Every step is compatible with the release before and after, so rolling and canary deploys and rollbacks all work.

Gotcha. One big ALTER in one deploy locks the table and can't be rolled back. Never couple a schema change to a code deploy.

What it is. Never patch a running server — build a new image and replace it. GitOps: the Git repo is the source of truth; a reconciler (Argo CD, Flux) makes the cluster match it. Rollback is a revert.

When you use it. Everything in production.

Number or rule to remember. Drift detection catches console changes; the commit log is the audit trail.

Gotcha. Emergency console fixes during an incident must be back-ported to code within the week or they're drift.

What it is. RTO — how long until you're back. RPO — how much data you can lose. Both are business decisions that set the engineering budget.

When you use it. Every system gets an RTO and RPO on paper, per tier, before anyone picks a DR strategy.

Number or rule to remember. Tier-1 might be RTO 15 minutes / RPO 1 minute; an internal report RTO a day / RPO a day.

Gotcha. Teams choose active/active for a system whose RTO is "by tomorrow."

What it is. Backup and restore (cheapest, hours to days). Pilot light (data replicated, minimal compute idle). Warm standby (scaled-down copy running). Active/active (both regions serving).

When you use it. Match to RTO/RPO. Most control paths need warm standby at most; most data platforms need tested backup/restore plus a replicated catalog.

Number or rule to remember. Each step up is roughly an order of magnitude more cost and complexity.

Gotcha. A DR plan that has never been exercised is a hope. Drill quarterly; measure the real RTO.

What it is. AZs are isolated data centers in one region — spread everything across three by default. Regions are far apart — go multi-region only for a stated reason: latency for users, data residency, or an RTO the business will pay for.

When you use it. Multi-AZ always. Multi-region for Germany-style residency or a hard RTO.

Number or rule to remember. Cross-AZ traffic costs a cent per GB each way; cross-region replication and failover add real complexity.
