Gotcha. Multi-region "for resilience" with no tested failover is cost with no benefit.

What it is. Automated backups to a separate account (ransomware resilience); point-in-time recovery on databases; versioning and Object Lock on S3; a quarterly restore drill with a measured time.

When you use it. Every system of record.

Number or rule to remember. A backup that exists but was never restored is untested. Keep backups out of the production account.

Gotcha. Backups that include secrets; backups in the same account as the thing that got compromised.

What it is. Deliberately inject failure — kill an AZ, add latency to a dependency, fill a disk — in staging first (AWS Fault Injection Service, Gremlin), then production game days with the team watching.

When you use it. Before major launches and after any resilience change.

Number or rule to remember. Start with the two failures you're most afraid of.

Gotcha. Chaos without observability just breaks things. Game days without runbook updates teach nothing.

What it is. Timeouts everywhere. Retries with exponential backoff and jitter plus retry budgets. Circuit breakers stop calling a failing dependency. Bulkheads isolate pools so one failure can't sink the rest. Load shedding and rate limiting. Graceful degradation — serve last-known data rather than an error. Idempotency on every boundary that can redeliver.

When you use it. Every service that calls another service.

Number or rule to remember. Three services at 99.9% in series are 99.7% together — remove synchronous dependencies from the critical path.

Gotcha. Retries without jitter cause synchronized storms. Circuit breakers without fallbacks just fail faster.

What it is. After an outage, every client reconnects at once. Fix on the client (jittered backoff) and the server (connection rate limits, warm capacity). Cells: partition the whole stack into independent units (by customer or region) so a failure hits one cell, not everyone.

When you use it. Any fleet; any very large multi-tenant service.

Number or rule to remember. Cell size is chosen so losing one cell is survivable; AWS itself runs this way.

Gotcha. Cross-cell dependencies quietly re-couple the cells.

What it is. The team that builds a service runs it. Shared ownership of delivery and operations, automation of everything repeatable, and measurement of the result.

When you use it. The operating model for every modern engineering team; Amazon's "you build it, you run it" is the origin.

Number or rule to remember. If "DevOps" is a separate team that owns deploys, the model isn't DevOps.

Gotcha. DevOps as a job title instead of a practice.

What it is. Lint and static analysis → unit tests → build and sign the artifact (with an SBOM) → contract tests → integration tests in an ephemeral environment → security scans (SAST, dependencies, container CVEs, secrets) → staging and smoke → progressive production deploy with automated rollback.

When you use it. Every service; every merge to main.

Number or rule to remember. Each gate catches a different class of failure; a failed gate stops the pipeline. Pipelines should run in minutes, not hours.

Gotcha. Flaky tests get skipped, and then the gate means nothing. Pipelines pulling images through NAT cost real money.

What it is. The four numbers that describe delivery health: deployment frequency, lead time for changes (commit to production), change failure rate, time to restore.

When you use it. The dashboard for "measurable improvement in deployment stability."

Number or rule to remember. Elite: deploy on demand, lead time under a day, change failure rate under 5%, restore under an hour. Speed and stability improve together, not as a tradeoff.

Gotcha. Gaming deployment frequency with trivial deploys; measuring lead time from ticket rather than commit.

What it is. Everyone commits to main in small, short-lived branches (a day or two), with feature flags hiding incomplete work. The opposite of long-lived Gitflow release branches.

When you use it. Product and platform teams. Firmware teams sometimes keep release branches for certification — a legitimate exception.

Number or rule to remember. The practice most correlated with high DORA scores.

Gotcha. Without flags and good tests, trunk-based just breaks main.

What it is. Many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests, very few slow end-to-end tests. Contract tests (Pact, OpenAPI-driven) check that a service still satisfies what its consumers expect — the mechanism that stops you breaking an old client or a downstream team.

When you use it. Every API with more than one consumer; every device-to-cloud or producer-to-consumer boundary.

Number or rule to remember. A field removal should fail the build, not production.

Gotcha. An inverted pyramid — mostly E2E tests — is slow, flaky, and skipped.

What it is. Terraform/OpenTofu (multi-cloud), CloudFormation/CDK (AWS-native), Pulumi. Remote state with locking, modules per environment, plan in pull requests, policy-as-code (OPA, Checkov) to block insecure configs, drift detection.

When you use it. A region must be rebuildable from code — that's the test.

Number or rule to remember. State in its own account, versioned, locked. CI gets credentials through OIDC, never static keys.

Gotcha. Losing state means importing every resource by hand. Console drift that never gets codified.

What it is. Shift security left: scans in CI, secrets never in code, least-privilege pipeline credentials. Supply chain: know what's in your artifacts (SBOM), sign them (Sigstore/cosign), verify at deploy, pin dependencies.

When you use it. Regulated environments ask for this as evidence; everyone else needs it after the next log4j.

Number or rule to remember. A known CVE in a public-facing app is the most common breach path — your vendor-portal story.

Gotcha. Scanning that produces thousands of findings nobody triages.

cards.f: Internal developer platform and paved roads
cards.b:
What it is. A platform team offers self-service infrastructure with guardrails: templates that come with CI/CD, observability, and security baked in; a portal (Backstage) for ownership and docs.

When you use it. Once there are more than three or four product teams.

Number or rule to remember. Measure time-to-first-deploy for a new service and developer satisfaction.

Gotcha. A platform team that becomes a ticket queue instead of a product.

What it is. Monitoring tells you a known thing is wrong (a threshold alarm). Observability lets you ask questions you didn't anticipate — why is p99 slow only for German users on one firmware? Three signals: metrics, logs, traces, tied together by a correlation ID.

When you use it. Every service. OpenTelemetry as the vendor-neutral instrumentation so you can change vendors without re-instrumenting.

Number or rule to remember. RED for services (rate, errors, duration); USE for resources (utilization, saturation, errors); Google's four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation).

Gotcha. Observability spend can rival compute spend — sample traces, cap log retention, drop debug logs at the agent.

What it is. SLI is what you measure; SLO is the target over a window; SLA is a contractual promise, looser than the SLO. Error budget = 1 − SLO: the unreliability you're allowed, and the objective trigger for when reliability work outranks features.

When you use it. Per domain, tighter for the critical path. For a data platform the SLIs are freshness, completion by deadline, and correctness.

Number or rule to remember. 99.9% = 43.8 minutes a month; 99.95% = 21.9; 99.99% = 4.4. Three 99.9% services in series ≈ 99.7%.

Gotcha. An SLO nobody alarms on. 100% as a target.

What it is. Page on how fast the error budget is being consumed, not on raw latency. Fast burn (14.4× over an hour — 2% of a monthly budget gone in an hour) pages; slow burn (1× over three days) opens a ticket.

When you use it. Replaces threshold alerts that page on thirty-second blips.

Number or rule to remember. Multi-window burn-rate alerts are the Google SRE recipe.

Gotcha. Alerting on causes (CPU) instead of symptoms (the SLI). Every alert needs a runbook and an owner.

What it is. Primary and secondary, one-week shifts, no more than one week in five per person, compensated, with handoff notes. Follow-the-sun if you have three regions; otherwise business-hours paging per region and true Sev-1 only overnight.

When you use it. Any team that owns production.

Number or rule to remember. More than a few pages per shift is a system problem. Track pages per shift and the fraction that were actionable. The on-call engineer's fixes go into the next sprint.

Gotcha. Contractors on call without the same access and runbooks — a two-tier system that fails at 3 a.m.

What it is. An incident commander coordinates and does not debug; a communications lead updates the status page and stakeholders on a schedule; responders do the work; a scribe keeps the timeline. Severity is defined by customer impact in advance. Declare early, downgrade freely.

When you use it. Every Sev-1 and Sev-2.

Number or rule to remember. The first question is always "what changed?" — a deploy, a campaign, a config, a vendor event. Containment beats diagnosis in the first fifteen minutes.

Gotcha. The IC starts reading logs and nobody is steering.

What it is. Amazon's name for the postmortem: timeline, customer impact, contributing factors (plural — never one root cause), what went well, action items with owners and dates, and a check that they shipped. Blameless because that's how you learn what actually happened.

When you use it. Within days of every significant incident; reviewed in a weekly ops meeting.

Number or rule to remember. The senior skill is noticing the third occurrence of a pattern and removing the category — fix the class, not the instance.

Gotcha. Action items that never close. Postmortems that name a person.

What it is. Toil is manual, repetitive, automatable work that grows with the service. Cap it and automate it. A weekly operational metrics review walks the dashboards — SLO attainment, incidents, pages, deploy failure rate, cost — with the team.

When you use it. The weekly ritual Amazon teams actually run.

Number or rule to remember. If the on-call spends more than ten hours a week on things a script could do, the next sprint has an automation story.

Gotcha. A review that's a status read-out instead of a question-asking session.

What it is. Model demand (users × requests; devices × messages × bytes), provision for the peak with headroom, and load-test with a realistic simulator before every major launch and every new region.

When you use it. Before Q4, before a product launch, before Germany.

Number or rule to remember. Back-of-envelope every time: events/s × bytes = MB/s → shards, partitions, storage per day.

Gotcha. Quotas and service limits nobody checked — raise them a month before you need them.

cards.f: Monolith vs microservices vs modular monolith
cards.b:
What it is. Start with a modular monolith; extract a service when a module has a different scaling or release cadence and a team to own it. Microservices add network failure, distributed debugging, and operational cost.

When you use it. Small teams and unknown boundaries → monolith. Known domains with separate teams → services.

Number or rule to remember. "When are microservices a bad idea?" — small teams, low DevOps maturity, simple domains, boundaries not yet known.

Gotcha. A distributed monolith: services that must all deploy together.
cards.s: Architecture patterns a manager should name

cards.b:
What it is. Put a facade in front of a legacy system and migrate functionality behind it piece by piece; retire the old system when it's empty. Observability first, highest-change lowest-coupling context first, contract tests between old and new, expand/contract on the database.

When you use it. Any monolith or legacy migration (design Q10, Q11).

Number or rule to remember. A modular monolith is a valid end state. Big-bang rewrites fail on the data migration.

Gotcha. Sharing the old database with the new service long-term.
cards.s: Architecture patterns a manager should name

cards.f: Event-driven architecture, CQRS, event sourcing, outbox
cards.b:
What it is. Services communicate by publishing events. CQRS separates read and write models when reads vastly outnumber writes (your Ford design). Event sourcing stores the events as truth and derives state. The outbox pattern writes the event in the same transaction as the data so you never lose or duplicate one between a database and a bus.

When you use it. Fan-out, decoupling teams, audit trails, derived-state-read-far-more-than-changed problems.

Number or rule to remember. "Compute on change, not on read" is the sentence from your Ford story.

Gotcha. Event sourcing everywhere — it's expensive in complexity; use it where audit or replay matters.
cards.s: Architecture patterns a manager should name

cards.b:
What it is. No two-phase commit across services. A saga is a multi-step workflow with a compensating action per step. Every step is idempotent so retries are safe.

When you use it. Device pairing plus subscription activation; order placement across services.

Number or rule to remember. Idempotency key on every mutating call; dedup on the consumer.

Gotcha. A saga without compensations is just a workflow that half-completes.
cards.s: Architecture patterns a manager should name

cards.b:
What it is. Under a partition, choose consistency or availability; without one, trade latency for consistency. Strong consistency for money, inventory, leases, catalog commits; eventual for feeds, device state, analytics outputs — with versioning so readers always see a complete version.

When you use it. Say which part of the system is which; that's the senior answer.

Number or rule to remember. DynamoDB reads are eventually consistent by default; strongly consistent reads cost double.

Gotcha. Treating "eventually consistent" as "wrong" — it's a design choice with a documented lag.
cards.s: Architecture patterns a manager should name

cards.b:
What it is. REST with URI or header versions; GraphQL versionless with deprecation; gRPC for service-to-service. Additive changes only; deprecate with usage measurement; support N−2 client versions; contract tests in CI; force-upgrade only for security.

When you use it. Any API with clients you can't upgrade at once — mobile apps, devices, partner teams.

Number or rule to remember. A rename is a breaking change. Add the new field, deprecate the old, remove when nobody sends it.

Gotcha. Broken object-level authorization — user A reading resource B by guessing an ID — is the top API vulnerability.
cards.s: Architecture patterns a manager should name

cards.b:
What it is. At the edge (CDN), at the service (Redis), at the database (query cache). Cache what's read far more than written and tolerates staleness. Key on everything that changes the answer, including the policy version.

When you use it. Read-heavy paths; the Ford read path.

Number or rule to remember. "Cache-aside" (app checks cache, then DB) is the default; "write-through" when consistency matters more.

Gotcha. Stampede when a hot key expires (jittered TTLs, request coalescing). Stale-after-permission-change leaks data.
cards.s: Architecture patterns a manager should name

cards.b:
What it is. Shared infrastructure serving many customers or teams. Isolation levels: separate accounts (strongest), separate databases, shared database with a tenant key (cheapest). Per-tenant quotas, rate limits, cost attribution, and noisy-neighbor detection.

When you use it. Every internal platform — Cradle is one. Every SaaS product.

Number or rule to remember. Quotas plus priority aging plus preemption only in a shared burst pool (design Q23).

Gotcha. One tenant's runaway job starving everyone; cost nobody can attribute.
cards.s: Architecture patterns a manager should name

cards.b:
What it is. Verify every request regardless of network location: strong identity for users and workloads, mTLS between services, least privilege, short-lived credentials, continuous authorization, and logging.

When you use it. The posture for anything new; the direction for anything old.

Number or rule to remember. No long-lived keys anywhere; roles and OIDC for machines, SSO for humans.

Gotcha. A VPN that grants everything once you're in.

What it is. The provider secures the cloud; you secure what you put in it. The line moves per service — on EC2 you patch the OS; on Lambda you don't; on RDS the engine is theirs, the schema and access are yours.

When you use it. Every "is it secure?" conversation.

Number or rule to remember. A public S3 bucket is always on your side of the line.

Gotcha. Assuming "managed" means "not my problem."

What it is. Secrets in a secrets manager with rotation; keys in KMS with envelope encryption; certificates from ACM with auto-renewal; nothing in code or environment files committed to git; secrets scanning in CI.

When you use it. Day one of any inherited environment.

Number or rule to remember. A leaked access key gets used by crypto-miners within minutes of hitting a public repo.

Gotcha. An expired certificate at 2 a.m.

What it is. Scan images and dependencies in CI; scan running instances (Inspector); patch on a cadence with automation (Systems Manager); treat a known CVE on a public-facing app as a Sev-1 until patched.

When you use it. The mechanism that would have prevented your vendor-portal breach.

Number or rule to remember. Mean time to patch critical CVEs is the metric.

Gotcha. Scanning without an owner for findings.

What it is. SOC 2 (service organizations), ISO 27001 (information security management), NIST CSF (the common language), NIST 800-171 / CMMC (DoD controlled data — your world), TISAX (automotive suppliers), GDPR / CCPA (privacy), PCI DSS (cards), HIPAA (health).

When you use it. When asked about audits, evidence, or regulated customers.

Number or rule to remember. Continuous evidence from Config, Security Hub, and IaC beats a yearly scramble.

Gotcha. Compliance as a checkbox instead of controls that actually run.

What it is. Classification at ingest, column-level masking and row-level security, pseudonymization, retention schedules, deletion that reaches derived data and caches, subject-access export, DPIAs for sensitive features, breach notification within 72 hours under GDPR.

When you use it. Any consumer data; any EU launch; any lake (design Q36–Q37).

Number or rule to remember. Deletion through a lake means rewriting files and expiring snapshots — plan it before you need it.

Gotcha. PII in logs; backups that outlive the retention policy.

What it is. Scrum: fixed sprints, defined roles (PO, Scrum Master, developers), events (planning, daily, review, retro), artifacts (backlogs, increment, definition of done). Kanban: continuous flow, WIP limits, cycle time and lead time. Hybrid is normal — Scrum for product work, Kanban for ops and support.

When you use it. Pick by the shape of the work, not by fashion.

Number or rule to remember. Velocity is a planning tool, never a target. Measure cycle time, lead time, and outcomes.

Gotcha. Daily standup as a status report to the manager; retros with no actions; half the sprint carried over every sprint.

What it is. SAFe (Agile Release Trains, Program Increments, PI planning, RTE, WSJF prioritization) for coordinating many teams with dependencies; LeSS and Scrum of Scrums for lighter coordination; Team Topologies (stream-aligned, platform, enabling, complicated-subsystem teams) for org design.

When you use it. Essential SAFe when you have more than four or five teams with real dependencies; lighter otherwise.

Number or rule to remember. PI planning's value is dragging dependencies and risks into daylight each quarter.

Gotcha. Process as the product — an RTE and a program board can't substitute for clear ownership and good APIs.

What it is. Amazon's unit: a team small enough to feed with two pizzas, owning a service end to end — build, run, on-call, metrics. Clear ownership boundaries with API contracts between teams.

When you use it. The default org design; Conway's law used deliberately.

Number or rule to remember. Every service has a named owner and a backup; publish the map.

Gotcha. Shared ownership of a critical service is no ownership.

What it is. Amazon starts a product by writing the press release and FAQ as if it launched, then works backwards to the plan. Six-page narratives instead of slides; meetings start with silent reading.

When you use it. How you'd propose a platform investment at Amazon — write the narrative, state the customer, state the metric.

Number or rule to remember. Know the vocabulary: PR/FAQ, six-pager, one-way vs two-way door decisions (irreversible decisions get more study; reversible ones get speed).

Gotcha. Treating every decision as one-way — Bias for Action exists because most aren't.

What it is. Make debt visible in the backlog with business impact; reserve capacity; use error budgets as the trigger. Governance: lightweight design docs and ADRs, a two-tier review (architecture forum for cross-cutting changes, team review for the rest), a golden path so the default is compliant without a meeting.

When you use it. Every quarter's planning; every inherited system.

Number or rule to remember. Ask for a specific outcome with a metric, never "a quarter to pay down debt."

Gotcha. Governance as a gate instead of a paved road.

What it is. A written competency framework; structured loops with rubrics and a work-sample round; independent scores before the debrief; a Bar Raiser-style outside voice; promotions on sustained next-level performance; underperformance handled early, specifically, and in writing with a date.

When you use it. The people-management round.

Number or rule to remember. Amazon's Bar Raiser is the formalized version — an interviewer from outside the team with veto power.

Gotcha. Lowering the bar to fill a seat; waiting a quarter too long on a performance problem.

decks.title: Agile, Scrum, Kanban, SAFe (cards)
decks.blurb: Ceremonies, artifacts, Kanban flow, SAFe, Team Topologies.

cards.b:
What it is. Four values: individuals and interactions over processes and tools; working software over comprehensive documentation; customer collaboration over contract negotiation; responding to change over following a plan. Twelve principles behind them — deliver early and often, welcome changing requirements, sustainable pace, simplicity, self-organizing teams, regular reflection.

How you run it. As the reason behind every ceremony: if a ritual doesn't serve one of these values, cut it.

Rule to remember. "Over" means both matter; the left side wins when they conflict.

Gotcha. Treating agile as "no planning" or "no documentation." Interviewers hear that as immaturity.

What it is. Build a thin slice end to end, ship it, learn, build the next slice. Incremental = adding pieces; iterative = refining what exists. Agile does both.

How you run it. Every roadmap: slice by customer value, not by architectural layer.

Rule to remember. A sprint that ends with nothing releasable has failed its purpose, even if every task is "done."

Gotcha. Building all the backend first, then all the frontend — layers, not slices.

cards.f: Definition of Done vs Definition of Ready
cards.b:
What it is. Definition of Done: the quality bar an increment must meet — code reviewed, tests passing, deployed to staging, documented, observable. Definition of Ready: what a backlog item needs before the team pulls it — clear acceptance criteria, dependencies known, sized.

How you run it. Both written by the team, visible on the board, and held equally for employees and contractors.

Rule to remember. DoD is where you encode "quality by default" — tests and docs are not optional extras.

Gotcha. A DoD nobody reads; "done" meaning "code written."

What it is. "As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]." Acceptance criteria in Given/When/Then make the story testable. INVEST: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.

How you run it. Backlog refinement; the contract between PO and team.

Rule to remember. If you can't write the acceptance criteria, the story isn't ready.

Gotcha. Stories that are really tasks ("update the config"); epics masquerading as stories.

cards.f: Estimation: story points, velocity, and alternatives
cards.b:
What it is. Story points express relative size and uncertainty, not hours; planning poker surfaces disagreement. Velocity is points per sprint, used by the team to forecast. Alternatives: t-shirt sizes, #NoEstimates with throughput, or just counting items.

How you run it. Forecasting a quarter from trailing velocity; sizing to find hidden complexity.

Rule to remember. The moment velocity becomes a management target, it inflates and stops meaning anything.

Gotcha. Comparing velocity across teams. Estimating in hours and calling them points.

What it is. One ordered product backlog owned by the Product Owner. Prioritization schemes: MoSCoW (must/should/could/won't), RICE (reach × impact × confidence ÷ effort), WSJF (cost of delay ÷ job size), Kano (basic/performance/delight), value vs effort.

How you run it. Quarterly planning and continuous refinement.

Rule to remember. WSJF is the SAFe one: the small, urgent, risk-reducing item beats the big feature.

Gotcha. A backlog of 800 items nobody has looked at in a year — delete the bottom half.

What it is. Make it visible as backlog items with business impact; reserve capacity (often 15–20%); tie each item to a metric; use error budgets as the trigger for a reliability sprint.

How you run it. Every planning session.

Rule to remember. Ask for a specific outcome with a number, never "a sprint to clean up."

Gotcha. Debt as a separate backlog nobody prioritizes.

What it is. Product Owner owns the backlog and priority — the "what." Scrum Master owns the process, removes impediments, coaches — not a project manager. Developers are the cross-functional team that owns the "how." The engineering manager is none of these: you set direction, grow people, and remove organizational blockers.

How you run it. Say explicitly in the interview where you sit: "I'm not the Scrum Master; my job is the people and the systemic blockers."

Rule to remember. A PO without authority is a proxy and the team will feel it.

Gotcha. The manager running the daily scrum.
cards.s: Scrum — roles, artifacts, and every ceremony

cards.b:
What it is. Product Backlog (commitment: the Product Goal), Sprint Backlog (commitment: the Sprint Goal), Increment (commitment: the Definition of Done).

How you run it. The Sprint Goal is one sentence the team can rally around; the increment must be releasable.

Rule to remember. Every artifact has a commitment in the 2020 Scrum Guide — interviewers who know Scrum will notice you know that.

Gotcha. Sprint backlogs that are just a to-do list with no goal.
cards.s: Scrum — roles, artifacts, and every ceremony

cards.b:
What it is. A fixed time box — one to four weeks, usually two — in which the team delivers a releasable increment. No scope changes that endanger the Sprint Goal once it starts.

How you run it. Consistent length so velocity means something.

Rule to remember. Shorter sprints for faster learning and more frequent planning; longer when context-switching cost is high.

Gotcha. Sprints that quietly become mini-waterfalls: all dev in week one, all testing in week two.
cards.s: Scrum — roles, artifacts, and every ceremony

cards.b:
What it is. The first event. Three questions: why is this sprint valuable (Sprint Goal)? what can be done (select backlog items)? how will it get done (plan the work)? Time-boxed to eight hours for a month-long sprint, proportionally less for shorter.

How you run it. PO brings a refined, ordered backlog; the team pulls what it believes it can finish.

Rule to remember. Plan to historical velocity, not to the pressure in the room.

Gotcha. Over-commitment every sprint; planning that's really the PO assigning work.
cards.s: Scrum — roles, artifacts, and every ceremony

cards.b:
What it is. Fifteen minutes, same time and place, for the developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and replan the next day. Any format works; the classic three questions are optional.

How you run it. Developers talk to each other; the manager listens or isn't there.

Rule to remember. It's a replanning meeting, not a status report. Problems get parked and solved right after.

Gotcha. Thirty-minute status reports to the manager. People reporting instead of coordinating.
cards.s: Scrum — roles, artifacts, and every ceremony

cards.b:
What it is. At sprint end, the team shows the increment to stakeholders and gets feedback that reshapes the backlog. A working session, not a demo for applause. Up to four hours for a month-long sprint.

How you run it. Invite real stakeholders; show working software; capture what changed in the backlog.

Rule to remember. The output is an updated backlog, not a slide deck.

Gotcha. A polished demo with no feedback loop.
cards.s: Scrum — roles, artifacts, and every ceremony

cards.b:
What it is. After the review, the team inspects how the sprint went — people, process, tools, Definition of Done — and picks one or two improvements for the next sprint. Up to three hours for a month-long sprint. Blameless.

How you run it. Rotate formats (start/stop/continue, 4Ls, sailboat) to keep it honest; track action items to completion.

Rule to remember. A retro that produces no action is a social hour. One improvement actually done beats five listed.

Gotcha. The same complaint every retro with nothing changing.
cards.s: Scrum — roles, artifacts, and every ceremony

cards.b:
What it is. An ongoing activity, not a formal event: the PO and team break down, clarify, estimate, and order upcoming items so they're Ready for planning. Typically up to 10% of the team's capacity.

How you run it. A standing weekly slot works for most teams.

Rule to remember. Refined two sprints ahead; nothing enters planning unrefined.

Gotcha. Refining the whole backlog instead of the top of it.
cards.s: Scrum — roles, artifacts, and every ceremony

cards.b:
What it is. Sprint Goal success rate; velocity trend (not absolute); cycle time; escaped defects; carryover percentage; sprint burndown for within-sprint, release burnup for the roadmap.

How you run it. Team dashboards for the team; outcome metrics for leadership.

Rule to remember. Burndown that only drops on the last day means work is batched, not flowing.

Gotcha. Story points per engineer as a performance metric.
cards.s: Scrum — roles, artifacts, and every ceremony

cards.b:
What it is. Visualize the workflow; limit work in progress; manage flow; make policies explicit; implement feedback loops; improve collaboratively. No sprints, no fixed roles.

How you run it. Operations, support, platform teams, and any team with continuous unplanned intake.

Rule to remember. WIP limits are the mechanism — everything else follows from finishing before starting.

Gotcha. A Kanban board with no WIP limits is just a to-do list.

What it is. Cycle time (start to finish of an item), lead time (request to delivery), throughput (items per week), WIP. Little's Law: cycle time = WIP ÷ throughput — cut WIP and cycle time falls.

How you run it. Forecast with throughput and a cycle-time distribution ("85% of items finish within nine days") instead of estimates.

Rule to remember. Little's Law is the one formula to be able to say out loud.

Gotcha. Reporting average cycle time when the distribution has a long tail.

What it is. A stacked area chart of items in each state over time. Band height is WIP; horizontal width is cycle time; a widening band is a bottleneck.

How you run it. The one chart to show a manager where work is stuck.

Rule to remember. If "in review" keeps widening, the fix is reviewing, not starting more work.

Gotcha. Reading it as a burndown.

What it is. Expedite (true emergencies, capped at one), fixed-date, standard, intangible. Swimlanes per class or per team so an emergency doesn't silently push everything else.

How you run it. Teams that mix planned work and interrupts — most platform teams.

Rule to remember. An expedite lane with a WIP limit of one keeps "urgent" meaning something.

Gotcha. Everything marked urgent.

What it is. Scrum cadence with Kanban flow inside it, or Kanban with periodic planning and retros. Most real teams run a hybrid.

How you run it. Say what you ran and why: "Scrum for software teams, Kanban for IT operations" — your Rheinmetall setup.

Rule to remember. Pick by the shape of the work; "pure" anything is a warning sign.

Gotcha. Changing the process every month.

What it is. Scaled Agile Framework. Agile Release Train (ART): 50–125 people on one value stream and cadence. Program Increment (PI): 8–12 weeks, four or five sprints plus an Innovation and Planning iteration. Levels: Essential, Large Solution, Portfolio, Full.

How you run it. Automotive and industrial companies — Stellantis, Ford, Tier 1s — speak this vocabulary.

Rule to remember. Essential SAFe when you have more than four or five teams with real dependencies; stay lighter otherwise.

Gotcha. Process as the product: an RTE and a program board can't substitute for ownership and good APIs.
cards.s: Scaling agile — SAFe, LeSS, and alternatives

cards.b:
What it is. Release Train Engineer (RTE, the ART's chief scrum master), Product Management (program backlog, features), System Architect (technical direction across the train), Business Owners (executives accountable for value), plus team-level POs and Scrum Masters.

How you run it. Know who you'd be: an SDM is usually the people leader for one or more teams on a train, partnering with the RTE and PM.

Rule to remember. The System Architect role is the closest to your current job.

Gotcha. Confusing the RTE with a project manager.
cards.s: Scaling agile — SAFe, LeSS, and alternatives

cards.b:
What it is. Epics (portfolio, need a lean business case) → Capabilities (solution) → Features (program, fit in a PI, have a benefit hypothesis) → Stories (team, fit in a sprint). Enablers are the technical counterparts — architecture, infrastructure, exploration, compliance — planned alongside business features.

How you run it. Platform investment is an enabler; architectural runway is SAFe's name for the foundation built ahead of features.

Rule to remember. Ask for enabler capacity explicitly or it gets squeezed to zero.

Gotcha. Enablers with no business owner.
cards.s: Scaling agile — SAFe, LeSS, and alternatives

cards.b:
What it is. The two-day event where the whole ART plans the PI: business context and vision, team breakouts, dependencies mapped on the program board, risks ROAMed (Resolved, Owned, Accepted, Mitigated), a confidence vote, and PI objectives per team.

How you run it. The single most valuable SAFe ritual — it drags cross-team dependencies into daylight every quarter.

Rule to remember. Your Stellantis provisioning workshop was PI planning in spirit: every team in one room, dependencies on the wall.

Gotcha. PI objectives that are just feature lists; a confidence vote nobody acts on.
cards.s: Scaling agile — SAFe, LeSS, and alternatives

cards.b:
What it is. ART Sync (or Scrum of Scrums plus PO Sync) weekly; System Demo every sprint of the integrated system; Inspect and Adapt at PI end — demo, metrics, and a problem-solving workshop.

How you run it. The system demo is the one that catches integration problems early.

Rule to remember. If the system demo only works on slides, the train isn't integrating.

Gotcha. ART Sync as a status meeting.
cards.s: Scaling agile — SAFe, LeSS, and alternatives

cards.b:
What it is. Weighted Shortest Job First = cost of delay ÷ job size, where cost of delay = user/business value + time criticality + risk reduction/opportunity enablement, each scored relatively.

How you run it. Ordering the program backlog.

Rule to remember. A small, urgent, risk-reducing item often beats a large feature — which matches an engineer's instinct.

Gotcha. Scoring in absolute units instead of relative.
cards.s: Scaling agile — SAFe, LeSS, and alternatives

cards.f: LeSS, Nexus, Scrum@Scale, Spotify, Team Topologies
cards.b:
What it is. LeSS: one backlog, one PO, many teams, minimal added roles — Scrum scaled by subtraction. Nexus: 3–9 teams with an integration team. Scrum@Scale: scrum of scrums with an executive action team. Spotify model: squads, tribes, chapters, guilds (Spotify says it never fully used it). Team Topologies: stream-aligned, platform, enabling, complicated-subsystem teams with three interaction modes.

How you run it. Team Topologies is the best current vocabulary for org design; use it when asked how you'd structure teams.

Rule to remember. A platform team offers its capabilities "as a service" to stream-aligned teams.

Gotcha. Adopting the Spotify model because of the name.
cards.s: Scaling agile — SAFe, LeSS, and alternatives

cards.b:
What it is. Every commit merged to main and built and tested within minutes. Integration problems found the same day they're created.

How you run it. Trunk-based development plus a fast pipeline.

Rule to remember. Main is always releasable.

Gotcha. Long-lived feature branches and "integration week."
cards.s: Engineering practices that make agile work

cards.b:
What it is. TDD: write a failing test, make it pass, refactor. BDD: specify behavior as Given/When/Then and automate it (Cucumber). ATDD: acceptance criteria become the tests before coding starts.

How you run it. BDD/ATDD bridge the PO's acceptance criteria and the engineer's tests.

Rule to remember. Tests are the executable Definition of Done.

Gotcha. Test coverage as a target — people write tests that assert nothing.
cards.s: Engineering practices that make agile work

cards.b:
What it is. Two (pair) or the whole team (mob) on one problem at one keyboard. Expensive per hour, fastest for knowledge transfer, onboarding, and de-risking the hardest piece.

How you run it. Onboarding; the gnarliest change; spreading knowledge off a single owner.

Rule to remember. Your remedy for single-person dependencies on contractors.

Gotcha. Mandated pairing all day for everyone.
cards.s: Engineering practices that make agile work

cards.b:
What it is. Improve the design without changing behavior, continuously, in small steps, under tests. Leave the code cleaner than you found it.

How you run it. Every sprint, inside feature work — not a separate project.

Rule to remember. Refactoring without tests is just changing things.

Gotcha. "Refactoring sprint" that ships nothing and gets cancelled.
cards.s: Engineering practices that make agile work

cards.b:
What it is. Small PRs, reviewed within a business day, review the design and the tests not just the style; automated checks handle formatting; disagreements go to a short call.

How you run it. The DoD includes review; the same standard for contractors.

Rule to remember. A PR waiting three days is a WIP problem.

Gotcha. Rubber-stamp reviews; reviews as gatekeeping.
cards.s: Engineering practices that make agile work

cards.b:
What it is. Bounded contexts — a boundary inside which a term means one thing; the ubiquitous language shared by engineers and domain experts; aggregates and domain events.

How you run it. Finding service boundaries in a monolith; naming teams.

Rule to remember. Team boundaries should follow bounded contexts (Conway's law, used deliberately).

Gotcha. Microservices cut along tables instead of contexts.
cards.s: Engineering practices that make agile work

cards.b:
What it is. A roadmap is themes over time horizons (now / next / later), not a Gantt chart. OKRs: an objective (qualitative, inspiring) with two to four measurable key results, set quarterly, scored honestly.

How you run it. Translating roadmap intent into a technical plan with scope, sequencing, dependencies, and risk.

Rule to remember. Key results are outcomes (yield from 94% to 96.5%), not output (ship ten models).

Gotcha. OKRs as a task list; 100% attainment every quarter means they weren't ambitious.

What it is. MVP: the smallest thing that tests the riskiest assumption. Discovery (learning what to build) runs in parallel with delivery (building it) — dual-track.

How you run it. New features and new platforms: a pilot with a metric in weeks beats a platform in quarters.

Rule to remember. An MVP that nobody can use isn't viable.

Gotcha. Discovery that never ends; delivery that never asks.

What it is. A Technical Program Manager owns cross-team delivery of a program — dependencies, risks, schedule — without owning the people. You own feasibility and the people; they own the integrated plan.

How you run it. Weekly risk-register review; shared definitions of done and "launched."

Rule to remember. Bring options with costs, not objections.

Gotcha. Treating the TPM as a status collector.

What it is. Map dependencies before committing; sequence around the slowest train (firmware, certification, a partner); make backend tolerant of both old and new during overlap; a shared release calendar.

How you run it. Any program spanning cloud, app, and hardware — your Stellantis and Cameo-upgrade stories.

Rule to remember. A dependency discovered in sprint planning is a planning failure.

Gotcha. Hoping the other team is on time.

What it is. A living risk register: likelihood, impact, owner, mitigation, trigger. Reviewed weekly. Risks surface early with options, never as surprises in a steering meeting.

How you run it. Part of every planning cadence.

Rule to remember. A red risk goes to leadership with a recommendation attached.

Gotcha. A register nobody reads; risks without owners.

cards.f: Agile in regulated and hardware environments
cards.b:
What it is. V-model traceability (requirements ↔ tests) for the compliance deliverable, iterative delivery for the software inside it; longer validation cycles for firmware; documentation generated from the work, not written after it.

How you run it. Defense, automotive, medical — your world.

Rule to remember. Say the hybrid confidently: "Scrum for software, Kanban for ops, V-model traceability for the systems-engineering deliverables to the Army."

Gotcha. Pretending a certification cycle can be two weeks.

decks.title: SRE in depth
decks.blurb: SLIs, SLOs, error budgets, toil, on-call, postmortems, capacity.

cards.f: The core idea: reliability is a number, and 100% is the wrong target
cards.b:
Every additional nine of availability costs roughly ten times more and delivers value users can't perceive past a point — a phone on a cellular network is less reliable than 99.99% anyway. So SRE starts by asking: how reliable does this need to be? That target is the Service Level Objective. Everything else follows from it.

TermMeaningExample for the Whisker command path
SLI — indicatorThe thing you measureFraction of commands acknowledged by the robot within 3 seconds
SLO — objectiveThe target for the SLI over a window99.5% over a rolling 30 days
SLA — agreementA contractual promise with consequences, usually looser than the SLOBusiness customers: 99% or a service credit
Error budget1 − SLO: the unreliability you're allowed0.5% of a month ≈ 3.6 hours of slow or failed commands
Burn rateHow fast you're consuming the budget relative to planBurn rate 14 means at this pace the month's budget is gone in two days

Why the error budget is a management tool, not a metric. It converts an emotional argument ("the system is too flaky" vs "we need to ship features") into a rule both sides agreed to in advance: while budget remains, product velocity wins; when it's spent, reliability work goes first until it recovers. At Ford the equivalent conversation was about downstream dependencies taking the read path down — an error budget would have ended that debate in a week.

cards.f: Availability arithmetic you should have memorized
cards.b:
99% = 7.3 hours/month down    99.9% = 43.8 minutes    99.95% = 21.9 minutes    99.99% = 4.4 minutes    99.999% = 26 seconds
Serial dependencies multiply: A(99.9%) → B(99.9%) → C(99.9%) ≈ 99.7% together
Redundant parallel components: two independent 99% components in parallel ≈ 99.99%
So: remove synchronous dependencies from the critical path (Ford), and make the components you can't remove redundant (multi-AZ).

cards.f: The four golden signals, and RED and USE
cards.b: Google's four golden signals for any service: latency (how long requests take, separating successful from failed), traffic (demand), errors (rate of failed requests), and saturation (how full the system is — CPU, memory, queue depth). Two mnemonics organize dashboards: RED for services (Rate, Errors, Duration) and USE for resources (Utilization, Saturation, Errors). A service dashboard built on RED tells you whether users are hurting; a resource dashboard on USE tells you why.

The classic mistake is alerting on CPU at 80%. CPU at 80% is not a user problem; it's a possible cause of one. SRE alerts on symptoms — the SLI degrading — and uses multi-window burn-rate alerts to decide urgency. The standard recipe: page if the burn rate over the last hour would exhaust 2% of the monthly budget (a fast burn — something broke now); open a ticket if the burn over three days would exhaust 10% (a slow leak — fix it this sprint). This cuts pages dramatically because a thirty-second blip doesn't threaten the monthly promise. Every alert must have a runbook (what to check, in order) and an owner; an alert with neither is noise with a pager attached.

Toil is manual, repetitive, automatable operational work that scales with the service — restarting pods by hand, rotating a certificate manually, approving the same access request weekly. Google caps toil at 50% of an SRE's time; the rest is engineering that reduces toil. As a manager, the metric is: how many hours per week does the on-call spend on things a script could do? If the answer is over ten, the next sprint has an automation story in it.

• Rotation: primary and secondary, one-week shifts, no more than one week in five per person, compensated. Handoff notes at every rotation.
  • Time zones: follow-the-sun if you have coverage in three regions; otherwise business-hours paging in each region and true Sev-1-only overnight.
  • Load: more than two or three pages per shift is a system problem, not an on-call problem. Track pages per shift and the fraction that were actionable.
  • The on-call engineer's fixes go into the next sprint. Otherwise the same page recurs and people burn out.

Incidents are run, not improvised. The incident commander coordinates and communicates and explicitly does not debug — the moment the IC starts reading logs, nobody is steering. A communications lead updates the status page and stakeholders on a schedule so responders aren't interrupted. Subject-matter responders do the work. Declare early and downgrade freely; the cost of an unnecessary declaration is twenty minutes, the cost of a late one is hours. Severity is defined by customer impact, written down in advance, so nobody debates it at 3 a.m.

The blameless postmortem follows within days: timeline, contributing factors (plural — there's never a single root cause in a complex system), what went well, action items with owners and dates, and a later check that the actions shipped. "Blameless" is not politeness; it's how you get people to tell you what actually happened. The management skill is noticing the third instance of a pattern and removing the category — see the postmortem example in Part 4.

Organic growth plus launch events. Model demand (devices × messages × bytes; users × requests) against the launch calendar, provision for the peak with headroom, and load-test before every major launch with a realistic simulator. For IoT the specific scenario is the reconnect storm: after an outage, every device reconnects at once and the TLS handshakes alone can take the broker down. The fix lives on the device (jittered exponential backoff) and on the broker (connection rate limits).

Deliberately inject failure to prove the system survives it: kill an availability zone, add 500 ms of latency to a dependency, fill a disk. Start in staging with AWS Fault Injection Service or Gremlin; graduate to production game days with the whole team watching. The point isn't to break things — it's to discover that the runbook is wrong before an incident does.

cards.f: How SRE shows up in the interview
cards.b:
• "How do you make reliability measurable?" → SLOs per domain, error budgets, burn-rate alerting, and the numbers on a monthly slide.
  • "Describe your on-call philosophy." → sustainable, symptom-based, runbooks, fixes prioritized.
  • "Tell me about an incident." → structure (IC, comms, responders) and the postmortem's systemic action.
  • "Your team pages 15 times a week." → classify, delete cause-based alerts, convert to burn-rate, fix the top two causes, report pages per shift weekly.

decks.title: Delivery, deployment & infrastructure practices
decks.blurb: CI/CD, release strategies, IaC, GitOps, platform engineering.

cards.b:
StrategyHow it worksBlast radiusRollbackUse when
RecreateStop old, start newEveryone, plus downtimeRedeploy oldDev environments; never prod
RollingReplace instances a few at a time behind a load balancerGradual, but mixed versions coexistRoll forward or reverse the rollDefault for stateless services with backward-compatible changes
Blue/greenTwo identical environments; switch traffic all at onceEveryone, instantly — but instantly reversibleFlip back in secondsChanges you want to test fully in a real environment then switch; database must be compatible with both
CanaryRoute 1% → 10% → 50% → 100% of traffic to the new version, gated on metricsSmall, controlledShift traffic backRisky changes; the standard for high-traffic services
Feature flags / dark launchDeploy code disabled; enable per user, cohort, or percentage at runtimeWhatever you chooseTurn the flag off — no deployDecoupling deploy from release; product experiments; kill switches
Shadow / mirroringSend a copy of real traffic to the new version; discard its responsesNoneNothing to roll backValidating a rewrite (D11) or a new model before it affects anyone
A/B testingTwo versions to two cohorts; compare a business metricHalf of the cohortPick the winnerProduct decisions, not reliability

Example: Whisker's notification service gets a new dedup rule. Deploy it behind a flag, turn it on for the internal cohort, then canary 5% of users while watching duplicate-push rate and delivery latency, then 100%. If anything looks wrong, the flag goes off in seconds and no deploy is needed. OTA firmware follows the same logic with cohorts instead of traffic percentages.

Immutable means you never patch a running server; you build a new image and replace it. It eliminates configuration drift — the "works on server 3 but not 4" problem. Infrastructure as code (Terraform, CloudFormation, CDK, Pulumi) makes the environment reproducible from a repository. GitOps takes it further: the Git repository is the source of truth for what should be running, and a reconciler (Argo CD, Flux) continuously makes the cluster match it. A rollback is a Git revert; an audit trail is the commit log.

The thing that actually breaks zero-downtime deploys is the database. The pattern: expand (add the new column, nullable), deploy code that writes both old and new, backfill, switch reads to the new column, then contract (drop the old column) in a later release. Every step is compatible with the version before and after, so rolling and canary deploys work. Never couple a schema migration to a single deploy.

cards.f: CI/CD pipeline stages, and what each gate catches
cards.b:
1. Lint and static analysis — style and obvious bugs; for safety-critical code, tools like Astrée (abstract interpretation) prove the absence of certain runtime errors.
  2. Unit tests — logic in isolation; fast; should be the majority of tests (the "test pyramid").
  3. Build and sign the artifact — a container image with a software bill of materials (SBOM), signed so production can verify provenance.
  4. Contract tests — consumer-driven (Pact) or schema-driven checks that the API still satisfies what its clients expect; this is how you don't break the two-year-old app version.
  5. Integration and end-to-end tests in an ephemeral environment spun up per pull request.
  6. Security scans — SAST (source), dependency vulnerabilities, container image CVEs, secrets detection.
  7. Deploy to staging, smoke test, then progressive production deploy with automated rollback on SLO breach.

cards.f: DORA metrics — the four numbers that describe delivery health
cards.b:
MetricWhat it measuresElite benchmark
Deployment frequencyHow often you ship to productionOn demand, multiple times a day
Lead time for changesCommit to running in productionUnder a day
Change failure rateFraction of deploys causing an incident or rollbackUnder 5%
Time to restoreHow fast you recover from a failed changeUnder an hour

The insight from the research behind them: speed and stability are not a tradeoff — teams that deploy more often also fail less, because small changes are easier to test and roll back. When a posting asks for "measurable improvement in deployment stability," these are the numbers.

Gitflow uses long-lived develop and release branches with merges at milestones; it made sense for boxed software with quarterly releases and creates painful merges and late integration. Trunk-based development means everyone commits to main in small, short-lived branches (a day or two), with feature flags hiding incomplete work. It's the practice most correlated with high DORA scores. Firmware teams often still need release branches because of validation and certification cycles — that's a legitimate exception.

Monitoring tells you a known thing is wrong (an alert on a threshold). Observability lets you ask questions you didn't anticipate — why is p99 slow only for German users on hardware rev B? It rests on three signals: metrics (cheap, aggregated numbers over time), logs (structured events with context), and traces (a request's path across services with timing per hop). OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard for emitting all three, so you can switch from Datadog to Grafana without re-instrumenting. Correlation IDs tie a user's tap to a device's ack across every system between.

cards.f: Security in the pipeline: DevSecOps and supply chain
cards.b: Shift security left: scans in CI, secrets never in code, least-privilege credentials issued by OIDC to the pipeline rather than long-lived keys. Software supply chain concerns (after SolarWinds and log4j): know what's in your artifacts (SBOM), sign them (Sigstore/cosign), verify signatures at deploy, and pin dependencies. In regulated settings (CMMC, ISO 27001, TISAX) this is evidence you'll be asked to produce.

• 99.9% = 43.8 min/month; 99.95% = 21.9 min; 99.99% = 4.4 min.
  • Three 99.9% services in series ≈ 99.7%.
  • Burn-rate paging: 14.4× over 1 h; ticket at 1× over 3 days.
  • DORA elite: deploys on demand, lead time < 1 day, CFR < 5%, restore < 1 h.
  • Kinesis shard: 1 MB/s in, 2 MB/s out. IoT Core bills per 5 KB message unit.

• Severity by customer impact; IC, comms lead, responders; declare early.
  • Blameless postmortem within days; action items tracked; quarterly pattern review.
  • Every alert: symptom-based, runbook, owner.

• Trunk-based, short-lived branches, feature flags.
  • Pipeline: lint → unit → build/sign → contract → integration → security → staging → progressive prod.
  • Expand/contract migrations; immutable artifacts; one-click rollback.

• Scrum for product teams, Kanban for ops; hybrid is fine.
  • Measure cycle time, lead time, and outcomes — not velocity as a target.
  • Retros produce tracked actions; dependencies planned, not discovered.
  • Director's role: remove organizational blockers, align to business goals, enable rather than micromanage.

decks.title: Methodologies & scaled frameworks
decks.blurb: Scrum, Kanban, XP, SAFe, LeSS, Spotify model, OKRs, estimation.

cards.f: The methodologies, and what each optimized for
cards.b:
MethodCore ideaWhere it fitsWhere it fails
WaterfallSequential phases: requirements → design → build → test → deployFixed-scope, regulated deliverables where change is expensive (some defense and hardware programs)Anything where requirements are learned by building
V-modelWaterfall with each design level paired with a test level (system design ↔ system test, unit design ↔ unit test)Automotive and safety-critical (ISO 26262, DO-178C); it's the mental model behind SysML/MBSE traceabilitySlow feedback; heavy documentation
Spiral / iterativeRepeated cycles of plan, risk analysis, build, evaluateLarge risky systemsHard to manage cadence
Agile (Manifesto, 2001)Working software, customer collaboration, responding to change; short iterationsProduct software where learning is the pointWhen treated as "no planning"
Lean / KanbanFlow: limit work in progress, visualize, reduce cycle time, eliminate wasteOperations, support, platform teams with continuous intakeTeams that need a forcing cadence
ScrumFixed-length sprints, defined roles and ceremonies, an increment each sprintProduct teams that benefit from rhythmWork that doesn't fit two-week boxes; teams that cargo-cult the ceremonies
XP (Extreme Programming)Engineering practices: pairing, TDD, continuous integration, refactoring, small releasesThe technical half that Scrum leaves outCultural resistance to pairing
DevOpsDev and Ops share ownership of delivery and operations; automation; measurementEverywhere modernWhen it's a team name instead of a practice
Shape Up (Basecamp)Six-week cycles, shaped pitches, fixed time and variable scope, no backlogSmall senior product teamsLarge or regulated orgs

Hybrid is normal. At Rheinmetall: Scrum for software teams, Kanban for IT operations, and V-model traceability for the systems-engineering deliverables to the Army — because each fits the work. Say that with confidence; "pure" anything is a warning sign.

• Roles: Product Owner (owns the backlog and priority — the "what"), Scrum Master (facilitates process and removes impediments), Developers (cross-functional team that owns the "how"). Note: the engineering manager is none of these roles in pure Scrum; in practice you set direction, grow people, and remove organizational blockers.
  • Artifacts: Product Backlog (ordered list of everything), Sprint Backlog (what the team committed to this sprint and the plan), Increment (the working product at sprint end, meeting the Definition of Done).
  • Events: Sprint Planning (what and how), Daily Scrum (15 min, replanning not status), Sprint Review (demo to stakeholders, inspect the increment), Sprint Retrospective (inspect the process; produce one or two actions), and the Sprint itself (1–4 weeks, usually 2).
  • Definition of Done vs Definition of Ready: DoD is the quality bar an increment must meet (tests, review, docs, deployed to staging); DoR is what a backlog item needs before the team pulls it (clear acceptance criteria, dependencies known). Both are the team's, written down.
  • Estimation: story points express relative size and uncertainty, not hours; velocity (points per sprint) is a planning tool for the team, not a performance metric for management. The moment velocity becomes a target, it inflates.
  • Common anti-patterns: the daily scrum as a status report to the manager; sprints that never produce a releasable increment; retros with no actions; a PO who is a proxy without authority; carrying over half the sprint every sprint.

Visualize the workflow on a board (to do → in progress → review → done, or whatever the real steps are); limit work in progress per column so the team finishes before starting; manage flow by measuring cycle time (start to finish of an item) and lead time (request to delivery); make policies explicit; improve continuously. WIP limits are the mechanism — a limit of 3 in "review" forces people to review each other's work instead of starting a fourth thing. Kanban has no sprints, so it suits interrupt-driven teams. A cumulative flow diagram shows where work piles up.

cards.f: SAFe — the Scaled Agile Framework, and what to say about it
cards.b:
SAFe is the most common framework for coordinating many agile teams in large organizations, especially automotive and industrial companies. You'll hear its vocabulary at Stellantis, Ford, and most Tier 1 suppliers. Know it well enough to speak it and to say where it helps and where it's overhead.

The structure

  • Agile Release Train (ART): a long-lived team of teams (50–125 people) delivering a value stream together on a common cadence. Multiple ARTs form a Solution Train for very large systems.
  • Program Increment (PI): the ART's planning cadence — typically 8–12 weeks, four or five sprints plus an Innovation and Planning (IP) iteration.
  • PI Planning: the two-day event where the whole ART plans the PI together: business context, team breakouts, dependency mapping on the program board, risk identification (ROAMed: Resolved, Owned, Accepted, Mitigated), and a confidence vote. It's the single most valuable ritual in SAFe because it forces cross-team dependencies into the open.
  • Roles: Release Train Engineer (RTE — the ART's chief scrum master), Product Management (owns the program backlog, defines features), System Architect/Engineering (technical direction across the ART), Business Owners (executives accountable for value), Product Owners and Scrum Masters at team level.
  • Backlog hierarchy: Epics (portfolio-level, need a business case / lean business case) → Capabilities (solution level) → Features (program level, fit in a PI, have benefit hypotheses and acceptance criteria) → Stories (team level, fit in a sprint). Enablers are the technical counterparts — architecture, infrastructure, exploration — that get planned alongside business features.
  • Architectural runway: the existing technical infrastructure needed to implement near-term features without excessive redesign. Enabler work builds runway ahead of the features that will need it — this is SAFe's word for "platform investment."
  • Other cadence events: ART Sync (or Scrum of Scrums + PO Sync), System Demo every sprint, Inspect & Adapt at the end of a PI (demo, metrics, problem-solving workshop).
  • Configurations: Essential SAFe (one ART), Large Solution, Portfolio (Lean Portfolio Management with strategic themes, guardrails, and participatory budgeting), Full.
  • Weighted Shortest Job First (WSJF): prioritization = cost of delay ÷ job size, where cost of delay = user/business value + time criticality + risk reduction/opportunity enablement. Do the highest WSJF first.

What to say about it

"What do you think of SAFe?"

"It solves a real problem — coordinating fifty to a hundred people with dependencies — and PI planning in particular is worth its cost because it drags dependencies and risks into daylight every quarter. Where I've seen it go wrong is when the process becomes the product: an RTE and a program board can't substitute for clear ownership boundaries and good APIs between teams. At Stellantis the OTA work ran on a PI cadence with firmware, cloud, and app teams on separate trains, and the thing that made it work was the dependency mapping, not the ceremonies. I'd use Essential SAFe when I have more than four or five teams with real dependencies, and stay lighter — Scrum of Scrums and a shared release calendar — when I don't."

cards.f: Other scaling approaches in one line each
cards.b:
• LeSS (Large-Scale Scrum): one product backlog, one PO, multiple teams, minimal added roles — Scrum scaled by subtraction.
  • Scrum@Scale: a scrum of scrums of scrums, with an Executive Action Team.
  • Spotify model: squads (teams), tribes (groups of squads), chapters (discipline communities across squads), guilds (interest communities). Spotify itself says it never fully used it.
  • Team Topologies: four team types — stream-aligned (product), platform, enabling, complicated-subsystem — and three interaction modes (collaboration, X-as-a-service, facilitating). The best current vocabulary for org design; a platform team offers its capabilities "as a service" to stream-aligned teams.
  • Nexus: Scrum.org's framework for 3–9 teams with an integration team.

cards.f: Engineering practices that make agile work
cards.b:
• TDD: write a failing test, make it pass, refactor. BDD: specify behavior in Given/When/Then and automate it (Cucumber). ATDD: acceptance criteria as tests.
  • Domain-Driven Design (DDD): model software around business domains; bounded contexts define where a term means one thing; the ubiquitous language is shared by engineers and domain experts. It's the tool for finding service boundaries in a monolith migration (D11).
  • Pair and mob programming: two or more engineers on one problem; knowledge transfer and quality; expensive but the fastest way to onboard or de-risk.
  • Continuous integration: every commit built and tested within minutes; integration problems found the same day.
  • Refactoring as ongoing work: the "boy scout rule" — leave the code cleaner than you found it — plus explicit debt items in the backlog.
  • Code review norms: small PRs, reviewed within a day, review the design not just the syntax, automated checks handle style.

• Roadmap (themes over time, not a Gantt chart), OKRs (objectives and key results, quarterly, measurable), MVP (smallest thing that tests the riskiest assumption), PRD (product requirements document), user story ("As a … I want … so that …"), acceptance criteria, epic, discovery vs delivery (dual-track agile), North Star metric, RICE scoring (Reach, Impact, Confidence, Effort), MoSCoW (Must, Should, Could, Won't).
  • TPM (Technical Program Manager): owns cross-team delivery of a program — dependencies, risks, schedule — without owning the people. Your partner at Whisker for "predictable, well-sequenced execution."

• "Scrum or Kanban?" → depends on the work; give the Rheinmetall hybrid.
  • "How do you scale agile?" → domain-aligned teams and API contracts first; then Essential SAFe or Scrum of Scrums depending on dependency density.
  • "How do you handle changing requirements?" → reprioritize between sprints, protect the sprint, shorten cycles where change is real, keep the PO close.
  • "How do you measure a team?" → cycle time, DORA, outcomes; never velocity as a target.

decks.title: Incidents & API evolution (worked)
decks.blurb: Five incidents as incident commander; designing and evolving an API without breaking old clients.

cards.f: Incident 1 — "Devices offline" alarm, 03:40, connected-device ratio dropped from 96% to 41%
cards.b:
First five minutes. Is it the broker, the network, or a firmware build? Check: broker connection count and CPU by node; TLS handshake rate; whether the drop is uniform or concentrated by region, firmware, or ISP. Check AWS Health for an IoT Core or regional event.

Likely diagnosis. Uniform drop plus a spike in handshake rate means a broker-side blip (a node recycled, a certificate rotation, a regional event) followed by a reconnect storm — 1.2 million devices trying to reconnect within the same thirty seconds, and the broker rate-limiting or timing out most of them. The devices aren't broken; they're queueing.

Contain. If self-managed: add broker capacity and raise connection rate limits gradually. If IoT Core: there's nothing to scale; the fleet will drain as backoff spreads it out. Communicate: status page says "connectivity delays; robots continue to operate normally" — the second half of that sentence is the one that stops the support flood.

Systemic change. The device reconnect logic has too little jitter — every unit retries at 1, 2, 4, 8 seconds from the same moment. The firmware fix is randomized exponential backoff with a cap and a fleet-wide spread (jitter proportional to a hash of the device ID). On the backend: an SLO for reconnect-storm drain time, and a load test that simulates a broker restart before every major launch. Post the pattern: "fleet-synchronized behavior" — the same root cause shows up in scheduled telemetry (everyone at :00 and :05) and in OTA download timing.

cards.f: Incident 2 — Push-notification volume alarm, 06:42, users receiving repeated "drawer full" pushes
cards.b: This is the postmortem in Part 4.6. The five-minute check: what changed? An OTA campaign entered stage 3 at 06:10. Correlate notification volume by firmware version — it's all 5.2.1. Contain: halt the campaign (one click), deploy a per-(user, event-type) dedup window in the notification service (should have existed). Systemic: the backend trusted the device to send an event once. Rule going forward: every device-originated event is at-least-once and dedup is a backend responsibility; notification rate is added to the OTA gate metrics so stage 1 catches it next time.

cards.f: Incident 3 — Command latency SLO burn-rate page, 19:10 Saturday, p99 command ack time 9 s
cards.b:
First five minutes. Is it the app → API path, the command publish, or the device ack? Traces show the API responds in 80 ms and the publish succeeds; the gap is between publish and ack. Check the events stream consumer lag — it's 14 minutes and climbing. The fast-path Lambda that processes acks is behind because it shares the events stream with a burst of telemetry from a new "health insights" feature that shipped Friday.

Contain. Increase the Lambda's parallelization factor / consumer count to drain the lag; if that's not enough, temporarily throttle the new feature's event type at the IoT rule (a rule change deploys in seconds).

Systemic. The control path shared a stream with analytics traffic — the architectural sin this whole document warns about. Fix: acks and command-state events get their own stream and consumer with a strict SLO; analytics gets its own with a relaxed one. Add consumer lag to the pre-launch checklist and a per-event-type rate limit at the rule. In the retro, the honest note is that this was known technical debt with a ticket from March; the exec memo in 7B is what you write next.

cards.f: Incident 4 — DynamoDB throttling errors on the device_data table, 12:15, app shows stale state for ~5% of users
cards.b:
First five minutes. Throttling on a table with on-demand capacity means a hot partition, not a capacity ceiling. Which partition key? CloudWatch Contributor Insights shows one DEV# key taking 40% of writes — a single device publishing 200 events a second. It's a robot with a stuck sensor on firmware 4.9 that loops on cat_detected.

Contain. Disable that device's ingest (a deny entry in the IoT rule or a device-level quarantine flag the fast path checks). State recovers in seconds for everyone else.

Systemic. Two guardrails: a per-device publish rate limit at the broker (IoT Core supports this via Device Defender behaviors and you can also enforce it in the fast path with a token bucket in Redis), and a quarantine mechanism that automatically parks a device exceeding N events/minute and opens a support case. Also a firmware fix for the sensor loop, rolled out to the 4.9 cohort. Pattern: "one device can hurt the fleet" — the same class as a compromised device, and the same fix.

cards.f: Incident 5 — Regional degradation: us-east-1 API latency and error rates spike, 14:00, AWS reports an issue
cards.b:
First five minutes. Confirm scope: which services are affected (API, broker, DynamoDB?), and whether the robots are fine (they are — cleaning doesn't need the cloud). Decide whether to fail over the control path to the warm standby region.

The decision. Failover isn't free: DNS TTLs mean some clients keep hitting the old region for minutes; devices must reconnect to the standby broker (their certs are valid there if you designed it that way); DynamoDB global tables replicate with seconds of lag so a few command states may be stale. If the regional issue is "elevated latency," waiting is usually better than a failover that creates its own incident. If it's a hard outage, fail over the API and broker endpoints and accept the reconnect storm (see Incident 1 — the backoff fix matters here too).

Systemic. Whatever you decided, the postmortem asks whether the decision criteria were written down in advance. They should be: "fail over when the primary's error rate exceeds X for Y minutes and AWS confirms a regional event." A game day that exercises the failover twice a year, with the runbook updated each time, is the difference between a plan and a hope. For Whisker specifically, the EU region for Germany changes the calculus — it's a real second region with its own residency rules, not a standby.

cards.f: What all five have in common
cards.b:
• The first question is always "what changed?" — a deploy, a campaign, a config, a vendor event.
  • Containment beats diagnosis in the first fifteen minutes: halt the campaign, quarantine the device, drain the queue.
  • The robot keeps working; say so on the status page immediately.
  • The systemic fix names a category — fleet-synchronized behavior, trusting device behavior, shared control/analytics path, one device hurting the fleet, undocumented failover criteria — and removes it.

cards.f: The GraphQL schema the app talks to
cards.b:
type Query {
  me: Account!
  household(id: ID!): Household
  device(id: ID!): Device
}
type Household { id: ID!  name: String!  members: [Member!]!  devices: [Device!]!  cats: [Cat!]! }
type Device {
  id: ID!  name: String!  model: DeviceModel!  hwRev: String!  fwVersion: String!
  online: Boolean!  lastSeen: DateTime!
  state: DeviceState!                        # from the DynamoDB STATE item
  capabilities: [Capability!]!               # advertised by the device on connect — the app greys out what's missing
  recentActivity(first: Int = 20, after: String): ActivityConnection!   # cursor pagination
  settings: DeviceSettings!                  # from the shadow's reported/desired
}
type DeviceState { drawerLevel: Int!  litterLevel: Int!  cycleStatus: CycleStatus!  lastCycleAt: DateTime  faults: [Fault!]! }
enum CycleStatus { IDLE CYCLING PAUSED FAULT UNKNOWN }     # UNKNOWN so old firmware never breaks the enum
type Mutation {
  sendCommand(deviceId: ID!, type: CommandType!, idempotencyKey: String!): Command!
  updateSettings(deviceId: ID!, patch: DeviceSettingsInput!): DeviceSettings!
}
type Command { id: ID!  type: CommandType!  state: CommandState!  createdAt: DateTime!  failureReason: String }
type Subscription { deviceStateChanged(deviceId: ID!): DeviceState!  commandUpdated(commandId: ID!): Command! }

Why GraphQL here rather than REST: the home screen composes household, devices, state, and recent activity — one query instead of four round trips on a mobile radio. Why persisted queries: the app ships with a fixed set of query hashes, so an attacker can't send an arbitrarily expensive query and you can cache by hash. Why capabilities in the schema: the fleet is on mixed firmware; the app must learn what a specific robot can do from the robot, not from the app version.

cards.f: Versioning in practice — three changes and how each is handled
cards.b:
ChangeBreaking?How
Add catWeightTrend to Device for the health featureNoAdd the field. Old apps never ask for it. Ship today.
Rename drawerLevel to wasteDrawerLevelYes, if you remove the old oneAdd the new field, mark drawerLevel @deprecated(reason: "use wasteDrawerLevel"), watch the gateway's per-field usage by app version, remove only when no supported app version requests it — likely 12–18 months.
Change sendCommand to require a reason argumentYesDon't. Add an optional argument with a default. Required-argument additions break every existing client; the rule is the same as the device schema: additive only.

For REST APIs (the ones the web dashboard or partners might use), the same logic with a version in the path: /v1/devices keeps working while /v2/devices exists; the gateway logs which versions still get traffic; a sunset header announces the date; force-upgrade is the last resort and comes with an in-app screen, not a 410.

# BFF handler for sendCommand (pseudo-Python)
def send_command(device_id, type_, idempotency_key, user):
    assert user_owns_device(user, device_id)                      # BOLA check — the #1 API vulnerability
    existing = redis.get(f"idem:{user.id}:{idempotency_key}")     # 24 h TTL
    if existing: return existing                                   # retry → same response, no second cycle
    cmd = commands.create(device_id, type_, expires_in=120)        # DynamoDB CMD# item, state=queued
    publish_qos1(f"devices/{device_id}/cmd", cmd.to_wire())        # → state=sent
    redis.set(f"idem:{user.id}:{idempotency_key}", cmd, ex=86400)
    return cmd

The line to point at in an interview is the ownership check: "broken object-level authorization" — user A reading or commanding device B by guessing an ID — is the most common API vulnerability in consumer apps, and it's a one-line check that must exist on every device-scoped operation.

cards.f: A contract test, so mobile can't be broken silently
cards.b:
# Pact-style consumer contract written by the mobile team, verified in the BFF's CI
consumer: whisker-ios-4.6
interaction: "home screen query"
  request:  POST /graphql  body: { queryHash: "a91f…", variables: { householdId: "HH#7781" } }
  response: 200, body matches:
    data.household.devices[*].id            : string
    data.household.devices[*].state.cycleStatus : oneOf [IDLE, CYCLING, PAUSED, FAULT, UNKNOWN]
    data.household.devices[*].capabilities  : array
# The BFF pipeline runs every supported app version's contracts (4.6, 4.7, 4.8). A field removal fails the build.

Per user: 60 commands a minute is generous and stops a bug in the app from hammering a robot. Per device: a command floor of one cycle command per 30 seconds protects the motor. Per app version: a misbehaving release can be throttled without touching the others. Implementation: token buckets in Redis with a Lua script for atomicity, local in-memory pre-limits at each gateway node, and fail-open with a conservative local cap if Redis is unreachable — you'd rather over-admit for a minute than block every customer.

The app subscribes to deviceStateChanged over a WebSocket (AppSync handles this natively; on ECS you'd run a WebSocket service fed by DynamoDB Streams through a Redis pub/sub). When the fast path writes a new STATE item, the stream triggers a fan-out to any connected session for that household. Fallback is polling every 15 seconds when the socket drops. The thing to design for is the 6 a.m. spike when everyone opens the app — connections are cheap, but the first query each session makes is the expensive home-screen query, so cache the household composition for a few seconds.

decks.title: Technical, DevOps & Agile rapid-fire Q&A
decks.blurb: Short answers with a trade-off and a number.

cards.b:
1. Design a system that handles 10x growth in 6 months

Answer:

  • First identify bottlenecks: database, CPU, memory, network

  • Move to horizontal scaling (adding more machines instead of bigger ones)

  • Add caching using tools like Redis or CDN to reduce load

  • Introduce asynchronous processing using queues (Kafka, RabbitMQ) so heavy tasks don’t block users

  • Break system into smaller services so each can scale independently
