decks.title: AWS services that matter — with use cases
decks.blurb: About thirty services: what it is, when to use it, an example, a number, the gotcha.

cards.b:
What it is. Servers you size and run. Families by shape: M general, C compute-heavy, R memory-heavy, I local NVMe disks for storage-heavy work, P/G GPUs. Graviton (ARM) versions of each are 20–40% better price-performance for most workloads. You pay three ways: on-demand, Savings Plans (commit to a dollar amount per hour for one or three years, 30–60% off — use for the steady baseline), and Spot (spare capacity at up to 90% off, reclaimable with two minutes' notice).

When you reach for it. Anything long-running or stateful you want control over: self-managed Kafka, EMR core nodes, a legacy app, a GPU box for training.

Example use case. Cradle runs Spark executors on a fleet where the core nodes are on-demand (they hold data) and the task nodes are Spot (they only compute). When Spot is reclaimed, Spark reruns the lost tasks from lineage. That mix is often 60–70% cheaper than all on-demand.

Number to remember. Savings Plans cover ~70% of the trailing baseline after rightsizing. Most instances in a typical account run at 10–20% CPU.

Gotcha. A stopped instance still bills for its disks. Spot on anything stateful loses the state. Instance metadata hands role credentials to anything running on the box — require IMDSv2 so an SSRF bug in your app doesn't become a credential theft.

What it is. Code that runs only when triggered — by an S3 upload, a Kinesis batch, an SQS message, an API call, a schedule — and bills per millisecond of execution. Scales from zero to thousands of concurrent copies automatically. Supports containers up to 10 GB and runs up to 15 minutes.

When you reach for it. Event glue and spiky work: IoT rule actions, a thumbnail on upload, a nightly report, a webhook receiver. Anything that is idle most of the time.

Example use case. A Kinesis stream of device events triggers a Lambda per batch that validates the schema, writes the hot aggregate to DynamoDB, and drops bad records on a dead-letter queue. At a few thousand events a second this costs tens of dollars a month and nobody runs a server.

Number to remember. Default 1,000 concurrent executions per account per region, shared by every function — one runaway function starves the rest; reserve concurrency for the ones that matter. Provisioned concurrency keeps copies warm to kill cold starts on a latency-critical path.

Gotcha. At sustained high throughput (hundreds of requests a second all day) containers are cheaper. Java and VPC-attached functions cold-start in seconds. Asynchronous invocations retry twice by default — the handler must be idempotent or you process events three times.

cards.f: ECS and Fargate — containers without Kubernetes
cards.b:
What it is. ECS is AWS's own container orchestrator: you define a task (container image, CPU, memory), a service keeps N copies running behind a load balancer. Fargate is the serverless way to run those tasks — no EC2 to patch or scale; you pay per vCPU-second and GB-second.

When you reach for it. APIs and background services that run all the time and need no Kubernetes features. The honest default for a team under about twenty engineers.

Example use case. A GraphQL BFF for a mobile app runs as an ECS service on Fargate: three tasks behind an ALB, autoscaled on request count, deployed blue/green by CodeDeploy. No cluster to upgrade, no nodes to right-size.

Number to remember. Fargate costs roughly 20–30% more per vCPU than EC2 you manage yourself; you save the platform engineer.

Gotcha. Slower to start than Lambda; no privileged containers or daemon sets. Teams pick EKS over ECS for prestige and then spend a year on cluster upgrades.

What it is. AWS runs the Kubernetes control plane; you run the worker nodes (or use Karpenter to provision them automatically, or Fargate profiles to go nodeless). You get namespaces, quotas, network policies, the Helm ecosystem, and portability. EMR on EKS runs Spark jobs as pods on the same cluster.

When you reach for it. Many services with a platform team to run them; multi-tenant isolation with namespaces and quotas; stateful sets; workloads you want portable to GCP.

Example use case. A managed Spark platform for hundreds of internal teams runs on EMR on EKS: each tenant gets a namespace with a CPU and memory quota, Karpenter adds Spot nodes when the queue grows and removes them when it drains, and small jobs are bin-packed onto shared nodes instead of each spinning up its own cluster.

Number to remember. Kubernetes versions get about 14 months of standard support; extended support costs extra per cluster-hour. Budget a cluster upgrade every quarter.

Gotcha. Pods without resource requests and limits get OOM-killed or starve neighbors. Skipping upgrades batches them into a painful jump. It needs a real platform owner — not a side job.

What it is. ALB works at layer 7: HTTP routing by path and host, TLS termination, WebSockets, and WAF integration. NLB works at layer 4: TCP/UDP, static IPs, millions of connections, microsecond latency. Auto Scaling groups add and remove instances on metrics; target tracking ("keep CPU at 50%") is the simple mode.

When you reach for it. ALB in front of any HTTP service. NLB in front of anything that isn't HTTP — an MQTT broker, a database proxy, gRPC at very high scale.

Example use case. Two million robots connect over MQTT through an NLB with static IPs (so device firmware can pin them) to a fleet of brokers; the app's HTTPS traffic goes through an ALB that routes /graphql to the BFF and everything else to the web tier.

Number to remember. Health checks decide when traffic shifts — point them at a real endpoint that touches dependencies, not a bare TCP check. Deregistration delay defaults to 300 seconds, which makes deploys look slow.

Gotcha. Sticky sessions hide scaling problems. One security group for the load balancer, a different one for the targets that only admits the load balancer's group.

cards.f: S3 — the lake, the backups, everything durable
cards.b:
What it is. Object storage: put a file under a key, get it back. Eleven nines of durability, strongly consistent reads after writes. Storage classes by access pattern — Standard, Intelligent-Tiering (moves objects between tiers automatically based on access), Infrequent Access, and the Glacier tiers (Instant, Flexible, Deep Archive) for cold data. Lifecycle rules move and delete by age. Versioning keeps old copies; Object Lock makes them undeletable for compliance. Event notifications trigger Lambda or SQS on upload.

When you reach for it. The system of record for a data lake, raw telemetry, logs, backups, firmware images, static sites behind CloudFront.

Example use case. A lake lands 50 TB a day of Parquet under s3://lake/orders/dt=2026-10-07/region=us/. A lifecycle rule moves partitions older than 90 days to Infrequent Access and older than two years to Glacier Deep Archive; the catalog still sees them, Athena still queries them (slowly), and storage cost drops by two-thirds.

Number to remember. ~$23 per TB-month in Standard; about $1 in Deep Archive. Thousands of requests per second per prefix. Target files of 128–512 MB for analytics.

Gotcha. The small-files problem: millions of tiny objects make every query engine spend its time opening files instead of reading them — compact them. Public-bucket misconfiguration — turn on Block Public Access at the account level. LIST over millions of objects is slow and billed. Overwriting a key behind CloudFront serves the old object until the cache expires — version the key.

What it is. Block volumes attached to one EC2 instance in one AZ. gp3 is the general default with baseline IOPS you can raise independently of size; io2 for databases that need guaranteed high IOPS. Snapshots go to S3 and are the backup.

When you reach for it. Under self-managed databases, EMR core nodes, anything that needs a local filesystem.

Example use case. A self-managed Postgres on EC2 uses io2 volumes with 20,000 provisioned IOPS and nightly snapshots; the snapshot is what you restore in a DR drill.

Number to remember. Volumes are single-AZ — losing the AZ loses the volume unless you have a snapshot or a replica elsewhere.

Gotcha. Unattached volumes and old snapshots bill forever and are the most common "why is our storage bill growing" answer.

What it is. RDS runs Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server, and Oracle with backups, patching, and Multi-AZ failover handled for you. Aurora replaces the storage engine under the Postgres and MySQL APIs: storage grows automatically to 128 TB, up to 15 read replicas share it with millisecond lag, Global Database replicates to other regions in about a second, and Serverless v2 scales capacity up and down in fine steps. RDS Proxy pools connections in front of either.

When you reach for it. Anything transactional with joins and constraints: accounts, orders, subscriptions, the catalog's metadata if you want SQL over it.

Example use case. An app backend keeps accounts, households, and subscriptions in Aurora Postgres with two read replicas; Lambda functions reach it through RDS Proxy so a burst of a thousand concurrent invocations doesn't open a thousand connections. Nightly, DMS reads the write-ahead log and streams every change into the lake.

Number to remember. Multi-AZ failover takes 30–60 seconds. Connection limits are per instance class — hundreds, not thousands.

Gotcha. Serverless callers exhaust connections without a proxy. A read right after a write can hit a replica and miss — route read-your-writes to the primary. A large ALTER TABLE locks the table; use expand/contract migrations. JVMs cache DNS by default and keep connecting to the dead primary after failover — set the JVM TTL.

What it is. A serverless key-value and document store with single-digit-millisecond reads and writes no matter how big the table gets. You model around a partition key (and optional sort key); global secondary indexes give you other access paths. Capacity is on-demand (pay per request) or provisioned (cheaper if steady). Streams emit every change for downstream consumers; TTL deletes expired items for free; global tables replicate across regions; conditional writes give you atomic check-and-set.

When you reach for it. State that is read and written by key at high rate: device state, job state and leases, sessions, catalog entries, the serving layer for lake outputs. Anything where you know the access patterns up front.

Example use case. A job scheduler keeps every job as an item with partition key JOB#id. A worker claims a job with a conditional write — "set lease_owner only if lease_owner is empty" — so two workers can never grab the same job. The worker heartbeats by updating lease_expires; a sweeper re-queues any job whose lease expired. TTL deletes finished jobs after 30 days.

Number to remember. 3,000 reads / 1,000 writes per second per partition. 400 KB item limit. 1 MB per query page. Strongly consistent reads cost double and are not available on global secondary indexes.

Gotcha. A hot partition — one key taking most of the traffic — throttles regardless of capacity mode; on-demand does not fix skew. There are no ad hoc queries; if you haven't designed the access pattern, you'll be scanning. Reads are eventually consistent by default.

What it is. A managed in-memory data store with sub-millisecond latency. Redis gives you data structures (sorted sets, hashes, lists), pub/sub, Lua scripts for atomic operations, and cluster mode to shard keys across nodes. MemoryDB is Redis with durable multi-AZ persistence if you need it to survive a node loss.

When you reach for it. Read caching in front of a database, rate-limit counters, session storage, leaderboards, pub/sub to WebSocket servers, the hot serving layer for lake-derived data.

Example use case. A rate limiter keeps a token bucket per user in Redis and uses a Lua script to check-and-decrement atomically; if Redis is unreachable the gateway fails open with a conservative local cap rather than blocking every customer. A separate cache holds the app's home-screen composition for five seconds so the 6 a.m. spike doesn't hit Postgres a hundred thousand times.

Number to remember. Treat ElastiCache as ephemeral; a node replacement loses the data.

Gotcha. The cache stampede: a hot key expires and thousands of requests recompute it at once — use jittered TTLs and request coalescing. A cached result that outlives a permission change leaks data — include the policy version in the cache key.

What it is. A massively parallel columnar warehouse. Data is loaded in, distributed across nodes by a DISTKEY and sorted by a SORTKEY, and queries that touch a few columns of a billion rows come back in seconds with hundreds of concurrent users. Spectrum lets it query files in S3 directly for the cold tail. Workload management (WLM) assigns queues and limits so one query can't starve the rest; query monitoring rules kill runaway queries. Serverless option. Row-level security and dynamic data masking built in.

When you reach for it. Curated gold tables that dashboards and analysts hit all day with sub-second expectations.

Example use case. The daily "orders by region" table lives in Redshift with region as the distribution key and date as the sort key. A thousand Power BI users hit it; WLM gives the BI queue 70% of memory and caps any single query at five minutes. Last year's raw history is in S3 and reachable through Spectrum when someone needs it.

Number to remember. COPY from S3 is the fast way in; row-by-row INSERT is the slow way. Materialized views for repeated aggregations. Concurrency scaling adds transient capacity for bursts.

Gotcha. Sized for the peak and idle at night — Serverless or pause/resume. The wrong distribution key means every join shuffles across all nodes. One runaway query with no WLM rule starves everyone.

What it is. Serverless SQL (Trino under the hood) that reads files in S3 through the Glue Catalog. Nothing to provision; you pay per terabyte scanned. Reads Parquet, ORC, JSON, CSV, and Iceberg tables; CTAS writes results back to S3 as a new table; federated queries reach other sources.

When you reach for it. Ad hoc questions over the lake; the long tail of queries that don't justify loading into a warehouse; data engineers exploring raw partitions.

Example use case. A data engineer investigating a late-data bug runs one Athena query over yesterday's raw events partition — 40 GB of Parquet, twenty cents — instead of standing up a cluster. The same query over the unpartitioned JSON landing bucket would scan 2 TB and cost ten dollars.

Number to remember. $5 per TB scanned (list price). Partition pruning and columnar formats are the only "index" it has.

Gotcha. An unpartitioned SELECT * over a big table costs real money every time someone runs it. Concurrency limits per account. You cannot make a badly laid-out table fast except by re-laying it out.

What it is. Managed Elasticsearch/OpenSearch: full-text search, aggregations, log analytics dashboards, and k-NN vector search for embeddings. Serverless option.

When you reach for it. Dataset discovery search in a catalog, diagnostics and log search, product search, RAG retrieval.

Example use case. The data-lake catalog streams every metadata change into OpenSearch so a user can type "orders region daily" and get a ranked list by relevance, freshness, and popularity, with access-aware results. The catalog's source of truth stays in DynamoDB; OpenSearch is rebuilt from it if it ever drifts.

Number to remember. Index size and shard count drive cost; keep log retention short.

Gotcha. Expensive at scale and easy to over-retain. Never the system of record.

What it is. Fully managed message queues. Standard queues: unlimited throughput, at-least-once delivery, best-effort ordering. FIFO queues: exactly-once and strictly ordered, 300 messages a second (3,000 with batching). A consumer receives a message, it becomes invisible for the visibility timeout, and the consumer deletes it when done — if it crashes, the message reappears. A dead-letter queue catches messages that fail N times.

When you reach for it. Decoupling producers from consumers; absorbing bursts; any work that can be processed later; retries with a safety net.

Example use case. When a device publishes "cycle complete," the fast path drops a message on an SQS queue; a fleet of notification workers consume it, look up user preferences, and send the push. If the push provider is down, messages wait in the queue instead of being lost; after five failures a message lands in the dead-letter queue and alarms.

Number to remember. Messages up to 256 KB; retention up to 14 days. Long polling cuts empty receives and cost.

Gotcha. Standard queues deliver duplicates — consumers must be idempotent. A visibility timeout shorter than processing time means two workers process the same message.

cards.f: SNS and EventBridge — fan-out and routing
cards.b:
What it is. SNS is pub/sub: publish to a topic, and it fans out to SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTP endpoints, email, SMS, and mobile push (APNs and FCM). EventBridge is an event bus with rules that filter and route events by content to many targets, a schema registry, built-in SaaS sources, and a Scheduler for cron-style triggers.

When you reach for it. SNS when one event needs many independent consumers, and for push notifications. EventBridge for application-level events, cross-account routing, and scheduled jobs.

Example use case. An "order placed" event goes to an SNS topic. Three SQS queues subscribe: one for the warehouse system, one for the analytics pipeline, one for the email service. Each consumer gets its own durable queue, so the analytics team's outage doesn't affect the warehouse.

Number to remember. SNS → SQS fan-out is the standard way to give each consumer a durable buffer.

Gotcha. SNS retries HTTP endpoints only briefly — without an SQS buffer you lose events during a consumer outage.

cards.f: Kinesis Data Streams and Firehose — managed streams
cards.b:
What it is. Kinesis Data Streams is an ordered, replayable log split into shards. Each shard takes 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s in and gives 2 MB/s out, shared by all consumers unless you pay for enhanced fan-out (each consumer gets its own 2 MB/s). Retention 24 hours by default, up to a year. On-demand mode scales shards automatically at a higher per-GB price. Firehose is the no-code delivery service: it buffers a stream and writes it to S3, Redshift, or OpenSearch, converting to Parquet on the way.

When you reach for it. Lean, all-AWS streaming where you want managed and simple. Firehose when "land it in S3 as Parquet every five minutes" is the whole requirement.

Example use case. Two million devices publish telemetry through IoT Core; a rule routes it to a Kinesis stream keyed by device ID so each device's events stay ordered. Firehose reads the stream and writes 128 MB Parquet files to S3 every five minutes; a Lambda consumer on the same stream updates the hot per-device state in DynamoDB.

Number to remember. Size shards from the math: events/s × bytes = MB/s ÷ 1 MB/s per shard, with headroom. Iterator age (how far behind the consumer is) is the health metric.

Gotcha. A hot shard from one chatty producer key. PUT costs add up — aggregate records with the KPL. Five consumers on one shard each get 400 KB/s unless you buy enhanced fan-out.

What it is. AWS runs the Kafka brokers; you get real Kafka: topics split into partitions, each an ordered log; consumer groups that each read at their own offset; retention from days to forever with tiered storage; replay by seeking to an offset. MSK Serverless removes broker sizing; MSK Connect runs connectors like Debezium for change data capture.

When you reach for it. When you need long retention, replay from any point, many independent consumer groups, exactly-once transactions, or portability off AWS. Data-platform ingestion at scale.

Example use case. Debezium on MSK Connect reads the transaction logs of 300 source databases and writes every change to a Kafka topic per table. The lake's ingestion job consumes them; when a transformation bug is found, the team resets the consumer offset to last Tuesday and replays — something Kinesis's 24-hour default retention wouldn't allow.

Number to remember. Partitions can be added but never removed. Ordering is per partition, so the partition key decides what stays in order.

Gotcha. Consumer-group rebalances pause consumption on every deploy — use cooperative rebalancing and static membership. More operational surface than Kinesis; MSK Serverless narrows the gap.

cards.f: Managed Service for Apache Flink — stream processing
cards.b:
What it is. A true streaming engine, run as a service. Flink understands event time (when something happened) separately from processing time (when it arrived), uses watermarks to decide when a window is complete, keeps large keyed state, and takes checkpoints to S3 so a job restarts from where it left off. Exactly-once end to end when the sink is idempotent or transactional.

When you reach for it. Sessionization, windowed aggregates, late-data handling, joins across streams — anything where "which five-minute bucket does this event belong to" must be right even when events arrive out of order.

Example use case. A Flink job turns raw litter-box events into "visits": a session window closes after two minutes of silence; a watermark of four hours lets a robot that was offline flush its buffer into the right day's visits; events later than that go to a corrections path that a nightly job reconciles.

Number to remember. The checkpoint interval is your recovery point. Parallelism equals partition count — plan it ahead.

Gotcha. Large keyed state needs RocksDB and sizing. Spark Structured Streaming is micro-batch — fine when seconds of latency are acceptable and the team already knows Spark.

cards.f: Glue — the catalog and serverless ETL
cards.b:
What it is. Four things under one name. The Data Catalog is the metastore every engine shares: databases, tables, columns, where the files are, how they're partitioned. Crawlers scan S3 and infer schemas into the catalog. ETL jobs run Spark (PySpark or Scala) without a cluster, billed per DPU-hour (a DPU is 4 vCPU and 16 GB). The Schema Registry versions Avro/JSON/Protobuf schemas for streams, and Data Quality evaluates rules against tables.

When you reach for it. The catalog is non-negotiable — it's how Athena, EMR, Redshift Spectrum, and Lake Formation all see the same tables. ETL jobs are right for a handful of batch transformations when you don't want to run a cluster; wrong at a million jobs a day.

Example use case. A nightly Glue job compacts the day's thousands of small Firehose files into eight 200 MB Parquet files per partition and registers the partition in the catalog. It runs in nine minutes on 10 DPUs, costs about a dollar, and makes every Athena query over that day ten times faster.

Number to remember. A one-minute minimum bill and a one-minute cold start per job. Default DPU counts over-provision small jobs.

Gotcha. Crawlers create one table per folder if partitions aren't laid out as key=value. The catalog becomes a junk drawer without owners. At tens of millions of partitions, catalog-per-partition metadata stops scaling — that's why Iceberg keeps partition metadata in its own manifests.
cards.s: Data platform — catalog, ETL, processing, governance

cards.b:
What it is. Managed clusters for Spark, Hive, Trino/Presto, Flink, and HBase. EMR on EC2: the classic — you size the cluster, core nodes hold HDFS and must be on-demand, task nodes can be Spot. EMR on EKS: Spark jobs run as pods on your Kubernetes cluster — multi-tenant isolation with namespaces and quotas, bin-packing of small jobs, one cluster instead of hundreds. EMR Serverless: submit a job, pay per second, scales to zero.

When you reach for it. The processing engine of a data platform. EKS when many tenants share; EC2 for big, steady batch; Serverless for spiky or infrequent jobs.

Example use case. Cradle-style platform: a customer submits a PySpark job through an API. The control plane checks their quota, the scheduler waits for the upstream dataset version to be complete, then launches the job on EMR on EKS in the tenant's namespace. Executors read Parquet from S3, shuffle on local NVMe, and write a new Iceberg snapshot. The cluster could vanish mid-job and the job would restart from its last checkpoint on another — all state is in S3.

Number to remember. Executors of 4–5 cores and 16–32 GB each are the usual sweet spot. Too many tiny executors waste memory; too few starve parallelism. Never Spot for core nodes.

Gotcha. Idle clusters billing overnight — auto-terminate. Version drift across clusters. Skew: one task with 40% of the rows runs for hours while the rest finish in minutes — salt the key or enable adaptive query execution.
cards.s: Data platform — catalog, ETL, processing, governance

cards.f: Lake Formation — permissions for the lake
cards.b:
What it is. A permission layer over the Glue Catalog: grant access at the database, table, column, and row level, or by LF-Tags (grant "PII: no" once instead of per table). Enforced by Athena, Redshift Spectrum, EMR, and QuickSight. Supports cross-account sharing of catalog tables.

When you reach for it. Central fine-grained access control when many engines read the same lake and you can't maintain policy in each one.

Example use case. The orders table is tagged PII on its customer columns. Analysts in the "finance" role see every column except those; the fraud team sees them all; a partner account gets a share of the aggregated view only. One policy, enforced the same way whether the query comes from Athena or a Spark job.

Number to remember. Tag-based access scales; per-table grants don't past a few hundred tables.

Gotcha. Engine support varies and needs configuration — verify EMR enforcement in your setup. Useless without disciplined classification of what's sensitive.
cards.s: Data platform — catalog, ETL, processing, governance

cards.b:
What it is. Database Migration Service does one-time migrations and ongoing CDC: it reads a source database's transaction log and writes every insert, update, and delete to S3, Kinesis, Redshift, or another database. Serverless option; the alternative is Debezium on MSK Connect.

When you reach for it. Replicating operational databases into the lake without querying them; migrating a warehouse to the lake with the old one still live.

Example use case. Three hundred Postgres and MySQL databases across product teams each get a DMS task: a full snapshot that records the log position, then continuous CDC from that position into a Kafka topic per table. The lake's bronze layer is the append-only change log; silver is the merged current state via Iceberg MERGE.

Number to remember. Monitor replication latency and task state — a task that silently stopped looks like "the data is stale."

Gotcha. Multi-terabyte initial loads need chunking; LOB columns are slow; a schema change on the source can break the task.
cards.s: Data platform — catalog, ETL, processing, governance

cards.f: SageMaker and Bedrock — ML and GenAI
cards.b:
What it is. SageMaker is the ML platform: notebooks, managed training jobs (Spot-capable), Pipelines for repeatable train-evaluate-register flows, a Feature Store so training and serving use the same feature definitions, a Model Registry with approval stages, real-time endpoints and batch transform for scoring, and Model Monitor for drift. Bedrock is hosted foundation models (Anthropic Claude, Amazon Nova, Meta Llama, Mistral) behind one API, with Knowledge Bases for RAG, Agents, and Guardrails.

When you reach for it. The ML layer on top of the lake; Bedrock for GenAI features without running GPUs.

Example use case. A health-insights model trains weekly in a SageMaker Pipeline from the feature store's per-cat features, must beat the current champion on precision at the evaluation gate, is registered with an approval step, and scores the fleet nightly with batch transform — no always-on endpoint. Model Monitor alarms when the input distribution drifts after a new litter type ships.

Number to remember. Batch transform is far cheaper than an always-on endpoint for nightly scoring. Spot for training with checkpointing.

Gotcha. Training-serving skew without a feature store: the model is 92% in the notebook and 70% in production. Bedrock keeps your data private but is still outside a CUI boundary.
cards.s: Data platform — catalog, ETL, processing, governance

cards.b:
What it is. A private IP range you choose (a /16 gives 65,536 addresses), split into subnets per AZ. Public subnets route to an internet gateway (load balancers, NAT). Private subnets route out only through a NAT gateway (services). Data subnets have no default route at all. Security groups are stateful firewalls on resources that reference each other by ID; NACLs are stateless firewalls on subnets. VPC endpoints let private subnets reach AWS services without the internet — gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are free; interface endpoints (PrivateLink) for most others cost per hour and per GB.

When you reach for it. Every workload. The three-tier, three-AZ layout is the default for a region.

Example use case. The EU region for a German launch: a new VPC with a non-overlapping CIDR, nine subnets across three AZs, gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB, interface endpoints for ECR and Secrets Manager, an ALB in the public subnets, the BFF in private app subnets, Aurora in data subnets with a security group that admits only the BFF's group. A Transit Gateway links it to the shared-services VPC for CI and observability.

Number to remember. Plan CIDRs across accounts and regions so they never overlap — overlapping VPCs can't be peered and fixing it means re-IPing production.

Gotcha. The NAT gateway bills per GB and is a top-five line item in many accounts because container pulls, S3 traffic, and log shipping go through it — endpoints fix most of that. Cross-AZ traffic costs a cent per GB each way. A NACL that forgets return traffic on ephemeral ports blocks responses and the app gets blamed.

cards.f: Route 53 and CloudFront — DNS and the edge
cards.b:
What it is. Route 53 is DNS with routing policies: latency-based (send users to the closest region), geolocation (data residency), weighted (canary a region), and failover with health checks. CloudFront is the CDN: edge locations near users cache static content and firmware, terminate TLS, absorb traffic spikes, and integrate with WAF and Shield for DDoS protection.

When you reach for it. Multi-region routing, static assets, firmware and large file delivery, anything public that needs protection.

Example use case. Firmware images sit in S3 behind CloudFront. When a 1.8 MB update goes to two million robots, the edge serves it from cache instead of S3 handling two million requests, and it costs less because CloudFront egress is cheaper than S3 egress. Route 53 latency routing sends German app traffic to eu-central-1 and everyone else to us-east-1.

Number to remember. Failover depends on TTL — set 60 seconds or less on failover records in advance.

Gotcha. Long TTLs keep clients on a dead region for minutes. Cached objects don't update until invalidated or the key changes.

cards.f: API Gateway — the front door for APIs
cards.b:
What it is. A managed entry point that handles authentication (JWT, Cognito, IAM), request validation, throttling and usage plans, caching, and routing to Lambda, containers, or HTTP backends. REST APIs have the full feature set and a 29-second timeout; HTTP APIs are cheaper and simpler; WebSocket APIs hold persistent connections. AppSync is the GraphQL equivalent with subscriptions built in.

When you reach for it. Public and partner APIs; serverless backends; anything that needs per-client throttling without writing it yourself.

Example use case. A partner-facing REST API runs behind API Gateway with a usage plan per partner — 100 requests a second, a million a month — and a Lambda authorizer that validates their token. When a partner's batch job misbehaves, it gets 429s; nobody else notices.

Number to remember. REST API Gateway is ~$3.50 per million requests; past a few hundred million a month an ALB with Envoy or Kong is cheaper.

Gotcha. The 29-second timeout bites long requests. At very high volume the per-request price dominates.

What it is. Principals (users, roles, service accounts), actions (s3:GetObject), resources, and policies that allow or deny combinations. The practice that matters: roles with temporary credentials — an EC2 instance or Lambda gets a role; a CI pipeline authenticates with OIDC and assumes a role for a few minutes; humans sign in through IAM Identity Center (SSO). Permission boundaries and Service Control Policies cap what anyone can grant. Access Analyzer finds unused and over-broad permissions.

When you reach for it. Everything. Least privilege by default.

Example use case. A GitHub Actions workflow deploys to production with no stored secret: it presents an OIDC token, assumes a role scoped to "deploy this one service in this one account," and the credentials expire in fifteen minutes. There is no access key to leak.

Number to remember. IAM is eventually consistent — a policy change takes up to a minute to apply everywhere.

Gotcha. Long-lived access keys in code are how breaches start; a leaked key is mining crypto within minutes of hitting a public repo. "Everyone is admin because it was faster" is the usual inherited state.

cards.f: KMS, Secrets Manager, ACM — keys, secrets, certificates
cards.b:
What it is. KMS holds encryption keys and does envelope encryption for S3, EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, and your own data. Secrets Manager stores secrets with automatic rotation (it can rotate database passwords for you). ACM issues free TLS certificates and renews them automatically on load balancers and CloudFront.

When you reach for it. Encrypt everything at rest with KMS; rotate database credentials with Secrets Manager; never let a certificate expire by hand.

Example use case. Every S3 bucket in the lake is encrypted with a KMS key per data domain; the fraud team's key policy lists only their roles, so even an admin elsewhere can't read their bucket. Aurora credentials rotate every 30 days through Secrets Manager and the app fetches them at startup.

Number to remember. KMS bills per API call — a hot path decrypting per request adds up; use data-key caching.

Gotcha. A certificate not on ACM expiring at 2 a.m. is a classic Sev-1. Secrets in environment files checked into git.

cards.f: CloudTrail, GuardDuty, Security Hub, Macie — see and detect
cards.b:
What it is. CloudTrail logs every API call in the account. Config inventories resources and checks them against rules. GuardDuty watches logs and DNS for threats (a credential used from a new country, a crypto-mining pattern). Security Hub collects findings from all of them into one posture view. Macie scans S3 for personal data. WAF and Shield protect public endpoints.

When you reach for it. Turn on CloudTrail (to a separate log-archive account), Config, GuardDuty, and Security Hub in every account on day one. Macie before an audit.

Example use case. GuardDuty flags an IAM role being used from an unfamiliar IP range at 3 a.m. The on-call revokes the role's sessions, CloudTrail shows exactly which S3 objects were listed, and Config confirms no public buckets. The postmortem finds a developer's laptop with a cached key — and the fix is eliminating long-lived keys, not just rotating that one.

Number to remember. CloudTrail management events show in the console for 90 days free; a real trail to S3 lasts forever and feeds investigations.

Gotcha. Findings nobody owns. A public bucket Config flagged three months ago that nobody read.

What it is. The default observability layer: metrics from every service plus your own, alarms with composite and anomaly-detection modes, dashboards, Logs with Logs Insights queries, and X-Ray for distributed traces. OpenTelemetry through the ADOT distribution if you want to stay vendor-neutral.

When you reach for it. Every service. Datadog or Grafana on top if the organization prefers, with CloudWatch as the source.

Example use case. The data platform's dashboard shows four SLOs — tier-1 jobs completed by deadline, dataset freshness, quality gates passed, downstream jobs blocked — each with a burn-rate alarm. A Kinesis iterator-age alarm pages when the consumer falls more than ten minutes behind; the runbook says scale consumers, then check the sink.

Number to remember. Log ingestion costs about $0.50 per GB — far more than storing it. Custom metrics bill per metric per month.

Gotcha. A debug flag left on in production costs thousands in log ingest. Alarms on CPU instead of on what users feel.

cards.f: Organizations and Control Tower — many accounts, governed
cards.b:
What it is. Accounts grouped into organizational units under one organization, with Service Control Policies as guardrails ("nobody can disable CloudTrail," "no resources outside these regions"). Control Tower builds the baseline landing zone — log archive, security tooling, guardrails — so every new account starts compliant. Consolidated billing across all of them.

When you reach for it. Any company past a handful of engineers. Accounts are the blast-radius, quota, and billing boundary.

Example use case. Security OU holds log-archive and security-tooling accounts; Infrastructure OU holds network (Transit Gateway) and shared-services (CI, observability); Workloads OU has prod, staging, and dev accounts per team. Cost per team falls out of the bill with no tagging effort, and a developer's mistake in dev can't touch prod.

Number to remember. Typical starting shape: five to eight accounts; large organizations run hundreds.

Gotcha. One account for everything means one mistake can delete production and no cost can be attributed.

cards.f: Cost tooling — Cost Explorer, CUR, Budgets, Anomaly Detection
cards.b:
What it is. Cost Explorer for dashboards and forecasts. The Cost and Usage Report is every billing line item, queryable in Athena when you need "what does this tenant cost." Budgets alert at thresholds; Cost Anomaly Detection is free and catches the 40% jumps; Compute Optimizer recommends rightsizing.

When you reach for it. Turn on the CUR and anomaly detection on day one; tag everything; review monthly with unit economics.

Example use case. The CUR lands in S3; an Athena view joins it to resource tags so the monthly review shows cost per active device split into messaging, streams, storage, compute, and observability. When the figure jumps 18% after a feature launch, the team sees it's all Kinesis PUT units and batches telemetry on the next firmware.

Number to remember. Savings Plans should cover ~70% of the trailing baseline after rightsizing; review quarterly.

Gotcha. Untagged spend can't be attributed. Commitments bought before rightsizing lock in the wrong shape.

decks.title: AWS told as the life of one dataset
decks.blurb: Ingest → store → catalog → process → query → serve → secure → operate → cost.

cards.f: Stop 1 — The row is born, and we catch it leaving
cards.b:
Remember: CAPTURE — CDC + stream

An order lands in a transactional database somewhere in Amazon. We don't query that database — it belongs to a product team and it's busy. Instead we read its transaction log. That's change data capture (CDC). On AWS the managed tool is DMS; the open-source one is Debezium running on MSK Connect. Either way, every insert, update, and delete becomes an event.

Those events need somewhere to go that can absorb bursts and let several readers consume them independently. That's a stream. Kinesis Data Streams is the lean managed option: you buy shards, each takes 1 MB per second in and gives 2 MB per second out. MSK is managed Kafka: more work to run, but you get long retention, replay by offset, and as many consumer groups as you like. For a platform like Cradle that needs to replay data when logic changes, Kafka's retention is the reason to pick it.

What you'd say

"I'd capture changes from the log rather than query the source — CDC through DMS or Debezium — and land them on a stream. Kinesis if we want managed and simple; Kafka on MSK if we need days of retention and replay. Consumer lag is the one metric I'd watch on that stream."

cards.f: Stop 2 — The event becomes a file, and the file becomes findable
cards.b:
Remember: STORE — S3 + Parquet + Iceberg + catalog

Streams are for moving data, not keeping it. The permanent home is S3. Something has to turn a stream of small events into well-sized files: Kinesis Firehose does it with no code (buffer five minutes or 128 MB, write Parquet, done), or a Flink job does it with more control. Either way the file should be Parquet — columnar, compressed, five to ten times smaller than JSON — and between 128 and 512 MB. Smaller than that and you get the small-files problem: every query engine spends its time opening files instead of reading them.

Now there's a file in a bucket. Nobody can find it. That's what the Glue Data Catalog is for: it's the phone book. Database, table, columns, where the files live, how they're partitioned. Every engine — Athena, Spark, Redshift — reads the same phone book, so a dataset registered once is visible everywhere.

But a phone book that lists every partition as a row doesn't scale to tens of millions of partitions. So the modern layout puts the table on Iceberg (or Hudi, or Delta): the table's own manifest files track which data files belong to which snapshot. You get atomic commits (readers see a whole version or nothing), schema evolution, time travel, and row-level deletes — which you'll need the day a customer asks to be forgotten.

What you'd say

"Land it as Parquet in S3, sized to a few hundred megabytes, registered in the Glue Catalog so every engine sees it. I'd make the table Iceberg from day one — atomic publication and deletes are much harder to add later than to start with."

cards.f: Stop 3 — Someone transforms it, and we have to decide where that runs
cards.b:
Remember: PROCESS — Spark/Flink placement

Raw orders aren't "orders by region, daily." A job has to aggregate them. This is the Cradle question: where does Spark run?

  • Glue ETL — serverless Spark, pay per DPU-hour. Nothing to manage. Takes a minute to start. Right for a few jobs a day; wrong for a platform running a million.
  • EMR on EC2 — a real cluster you size and run. Cheapest per job at sustained volume, especially with Spot task nodes (never Spot for the core nodes that hold data). You own upgrades and idle time.
  • EMR on EKS — Spark on Kubernetes. The reason to choose it is multi-tenancy: namespaces and quotas isolate tenants, and the scheduler bin-packs many small jobs onto shared nodes. This is the shape a Cradle-like platform wants.
  • EMR Serverless — for spiky, unpredictable jobs where you'd rather pay per second than keep a cluster warm.

Whichever you pick, the principle is the same and it's the one from the Andes talk: storage and compute are decoupled. The cluster is disposable. S3 is the only state that matters. A cluster can die mid-job and the job reruns from the last checkpoint on a new one.

For the streaming half of Cradle — things that need an answer in seconds, not hours — the engine is Flink (AWS runs it as Managed Service for Apache Flink). Flink understands event time and watermarks, so a late-arriving order still lands in the right day's bucket.

What you'd say

"For a multi-tenant platform I'd run Spark on EMR on EKS so I can isolate tenants with namespaces and quotas and bin-pack small jobs; EC2 with Spot for the big batch work; Serverless for spikes. Compute is disposable — all state is in S3 — and streaming goes to Flink because it handles event time properly."

cards.f: Stop 4 — The job needs a scheduler, a quota, and a place to keep its state
cards.b:
Remember: SCHEDULE — durable control plane

A million jobs a day don't start themselves. Something has to know that "orders by region" depends on "raw orders" being complete for the day, that it has a 6 a.m. deadline, and that it's allowed to use this tenant's share of the cluster. That's the control plane, and it's tiny compared to the data plane — but it must never lose a job.

Its state lives in DynamoDB: job records, their states, the lease a worker holds while running one, the heartbeat that proves the worker is alive. DynamoDB gives single-digit-millisecond reads and conditional writes, which is how you make sure two workers never grab the same job. The things to know about it: design for your access patterns first, items are capped at 400 KB, and a hot partition will throttle you no matter how much capacity you buy.

For orchestration you can build (Cradle did) or adopt: Step Functions for workflows as state machines, MWAA (managed Airflow) for DAGs, EventBridge Scheduler for cron-style triggers. At Cradle's volume a custom scheduler is justified; at ten jobs a day it isn't.

What you'd say

"The control plane is small and must be durable — job state and leases in DynamoDB with conditional writes, heartbeats to detect dead workers, and dependency-based triggering so a job runs when its inputs are complete, not when a clock says so."

cards.f: Stop 5 — Someone wants to query it, and there are three doors
cards.b:
Remember: QUERY — Athena vs Redshift vs Spark

The aggregated table exists. An analyst wants numbers. Three engines can answer, and the choice is the most common tradeoff question in this space.

  • Athena — serverless SQL straight over S3 through the catalog. You pay per terabyte scanned. Perfect for ad hoc questions; terrible if the table isn't partitioned, because every query reads everything.
  • Redshift — a real warehouse. Data is loaded in, sorted and distributed across nodes, and queries come back in seconds even with hundreds of concurrent users. Redshift Spectrum lets it also reach into S3 for the cold stuff. Workload management (WLM) is how you stop one runaway query starving everyone else.
  • Spark / EMR — for when the "query" is really a transformation over terabytes, or feeds a model.

The rule: curated, high-concurrency BI goes to Redshift; exploration and the long tail go to Athena; heavy lifting goes to Spark. A query gateway can route automatically by estimated size and latency need — that's design question Q41.

What you'd say

"Redshift for curated tables that many people hit all day; Athena for ad hoc questions over the lake; Spark when it's really a transformation. If the analyst's query is slow in Athena, the answer is almost always partitioning and file size, not a bigger engine."

cards.f: Stop 6 — The result goes somewhere an application can read it
cards.b:
Remember: SERVE — fast projection store

Sometimes the consumer isn't an analyst but a web page — a seller dashboard that needs "your orders today" in ten milliseconds. The lake can't answer that fast. So the job publishes its output into a serving store: DynamoDB for key lookups, ElastiCache (Redis) for hot reads, OpenSearch for search. This is what the Cradle posting means by "write curated datasets for front-end applications." The subtlety: publish to a new versioned key, validate, then flip the pointer — a failed publish leaves the old version live. And the lake stays the source of truth, so a serving store can always be rebuilt.

What you'd say

"Lake-derived data gets published to DynamoDB or Redis under a versioned key and the alias flips only after validation. If the cache is ever wrong, we rebuild it from the lake — the lake is the truth, the cache is a projection."

cards.f: Stop 7 — Who's allowed to see it, and how do we prove it
cards.b:
Remember: SECURE — policy, encryption, audit

Orders contain customer data. Not everyone who can query the lake should see every column. Lake Formation sits over the Glue Catalog and grants access at the table, column, and row level, enforced in Athena, Spectrum, and EMR. IAM roles say who you are; Lake Formation says what you can see. Keys come from KMS. Every API call is logged by CloudTrail. Macie can scan buckets and tell you where the PII is hiding. Together that's the "compliance" component of the BDT mission.

What you'd say

"Identity from IAM, column- and row-level policy from Lake Formation enforced in every engine, keys in KMS, audit in CloudTrail, and Macie to find PII we didn't know we had. Policy decided once, enforced everywhere."

cards.f: Stop 8 — Somebody has to pay for all this
cards.b:
Remember: COST — unit economics

Storage is cheap; compute and scans are where data platforms bleed money. The Cost and Usage Report is the raw bill; put it in Athena and you can answer "what does this tenant cost" — if everything is tagged. The levers, in payoff order: convert to Parquet and compact (fewer bytes scanned), partition properly, Spot for task nodes, right-size and auto-terminate clusters, workload management to kill runaway queries, tier old data to S3 Intelligent-Tiering or Glacier, and show each tenant their bill so they fix their own waste. The Andes talk reported 40–90% operational savings from this list.

What you'd say

"I'd report cost per terabyte processed per tenant. The first three levers — Parquet and compaction, partitioning, Spot — usually cover most of a cost target before anyone has to give anything up."

cards.f: Stop 9 — And when it breaks at 3 a.m.
cards.b:
Remember: OPERATE — SLOs, alarms, COE

CloudWatch holds the metrics and logs; alarms fire on what matters — consumer lag, job deadline misses, dataset freshness. X-Ray traces a request across services. The alarm pages someone with a runbook. The thing to say here is that for a data platform the SLO isn't "is the API up" — it's "was the dataset fresh and correct by its deadline," per tier, and that's what goes on the dashboard a VP reads.

cards.f: The whole trip, in one breath
cards.b:
If they ask "walk me through the AWS stack you'd use"

"Change data capture off the source onto a Kafka or Kinesis stream. Firehose or Flink writes Parquet to S3, registered in the Glue Catalog as Iceberg tables so publication is atomic. Spark on EMR — on EKS for multi-tenant isolation — transforms it, with job state and leases in DynamoDB and dependency-based scheduling. Redshift for curated BI, Athena for ad hoc, and published projections in DynamoDB or Redis for applications. Lake Formation for column- and row-level access, CloudTrail for audit, tags and the cost report for chargeback, CloudWatch alarms on freshness and lag. Storage and compute decoupled throughout — clusters are disposable, S3 is the truth."

cards.f: Numbers to carry into the room
cards.b:
• Kinesis shard: 1 MB/s in, 2 MB/s out. DynamoDB partition: 3,000 reads / 1,000 writes per second; 400 KB item limit. S3: thousands of requests per second per prefix. Athena bills per TB scanned.
  • Parquet: 5–10× smaller than JSON. Target file size 128–512 MB.
  • Andes: ~38K datasets, ~900K jobs a day, ~80K users; 40–90% cost savings after the redesign.

10B. Technical memory sheet — memorize this, not 50 answers

Most of the technical section collapses into three layers with three decisions each.

The 3 × 3 data-platform map

1. Capture CDC → DMS/Debezium → Kinesis or MSK. Watch consumer lag.
2. Store S3 → Parquet → Iceberg → Glue Catalog. Avoid small files.
3. Process Glue / EMR / Flink. Batch = Spark; streaming/event time = Flink.
4. Schedule Job state, dependencies, leases, quotas. Control plane must be durable.
5. Query Athena / Redshift / Spark. Ad hoc / BI / heavy transform.
6. Serve DynamoDB / Redis / OpenSearch. Lake = truth; serving store = projection.
7. Secure IAM + Lake Formation + KMS + audit. Policy must follow the data.
8. Cost Cost per TB / job / tenant. Compaction, partitioning, Spot.
9. Operate Freshness, job deadline, quality, customer impact. Every SLO gets an alarm.

Six technical phrases that unlock many answers

  • “S3 is the source of truth; compute is disposable.”
  • “The latency-critical path and analytics path are isolated.”
  • “At-least-once input + idempotent sink gives effective exactly-once behavior.”
  • “Publish a new version, validate it, then atomically flip the pointer.”
  • “Partition for the access pattern; compact for the engine.”
  • “At scale, optimize unit cost — cost per request or per TB — not just total cost.”
30-second recall: Capture → Store → Process; Schedule → Query → Serve; Secure → Cost → Operate. Then apply SCALE to whichever box the interviewer asks about.

Pre-built AI APIsRekognition (vision), Textract (documents), Comprehend (NLP), Transcribe, Polly, Translate, Lookout for Equipment/Vision (industrial anomaly detection), Forecast (retired)Vision AI, Document AI, Natural Language, Speech, Translation, Visual Inspection AIDocument AI / Textract for supplier paperwork, warranty claims; Lookout for Vision / Visual Inspection AI for defect detection
GPUsEC2 P/G instances, Trainium/Inferentia chipsA2/A3 GPUs, TPUsSpot GPUs for training; reserved for inference

• AWS: CloudWatch (metrics, logs, alarms, dashboards, Logs Insights), X-Ray (traces), CloudTrail (API audit), Config (compliance), Systems Manager (patching, run commands, parameter store), Health Dashboard, Trusted Advisor. Cost: Cost Explorer, Cost and Usage Report (CUR), Budgets, Compute Optimizer, Savings Plans.
  • GCP: Cloud Monitoring, Cloud Logging, Cloud Trace, Cloud Profiler, Audit Logs, Recommender; billing export to BigQuery is the FinOps workhorse.
  • Third-party: Datadog (broad, expensive at scale), Grafana stack (Prometheus, Loki, Tempo — cheaper, more ops), New Relic, Honeycomb, Splunk. Observability spend can rival compute spend; sample traces and cap log retention.
  • Security services: AWS GuardDuty (threat detection), Security Hub (posture), Inspector (vulnerabilities), Macie (PII in S3), Detective; GCP Security Command Center, Chronicle.

A region is a geographic area with multiple isolated availability zones (data centers). Multi-AZ is the default for anything that matters — RDS Multi-AZ, ASGs spanning zones, EKS nodes across zones. Multi-region is a deliberate cost for either latency (users in Germany) or disaster recovery. DR strategies in ascending cost: backup and restore (hours to days), pilot light (core data replicated, minimal compute idle), warm standby (scaled-down copy running), active/active (both serving). Each has an RTO (how long to recover) and RPO (how much data you can lose). For Whisker's control path, warm standby with buffered devices is usually enough; for a Federal-Mogul data platform, backup/restore with tested restores may be. Test the restore — a DR plan that has never been exercised is a hope.

cards.f: Well-Architected — the vocabulary both clouds use
cards.b: AWS's Well-Architected Framework has six pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, sustainability. GCP's Architecture Framework mirrors them. Reviews against the pillars are a useful, non-threatening way to audit an inherited system in your first 60 days — "let's do a Well-Architected review" lands better than "let me audit your work."

cards.f: Cloud cost — the FinOps playbook, explained
cards.b:
1. Inform: tagging (service, team, environment, cost center) enforced by policy; allocation reports; anomaly alerts; a unit metric — cost per active device, per query, per model.
  2. Optimize: rightsizing (most instances run at 10–20% utilization); Savings Plans or committed-use discounts for the steady baseline (1–3 years, 30–60% off); Spot/preemptible for interruptible work (stream processors with checkpoints, training jobs, batch); Graviton/ARM (20–40% better price-performance); storage tiering and lifecycle; log retention limits; kill idle dev environments nightly; eliminate NAT and cross-AZ chatter.
  3. Operate: monthly review with engineering leads, budgets with alerts, cost as a design-review criterion ("what does this cost per device?"), showback then chargeback.

Where data platforms overrun: compute, not storage — unpartitioned BigQuery scans, always-on Databricks clusters, Redshift sized for the peak. Where IoT overruns: message counts and rule actions, NAT egress for firmware, and observability ingest.

cards.f: Multi-cloud and hybrid, the honest position
cards.b: Avoid multi-cloud by design; accept it by inheritance (acquisitions, an analytics stack already on BigQuery, a partner). Govern it with portable layers — containers, Terraform, Iceberg tables, OpenTelemetry, SQL — and standardize each workload class on one cloud. Running the same service on two clouds "for resilience" doubles the failure modes and the on-call load. Hybrid (on-prem plus cloud) is normal in manufacturing and defense: plants keep edge compute for latency and resilience; CUI stays on-prem; the cloud gets analytics and non-sensitive services. AWS Outposts, Local Zones, and Google Distributed Cloud exist for the cases that need cloud APIs on-prem.

cards.f: Architecture patterns to name on the whiteboard
cards.b:
• Strangler fig — put a facade in front of a legacy system and migrate functionality behind it piece by piece (D11).
  • CQRS — separate read and write models when reads vastly outnumber writes or need a different shape (D4 is a form of it).
  • Event sourcing — store the sequence of events as the source of truth and derive state; powerful for audit, expensive in complexity.
  • Outbox pattern — write the event to a table in the same transaction as the data, then publish asynchronously, so you never lose or duplicate events between a database and a message bus.
  • Saga — a multi-step workflow across services with compensating actions instead of a distributed transaction (device pairing + subscription activation).
  • Circuit breaker, bulkhead, retry with backoff and jitter, timeout, load shedding — the resilience toolkit; all five belong in every service that calls another.
  • Backend-for-Frontend, API gateway, service mesh (Istio/Linkerd/App Mesh for east-west mTLS and traffic policy) — the edges.
  • Cell-based architecture — partition the whole stack into independent cells (by customer or region) so a failure affects one cell; how the largest services limit blast radius.
  • Lambda vs Kappa data architecture — two paths (batch + speed) vs one streaming path with replay; prefer Kappa.
  • Medallion (bronze/silver/gold) — raw, conformed, curated layers in a lakehouse; data mesh — domain-owned data products with federated governance and a self-serve platform; hub-and-spoke — central platform, embedded domain teams (the realistic model for manufacturing).

decks.title: Cloud concepts & problems managers face
decks.blurb: IAM, networking, cost, multi-account, reliability — and the real problems.

cards.b: The provider is responsible for security of the cloud (physical data centers, hypervisors, the managed service's internals); you are responsible for security in the cloud (your IAM, your data, your configuration, your patches on EC2). The line moves with the service: on EC2 you patch the OS; on Lambda or Cloud Run you don't; on RDS the provider patches the database engine but you own the schema, backups policy, and who can connect. Managers get burned when they assume "managed" means "someone else's problem" — an S3 bucket left public is entirely your side of the line.

cards.f: Regions, zones, and what "highly available" actually costs
cards.b: A region is a cluster of at least three isolated data centers (availability zones) close enough for synchronous replication. Running in one AZ means one building fire takes you down. Multi-AZ means your instances, databases, and load balancers are spread across zones — the provider charges you for cross-zone traffic and for the redundant capacity, so a "Multi-AZ RDS" is roughly double the price of a single instance. Multi-region is an order of magnitude more complex: data replication lag, DNS failover, and duplicate everything. The manager's decision: multi-AZ is table stakes for anything customer-facing; multi-region only for a stated reason (latency for German customers, a regulatory residency requirement, or an RTO the business will pay for).

cards.f: Accounts and projects as the unit of blast radius and billing
cards.b: In AWS, an account is a hard boundary for permissions, quotas, and billing; in GCP a project plays the same role, grouped into folders under an organization. The mature pattern is many small accounts/projects — prod, staging, dev, security tooling, log archive, one per team or workload — governed centrally (AWS Organizations with Service Control Policies; GCP org policies). One account for everything means a developer's mistake can delete production, quotas are shared, and the bill can't be attributed. Landing zone is the term for the pre-built, governed multi-account foundation (AWS Control Tower, GCP's Cloud Foundation Toolkit).

cards.f: Identity and access: roles, not keys
cards.b: IAM has three parts: a principal (who — a user, a role, a service account), an action (what — s3:GetObject), and a resource (on what). Policies allow or deny combinations. The principle is least privilege, and the practice that makes it real is roles assumed with temporary credentials rather than long-lived access keys: an EC2 instance or Lambda gets a role; a CI pipeline authenticates via OIDC and assumes a role for a few minutes; humans log in through SSO. Access keys in a config file are how breaches start. GCP's equivalent is service accounts with Workload Identity Federation.

A VPC is your private network with an IP range. Subnets are public (can reach the internet through an internet gateway) or private (reach out only via a NAT gateway; nothing reaches in). Security groups are stateful firewalls on instances; network ACLs are stateless firewalls on subnets. Load balancers sit in public subnets and forward to private ones. VPC endpoints let private subnets talk to S3 or DynamoDB without going through NAT — cheaper and more secure. Peering, Transit Gateway, and PrivateLink connect VPCs; Direct Connect or Interconnect connects to your data centers and plants.

Every service has limits per account per region — some soft (raise by request, takes hours to days), some hard. Lambda concurrent executions (1,000 by default), Kinesis shards per region, IoT Core connections and messages per second, EC2 vCPUs per family, API Gateway requests per second, RDS instances. Launches fail because nobody checked. The manager's control: a quota review on the pre-launch checklist and a habit of raising limits a month before you need them.

On-demand (pay per hour/second, no commitment), reserved or committed use (1–3 years, 30–60% cheaper, for the steady baseline), Spot/preemptible (up to 90% cheaper, can be reclaimed with two minutes' notice — for anything that checkpoints or is stateless), and serverless (pay per request/GB-second, cheap when idle, expensive at sustained load). Data transfer is the hidden dimension: in is free, out to the internet costs, across regions costs, across zones costs a little. Every architecture review should ask where bytes cross a billing boundary.

Key-value metadata on every resource — service=notifications, team=backend, env=prod, cost-center=4410. Without them the bill is one number. Enforce with policy (a resource without required tags can't be created), and use them for cost allocation, access control (attribute-based IAM), and automation (shut down anything tagged env=dev at night).

cards.f: Managed vs self-managed, the recurring decision
cards.b: A managed service (RDS, MSK, IoT Core, GKE Autopilot) costs more per unit and removes operations, upgrades, and much of the on-call. Self-managed (Postgres on EC2, Kafka on EKS, EMQX) costs less per unit at scale and costs an engineer. The break-even is usually a fraction of an engineer's salary: a $3,000/month premium for a managed broker is cheap against half an SRE. Choose self-managed only when scale, a feature gap, or portability makes the managed option genuinely wrong.

Account → project. IAM role → service account. VPC → VPC (GCP VPCs are global, subnets regional — a real difference). ALB/NLB → global HTTP(S) load balancer / regional network LB. S3 → Cloud Storage. DynamoDB → Firestore/Bigtable. Aurora → Cloud SQL/AlloyDB/Spanner. Kinesis → Pub/Sub. Lambda → Cloud Functions/Cloud Run. EKS → GKE. CloudWatch → Cloud Monitoring/Logging. Cost Explorer → billing export to BigQuery. Organizations/SCPs → organization/org policies. Control Tower → Foundation Toolkit. Support: both sell tiers (AWS Business/Enterprise; GCP Standard/Enhanced/Premium) and you'll want at least the middle tier in production for response-time commitments.

cards.f: Part 3 — Three cloud problems as interview stories
cards.b:
"Tell me about a time you reduced cloud cost."

"The Feature Management API at Ford recomputed vehicle capability on every request — thirty million a month — which meant compute scaled with traffic instead of with actual changes. Moving to event-driven computation with persisted results meant we paid for configuration changes, which happen a few times per vehicle, instead of reads, which happen constantly. On GCP's serverless target that translated directly into [X% lower compute]. The general lesson I apply now is to ask where cost scales with the wrong variable."

"Tell me about a cloud security issue you handled."

"At Rheinmetall the environment I inherited had an Arctic Wolf security score of 7.3 against an 8.1 standard, no DLP, and identity scattered across applications. The work was unglamorous: AD-based identity everywhere, endpoint hardening, patch automation, and a monitoring baseline so we could see what was happening. We got to 8.1 and above, and the pattern I'd bring to a cloud estate is the same — identity first, then visibility, then automation — with the specific cloud versions: SSO and roles instead of keys, Config and Security Hub for continuous evidence, and secrets scanning in CI so the most common incident can't happen."

"Tell me about a migration."

"Azure to GCP at Ford on a leadership-mandated timeline. The trap was lift-and-shift: it would have met the date and preserved every problem. I phased it so the core event-driven redesign and the migration landed together and non-critical enhancements followed, presented benchmarks and cost projections to align the platform and migration teams, and we hit the date with a system that was faster and cheaper than the one we left. The rule I took from it: a migration is the one time you have budget and attention to fix the architecture — use it, but phase it so the deadline is safe."

decks.title: Cloud gotchas, networking, FinOps, Glue, MLOps
decks.blurb: The things that bite in production, explained with examples.

cards.b:
• Data transfer is asymmetric and everywhere. Inbound is free; outbound to the internet is roughly $0.05–0.09/GB; between regions $0.02/GB; between availability zones $0.01/GB each direction. A chatty microservice architecture spread across three AZs can generate a surprising cross-AZ bill, and an analytics job in us-west reading a lake in us-east pays for every byte. Example: a team moved their Kafka consumers to a different AZ from the brokers "for resilience" and added $4K/month in cross-AZ traffic before anyone noticed.
  • NAT gateways charge per GB processed as well as per hour. Anything in a private subnet that reaches S3, ECR, or the internet pays. Container image pulls at scale, firmware downloads, and log shipping are the usual culprits. Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are free and fix most of it.
  • Serverless is cheap at low volume and expensive at sustained high volume. Lambda at 1,000 requests/second, 24/7, costs more than a few containers doing the same. API Gateway REST charges ~$3.50 per million requests; at 500M requests a month that's $1,750 for the gateway alone before compute. Know the crossover.
  • Stopped is not free. A stopped EC2 instance still bills for its EBS volumes; an unattached Elastic IP bills hourly; snapshots accumulate; an idle RDS instance bills fully. GCP: persistent disks and reserved static IPs likewise.
  • Provisioned capacity bills whether you use it or not. DynamoDB provisioned throughput, Kinesis shards, Redshift nodes, MSK brokers, Timestream memory store. On-demand modes trade a higher unit price for paying only for use — right for unpredictable workloads, wrong for steady ones.
  • Log ingestion costs more than log storage. CloudWatch Logs charges ~$0.50/GB ingested; a debug-level flag left on in production can cost thousands. Datadog and Splunk are worse. Structured logging with levels, sampling, and retention policies are cost controls, not just hygiene.
  • Free tiers and credits expire. The first real bill after startup credits end has ended careers. Forecast it.
  • Reserved commitments don't follow you. Reserve instance types you then migrate off (Intel → Graviton), and you pay twice. Compute Savings Plans are flexible across families; instance-specific RIs are not.
  • BigQuery bills per byte scanned unless you reserve slots. SELECT * on a 10 TB table is $50 every time someone runs it. Partition, cluster, and set per-user byte quotas.
cards.s: Part 1 — Cloud gotchas: the things you learn by being surprised

cards.b:
• Lambda's default 1,000 concurrent executions is per account per region and shared by every function — one runaway function starves the rest. Reserve concurrency for the ones that matter.
  • IoT Core has per-account limits on connections per second, publishes per second, and shadow operations; a fleet reconnect can hit them. They're published; check them before growth, not during an incident.
  • Kinesis: 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s in per shard; 2 MB/s out per shard shared by all consumers unless you pay for enhanced fan-out. Five consumers on one shard each get 400 KB/s.
  • DynamoDB: 3,000 read units / 1,000 write units per second per partition; a 400 KB item limit; a 1 MB query page. Hot keys throttle regardless of table capacity.
  • SQS: FIFO queues cap at 300 messages/s without batching (3,000 with); standard queues are unlimited but unordered.
  • EC2 vCPU quotas per instance family — a new GPU instance type often needs a quota request that takes a day.
  • Route 53 and DNS TTLs: a failover with a 300-second TTL means five minutes of clients still hitting the dead region; set short TTLs on failover records in advance.
  • GCP: project-level API quotas (Compute Engine API calls per minute) can throttle Terraform applies; regional resource quotas (CPUs per region) block scale-ups.
cards.s: Part 1 — Cloud gotchas: the things you learn by being surprised

cards.b:
• S3 is now strongly consistent, but your cache isn't. CloudFront caches objects; updating a firmware image at the same key serves the old one until TTL. Version the key.
  • DynamoDB reads are eventually consistent by default. Read-after-write can return stale data unless you ask for strongly consistent reads (which cost double and aren't available on global secondary indexes).
  • Aurora read replicas lag. Route a read to a replica right after a write and you can miss it. Read-your-writes flows go to the writer.
  • Lambda retries asynchronous invocations twice by default and SQS redelivers after the visibility timeout. If your handler isn't idempotent, you'll process events two or three times under load.
  • Cold starts are real on the latency path. A Java Lambda behind a VPC can take seconds to start; provisioned concurrency or a container service fixes it.
  • EKS and GKE control-plane upgrades are mandatory. Providers drop old versions; EKS extended support bills extra per cluster-hour. Skipping upgrades doesn't avoid them, it batches them into a painful jump.
  • Multi-AZ RDS failover changes the endpoint's IP. JVMs cache DNS forever by default; set the TTL in the JVM or you'll reconnect to a dead primary.
  • Availability zone names are per account. "us-east-1a" in one account isn't the same physical zone as in another; use zone IDs for cross-account topology decisions.
  • Managed services have maintenance windows. RDS, ElastiCache, and MSK can restart during theirs. Set them to your quietest hour and know they exist.
cards.s: Part 1 — Cloud gotchas: the things you learn by being surprised

cards.b:
• Security groups are stateful (a reply to an allowed outbound request is allowed in); NACLs are stateless (you must allow both directions, including ephemeral ports). People write NACLs that block return traffic and blame the application.
  • A "private" bucket with a permissive bucket policy is public. Block Public Access at the account level overrides mistakes.
  • IAM is eventually consistent; a policy change can take seconds to a minute to apply — tests "pass" before the permission exists.
  • Default VPCs and default security groups allow more than you think; delete or lock them.
  • Instance metadata (IMDS) on EC2 hands out role credentials to anything on the box — SSRF vulnerabilities in your app become cloud-credential theft. Require IMDSv2.
  • CloudTrail is on by default only for the last 90 days of management events in the console; for real audit you configure a trail to S3 in a separate account.
cards.s: Part 1 — Cloud gotchas: the things you learn by being surprised

cards.b:
• Moving a database is the migration. Everything else is plumbing. Plan the data cutover first, with a dual-write or CDC period and a parity check.
  • Terraform state is a single point of failure — remote, locked, backed up, in its own account. Losing it means importing every resource by hand.
  • A region "rebuildable from code" is a claim until you've done it. The Germany launch is the excuse to prove it.
  • Cloud provider sales quotas mean you'll be offered credits to adopt services; credits expire, architectures don't.
cards.s: Part 1 — Cloud gotchas: the things you learn by being surprised

cards.b:
VPC and CIDR. A VPC is a private IP range you choose — 10.20.0.0/16 gives you 65,536 addresses. Plan ranges across accounts and regions so they never overlap; overlapping CIDRs can't be peered, and fixing it later means re-IPing production. Reserve space for the EU region and for on-prem/plant networks before you need it.

Subnets. Slices of the VPC in a single AZ. A standard layout per AZ: a public subnet (load balancers, NAT gateway), a private application subnet (services), and a private data subnet (databases, caches) with no route to the internet at all. Three AZs × three tiers = nine subnets per region. Data subnets should be reachable only from application subnets.

Routing. Each subnet has a route table. Public: 0.0.0.0/0 → internet gateway. Private: 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT gateway (outbound only). Data: no default route. Endpoints add routes to AWS services without touching the internet.

Security groups vs NACLs. Security groups are attached to resources (instances, load balancers, RDS) and are stateful: allow inbound 443 from the load balancer's security group and the reply flows automatically. Reference security groups by ID, not by IP — "the API tier's group may reach the database tier's group on 5432." NACLs are subnet-level, stateless, and evaluated in rule order; use them sparingly as a coarse backstop (deny a known bad range), not as the primary control.

Load balancers. The Application Load Balancer works at layer 7: HTTP routing by path and host, TLS termination, WebSockets, sticky sessions, health checks, and integration with WAF. The Network Load Balancer works at layer 4: TCP/UDP, static IPs, millions of connections, ultra-low latency — what you put in front of a self-managed MQTT broker or anything that isn't HTTP. GCP's global external HTTP(S) load balancer is different in kind: a single anycast IP that routes users to the nearest healthy backend worldwide, with Cloud CDN and Cloud Armor integrated — genuinely easier for a global consumer app.

DNS and edge. Route 53 / Cloud DNS host your zones with routing policies: latency-based (send Germans to Frankfurt), geolocation (residency), weighted (canary a region), failover (health-checked). CloudFront / Cloud CDN cache static assets and firmware at edge locations near users, terminate TLS, and absorb traffic spikes; WAF and Shield / Cloud Armor sit at the same edge.
