cards.f: IPv6, and why it's coming up now
cards.b: IPv4 addresses are scarce and AWS now charges for every public IPv4 address (~$3.60/month each). Dual-stack VPCs and IPv6-only subnets reduce that cost and simplify addressing at scale. For a device fleet, some ISPs are IPv6-only behind carrier-grade NAT; your broker endpoints should be reachable over both.

cards.f: A networking walkthrough: the Whisker EU region
cards.b: A new VPC in eu-central-1 with a non-overlapping CIDR (10.30.0.0/16), nine subnets across three AZs, gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB, interface endpoints for ECR, Secrets Manager, and CloudWatch. The IoT Core endpoint is regional; German devices are provisioned with the EU endpoint in their config and their certificates are registered in both regions. The ALB in public subnets fronts the BFF in private application subnets; Aurora sits in data subnets with a security group that only admits the BFF's group. Route 53 latency routing sends European app traffic to the EU ALB. A Transit Gateway connects the EU VPC to the shared-services VPC (CI runners, observability) with routes that allow only what's needed. Firmware images are served from CloudFront with an origin in each region. Cost review: the interface endpoints and Transit Gateway attachments are the recurring line items; the NAT gateway is small because endpoints carry most traffic.

cards.f: Networking problems that reach a manager
cards.b:
• "We can't peer the acquired company's VPC" — overlapping CIDRs. The fix is re-IPing one side or a NAT layer; both are projects. Prevention: an IP allocation plan across the organization.
  • "The API is slow from the plant" — a VPN tunnel saturated at 1.25 Gbps or a route through the wrong region. Interconnect and a regional endpoint.
  • "The security team wants no internet egress from prod" — endpoints for every service used, an egress proxy for the rest, and a list of what breaks (package repositories, third-party APIs) with an allowlist.
  • "Devices in Australia time out" — TCP keepalive shorter than a carrier NAT timeout, or the broker endpoint two continents away; Global Accelerator / anycast or a regional broker.

FinOps is the discipline of making engineering teams accountable for cloud cost the way they're accountable for reliability — with visibility, ownership, and a feedback loop — while finance gets predictability. The FinOps Foundation's three phases are Inform (see the cost and attribute it), Optimize (reduce waste and buy commitments), and Operate (make it continuous: budgets, reviews, culture). Most organizations never leave Inform because attribution is hard; that's where a manager adds value.
cards.s: Part 3 — FinOps, as a practice you'd run

cards.f: Inform: making the bill mean something
cards.b:
1. Tagging policy enforced by code. Required tags (service, team, env, cost-center); a Service Control Policy or org policy that blocks creation without them; a weekly report of untagged spend that goes to zero.
  2. Account structure that attributes by default. If prod, staging, and dev are separate accounts, environment cost is free. If each pod owns an account, team cost is free.
  3. Cost and Usage Report (AWS) or billing export (GCP) into a warehouse. Athena or BigQuery over the raw line items; dashboards by service, team, environment; anomaly detection (Cost Anomaly Detection on AWS is free and catches the 40% jumps).
  4. Unit economics. The metric that connects cost to the business: cost per active device per month; cost per thousand telemetry events; cost per ML training run; cost per query. Trend it. Growth-driven cost is fine; per-unit cost rising is the alarm.
  5. Showback before chargeback. Show each team their cost for a quarter before you charge it to their budget; chargeback without understanding breeds gaming.
cards.s: Part 3 — FinOps, as a practice you'd run

cards.s: Part 3 — FinOps, as a practice you'd run

cards.b:
• Budgets with alerts at 80% and 100% per account and per team; a forecast reviewed monthly with finance.
  • Cost as a design-review question: "what does this cost at 5× current load, and where do bytes cross a billing boundary?"
  • A monthly 30-minute FinOps review: top movers, anomalies, unit-cost trend, one optimization shipped.
  • Commitments reviewed quarterly — utilization above 90% or you over-bought; coverage below 60% or you under-bought.
  • Engineers see their cost in the same dashboard as their latency. Cost that's invisible doesn't get managed.
cards.s: Part 3 — FinOps, as a practice you'd run

cards.f: A FinOps walkthrough: the first 90 days at Whisker
cards.b: Month one: get the CUR into Athena, enforce tags, and produce one chart — cost per active device per month, split by messaging, streams, storage, compute, observability — for the last twelve months. Month two: the easy wins (idle resources, NAT endpoints, log retention) and the Savings Plan purchase after rightsizing, with finance. Month three: the structural lever — telemetry batching in the next firmware release, projected at 8–12× fewer messages — presented to leadership as a unit-cost reduction with the launch of Germany as the reason it matters now. The story you tell in the interview is that FinOps is a monthly habit with one number, not a quarterly cleanup.
cards.s: Part 3 — FinOps, as a practice you'd run

cards.b: Glue is AWS's serverless data-integration service — three things under one name. The Glue Data Catalog is a metadata store (databases, tables, schemas, partitions) that Athena, Redshift Spectrum, EMR, and Glue jobs all read; it's the AWS-native Hive metastore. Glue Crawlers scan S3 (or JDBC sources) and infer schemas and partitions into the catalog. Glue ETL jobs run Spark (PySpark or Scala) or lightweight Python shell scripts without you managing a cluster, billed per DPU-hour; Glue Studio gives a visual editor and Glue DataBrew a no-code data-prep tool. Glue also has a schema registry for streaming schemas (Avro/JSON/Protobuf) and Glue Data Quality for rule-based checks.
cards.s: Part 4 — AWS Glue (and what GCP uses instead), explained

cards.b:
# PySpark Glue job: compact yesterday's raw telemetry into partitioned Parquet and register it
from awsglue.context import GlueContext
from pyspark.context import SparkContext
glue = GlueContext(SparkContext.getOrCreate()); spark = glue.spark_session
dt = "2026-09-13"
raw = spark.read.json(f"s3://whisker-raw/events/dt={dt}/")               # thousands of small JSON files from Firehose
canon = raw.selectExpr("device_id", "seq", "to_timestamp(event_ts) as event_ts", "event_type", "schema_version", "payload")
canon.repartition(8).write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy("region") \
     .parquet(f"s3://whisker-lake/events/dt={dt}/")                      # 8 files of ~200 MB instead of 1,440 tiny ones
# Then: a crawler or `MSCK REPAIR TABLE` / ALTER TABLE ADD PARTITION registers dt=2026-09-13 in the catalog
# Athena can now query it; the job is idempotent (overwrite) so a rerun for that date is safe
cards.s: Part 4 — AWS Glue (and what GCP uses instead), explained

cards.f: When to use Glue, and when not
cards.b:
Use Glue whenUse something else when
You're on AWS, the transformations are batch, and you don't want to run Spark clustersYou need long-running clusters with fine control or Spark tuning → EMR
You need a catalog that Athena/Redshift share → the Data Catalog is the default regardless of ETL toolTransformations are SQL on warehouse tables → dbt on Redshift/Athena is cheaper and more maintainable
A crawler can infer a stable schema from filesSchemas are messy or change often → crawlers create duplicate tables; define schemas explicitly in IaC
Occasional jobs where per-DPU billing beats an idle clusterJobs run continuously → a small EMR or EKS Spark cluster is cheaper
You want a managed multi-engine platform with ML → Databricks (also runs on AWS) is the richer option at higher cost

Glue gotchas managers hear about: cold-start latency of a minute or more per job (fine for batch, wrong for anything interactive); DPU costs that surprise when jobs are left at default sizing; crawlers creating a new table per folder when partitions aren't laid out as key=value; the catalog becoming a junk drawer without ownership; Glue version upgrades changing Spark versions under a job.
cards.s: Part 4 — AWS Glue (and what GCP uses instead), explained

cards.b: Dataflow (Apache Beam — batch and streaming in one model, autoscaling, the default for pipelines on GCP); Dataproc (managed Spark/Hadoop clusters, closest to EMR); Data Fusion (visual ETL, closest to Glue Studio); BigQuery itself does most transformation as SQL (with dbt); Dataplex and Data Catalog for metadata and governance; Datastream for CDC. The honest comparison: on GCP, BigQuery plus Dataflow covers what Glue plus Athena plus Kinesis Analytics cover on AWS, with less assembly.
cards.s: Part 4 — AWS Glue (and what GCP uses instead), explained

cards.b: A model in a notebook is an experiment. A model in production is software with two extra failure modes: the world changes (drift) and nobody can reproduce how it was built. MLOps is the set of practices that make models reproducible, deployable, monitored, and retrainable — the DevOps ideas applied to something that depends on data as much as code.
cards.s: Part 5 — MLOps, end to end, as a pipeline you could draw

cards.b:
Data sources ─▶ Feature pipeline ─▶ Feature store ─┬─▶ Training pipeline ─▶ Evaluation gate ─▶ Model registry (staging → prod)
                (batch + streaming)  (offline +    │     (tracked runs)       (metrics vs baseline,      │
                                       online)     │                            fairness, latency)       ▼
                                                   └────────────────────────────────────────────▶ Serving (batch / endpoint / edge)
                                                                                                          │
                                                          Monitoring ◀────────────────────────────────────┘
                                                          (data drift, prediction drift, performance vs ground truth, cost, latency)
                                                                    │ drift or schedule
                                                                    └──▶ retrain trigger → training pipeline (champion/challenger)
cards.s: Part 5 — MLOps, end to end, as a pipeline you could draw

cards.b:
1. Feature pipeline and feature store. Features are computed once, from the same code, for training (historical, "offline") and serving (current, "online"). Without a feature store, the data scientist computes "visits vs 28-day baseline" one way in a notebook and the engineer reimplements it differently in the service — training-serving skew, the most common reason a model that tested well fails in production. Tools: SageMaker Feature Store, Vertex AI Feature Store, Feast (open source), Databricks. Point-in-time correctness matters: when building training data for a prediction made on June 1, use only feature values known on June 1.
  2. Training pipeline and experiment tracking. A pipeline (SageMaker Pipelines, Vertex Pipelines, Kubeflow, Airflow, Dagster) runs data validation → training → evaluation as reproducible steps with pinned code, data snapshot, and parameters. Every run logs to a tracker (MLflow, SageMaker Experiments, Weights & Biases) so "which version did we ship in March and what data was it trained on?" has an answer.
  3. Evaluation gate. The model must beat the current champion on the held-out set on the chosen metric (precision at the operating threshold for the health nudge; PR-AUC for scrap), pass fairness checks where relevant, and meet latency and size budgets (an edge model must fit the device). A gate that fails stops the pipeline — the same idea as a failing test.
  4. Model registry. Versioned artifacts with metadata and stage (staging, production, archived), approval workflow, and lineage back to the run. Promotion is an explicit act, ideally by a human for consequential models.
  5. Serving. Three modes, choose the cheapest that meets the need. Batch: score nightly, write results to a table — the health-insights default. Real-time endpoint: a container behind an autoscaled endpoint (SageMaker Endpoint, Vertex Endpoint, or your own on EKS) when a decision needs the prediction now — fraud, divert-to-inspection. Edge: the model ships inside firmware or a plant gateway container — WasteID, SPC scoring — with the model version in every emitted event.
  6. Monitoring. Data drift: input distributions shift (new litter type, new material lot) — statistical tests (population stability index, KS test) per feature. Prediction drift: the output distribution shifts. Performance: when ground truth arrives (CMM results next hour; vet visits weeks later) compare to predictions. Operational: latency, errors, cost per prediction. Tools: SageMaker Model Monitor, Vertex Model Monitoring, Evidently, Arize, WhyLabs. Alerts route to the model's owner like any service alert.
  7. Retraining. Triggered by drift, by schedule, or by enough new labels. The new model is a challenger; it runs in shadow or on a canary slice against the champion; promotion follows the gate. Automated retraining without a gate is how a bad batch of labels silently degrades production.
cards.s: Part 5 — MLOps, end to end, as a pipeline you could draw

cards.b: Lineage from data to model to decision; model cards documenting purpose, data, metrics, limitations; reproducibility (pinned everything); access control on training data; and, in quality-system environments (IATF 16949, FDA), a model that influences a decision is a controlled process — changes go through change control like a firmware release. For CUI or IP-sensitive data, the whole pipeline stays in the governed boundary: on-prem or VPC-isolated compute, no data to external APIs — the constraint you already operate under.
cards.s: Part 5 — MLOps, end to end, as a pipeline you could draw

cards.f: LLMOps — what changes for generative AI
cards.b:
• The "model" you ship is usually a prompt + retrieval configuration + a hosted or self-hosted model; version all three together.
  • Evaluation is a golden question set scored for faithfulness, relevance, and task success (often LLM-as-judge calibrated against humans), run on every change like a test suite.
  • Monitoring adds cost per query, token usage, latency, refusal rate, and a sample of conversations reviewed by humans.
  • Guardrails on input (injection, PII) and output (grounding, policy) are part of the deployment, not the prompt.
  • Retrieval indexes need their own pipeline — document ingestion, chunking, embedding versioning, ACL sync — and reindexing when the embedding model changes.
cards.s: Part 5 — MLOps, end to end, as a pipeline you could draw

cards.f: The MLOps problems a manager sees
cards.b:
SymptomCauseFix
"The model was 92% in the notebook and 70% in prod"Training-serving skew or leakageFeature store; point-in-time joins; time-based splits; shadow mode before launch
Nobody can rebuild last quarter's modelNo tracking, no pinned dataPipelines with tracked runs; data snapshots or versioned tables (Iceberg time travel)
Precision quietly fell over six months; support noticed firstDrift with no monitoringDrift and performance monitors with owners; a documented fallback (the rule-based baseline)

Data scientists wait weeks for engineering to productionizeTwo-team handoff with no shared platformA paved-road pipeline template; ML engineers embedded; the data scientist owns the model through the registry, the platform owns serving
Auditor asks why the model made a decisionNo explainability, no model cardSHAP on tabular models; model cards; decision logging with model version
"How would you set up MLOps for a manufacturer starting from notebooks?"

"I'd start with a single use case and build the paved road around it rather than a platform in the abstract. Predictive quality on one line: features computed in a governed pipeline into a feature store, a training pipeline with tracked runs and an evaluation gate against the current rule-based baseline, a registry with an approval step because quality decisions are controlled processes, batch scoring first and edge scoring when latency demands it, and drift monitoring with a fallback to the rule. Then the second use case reuses the same road and takes a quarter instead of a year. The platform choice — SageMaker, Vertex, Databricks — follows the cloud decision; the practices are the same on all three."
cards.s: Part 5 — MLOps, end to end, as a pipeline you could draw

decks.title: Backend & connected-device services
decks.blurb: MQTT, device identity, shadows, schema versioning, OTA, Kafka vs Kinesis, APIs, notifications, FinOps, reliability.

cards.b:
• Model: publish/subscribe over a persistent TCP connection through a broker. Lightweight (2-byte fixed header), designed for constrained devices and flaky networks.
  • Topics: hierarchical strings, / separated. Wildcards: + (single level), # (multi-level, must be last). Convention: devices/{deviceId}/telemetry, devices/{deviceId}/cmd, devices/{deviceId}/cmd/ack.
  • QoS levels:
  • QoS 0 — at most once (fire and forget). Use for high-frequency, loss-tolerant telemetry.
  • QoS 1 — at least once (PUBACK). Use for commands and important state; consumer must be idempotent.
  • QoS 2 — exactly once (4-way handshake). Rarely worth the cost; most IoT platforms (including AWS IoT Core) don't support it.
  • Sessions: clean session vs persistent sessions — persistent lets a broker queue QoS 1/2 messages for an offline device.
  • Keepalive and Last Will and Testament (LWT): client sets keepalive interval; broker publishes the LWT message when a client disconnects ungracefully. This is how you implement device presence ("online/offline") without polling.
  • Retained messages: broker keeps the last message on a topic and delivers it to new subscribers. Useful for config; dangerous for stale commands.
  • MQTT 5 additions: message expiry, shared subscriptions (load-balanced consumers), user properties (headers), reason codes, topic aliases. Shared subscriptions matter for scaling backend consumers.
  • Alternatives: CoAP (UDP, REST-like, constrained networks), AMQP (heavier, enterprise messaging), plain HTTPS polling (simple but battery/connection-costly and no push), WebSockets (MQTT over WebSockets is common for web clients and firewall traversal).

• Per-device X.509 certificates are the standard for mutual TLS. Options: (a) inject unique cert at manufacturing (secure element / TPM holds the private key), (b) fleet provisioning by claim — device ships with a shared claim cert, calls a provisioning API, receives a unique cert on first boot, claim cert revoked or narrowly scoped.
  • Rotation: plan for cert expiry across a fleet that may be offline for months; support overlapping validity; never let rotation require a factory reset.
  • Authorization: policies scoped so a device can only publish/subscribe to its own topics (devices/${iot:ClientId}/*). Compromise of one device must not expose the fleet.
  • Registry / thing model: device ID, hardware revision, firmware version, owner account link, region. Keep the "which account owns which device" mapping in the app backend, not in the broker.

• Server holds a JSON document per device with desired and reported state; the delta drives commands. Device reports on connect and on change; backend sets desired state via API.
  • Solves: offline devices (desired state persists until device reconnects), app reads (read the shadow, not the device), race conditions (version numbers on shadow updates).
  • Watch out for: shadow size limits, conflict resolution when both sides change, and treating the shadow as a telemetry sink (it isn't — use the telemetry pipeline).

• Every command gets a command ID (idempotency key). Device acks with the same ID; backend tracks state: queued → sent → acked → completed | failed | expired.
  • Timeouts and retries at the application layer, not just MQTT QoS. Expire stale commands so a device coming online after a week doesn't execute a "start cleaning cycle" from last Tuesday.
  • Safety commands (motor stop, cycle abort) should have a separate, higher-priority path and be idempotent by definition.
  • Distinguish commands (imperative, one-shot) from configuration (declarative, shadow-style). Most bugs come from mixing the two.

cards.f: 1.5 AWS IoT Core specifics (and the self-managed alternative)
cards.b:
• IoT Core: managed MQTT broker, device registry, shadows, rules engine (route messages to Kinesis/Lambda/S3/Timestream with SQL-like rules), jobs (OTA orchestration), Device Defender (fleet security audit), fleet indexing.
  • Pricing is per connection-minute + per message (5 KB increments) + rules. At scale, message count and rule actions dominate cost — batching telemetry on-device is the first cost lever.
  • Self-managed brokers (EMQX, HiveMQ, VerneMQ, Mosquitto for small scale) on EKS/ECS: more control, more ops burden, often cheaper at very high message volume. Know the tradeoff; don't advocate one blindly.
  • GCP note: Google retired Cloud IoT Core in 2023; GCP customers typically run a partner broker or migrate. If Whisker has GCP footprint, ask what runs there.

60-second summary: "I'd run MQTT over mutual TLS with per-device certs provisioned at manufacturing, topic ACLs scoped to the device, presence via LWT, declarative config through a shadow, and imperative commands with idempotency keys and expiry. Telemetry goes QoS 0 batched; commands go QoS 1 with app-level acks."

cards.f: 2.1 Why this is the hard part
cards.b: A consumer fleet is never on one firmware version. Some devices update the day a release ships; some are behind a router that blocks OTA; some sit in a box for a year before first boot on firmware from two generations ago. The cloud must serve all of them, indefinitely, without breaking anyone's litter box at 3 a.m.

• Version the payload explicitly. A schema_version (or fw_version plus a server-side mapping) field in every message. Don't encode version in the topic — you'd multiply subscriptions.
  • Additive changes only in a major version: add optional fields, never rename, never change types, never change semantics of an existing field.
  • Tolerant reader: consumers ignore unknown fields and supply defaults for missing ones. This is the single most important discipline.
  • Enumerations: add an "unknown/other" catch-all so old servers can handle new device states and vice versa.
  • Units and precision in the schema, not in tribal knowledge. Grams vs ounces bugs are real.
  • Serialization: JSON is human-readable and flexible but verbose. Protobuf/CBOR cut bandwidth 50–80% and give you a schema registry; cost is tooling on constrained devices. A common pattern: CBOR or protobuf on the wire, JSON internally.
  • Schema registry (Confluent Schema Registry, AWS Glue Schema Registry, or a git-controlled protobuf repo with CI compatibility checks). Enforce backward/forward compatibility rules in CI so a breaking change fails a build, not a fleet.

• Adapter layer at ingest: normalize every incoming version to the current canonical model before it hits business logic. Old firmware's quirks live in one place.
  • Feature negotiation: device reports capabilities on connect; backend only sends commands the device advertises support for.
  • Deprecation policy: define minimum supported firmware, measure fleet distribution, communicate through the app before dropping support, and keep a long tail (years) for hardware that still works.
  • Contract tests: golden message fixtures from every supported firmware version, replayed in CI against the current backend.

• Interface control document = the device-to-cloud contract. Co-own it; changes go through a joint review.
  • Firmware release trains are slow (validation, certification, staged OTA). Backend must ship ahead of firmware and be tolerant of both the old and new payloads for the overlap period.
  • Field failure analysis: telemetry should carry enough context (firmware version, hardware rev, error codes, cycle counters) to diagnose a field failure without a device return.

• Staged rollout: internal fleet → beta cohort → 1% → 10% → 50% → 100%, gated on telemetry (error rate, cycle success rate, connectivity) at each stage. Automated halt if a metric regresses.
  • Cohort targeting: by hardware revision, region, current firmware, opt-in status.
  • Integrity: signed firmware images, hash verification on device, A/B partitions with automatic rollback if the new image fails to boot/connect.
  • Delivery: device receives a job with a pre-signed S3 URL; downloads over HTTPS (not MQTT); reports progress/status via job topics.
  • Delta updates for bandwidth; resumable downloads for flaky Wi-Fi.
  • Metrics: rollout velocity, failure rate by stage, rollback count, time-to-fleet-majority.

60-second summary: "Explicit schema version in every payload, additive-only evolution enforced by a registry in CI, tolerant readers, an adapter layer at ingest so legacy quirks are isolated, and contract tests replaying real fixtures from every supported firmware. OTA goes out in telemetry-gated stages with signed images and A/B rollback."

Ecosystem Kafka Connect, Streams, ksqlDB, huge community Firehose (delivery to S3/Redshift/OpenSearch), Kinesis Analytics (Flink)
Cost shape Instance/storage; cheap per message at high volume Per shard-hour + per PUT; on-demand priced per GB

Rule of thumb you can state: Kinesis for a lean team that wants managed and is all-in on AWS; Kafka when you need long retention, replay, rich stream processing, or multi-cloud portability.

• Partition key choice: device ID gives per-device ordering (good) but hot-partition risk if a few devices spam. Hash device ID; watch for skew.
  • Event time vs processing time: devices buffer while offline and flush later. Use the device's timestamp for analytics, ingest time for ops. Requires NTP-ish clock discipline on device or server-side clock correction.
  • Windowing: tumbling (fixed, non-overlapping), sliding, session (gap-based — good for "a visit to the litter box"). Watermarks define how long you wait for late data.
  • Exactly-once vs at-least-once: most pipelines are at-least-once plus idempotent writes (dedup on deviceId + sequenceNumber). Kafka transactions and Flink checkpoints can give effective exactly-once end to end.
  • Backpressure: producer-side batching, consumer autoscaling on iterator age (Kinesis) or consumer lag (Kafka). Iterator age / lag is the number-one health metric for the pipeline.
  • Dead-letter queues: malformed or unparseable messages go to a DLQ with the raw bytes and error; alert on DLQ rate; never drop silently.
  • Schema enforcement at the edge of the pipeline so bad data can't poison downstream stores.

• Time-series stores (Timestream, InfluxDB, TimescaleDB, ClickHouse): optimized for append-heavy, time-keyed queries, downsampling, retention tiers. Use for device metrics, dashboards, recent history in the app.
  • Object store + Parquet + Athena/BigQuery: the cheap, durable system of record for raw telemetry. Partition by date and a low-cardinality dimension; compact small files.
  • Warehouse (Redshift/BigQuery/Snowflake): aggregated, joined with account/subscription data for product analytics.
  • Operational reads for the app (last known state, recent events): DynamoDB or a Postgres table fed by the stream — not the analytics warehouse.
  • Hot/warm/cold tiering: e.g., 7 days in time-series hot, 90 days warm, forever in S3 cold. Retention policy = cost policy.

cards.f: 3.5 Cost and performance levers (they explicitly ask about this)
cards.b:
1. Batch on device (one message with N samples instead of N messages).
  2. Compress and use compact serialization.
  3. Sample high-frequency sensors; send deltas or change-only events.
  4. Tier retention; downsample old data.
  5. Right-size shards/partitions; use on-demand only during uncertainty.
  6. Separate control-path traffic from analytics traffic — never let an analytics backlog delay a command ack.
  7. Attribute cost per device and per feature so product can see what a telemetry-hungry feature actually costs.

• Feature pipelines: from raw events → sessionized visits → per-cat features (weight trend, visit frequency, duration). Behavioral-change detection is a classic anomaly detection / change-point problem.
  • Data quality checks (Great Expectations, Deequ) before training.
  • Model serving: batch scoring nightly is usually enough for health insights; only put models in the real-time path if latency matters.
  • Diagnostics: error-code frequency by firmware version and hardware rev; MTBF-style dashboards; correlate with support tickets.

60-second summary: "IoT Core rules route to a stream; a Flink-style processor validates against the schema registry, dedups on device sequence number, sessionizes with event-time windows, writes hot data to a time-series store and raw Parquet to S3, and lands aggregates in the warehouse for analytics and ML. I watch consumer lag, DLQ rate, and cost per active device, and the control path never shares a queue with analytics."

• Backend-for-Frontend (BFF): a thin layer per client type that aggregates domain services into screen-shaped responses; keeps domain services clean and lets mobile iterate without churning core services.
  • REST vs GraphQL: GraphQL fits app screens that compose many resources (device list + status + subscription + notifications) and reduces round trips on mobile; costs are query complexity control, caching difficulty, N+1 resolvers. REST is simpler to cache and version. A common answer: GraphQL at the BFF, REST/gRPC between services.
  • API gateway: authN/authZ, rate limiting, request validation, throttling per client version, WAF. AWS API Gateway vs ALB + Kong/Envoy — know the tradeoffs (cost per request, feature set, latency).
  • Versioning for clients you can't force to upgrade: URI (/v2/) or header versioning; support N–2 app versions; measure version distribution; feature flags to dark-launch; force-upgrade only for security or when a version is <1% of traffic.
  • Contract testing (Pact or OpenAPI-driven) between mobile and backend so a change that breaks an old client fails in CI.
  • Idempotency for mutating endpoints from mobile (retries on flaky networks): idempotency key header stored with the response.
  • Pagination, filtering, sparse fieldsets — mobile bandwidth and battery.

• OAuth 2.0 / OIDC with short-lived access tokens and refresh tokens; PKCE for mobile.
  • Managed identity (Cognito, Auth0, Firebase Auth) vs self-managed — a small team should not run its own password store.
  • Device-to-account linking flow: pair device → prove physical possession (button press, QR, BLE proximity) → bind device ID to account → issue device its long-term credentials. Unlinking on resale is a real support issue.
  • Household / multi-user sharing: roles per device (owner, member), invitations, revocation.

• Push (APNs/FCM via SNS or Firebase), email, SMS. Abstract behind a notification service with templates, user preferences, quiet hours, and per-event dedup ("drawer full" should not fire every cycle).
  • Delivery tracking and retries; token refresh handling; fan-out via queue so a notification storm can't take down the API.
  • The device-event → notification path is latency-sensitive from the user's perspective (they expect the ping within seconds of the cycle completing).

• Entitlements service: what features a user has (Whisker+ tier, litter subscription), sourced from the billing system (Stripe, Recurly, app-store subscriptions). Cache entitlements; handle grace periods, downgrades, and app-store receipt validation.
  • Feature flags (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, or homegrown) keyed on entitlement + cohort + app version. Graceful degradation when the entitlement service is down (fail open for a short TTL, then fail closed).
  • Webhooks from billing provider must be idempotent and verified.

• Relational (Postgres/Aurora) for accounts, devices, subscriptions — strong consistency matters.
  • DynamoDB / Redis for device state and session-shaped reads.
  • Multi-tenancy is per-account; data residency for EU/Canada may require regional partitioning of PII.

60-second summary: "OIDC-backed accounts, a GraphQL BFF for the app fronting REST/gRPC domain services, explicit API versioning with contract tests and an N–2 support policy, idempotent mutations, a queue-backed notification service with user preferences and dedup, and an entitlements service that decouples feature access from the billing provider."

• Containers on EKS/ECS (or GKE): long-running services, predictable load, need for sidecars/service mesh. EKS = more control and portability; ECS Fargate = less ops. GKE Autopilot on the GCP side.
  • Serverless (Lambda / Cloud Functions / Cloud Run): event-driven glue, spiky workloads, rules-engine targets. Watch cold starts on the command path and cost at sustained high throughput.
  • Typical shape for this domain: containers for API/BFF and stream processors; Lambda for IoT rule actions and light transforms; managed services everywhere you can.
  • Deployment strategies: blue/green, canary with automated rollback on SLO breach, feature flags for decoupling deploy from release.

• Terraform (multi-cloud, state management, modules, workspaces per environment), CDK/CloudFormation (AWS-native), Pulumi. Terraform is the sensible default for a mixed AWS/GCP estate.
  • Practices: remote state with locking, environment parity via modules, plan in PRs, policy-as-code (OPA/Sentinel/Checkov) to block insecure configs, drift detection.
  • Everything reproducible: a region should be rebuildable from code — this matters for international expansion.

• Pipeline stages: lint/static analysis → unit tests → build image → contract tests → integration tests against ephemeral env → security scan (SAST, dependency, container) → deploy to staging → smoke tests → progressive prod deploy.
  • Metrics (DORA): deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, MTTR. These are exactly the "measurable delivery quality" numbers the posting wants.
  • Trunk-based development with short-lived branches; feature flags instead of long-lived release branches.
  • Firmware coordination: backend pipeline should be able to run the firmware team's device simulator or fixtures for contract tests.

• Three pillars: metrics (Prometheus/CloudWatch/Datadog), logs (structured JSON, centralized), traces (OpenTelemetry → Jaeger/X-Ray/Datadog/Honeycomb). OpenTelemetry as the vendor-neutral instrumentation layer.
  • Trace across the device boundary: propagate a correlation ID from app request → API → command → device ack → notification. Device-side is usually a command ID, not a W3C trace context, so stitch on the backend.
  • Dashboards by firmware version and hardware rev — most field issues cluster there.
  • SLIs to define: command round-trip latency (p50/p99), command success rate, device connectivity ratio, telemetry pipeline lag, API availability and latency, notification delivery latency, OTA success rate.
  • Alert on symptoms (SLO burn rate), not causes (CPU). Multi-window burn-rate alerts (Google SRE book) reduce paging noise.

• Tagging strategy → cost allocation by service, team, environment, and per-device unit economics.
  • Levers: rightsizing, Savings Plans/Reserved Instances/Committed Use Discounts for the steady baseline, Spot for batch/stream processing that can tolerate interruption, Graviton/ARM, storage tiering, log retention limits, NAT gateway and data-transfer awareness (cross-AZ and egress are silent killers), IoT message batching.
  • Capacity planning: model growth by devices × messages/device/day × bytes/message; project stream shards/partitions and storage quarterly; tie to product launch calendar (LR5 international rollouts).
  • Present cost as cost per active device per month — it's the number executives understand.

• Least-privilege IAM, no long-lived keys, secrets in a secrets manager, encryption at rest and in transit, private subnets for data stores, VPC endpoints.
  • Consumer data: PII handling, GDPR/UK GDPR for EU expansion, PIPEDA in Canada, CCPA in the US — data residency, deletion on request, retention policies.
  • Device security: Device Defender / anomaly detection on connection patterns; revocation path for compromised devices.
  • Supply chain: SBOMs, signed images, dependency scanning.

60-second summary: "Containers for services and stream processors, serverless for event glue, all Terraform with policy-as-code, trunk-based CI/CD with progressive delivery and DORA metrics on a dashboard, OpenTelemetry tracing stitched across the device boundary, SLO burn-rate alerting, and FinOps reported as cost per active device."

• SLI = a measurement (fraction of commands acked within 2s). SLO = the target (99.5% over 30 days). SLA = a contractual promise with consequences (usually looser than the SLO).
  • Set SLOs per domain, tighter for the control path (a device that won't respond is a broken product) than for analytics.
  • Error budget = 1 − SLO. When it's spent, reliability work takes priority over features — this gives you an objective way to negotiate with Product.
  • Burn-rate alerting: page when the budget is being consumed at a rate that would exhaust it in hours; ticket when it would take days.

• Sustainable rotation: primary/secondary, one-week shifts, no more than ~1 in 5 weeks per engineer, compensated. Across time zones, follow-the-sun if coverage allows; otherwise align on-call to business hours where possible and reserve overnight paging for true Sev-1.
  • Contractors on call: only if they have the same access, training, and runbooks — otherwise you've created a two-tier system that fails at 3 a.m.
  • Page only on user-impacting symptoms. Track pages per shift; anything above a handful per week is a signal to fix alerting or the system.
  • Runbooks for every alert; an alert without a runbook is a bug.

• Severity definitions tied to customer impact (Sev-1: devices can't operate / app down; Sev-2: degraded feature; Sev-3: internal).
  • Roles: incident commander (coordinates, does not debug), communications lead, subject-matter responders. Declare early; downgrade freely.
  • Status page and support-team comms templates. A litter box that stops cycling generates support tickets fast — support needs to know before customers tell them.
  • Blameless postmortem within a few days: timeline, contributing factors (plural — there's never one root cause), what went well, action items with owners and dates, and a review of whether the action items actually shipped. Track "postmortem action-item completion rate."

Look for patterns across postmortems: config changes without validation, deploys without canaries, missing timeouts, unbounded queues, single-AZ dependencies, expired certificates, schema changes, hot partitions. Each pattern gets a systemic guardrail: linting, policy-as-code, chaos tests, load tests, automated cert rotation, schema CI checks. The interviewer wants to hear "I removed the category" not "I fixed the bug."

• Timeouts everywhere; retries with exponential backoff and jitter; circuit breakers; bulkheads (isolate the command path from analytics); idempotency; graceful degradation (app shows last-known state if live query fails); rate limiting and load shedding; multi-AZ by default, multi-region for international.
  • Chaos engineering: start with AZ failure and dependency latency injection in staging; graduate to prod game days.
  • Load testing with device simulators — a fleet reconnect storm after a broker restart or a regional outage is the classic IoT thundering herd. Mitigate with jittered reconnect backoff on the device and connection rate limiting on the broker.

60-second summary: "Per-domain SLOs with error budgets that give Product and me a shared language, symptom-based burn-rate paging, a sustainable compensated rotation with runbooks, an incident command structure that separates coordinating from debugging, blameless postmortems whose action items I actually track, and a habit of turning recurring incident patterns into guardrails that remove the whole class."

• Written design docs (context, goals/non-goals, options considered, chosen option with tradeoffs, risks, rollout plan, open questions). Async comments first; a short synchronous review only to resolve disagreements.
  • Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) — short, numbered, immutable; new decisions supersede old ones. Distributed teams live on these.
  • Reviewer's job is to find the risk, not to redesign. Keep a "decisions needed" list and time-box.

Framework: is it core to the product's differentiation? What's the total cost including ops and on-call? Does the managed option meet latency/compliance/portability needs? Can we exit later? For a small team, default to managed services for undifferentiated infrastructure (broker, auth, streaming, time-series) and spend engineering on the device contract, the data model, and the customer experience.

• Quantify: incidents attributable, engineering hours lost per sprint, cost overrun, delivery slippage, security exposure.
  • Frame as risk and optionality: "this blocks international expansion because…" or "this is the reason feature X took three months."
  • Propose a bounded investment with milestones and a metric that proves it worked. Never ask for "a quarter to pay down debt" — ask for a specific outcome.

Good places for a manager to write code: prototypes that de-risk a decision, tooling that removes toil (simulators, fixtures, dashboards), the first version of a contract test harness, review of the riskiest PRs. Bad places: the critical path of a sprint commitment.

• Listening tour (every person, including contractors): what's working, what's broken, what would you fix first, what do you want next.
  • Ownership map: every service has a named owner and backup; publish it.
  • Cadence: weekly 1:1s, biweekly skip-levels with team leads' reports, a written weekly team update.
  • Quick wins that signal change: kill the noisiest alert, fix the flakiest test, close the oldest postmortem action item.
  • Psychological safety: publicly thank the person who reports a risk or a near-miss; run blameless retros; model saying "I don't know."
  • Retention risk triage: identify flight risks and single points of failure in the first 30 days; pair, document, cross-train.

cards.f: 8.2 Contractors and partners to the same standard
cards.b:
• Same definition of done (tests, docs, review), same CI gates, same access model where security allows, same onboarding.
  • Scope defined in writing with acceptance criteria; capacity planned in the same sprint tool; budget tracked against delivery.
  • Reduce single-person dependencies: no contractor is the sole owner of a service; knowledge transfer is a deliverable in the SOW.
  • Transitioning to a stronger FTE core: hire into the most critical, least-documented areas first; convert top contractors where possible; wind down partner scope only after handover is proven by the FTE running on-call for it.

• Written-first: design docs, ADRs, decision logs, async standups, PR descriptions that explain why.
  • Handoff quality standard: at end of day, state of work, blockers, next step, and where to look — in the ticket, not in someone's head.
  • Minimal mandatory overlap (e.g., 2 hours) reserved for decisions, not status.
  • Rotate meeting times so pain is shared.

• Competency framework dimensions typically: technical depth, scope/impact, execution, communication, leadership/mentoring, operational ownership. Use it for leveling consistency and for growth conversations ("here's the gap between you and Staff").
  • Structured interviews with rubric; work-sample or system-design rounds that resemble the actual job; debrief without anchoring.
  • Promotion evidence: sustained performance at the next level, not potential. Build a promotion packet with the engineer over two quarters.
  • Developing leads: give them a pod to run with you as backup, coach on delegation and feedback, let them own a postmortem and a design review.

• Roadmap intent → technical plan with explicit scope, sequencing, dependencies (especially firmware), and risk register. Re-plan when inputs change; communicate options, not just problems.
  • Sequence around the slowest train (firmware certification and staged OTA); ship backend tolerant of both old and new early.
  • Shared definitions of done and of "launched" (including observability and support readiness).
  • BFF — Backend-for-Frontend. ADR — Architecture Decision Record. ICD — Interface Control Document (defense term; = device-to-cloud contract).
  • LWT — Last Will and Testament (MQTT presence). QoS — quality of service. PKCE — Proof Key for Code Exchange (OAuth for mobile).
  • DORA metrics — deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, MTTR.
  • SLI/SLO/SLA — indicator/objective/agreement. Error budget — 1 − SLO.
  • Iterator age / consumer lag — how far behind a stream consumer is; the key pipeline health metric.
  • Watermark — how late an event can arrive and still be included in a window.
  • Shadow / digital twin — server-side desired/reported state for a device.
  • OTA — over-the-air firmware update. A/B partitions — dual firmware slots enabling rollback.
  • Thundering herd — mass reconnect after an outage; mitigate with jitter.
  • Bulkhead — isolating resources so one failure can't cascade.
  • Tolerant reader — consumer that ignores unknown fields and defaults missing ones.
  • Schema registry — central store enforcing compatibility of message schemas.
  • FinOps — cloud cost management as an engineering discipline; unit economics = cost per active device.
  1. A device on two-year-old firmware sends a telemetry message with a field your current parser doesn't expect. What happens, and why is that the correct behavior?
  2. A broker restart causes 500K devices to reconnect at once. What breaks first, and what device-side and server-side mitigations exist?
  3. Product wants a new "health insights" feature that needs 10× the telemetry. Walk through the cost model and the three levers you'd pull.
  4. Kinesis iterator age is climbing for 20 minutes. What's your diagnostic sequence?
  5. The mobile team wants to ship a screen that needs data from four services. What do you propose, and what versioning promise do you make?
  6. Design the command path for "start a clean cycle" including failure modes when the device is offline, the ack is lost, or the command is duplicated.
  7. Your team pages 15 times a week. What do you do in the first two weeks?
  8. A contractor's pod has zero test coverage on a critical service and the contract renews in 60 days. What's your plan?
  9. An executive asks why cloud cost grew 40% last quarter. How do you answer in three sentences?
  10. Firmware wants to rename a telemetry field for clarity. What do you say?

decks.title: Data science & AI — concepts and algorithms
decks.blurb: Supervised/unsupervised, named algorithms, evaluation, LLMs, RAG, MLOps — and when to use which.

cards.b:
1. Frame the problem as a decision. "Predict scrap" is not a project; "flag parts likely to fail CMM before inspection so we can divert them" is. The decision defines the metric and the latency.
  2. Get the data and understand it — exploratory analysis, distributions, missing values, leakage (a feature that wouldn't be available at prediction time, like the inspection result itself).
  3. Baseline first — a rule or a simple model; if a threshold on coolant temperature catches 60% of scrap, that's the bar.
  4. Feature engineering — usually where the value is; domain knowledge beats model choice.
  5. Train / validate / test split — hold out data the model never saw; for time series, split by time, never randomly.
  6. Evaluate with the right metric (below), then shadow-mode in production before anyone acts on it.
  7. Deploy, monitor, retrain — MLOps (K5.8).

cards.f: 5.1 Supervised learning — you have labeled examples
cards.b:
TaskAlgorithms by nameExampleNotes
Regression (predict a number)Linear regression, Ridge/Lasso/ElasticNet (regularized), polynomial regression, decision tree regressor, random forest regressor, gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost), support vector regression, k-nearest neighbors, neural networksPredict cycle time of a machining operation from tool wear and material; forecast warranty cost per unitGradient boosting wins most tabular problems. Linear models when you need interpretability or have few rows.
Classification (predict a category)Logistic regression, naive Bayes, decision trees, random forest, gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost), support vector machines (SVM), k-NN, neural networks; for images CNNsWill this part fail inspection? Is this litter-box visit a health anomaly? Is this warranty claim narrative a known failure mode?Class imbalance is the norm (2% scrap): use precision/recall/F1 and PR-AUC, not accuracy; resample or reweight.

Evaluation metrics, explained: accuracy is misleading on imbalanced data — predicting "no scrap" always gets 98%. Precision is "of the parts I flagged, how many were really bad" (cost of false alarms); recall is "of the bad parts, how many did I catch" (cost of misses); F1 balances them. ROC-AUC and PR-AUC summarize across thresholds. Confusion matrix shows the four outcomes. For regression: MAE (average absolute error, in units), RMSE (penalizes big misses), R² (variance explained). Choose the threshold by the business cost — a false alarm diverts a good part (cheap); a miss ships a bad one (expensive), so tune for recall.

TaskAlgorithmsExample
Clusteringk-means, k-medoids, hierarchical (agglomerative), DBSCAN/HDBSCAN (density, finds arbitrary shapes and outliers), Gaussian mixture models (GMM), spectral clusteringGroup machines by vibration signature to find ones drifting from their peers; segment customers by usage for subscription offers; cluster warranty claims into failure modes
Dimensionality reductionPCA (linear), t-SNE and UMAP (visualization), autoencoders (neural), factor analysisCompress 200 sensor tags into 10 components before a model; visualize whether "good" and "bad" cycles separate
Anomaly detectionIsolation Forest, one-class SVM, Local Outlier Factor, autoencoder reconstruction error, statistical (z-score, Mahalanobis distance), control charts (SPC)Detect a robot behaving unlike the fleet; flag a machine before it fails; catch a firmware build with abnormal telemetry
Association rulesApriori, FP-GrowthWhich combinations of alarms precede a stoppage; market-basket analysis for consumables

• Classical forecasting: moving averages, exponential smoothing (Holt-Winters for trend and seasonality), ARIMA/SARIMA (autoregressive integrated moving average), Prophet (Facebook's decomposable model, easy for business seasonality).
  • ML forecasting: gradient boosting on lag features (very effective), LSTM/GRU recurrent networks, Temporal Convolutional Networks, Transformers for time series (Temporal Fusion Transformer), Amazon's DeepAR.
  • Change-point detection: CUSUM, PELT, Bayesian online change-point — "when did this cat's weight trend change?"
  • Survival analysis: Kaplan-Meier curves, Cox proportional hazards, Weibull models — time-to-failure for components; the backbone of warranty and predictive-maintenance analytics.
  • Pitfalls: never random-split time series; beware leakage from future data; seasonality (shift patterns, weekly cycles) must be modeled or removed.

• Feed-forward networks (MLPs): layers of neurons with nonlinear activations (ReLU); trained by backpropagation and gradient descent (SGD, Adam). Good for tabular data only when you have a lot of it.
  • Convolutional networks (CNNs): ResNet, EfficientNet, YOLO (detection), U-Net (segmentation). Image defect detection on a line, camera-based WasteID on a litter box, visual inspection of welds.
  • Recurrent networks (RNN, LSTM, GRU): sequences; largely replaced by transformers for text, still used for sensor sequences.
  • Transformers: attention mechanism; BERT (encoder, understanding/classification), GPT-family (decoder, generation), T5 (encoder-decoder); Vision Transformers for images. The architecture under every LLM.
  • Autoencoders and VAEs: compress and reconstruct; anomaly detection via reconstruction error.
  • GANs and diffusion models: generate data — synthetic defect images to augment rare classes.
  • Graph neural networks: learning on graphs — supply networks, the digital thread.
  • Training vocabulary: epochs, batch size, learning rate, overfitting (memorizes training data; fix with regularization, dropout, more data, early stopping), underfitting, transfer learning (start from a pretrained model — the default for vision), fine-tuning, data augmentation, GPU/TPU.

• Classical: tokenization, TF-IDF, bag-of-words, word2vec/GloVe embeddings, topic modeling (LDA), named-entity recognition, sentiment classification.
  • Modern: transformer embeddings (sentence-transformers), zero-shot classification with LLMs, extraction with structured output.
  • Examples: classify warranty claim narratives into failure modes; extract part numbers and defect codes from supplier emails; summarize maintenance logs; search work instructions semantically.

• RL: an agent learns a policy by reward — Q-learning, DQN, PPO. Used in robotics, scheduling, and HVAC/energy control; rarely the first tool in manufacturing because simulation is needed.
  • Optimization (operations research): linear and mixed-integer programming (production scheduling, inventory), constraint programming, genetic algorithms, simulated annealing. Often more valuable than ML for planning problems — inventory optimization is an OR problem with ML-forecasted inputs.
  • Simulation: discrete-event simulation of a line; digital twins combining physics models (GT-SUITE, Adams, which your Cameo–Volta integration connects to) with data.

cards.f: 5.7 Large language models, RAG, and agents
cards.b:
• How LLMs work, one paragraph: a transformer trained to predict the next token on a very large corpus, then aligned with instruction tuning and RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) so it follows instructions. It has no memory between calls beyond what you put in the context window (measured in tokens; a token ≈ ¾ of a word). It can be confidently wrong (hallucination) because it generates plausible text, not verified facts.
  • Prompting: system prompt (role and rules), few-shot examples, chain-of-thought (ask for reasoning), structured output (JSON schemas), temperature (randomness). Prompt injection is the security risk: untrusted text in the context can hijack instructions.
  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): instead of hoping the model knows your documents, retrieve the relevant passages at query time and put them in the context. Pipeline: chunk documents → embed chunks (an embedding model turns text into vectors) → store in a vector database (Qdrant, pgvector, Pinecone, Milvus, OpenSearch) → at query time embed the question, find nearest chunks (cosine similarity), optionally combine with keyword search (hybrid) and rerank → generate with citations. Access control must be applied at retrieval. Quality is measured by retrieval recall and answer faithfulness on an evaluation set. This is RheinMan.
  • Fine-tuning vs RAG: fine-tune to change style or teach a task format; RAG to give the model current or private knowledge. Most enterprise needs are RAG. LoRA/QLoRA make fine-tuning cheap.
  • Agents: an LLM in a loop that can call tools (search, database, code execution, APIs), observe results, and decide the next step — ReAct pattern, tool calling / function calling. Frameworks: LangChain/LangGraph, LlamaIndex, Semantic Kernel, CrewAI, AutoGen; the Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes how tools are exposed. Multi-agent systems assign roles (planner, coder, reviewer). Governance: scoped tool permissions, human approval on side effects, full audit logs, cost limits. This is RheinCoder.
  • Evaluation: golden question sets, LLM-as-judge with human calibration, faithfulness/groundedness, retrieval metrics (recall@k), task success rate, latency and cost per query. Never ship a change to a prompt or model without running the eval set.
  • Deployment choices: hosted APIs (Anthropic, OpenAI, Bedrock, Vertex) for convenience; open-weight models (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma, Nemotron) self-hosted with vLLM or TGI on GPUs for data control — mandatory for CUI. Quantization (running a model at lower precision) cuts memory and cost.
  • Responsible AI: data minimization, bias testing proportional to impact, model cards, human oversight for consequential decisions, a policy for what may leave the boundary, and monitoring for drift and misuse. The EU AI Act classifies risk tiers; industrial quality systems are generally low risk, HR decisions are high risk.

• Feature store (Feast, SageMaker/Vertex Feature Store, Databricks): one definition of each feature for training and serving, so the model in production sees what it was trained on.
  • Experiment tracking and model registry (MLflow, SageMaker, Vertex, Weights & Biases): every run's parameters, metrics, and artifact; promotion from staging to production with approval.
  • Pipelines (SageMaker Pipelines, Vertex Pipelines, Kubeflow, Airflow, Dagster): reproducible train → evaluate → register → deploy.
  • Serving: batch scoring (nightly, cheapest, usually enough), real-time endpoints (when a decision needs a prediction now), edge deployment (containers on plant gateways, on-device models on robots).
  • Monitoring: data drift (inputs changed — a new material lot), concept drift (the relationship changed — a machine was rebuilt), performance against ground truth as it arrives, and business metrics. Tools: Evidently, SageMaker Model Monitor, Arize, WhyLabs.
  • Retraining cadence triggered by drift or schedule; champion/challenger comparison before switching.
  • Governance: lineage from data to model to decision; reproducibility; in IATF 16949 environments, a model influencing quality is a controlled process change.

cards.f: 5.9 Data engineering concepts to have on tap
cards.b:
• ETL vs ELT: transform before loading (traditional, tool-based) vs load raw then transform in the warehouse with SQL/dbt (modern, cheaper, auditable).
  • Batch vs streaming; micro-batch (Spark Structured Streaming) as the middle.
  • CDC (change data capture): read the database's transaction log (Debezium, DMS, Datastream) to stream every change without querying the source.
  • Data modeling: star schema (facts and dimensions — Kimball), 3NF (Inmon), Data Vault (hubs/links/satellites for auditability); slowly changing dimensions (SCD type 2 keeps history); conformed dimensions (one definition of "plant," "part," "customer").
  • File formats: Parquet (columnar, compressed, the lake default), ORC, Avro (row-based with schema, streaming), JSON/CSV (raw only). Table formats: Iceberg, Delta Lake, Hudi — add transactions, schema evolution, time travel, and compaction to files on object storage.
  • Data quality dimensions: completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness, validity — enforced by tests (dbt tests, Great Expectations, Soda) and contracts.
  • Lineage and catalog: where data came from and what depends on it; the tool for "can I change this column?"
  • Master data management (MDM): golden records for parts, suppliers, customers across ERPs — the unglamorous prerequisite for every cross-plant analytic.
  • Privacy techniques: pseudonymization, tokenization, differential privacy, synthetic data; row- and column-level security.

decks.title: Data engineering & data science — deeper
decks.blurb: Pipelines, modeling, quality, features, experiments — worked examples.

cards.f: A real pipeline, piece by piece
cards.b: Take the visits pipeline from W1 and make it production-grade. Each piece below is a thing that fails in real pipelines and the standard fix.

# Lambda triggered by an IoT rule — put events on Kinesis with the device as partition key
def handler(event, ctx):
    rec = normalize(event)                       # schema-version adapter: v2 → canonical, v4 → canonical
    if rec is None:                              # unparseable → DLQ, never dropped silently
        dlq.send(raw=event, error="schema", fw=event.get("fw")); return
    kinesis.put_record(StreamName="events", PartitionKey=rec["device_id"], Data=json.dumps(rec))

Why the device ID as partition key: per-device ordering, which the sessionizer needs. The risk: a chatty device creates a hot shard (Incident 4). Mitigation: per-device rate limits upstream; if you ever need to split a single device's traffic, append a small suffix — but then you lose ordering, so don't unless you must.
cards.s: A real pipeline, piece by piece

cards.b: Flink checkpoints its state (the open sessions) every 30 seconds to S3. If a task fails, it restarts from the last checkpoint and replays the stream from that offset — events between the checkpoint and the failure are processed twice. That's why the sink must be idempotent: visits are keyed by (device_id, start_ts) and written with an upsert, so replaying produces the same rows. This combination — replayable source, checkpointed state, idempotent sink — is what people mean by "effectively exactly-once" and it's the answer to "how do you avoid double-counting."
cards.s: A real pipeline, piece by piece

cards.b: A robot loses Wi-Fi for two hours, buffers 24 events, and flushes them at reconnect with their original timestamps. If the sessionizer had already closed those windows, the late events would be lost. A watermark of "event time minus 4 hours" tells Flink to keep windows open that long. The cost is state (more open sessions in memory) and latency for the last events. For the app's live screen you accept the latency; for the nightly aggregate, a reconciliation job re-sessionizes the day from S3 and overwrites — cheap insurance.
cards.s: A real pipeline, piece by piece

cards.f: Store: partitioning, small files, and compaction
cards.b:
s3://whisker-lake/events/dt=2026-09-13/region=us/part-0001.parquet   ← partition by date and region, not by device
Problem: a streaming sink writes a file every minute → 1,440 tiny files/day/partition → Athena scans crawl
Fix:     hourly compaction job merges into ~128–512 MB files; with Iceberg, run "rewrite_data_files" on a schedule
Never partition by high-cardinality keys (device_id) — millions of tiny directories kill every query engine.
cards.s: A real pipeline, piece by piece

cards.b:
-- models/marts/daily_cat.sql
select cat_id, date_trunc('day', start_ts) as dt,
       count(*) as n_visits, avg(duration_s) as mean_duration_s,
       approx_percentile(weight_g, 0.5) as weight_g_median, stddev(weight_g) as weight_g_std
from {{ ref('visits') }} where cat_id is not null group by 1, 2
# models/marts/daily_cat.yml
tests: - unique: [cat_id, dt]   - not_null: n_visits   - accepted_range: {column: weight_g_median, min: 500, max: 15000}
# a failing test blocks the downstream health-insights job — bad data never reaches the model
cards.s: A real pipeline, piece by piece

cards.b: Every batch job takes a date parameter and can be re-run for any date producing identical output (delete-then-insert or merge by key). When the sessionizer bug from March is fixed, you re-run March from the raw S3 events. If a job can't be re-run safely, it isn't finished.
cards.s: A real pipeline, piece by piece

cards.f: CDC from the app database into the warehouse
cards.b: The warehouse needs households, cats, and subscriptions from Postgres. Debezium (or AWS DMS) reads the Postgres write-ahead log and emits every insert, update, and delete as an event to Kafka/Kinesis; a sink writes them into the bronze layer; dbt builds slowly-changing dimensions (type 2: a new row per change, with valid_from/valid_to) so you can ask "what plan was this household on in June?" No queries against the production database, no nightly full dumps.
cards.s: A real pipeline, piece by piece

cards.f: Data quality as a first-class pipeline stage
cards.b: Expectations at the boundary: event schemas validated at ingest; row counts within ±20% of the trailing 7-day average; null rates; freshness (the daily_cat table is complete by 06:00 or a page fires); referential checks (every visit's device exists). Tools: dbt tests, Great Expectations, Soda. The management point: quality checks are the on-call for the data team, with the same runbook discipline as service alerts.
cards.s: A real pipeline, piece by piece

cards.f: Data science, worked: the predictive quality model from 4B, with numbers
cards.b:
Data. 180,000 parts over six months, 1.1% failed CMM. Features per part: sensor summary during its cycle (mean/max/std of spindle load, coolant temp, vibration RMS; 12 features), machine, shift, tool age (cycles since last change), material lot, ambient temperature. Target: CMM fail (1) or pass (0).

Split. By time — train on months 1–4, validate on month 5, test on month 6. A random split would leak: parts from the same lot and shift would appear on both sides and the model would learn "lot 4471 is bad" rather than the physics.

Baseline. A rule: flag when coolant_temp_max > 28 °C. Recall 58%, precision 9%. That's the bar.

Model. LightGBM with class weights (positives weighted ~90×). Hyperparameters tuned on the validation month. Test-month results at the chosen threshold:

Confusion matrix (month 6, 30,000 parts, 330 true fails):
  Predicted fail & actually fail: 241 (true positives)     Predicted fail & actually pass: 420 (false positives)
  Predicted pass & actually fail: 89 (misses)                  Predicted pass & actually pass: 29,250
Recall = 241/330 = 73%     Precision = 241/661 = 36%     PR-AUC 0.41 (baseline rule 0.07)
Business math: each flagged part costs $4 to divert for inspection → 661 × $4 = $2.6K/month;
each caught fail avoids $60 of downstream rework/scrap → 241 × $60 = $14.5K/month. Net ≈ $12K/month on one line.

What the model learned (SHAP values): tool age and vibration RMS dominate; coolant temperature matters only above 27 °C and only on second shift — which is a maintenance finding (the chiller on that line is undersized), not just a model. That's the sentence that gets a plant manager's attention.

Deploy and monitor. Shadow mode for four weeks; then the flag drives a divert-to-inspection rule at the edge. Monitor input drift (a new material supplier changes the vibration distribution), precision against actual CMM results weekly, and retrain monthly. When precision drops below 25% for two weeks, the model is paused and the rule-based baseline takes over — a documented fallback is part of the deployment.

cards.f: Feature engineering — where the value actually is
cards.b:
• Aggregations over windows: mean, max, std, slope of a sensor over the cycle; over the last N cycles; since the last tool change.
  • Lags and deltas: this cycle's max vibration minus the trailing median — "is this unusual for this machine" is more predictive than the raw value.
  • Categorical encoding: one-hot for small sets (shift), target encoding or embeddings for large ones (material lot), and beware leakage in target encoding — compute it only on the training fold.
  • Time features: hour, day of week, time since maintenance, position in the production run.
  • Domain features: the quality engineer's rules turned into columns — "coolant above spec," "tool past 80% of rated life." Ask them; it's the fastest route to a good model.
  • For the litter box: visit count vs 28-day baseline (ratio), weight slope over 14 days, duration trend, night-visit fraction, variability. The same pattern: compare the entity to its own history.

cards.f: Choosing an algorithm — a decision guide you can say out loud
cards.b:
If…Start withBecause
Tabular data, any size, prediction is the goalGradient boosting (LightGBM/XGBoost)Best accuracy on tabular data with little tuning; handles missing values and mixed types
You need to explain every decision to a regulator or a plant managerLogistic/linear regression or a shallow decision tree; SHAP on a boosted model as a second stepCoefficients and rules are auditable
Few labels, lots of unlabeled dataAnomaly detection (Isolation Forest, autoencoder) then active labelingYou can't train a classifier on 12 examples
ImagesA pretrained CNN, fine-tuned (transfer learning)Training from scratch needs millions of images
TextEmbeddings + a small classifier, or an LLM with few-shot prompts for low volumeModern embeddings encode meaning; LLMs skip training entirely for small tasks
Forecasting with seasonalityProphet or gradient boosting on lag features; ARIMA for a single clean seriesPractical accuracy; interpretable components
Time-to-failureSurvival models (Cox, Weibull)Handles censoring — most components haven't failed yet
Grouping things with no labelsk-means for round clusters; DBSCAN/HDBSCAN for odd shapes and outliers—
A planning or allocation problemOptimization (MIP), not MLYou know the constraints; you need the best assignment, not a prediction

cards.f: Experiments and causality — what a manager must know
cards.b: An A/B test is the only clean way to know a change caused an effect. Randomize at the right unit (household, not device, if a household has two robots), pre-register the metric and the sample size (a power calculation: to detect a 2-point change in a 20% conversion rate at 80% power you need roughly 8,000 per arm), run for full weekly cycles, and don't peek and stop early — that inflates false positives. Watch for Simpson's paradox (the effect reverses inside subgroups), novelty effects (users click the new thing because it's new), and network effects. Where you can't randomize (a plant-wide change), difference-in-differences against a comparable plant is the fallback, with humility about confounders.

cards.f: GenAI in the engineering workflow, concretely
cards.b:
• Support assistant for Whisker's support team: RAG over runbooks, known issues, and the device's own diagnostics; suggests the fix and the macro. Metric: handle time and first-contact resolution. Guardrail: never sends a command to a robot without an agent clicking.
  • Postmortem and runbook drafting: an LLM drafts the timeline from the incident channel and alerts; humans edit. Saves the hour nobody has.
  • Code review assistant and test generation: your RheinCoder work; the evaluation is acceptance rate and defects escaped, and the rule is human approval on every change.
  • Firmware log triage: classify crash signatures and reset reasons into known buckets; surface the new ones.
  • What not to do: put an LLM on the command path, let it see customer PII without retrieval ACLs, or ship a prompt change without running the eval set.

decks.title: Data & AI strategy
decks.blurb: Data strategy, platforms, governance and AI programs for a director role.

cards.b:
• Why: three business outcomes to anchor everything — warranty cost, plant OEE/scrap, working capital (inventory). Everything else is enabling.
  • Foundation: a lakehouse with an open table format (Apache Iceberg or Delta) so compute engines and clouds are interchangeable; medallion layers (bronze raw → silver conformed → gold data products); dbt for transformations with tests; a catalog with lineage (Unity Catalog, Collibra, Alation, DataHub, Glue Data Catalog); data contracts between producers and consumers.
  • Governance as a product: automated quality checks (Great Expectations, Soda, dbt tests) in pipelines; data owners per domain; a data council that meets monthly and decides, not a committee that reviews.
  • Operating model: a central platform team (infrastructure, catalog, standards, shared ML tooling) plus domain data teams embedded with plants, quality, supply chain, and engineering — hub-and-spoke rather than pure data mesh, because manufacturing domains rarely have the engineering depth for full mesh autonomy.
  • AI: MLOps with a feature store and model registry; a small number of use cases with a P&L owner each; GenAI for knowledge access (work instructions, quality records, engineering docs) with retrieval grounded in governed data; responsible AI guardrails you've already built for CUI.
  • Measures: certified data products count and freshness SLAs, use cases in production with measured impact, cost per query/model, and adoption.

QuestionPoint of view
AWS vs Azure vs IBM for manufacturing analyticsPick a primary by the ERP: Azure if SAP S/4HANA (native integration, Fabric, Power BI); AWS if Oracle or greenfield (SageMaker, Kinesis, Bedrock). IBM for regulated/EU-sovereign workloads. Acknowledge multi-cloud by inheritance and govern it with a cloud-agnostic data layer — Iceberg tables, dbt, a single catalog — so data isn't trapped.
Redshift vs S3 lakeRedshift (or BigQuery/Synapse) for gold, sub-second BI SQL with strict schema; S3/Parquet for bronze/silver, ML training, semi-structured and time-series. Spectrum/Athena bridge them.
Databricks vs Glue vs Synapse/FabricDatabricks: best unified Spark + ML + catalog, multi-cloud, premium price. Glue: cheap serverless ETL if you're AWS-only and SQL-heavy. Fabric/Synapse: best if the org lives in Microsoft and Power BI. Decide on where the ML engineering will happen; that's the sticky layer.
Spark vs dbt/SQLdbt/SQL for transformations on structured data in the warehouse — cheaper, more people can maintain it. Spark when data is semi-structured, very large, or the workload is ML feature engineering and training.
FinOps for a data platformTagging, per-team budgets, auto-pause dev clusters, Spot for training, cost per query and per model, showback then chargeback. Compute, not storage, is where data platforms overrun.
Migrating a legacy on-prem warehouseInventory consumers and lineage first; replicate raw to the lake (CDC via Debezium/DMS); rebuild transformations in dbt with parity tests; run dual for a defined period; cut over by consumer, not big bang; decommission with a date.
Vendor lock-inOpen formats (Iceberg/Parquet), open orchestration (Airflow/Dagster), SQL as the interface, exit clauses and data-export rights in contracts, and one proof-of-portability per year.
Security end to endIdentity (SSO/MFA, workload identity, least privilege), network (private VPC, endpoints, Direct Connect), data (encryption, column-level masking, row-level security for plant data, tokenization for PII), governance (classification, lineage, access reviews), and monitoring (audit logs to SIEM). NIST CSF as the framework; CMMC if defense customers; TISAX for automotive suppliers.

cards.f: 5.3 Manufacturing domain — the vocabulary and the use cases
cards.b:
Layer (ISA-95)SystemData it produces
L0–1Sensors, actuators, PLCsTag values at ms–s cadence; OPC-UA/Modbus
L2SCADA / HMI, historians (PI, Ignition)Time-series, alarms, operator actions
L3MES (Plex, Siemens Opcenter, Rockwell)Work orders, routings, as-built genealogy, quality results, downtime codes, OEE
